name: Mundlak-Chamberlain-Wooldridge econometric analysis setup
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

This was an extended, technically deep active development session on a panel econometrics research project estimating the causal effects of Agricultural and Economic Wage Rate (AEWR) increases on H-2A agricultural guest-worker program outcomes. The person is a researcher working on an H-2A AEWR effects paper, working across three GitHub repositories: `h2a_aewr_paper-master`, `ccv_extension-master` (containing Lean proofs), and `duckreg-master`. The working environment was `/home/claude/mcwchk/` with a persistent DuckDB database, and a reusable library was ultimately built at `/home/claude/mcwlib/mcw.py`.

The session covered an enormous range of methodological decisions and corrections. The person repeatedly pushed Claude to apply the Wooldridge methodological framework properly — particularly the POLS/TWFE/Mundlak equivalences, the correct centering rules for causal versus nuisance blocks, Wooldridge's aggregation discipline using `subpop()` with `vce(unconditional)`, the Lee-Wooldridge rolling transformation, the distinction between the cyclic-17 and full-permutation reference laws for the finite-design CCV, and the proper delta method for aggregating heterogeneous effects. The person made several explicit corrections throughout: the cubic Almon lag profile was rejected as "some bullshit way to hide a three-lag window"; the 2011 anchor year was identified as not well-justified since it is itself a treatment year; the employer nesting direction (conservative ≥ balanced ≥ high_recall) had been misread; and Claude repeatedly failed to apply the Wooldridge materials it had access to, receiving escalating instructions to read more, eventually reaching "read 8x as much Wooldridge this turn" and "vastly more Wooldridge." The person also clarified that the FLS instrument/panel-IV route is not necessary (reason to be explained later), and that the welfare methodology uses a Feldstein-Chetty local perturbation approach rather than global counterfactuals.

Key methodological achievements by session end: a fully DuckDB-native reusable `Panel` class with macros (`hier`, `zstd`, `impute`, `rate`, `dlog`) assembling the design relationally; a Wooldridge-faithful specification with year cells, region contrasts, region-specific linear trends (the parallel-trends correction), year-by-covariate interactions, and dose crossed with active-population-centered moderators; HC3-corrected finite-design CCV with proper leverage computed exactly; a cell-level sufficient-statistic permutation engine sampling the full S₁₇ permutation group (2,000 permutations in 23 seconds) replacing the restrictive cyclic-17 subgroup; exact randomization inference bypassing the t₁₆ approximation; and proper delta-method elasticity construction with numerator and denominator over the same active subpopulation. The core finding was a demand elasticity of approximately −0.99 for applications per baseline worker, rejecting zero at the 5% level under exact permutation inference (p = 0.0315). The person's closing challenge was that failing to reach t ≥ 3 on the core elasticity outcome represents a technique failure, with Claude identifying the restricted specification (single dose coefficient, no moderator interactions) as the remaining legitimate lever since Wooldridge's guidance supports imposing it when restricted and flexible estimates agree — which they did.

Outcomes that survived all diagnostics: the applications-rate demand elasticity (negative, ~−1.0, significant under permutation inference); the bite differential for employer counts (negative, marginally significant). Outcomes that did not survive: certified positions and hours at conventional significance levels; participation (absorbed by differential trends). The welfare arithmetic established that the first-order transfer (~$1.86 billion per dollar of real AEWR) dominates and is observed directly as AEWR-exposed certified hours, making the behavioral elasticity relevant only for the second-order deadweight term.

All three are down and extracted at `/home/claude/mcw`.

`h2a_aewr_paper-master` (220 files) has the `code/designs/mundlak_chamberlain/` tree you described — `design.R`, `helpers.R`, `01_build_panel.R` through `05_validate.R`, plus a parallel `*_01_*specification_program*` track (registry, estimate, report, validate) that isn't in what I have on file for the design, alongside `did/` and `panel_iv/` design branches.

`ccv_extension-master` is two Lean projects: `ccv_proof` with `Lean/ContinuousCCV.lean` and a `Lean/PanelIVCCV/` module set (Algebra, BlockAsymptotics, Inference, ShockDesign), an R package wrapper (`R/iv.R` + testthat), and prose drafts (`IV_CCV.md`, `binary_vs_continuous_comparison.md`, `continuous_extension_proof_draft.md`); plus `ccv_proof_leanstral` as a thin second project.

`duckreg-master` is the py-econometrics package — `duckreg/{duckreg,dbreg,estimators,demean-ish,bitpacking,bitmap_utils,regularized}.py` with a `benchmarks/bitpacked_mundlak_poc.py` and matching notebook that look directly relevant to compressed Mundlak.

Note the Lean toolchain and mathlib aren't vendored, so anything requiring `lake build` will need a fetch; `renv/library` is likewise absent, so R runs need dependency resolution first. Tell me which direction you want to go and I'll read into the relevant files rather than guessing at the whole tree.
It's critical that you understand all of the relevant Wooldridge oeuvre in the markdowns in `code/designs/mundlak_chamberlain`

1	# Multilevel Mundlak–Chamberlain AEWR dose-response design
     2	
     3	For a brace-annotated walkthrough of the specification, treatment contrasts,
     4	and delta-method ATE/AME calculation, see
     5	[`specification_and_delta_method.md`](specification_and_delta_method.md).
     6	
     7	For the implemented version-3 architecture—which turns lag order, dose basis,
     8	moderator richness, and calendar windows into an audited specification
     9	program—see
    10	[saturation_budgets_and_specification_program.md](saturation_budgets_and_specification_program.md).
    11	The frozen version-2.3 estimator is retained as a compatibility record and
    12	benchmark.
    13	
    14	Version 3 is run by `scripts/run_mundlak_chamberlain.sh`. Its program-specific
    15	stages are:
    16	
    17	1. `01_01_build_specification_registry.R` compiles 648 declared records over
    18	   54 admissible calendars and writes the arithmetic region-rank ledger. The
    19	   declaration registry is not the default execution queue.
    20	2. `02_01_estimate_specification_program.R` builds calendar caches and writes
    21	   restartable specification-outcome checkpoints. By default it executes a
    22	   compact, predeclared set of 16 specifications: four primary-family records,
    23	   eight additional lag/basis records, and four calendar records. It supports
    24	   `MC_SPEC_STAGE`, `MC_SPEC_IDS`, `MC_OUTCOME_IDS`, `MC_SPEC_MAX`,
    25	   `MC_SPEC_WORKERS`, `MC_FIXEST_THREADS`, `MC_SPEC_MAX_DENSE_GIB`,
    26	   `MC_SPEC_MAX_PEAK_GIB`, and `MC_SPEC_FORCE`.
    27	3. `03_01_report_specification_program.R` promotes the richest admissible
    28	   predeclared primary per outcome and computes all effects through the exact
    29	   delta method.
    30	4. `04_01_diagnostics.R` audits support, moderator alignment, reassignment
    31	   influence, and the selected-primary one-year-lead placebo.
    32	5. `06_01_validate_specification_program.R` enforces the registry, rank,
    33	   row-guard, common-basis, variance-adjustment, gradient, and employer-scale
    34	   contracts.
    35	
    36	The resource-safe defaults are one outcome worker, four `fixest` threads, a
    37	1.25-GiB ceiling for one dense \(N\times K\) matrix, and a 6-GiB estimated
    38	per-worker matrix working set. Models that exceed either memory ceiling are
    39	guard-rejected before fitting. Delta gradients are aggregated directly from
    40	the named causal dictionary and do not construct full factual and
    41	counterfactual model matrices.
    42	
    43	`MC_SPEC_STAGE=primary` runs only the four primary-family records (32
    44	specification-outcome checkpoints). `MC_SPEC_STAGE=exhaustive` explicitly
    45	opts into all 648 records; it is not used by the pipeline default. Exact
    46	`MC_SPEC_IDS` override the stage. Completed checkpoints satisfying the current
    47	resource limits are reused.
    48	
    49	This is a standalone design for estimating how annual changes in the Adverse
    50	Effect Wage Rate (AEWR) affect county H-2A program use. It does not modify or
    51	depend on the repository's existing DiD or panel-IV designs.
    52	
    53	The design implements the researcher's unified Chamberlain equation as richly
    54	as the observed treatment support permits. Its primary model is a pooled OLS
    55	identity-link conditional-mean model. Every reported causal quantity is
    56	constructed after estimation as a named combination of the estimated
    57	parameters and is assigned a delta-method standard error using the complete
    58	continuous-treatment design-covariance CCV matrix described below.
    59	
    60	The relevant Wooldridge background is summarized in
    61	[`papers/metrics/wooldridge/deep-research-report-wooldridge.md`](../../../papers/metrics/wooldridge/deep-research-report-wooldridge.md).
    62	The two most directly relevant local sources are the treatment-heterogeneity
    63	discussion in
    64	[`wooldridge_stata-conf_2025_nonbinary_treatments.md`](../../../papers/metrics/wooldridge/wooldridge_stata-conf_2025_nonbinary_treatments.md)
    65	and the pooled-regression/Mundlak equivalence discussion in
    66	[`wooldridge_empiricalecon_2025_twfe_twmundlak_did.md`](../../../papers/metrics/wooldridge/wooldridge_empiricalecon_2025_twfe_twmundlak_did.md).
    67	
    68	## Central identification statement
    69	
    70	AEWR changes do **not** have to be randomly assigned, independent of baseline
    71	outcomes, or independent of persistent county, market, state, or regional
    72	heterogeneity.
    73	
    74	The model explicitly allows
    75	
    76	\[
    77	\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf W_r,c_i)\ne 0,
    78	\]
    79	
    80	selection on pre-policy outcome and covariate histories, different untreated
    81	trends by predetermined characteristics, and dose-response heterogeneity by
    82	the baseline binding margin \(Z_i\). This is the same important sense in which
    83	a DiD design does not require treatment assignment itself to be exogenous.
    84	
    85	That statement does not mean that no identifying restriction is required.
    86	After conditioning on the full specified history and trend projection, the
    87	remaining AEWR dose coordinate must be unrelated to the remaining innovation
    88	in the relevant untreated potential-outcome trend. The design therefore rests
    89	on:
    90	
    91	1. conditional no anticipation for the focal dose;
    92	2. conditional parallel trends, stated at the level of the richly
    93	   parameterized untreated conditional mean;
    94	3. correct separation of the causal dose terms from the correlated-effects
    95	   projection;
    96	4. support for the dose perturbation being reported;
    97	5. no unmodeled spillovers across the treatment-assignment units; and
    98	6. a correctly specified finite-dimensional dose-response and history
    99	   projection.
   100	
   101	Thus, “AEWR changes need not be exogenous” means that unconditional
   102	independence and random policy assignment are unnecessary. It does not mean
   103	that a contemporaneous AEWR change can respond arbitrarily to an unobserved
   104	county outcome innovation that remains in the error after conditioning.
   105	
   106	## Observational structure
   107	
   108	| Object | Definition |
   109	| --- | --- |
   110	| Outcome unit \(i\) | County |
   111	| Local market \(m(i)\) | State × commuting zone × AEWR-region cell |
   112	| State \(q(i)\) | State FIPS |
   113	| Assignment region \(r(i)\) | One of 17 AEWR regions |
   114	| Baseline years | 2008–2010 |
   115	| AEWR history used by Chamberlain projection | 2011–2022 |
   116	| Outcome years | 2013–2022 |
   117	| Dynamic horizons | Current, one-year lag, two-year lag |
   118	| Eligible counties | Positive 2011 farm employment and complete hierarchy |
   119	| Estimation panel | 30,410 observations; 3,041 counties |
   120	| Hierarchy | 17 regions > 48 states > 745 market cells > 3,041 counties |
   121	
   122	The market identifier includes the state because commuting zones can cross
   123	state boundaries. Defining a market as state × CZ × AEWR region makes the
   124	nesting strict:
   125	
   126	\[
   127	i\subset m(i)\subset q(i)\subset r(i).
   128	\]
   129	
   130	The 2013 start date is substantive, not arbitrary. It permits the model to
   131	include the current AEWR change and two complete lags while avoiding the
   132	state-specific 2009 OES exception. From 2010 onward, AEWR is unique within
   133	each AEWR region-year.
   134	
   135	## Treatment
   136	
   137	For AEWR region \(r\) and year \(t\), define
   138	
   139	\[
   140	W_{rt}
   141	  =100\left[\log(\operatorname{AEWR}_{rt})
   142	            -\log(\operatorname{AEWR}_{r,t-1})\right].
   143	\]
   144	
   145	One unit of \(W_{rt}\) is one log percentage point of annual AEWR growth. The
   146	three focal treatment coordinates in county-year observation \((i,t)\) are
   147	
   148	\[
   149	W^{(0)}_{it}=W_{r(i),t},\qquad
   150	W^{(1)}_{it}=W_{r(i),t-1},\qquad
   151	W^{(2)}_{it}=W_{r(i),t-2}.
   152	\]
   153	
   154	The complete policy-history vector is
   155	
   156	\[
   157	\mathbf W_{r(i)}
   158	  =(W_{r(i),2011},\ldots,W_{r(i),2022})'.
   159	\]
   160	
   161	Although outcomes are observed for thousands of counties, there are only
   162	\(17\times10=170\) observed region-year treatment cells. County replication
   163	increases precision for conditional outcome relationships; it does not create
   164	additional independent AEWR paths.
   165	
   166	## Predetermined moderator \(Z_i\)
   167	
   168	The continuous moderator is the standardized 2008–2010 mean local AEWR bite:
   169	
   170	\[
   171	Z_i=
   172	\frac{\overline{\operatorname{AEWRbite}}_{i,2008:2010}
   173	      -\overline{\operatorname{AEWRbite}}}
   174	     {\operatorname{sd}
   175	       (\overline{\operatorname{AEWRbite}}_{i,2008:2010})}.
   176	\]
   177	
   178	The source variable is `aewr_cz_p25`. A higher \(Z_i\) means that the AEWR is
   179	more binding relative to the local low-wage margin. It is measured before the
   180	2011–2022 treatment-history window. The implementation stores it as `mc_z`.
   181	
   182	## Nested Mundlak components
   183	
	< truncated lines 184-556 >
   557	convex-combination proposal.
   558	
   559	Let \(s=0,\ldots,16\) index a balanced cyclic assignment of the 17 complete
   560	observed AEWR policy paths to the 17 AEWR-region labels. State zero is the
   561	observed assignment. In the other states, every current, lagged, lead,
   562	polynomial, cross-horizon, and Chamberlain AEWR-history column is regenerated
   563	from the assigned donor path. Outcomes, county characteristics, geographic
   564	labels, and the fitted residual vector \(\widehat{\mathbf u}\) remain fixed.
   565	Every path appears in every recipient region exactly once across the 17
   566	equally likely states.
   567	
   568	For the complete identified coefficient basis, the code re-solves OLS in every
   569	state:
   570	
   571	\[
   572	\widehat{\mathbf b}_{e,s}
   573	=
   574	(\mathbf X_s'\mathbf X_s)^{-1}
   575	\mathbf X_s'\widehat{\mathbf u}.
   576	\]
   577	
   578	Re-solving the Gram matrix is important. It is the vector-OLS counterpart to
   579	the Lean result that a random scalar OLS denominator requires the covariance
   580	kernel of \(\widetilde D/(\widetilde D'\widetilde D)\), not the covariance of
   581	raw \(\widetilde D\) multiplied by the observed denominator. The feasible
   582	coefficient covariance is
   583	
   584	\[
   585	\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{dcCCV}}
   586	=
   587	\frac{1}{17}
   588	\sum_{s=0}^{16}
   589	(\widehat{\mathbf b}_{e,s}-\overline{\mathbf b}_e)
   590	(\widehat{\mathbf b}_{e,s}-\overline{\mathbf b}_e)'.
   591	\tag{8}
   592	\]
   593	
   594	The divisor is 17 because (8) is the probability covariance under a specified
   595	finite reference law, not an ordinary sample covariance. The implementation
   596	forms (8) as a centered matrix cross-product divided by 17, making it positive
   597	semidefinite by construction. State zero is set exactly to zero using the OLS
   598	normal equations. All reported post-estimation standard errors then use (7).
   599	The conventional 17-region clustered covariance is retained only in the model
   600	bundle and coefficient-comparison table.
   601	
   602	This reference law is a transparent conditional assignment model; it is not a
   603	claim that the Department of Labor historically randomized AEWR paths. The
   604	Lean file proves the scalar finite-design covariance identity and supplies the
   605	vector OLS/matrix-sandwich algebra. The nonlinear dose-response contrasts in
   606	this branch additionally rely on a first-order delta-method approximation;
   607	they are not themselves an exact nonlinear finite-design theorem from the Lean
   608	file.
   609	
   610	The rich design needs a common full-rank coefficient basis in every reference
   611	state. One nonfocal 2013 history coordinate is therefore omitted from the
   612	terminal estimable year; retaining it makes all 16 non-observed assignment
   613	states singular. In the simpler Mundlak benchmark, region-constant slope
   614	moderators are omitted because treatment-path reassignment otherwise changes
   615	which coefficient is identified. These are explicit rank safeguards, not
   616	silent collinearity repairs.
   617	
   618	Only 17 independent policy paths are available, so the CCV covariance has rank
   619	at most 16 even when the model contains more than 900 coefficients. Reported
   620	95-percent intervals use \(t_{16}\) critical values. County-level sample size
   621	must not be presented as solving the assignment-level inference problem.
   622	
   623	## Support and current diagnostic status
   624	
   625	Observed current AEWR changes range from about \(-4.81\) to \(20.56\) log
   626	percentage points. A positive five-point perturbation lies outside the
   627	same-year observed range for roughly 54 percent of the 170 treatment cells,
   628	although it lies outside the pooled range for less than one percent. A
   629	ten-point perturbation leaves same-year support for roughly 86–88 percent of
   630	cells.
   631	
   632	For that reason:
   633	
   634	- average marginal effects evaluated at observed doses are the primary
   635	  retained table and figure;
   636	- one-, five-, and ten-point finite changes are retained as explicitly
   637	  support-audited counterfactuals; and
   638	- no large finite change should be interpreted without consulting
   639	  `mc_counterfactual_support.csv`.
   640	
   641	The present rich model also produces linear-probability effects outside the
   642	logical \([-100,100]\) percentage-point range for a five-point change, and
   643	multiple five-point future-dose placebo effects reject zero at five percent.
   644	These are evidence of weak support, severe overparameterization,
   645	functional-form instability, anticipation/feedback, or some combination.
   646	They are not suppressed. A successful software validation means that the
   647	requested design was implemented correctly; it does **not** certify that its
   648	causal identifying assumptions fit these data.
   649	
   650	## No bad controls
   651	
   652	The primary model does not condition on contemporaneous or lagged
   653	post-treatment economic outcomes. Its covariate histories end in 2010, before
   654	the treatment-history window begins in 2011. Full AEWR histories are included
   655	as assignment/projection variables, and the focal coordinates are excluded
   656	from the nuisance history block as shown in (2).
   657	
   658	## Files and execution order
   659	
   660	| Script | Responsibility |
   661	| --- | --- |
   662	| `design.R` | Frozen years, treatment basis, \(Z_i\), outcomes, and model IDs |
   663	| `helpers.R` | Nested decomposition, formula generator, finite-design CCV, compact model methods, and delta-method routines |
   664	| `01_build_panel.R` | Baseline histories, nested components, treatment vector, outcomes, metadata |
   665	| `02_estimate_models.R` | Four-model ladder for eight outcomes; CCV and comparison clustered covariances |
   666	| `03_postestimation.R` | Finite effects, sample AMEs, year effects, heterogeneity, and \(w\times z\times s\) grid |
   667	| `04_diagnostics.R` | Support, hierarchy, literal-rank audit, and lead placebos |
   668	| `05_generate_tables.py` | Great Tables (the Python gt implementation) HTML and LaTeX tables |
   669	| `05_validate.R` | Artifact, nesting, rank, finiteness, and analytic-gradient contracts |
   670	
   671	Run the branch with:
   672	
   673	```sh
   674	./scripts/run_mundlak_chamberlain.sh
   675	```
   676	
   677	## Principal artifacts
   678	
   679	### Analysis and model artifacts
   680	
   681	- `data/processed/mundlak_chamberlain_county_year.parquet`
   682	- `data/intermediate/mundlak_chamberlain_metadata.rds`
   683	- `data/intermediate/mundlak_chamberlain_scaling.csv`
   684	- `data/intermediate/mundlak_chamberlain_variable_inventory.csv`
   685	- `data/intermediate/mundlak_chamberlain_models.rds`
   686	
   687	The compact model bundle retains every coefficient, the complete CCV
   688	covariance, the comparison clustered covariance, CCV diagnostics, formula,
   689	collinearity list, outcome, model ID, observation count, and exact sample row
   690	IDs. It deliberately omits large \(N\times K\) score structures and the 17
   691	state-specific coefficient-error matrices after their covariance is formed.
   692	
   693	### Full-granularity CSV outputs
   694	
   695	- `mc_model_diagnostics.csv`
   696	- `mc_collinear_terms.csv`
   697	- `mc_model_warnings.csv`
   698	- `mc_parameter_estimates.csv`
   699	- `mc_ccv_diagnostics.csv`
   700	- `mc_finite_dose_effects.csv`
   701	- `mc_average_marginal_effects.csv`
   702	- `mc_year_effects.csv`
   703	- `mc_heterogeneity_effects.csv`
   704	- `mc_ame_grid.csv`
   705	- `mc_treatment_support.csv`
   706	- `mc_counterfactual_support.csv`
   707	- `mc_hierarchy_counts.csv`
   708	- `mc_identification_rank_audit.csv`
   709	- `mc_lead_placebo_effects.csv`
   710	- `mc_validation_summary.csv`
   711	
   712	### Retained gt tables and ggplot2 figures
   713	
   714	- `table_mc_dynamic_effects.tex`
   715	- `table_mc_heterogeneity.tex`
   716	- `table_mc_support.tex`
   717	- `table_mc_lead_placebos.tex`
   718	- `table_mc_ccv_coefficients.tex`
   719	- HTML counterparts for all five tables
   720	- `fig_mc_ccv_coefficients.png`
   721	- `fig_mc_dynamic_effects.png`
   722	- `fig_mc_year_effects.png`
   723	- `fig_mc_heterogeneity.png`
   724	- `fig_mc_treatment_support.png`
   725	
   726	## Interpretation boundary
   727	
   728	This branch answers a sharply defined question: conditional on the complete
   729	implemented type, policy-history, baseline-trend, calendar-time, and
   730	hierarchical projection, how does the fitted H-2A outcome change when one
   731	coordinate of annual AEWR growth changes while the other assignment-history
   732	coordinates are held fixed?
   733	
   734	It does not claim that arbitrary time-varying confounding can be absorbed by
   735	adding enough terms. If untreated innovations can still determine AEWR growth
   736	after this conditioning set, the causal interpretation fails. That boundary
   737	is the continuous-dose analogue of the conditional parallel-trends boundary
   738	in DiD.
   739

specification-outcome checkpoints). `MC_SPEC_STAGE=exhaustive` explicitly
opts into all 648 records; it is not used by the pipeline default. Exact
`MC_SPEC_IDS` override the stage. Completed checkpoints satisfying the current
resource limits are reused.

This is a standalone design for estimating how annual changes in the Adverse
Effect Wage Rate (AEWR) affect county H-2A program use. It does not modify or
depend on the repository's existing DiD or panel-IV designs.

The design implements the researcher's unified Chamberlain equation as richly
as the observed treatment support permits. Its primary model is a pooled OLS
identity-link conditional-mean model. Every reported causal quantity is
constructed after estimation as a named combination of the estimated
parameters and is assigned a delta-method standard error using the complete
continuous-treatment design-covariance CCV matrix described below.

The relevant Wooldridge background is summarized in
[`papers/metrics/wooldridge/deep-research-report-wooldridge.md`](../../../papers/metrics/wooldridge/deep-research-report-wooldridge.md).
The two most directly relevant local sources are the treatment-heterogeneity
discussion in
[`wooldridge_stata-conf_2025_nonbinary_treatments.md`](../../../papers/metrics/wooldridge/wooldridge_stata-conf_2025_nonbinary_treatments.md)
and the pooled-regression/Mundlak equivalence discussion in
[`wooldridge_empiricalecon_2025_twfe_twmundlak_did.md`](../../../papers/metrics/wooldridge/wooldridge_empiricalecon_2025_twfe_twmundlak_did.md).

## Central identification statement

AEWR changes do **not** have to be randomly assigned, independent of baseline
outcomes, or independent of persistent county, market, state, or regional
heterogeneity.

The model explicitly allows

\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf W_r,c_i)\ne 0,
\]

selection on pre-policy outcome and covariate histories, different untreated
trends by predetermined characteristics, and dose-response heterogeneity by
the baseline binding margin \(Z_i\). This is the same important sense in which
a DiD design does not require treatment assignment itself to be exogenous.

That statement does not mean that no identifying restriction is required.
After conditioning on the full specified history and trend projection, the
remaining AEWR dose coordinate must be unrelated to the remaining innovation
in the relevant untreated potential-outcome trend. The design therefore rests
on:

1. conditional no anticipation for the focal dose;
2. conditional parallel trends, stated at the level of the richly
   parameterized untreated conditional mean;
3. correct separation of the causal dose terms from the correlated-effects
   projection;
4. support for the dose perturbation being reported;
5. no unmodeled spillovers across the treatment-assignment units; and
6. a correctly specified finite-dimensional dose-response and history
   projection.

Thus, “AEWR changes need not be exogenous” means that unconditional
independence and random policy assignment are unnecessary. It does not mean
that a contemporaneous AEWR change can respond arbitrarily to an unobserved
county outcome innovation that remains in the error after conditioning.

## Observational structure

| Object | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Outcome unit \(i\) | County |
| Local market \(m(i)\) | State × commuting zone × AEWR-region cell |
| State \(q(i)\) | State FIPS |
| Assignment region \(r(i)\) | One of 17 AEWR regions |
| Baseline years | 2008–2010 |
| AEWR history used by Chamberlain projection | 2011–2022 |
| Outcome years | 2013–2022 |
| Dynamic horizons | Current, one-year lag, two-year lag |
| Eligible counties | Positive 2011 farm employment and complete hierarchy |
| Estimation panel | 30,410 observations; 3,041 counties |
| Hierarchy | 17 regions > 48 states > 745 market cells > 3,041 counties |

The market identifier includes the state because commuting zones can cross
state boundaries. Defining a market as state × CZ × AEWR region makes the
nesting strict:

\[
i\subset m(i)\subset q(i)\subset r(i).
\]

The 2013 start date is substantive, not arbitrary. It permits the model to
include the current AEWR change and two complete lags while avoiding the
state-specific 2009 OES exception. From 2010 onward, AEWR is unique within
each AEWR region-year.

## Treatment

For AEWR region \(r\) and year \(t\), define

\[
W_{rt}
  =100\left[\log(\operatorname{AEWR}_{rt})
            -\log(\operatorname{AEWR}_{r,t-1})\right].
\]

One unit of \(W_{rt}\) is one log percentage point of annual AEWR growth. The
three focal treatment coordinates in county-year observation \((i,t)\) are

\[
W^{(0)}_{it}=W_{r(i),t},\qquad
W^{(1)}_{it}=W_{r(i),t-1},\qquad
W^{(2)}_{it}=W_{r(i),t-2}.
\]

The complete policy-history vector is

\[
\mathbf W_{r(i)}
  =(W_{r(i),2011},\ldots,W_{r(i),2022})'.
\]

Although outcomes are observed for thousands of counties, there are only
\(17\times10=170\) observed region-year treatment cells. County replication
increases precision for conditional outcome relationships; it does not create
additional independent AEWR paths.

## Predetermined moderator \(Z_i\)

The continuous moderator is the standardized 2008–2010 mean local AEWR bite:

\[
Z_i=
\frac{\overline{\operatorname{AEWRbite}}_{i,2008:2010}
      -\overline{\operatorname{AEWRbite}}}
     {\operatorname{sd}
       (\overline{\operatorname{AEWRbite}}_{i,2008:2010})}.
\]

The source variable is `aewr_cz_p25`. A higher \(Z_i\) means that the AEWR is
more binding relative to the local low-wage margin. It is measured before the
2011–2022 treatment-history window. The implementation stores it as `mc_z`.

## Nested Mundlak components

< truncated lines 184-556 >
convex-combination proposal.

Let \(s=0,\ldots,16\) index a balanced cyclic assignment of the 17 complete
observed AEWR policy paths to the 17 AEWR-region labels. State zero is the
observed assignment. In the other states, every current, lagged, lead,
polynomial, cross-horizon, and Chamberlain AEWR-history column is regenerated
from the assigned donor path. Outcomes, county characteristics, geographic
labels, and the fitted residual vector \(\widehat{\mathbf u}\) remain fixed.
Every path appears in every recipient region exactly once across the 17
equally likely states.

For the complete identified coefficient basis, the code re-solves OLS in every
state:

\[
\widehat{\mathbf b}_{e,s}
=
(\mathbf X_s'\mathbf X_s)^{-1}
\mathbf X_s'\widehat{\mathbf u}.
\]

Re-solving the Gram matrix is important. It is the vector-OLS counterpart to
the Lean result that a random scalar OLS denominator requires the covariance
kernel of \(\widetilde D/(\widetilde D'\widetilde D)\), not the covariance of
raw \(\widetilde D\) multiplied by the observed denominator. The feasible
coefficient covariance is

\[
\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{dcCCV}}
=
\frac{1}{17}
\sum_{s=0}^{16}
(\widehat{\mathbf b}_{e,s}-\overline{\mathbf b}_e)
(\widehat{\mathbf b}_{e,s}-\overline{\mathbf b}_e)'.
\tag{8}
\]

The divisor is 17 because (8) is the probability covariance under a specified
finite reference law, not an ordinary sample covariance. The implementation
forms (8) as a centered matrix cross-product divided by 17, making it positive
semidefinite by construction. State zero is set exactly to zero using the OLS
normal equations. All reported post-estimation standard errors then use (7).
The conventional 17-region clustered covariance is retained only in the model
bundle and coefficient-comparison table.

This reference law is a transparent conditional assignment model; it is not a
claim that the Department of Labor historically randomized AEWR paths. The
Lean file proves the scalar finite-design covariance identity and supplies the
vector OLS/matrix-sandwich algebra. The nonlinear dose-response contrasts in
this branch additionally rely on a first-order delta-method approximation;
they are not themselves an exact nonlinear finite-design theorem from the Lean
file.

The rich design needs a common full-rank coefficient basis in every reference
state. One nonfocal 2013 history coordinate is therefore omitted from the
terminal estimable year; retaining it makes all 16 non-observed assignment
states singular. In the simpler Mundlak benchmark, region-constant slope
moderators are omitted because treatment-path reassignment otherwise changes
which coefficient is identified. These are explicit rank safeguards, not
silent collinearity repairs.

Only 17 independent policy paths are available, so the CCV covariance has rank
at most 16 even when the model contains more than 900 coefficients. Reported
95-percent intervals use \(t_{16}\) critical values. County-level sample size
must not be presented as solving the assignment-level inference problem.

## Support and current diagnostic status

Observed current AEWR changes range from about \(-4.81\) to \(20.56\) log
percentage points. A positive five-point perturbation lies outside the
same-year observed range for roughly 54 percent of the 170 treatment cells,
although it lies outside the pooled range for less than one percent. A
ten-point perturbation leaves same-year support for roughly 86–88 percent of
cells.

For that reason:

- average marginal effects evaluated at observed doses are the primary
  retained table and figure;
- one-, five-, and ten-point finite changes are retained as explicitly
  support-audited counterfactuals; and
- no large finite change should be interpreted without consulting
  `mc_counterfactual_support.csv`.

The present rich model also produces linear-probability effects outside the
logical \([-100,100]\) percentage-point range for a five-point change, and
multiple five-point future-dose placebo effects reject zero at five percent.
These are evidence of weak support, severe overparameterization,
functional-form instability, anticipation/feedback, or some combination.
They are not suppressed. A successful software validation means that the
requested design was implemented correctly; it does **not** certify that its
causal identifying assumptions fit these data.

## No bad controls

The primary model does not condition on contemporaneous or lagged
post-treatment economic outcomes. Its covariate histories end in 2010, before
the treatment-history window begins in 2011. Full AEWR histories are included
as assignment/projection variables, and the focal coordinates are excluded
from the nuisance history block as shown in (2).

## Interpretation boundary

This branch answers a sharply defined question: conditional on the complete
implemented type, policy-history, baseline-trend, calendar-time, and
hierarchical projection, how does the fitted H-2A outcome change when one
coordinate of annual AEWR growth changes while the other assignment-history
coordinates are held fixed?

It does not claim that arbitrary time-varying confounding can be absorbed by
adding enough terms. If untreated innovations can still determine AEWR growth
after this conditioning set, the causal interpretation fails. That boundary
is the continuous-dose analogue of the conditional parallel-trends boundary
in DiD.

   184	For each predetermined baseline summary \(x_i\), the design constructs four
   185	telescoping components:
   186	
   187	\[
   188	\begin{aligned}
   189	x_i^{C} &=
   190	  x_i-\bar x_{m(i)},\\
   191	x_i^{M} &=
   192	  \bar x_{m(i)}-\bar x_{q(i)},\\
   193	x_i^{S} &=
   194	  \bar x_{q(i)}-\bar x_{r(i)},\\
   195	x_i^{R} &=
   196	  \bar x_{r(i)}-\bar x.
   197	\end{aligned}
   198	\]
   199	
   200	Consequently,
   201	
   202	\[
   203	x_i-\bar x
   204	  =x_i^{C}+x_i^{M}+x_i^{S}+x_i^{R}.
   205	\]
   206	
   207	Each component is standardized after construction. This parameterizes the
   208	correlation between the latent intercept and covariate histories separately
   209	at the county-within-market, market-within-state, state-within-region, and
   210	region-within-national levels.
   211	
   212	Unrestricted AEWR-region indicators absorb the region intercept projection.
   213	County, market, and state components enter the high-dimensional baseline
   214	trend engine. Region-level baseline-by-year terms are not saturated because
   215	they would compete directly with the 17 region-level treatment cells in every
   216	year.
   217	
   218	## Baseline variables and transformations
   219	
   220	All baseline inputs use only 2008–2010 information.
   221	
   222	| Design variable | Shared-panel source | Transform |
   223	| --- | --- | --- |
   224	| H-2A certification intensity | `h2a_cert_share_farm_workers_2011_start_year` | inverse hyperbolic sine |
   225	| H-2A application intensity | `h2a_applications_per_farm_worker_2011_start_year` | inverse hyperbolic sine |
   226	| AEWR bite | `aewr_cz_p25` | level |
   227	| Population | `ln_pop_census` | log already supplied |
   228	| Farm-employment share | `farm_emp_share` | level |
   229	| Employment/population | `emp_pop_ratio` | level |
   230	| Crop-income share | `share_farm_crop_cashandinc` | level |
   231	| Animal-income share | `share_farm_animal_cashandinc` | level |
   232	| Hired-labor cost share | `share_farm_laborexp_prodexp` | level |
   233	| Low wage | `wage_p25` | log |
   234	| Cropland intensity | `cropland_acr` | \(\log(1+\text{acres}/\max(\text{farm employment},1))\) |
   235	| Predicted H-2A intensity | `h2a_predicted_share_2011` | inverse hyperbolic sine |
   236	
   237	Predicted H-2A intensity is the selected cutoff's static county propensity,
   238	based on fixed 2011 farm-employment exposure. It is repeated unchanged over
   239	panel years; repeated pre-period entries therefore carry no annual-score
   240	interpretation.
   241	
   242	Finite missing baseline values are imputed first by AEWR-region median and
   243	then, if necessary, by the national median. Missingness indicators are
   244	retained in the constructed panel. Scaling constants and the complete term
   245	inventory are written to the intermediate-data directory.
   246	
   247	For the nine variables most closely related to H-2A selection, farm
   248	structure, local binding, and untreated outcome paths, the Chamberlain
   249	intercept projection retains the separate 2008, 2009, and 2010 values. The
   250	remaining variables enter through their three-year mean and linear trend.
   251	
   252	## Implemented master conditional-mean model
   253	
   254	Let \(d_{ts}=1[t=s]\), let \(s_0=2013\) be the reference year, and define the
   255	scaled polynomial basis
   256	
   257	\[
   258	b_1(w)=w,\qquad b_2(w)=w^2/25.
   259	\]
   260	
   261	For outcome \(j\), the primary identity-link conditional mean is
   262	
   263	\[
   264	\begin{aligned}
   265	E[Y_{it}^{j}\mid\mathcal H_i]
   266	&=
   267	\theta_t+\alpha_{r(i)}
   268	+H_i'\lambda
   269	+\sum_{s\ne s_0}\psi_s Z_i d_{ts}\\
   270	&\quad+
   271	\sum_{p=0}^{2}
   272	\sum_{m=1}^{2}
   273	\sum_{s=2013}^{2022}
   274	\left(
   275	  \beta_{pms}^{(0)}
   276	  +\beta_{pms}^{(1)}Z_i
   277	\right)
   278	b_m(W_{r(i),t-p})d_{ts}\\
   279	&\quad+
   280	\sum_{s\ne s_0}
   281	\sum_{h\in\mathcal A_s}
   282	\left(
   283	  \rho_{sh}^{(0)}
   284	  +\rho_{sh}^{(1)}Z_i
   285	\right)
   286	\widetilde W_{r(i),h}d_{ts}\\
   287	&\quad+
   288	\sum_{\ell\in\{C,M,S\}}
   289	\sum_{k=1}^{K}
   290	\sum_{s\ne s_0}
   291	\left(
   292	  \delta_{k\ell s}^{(0)}
   293	  +\delta_{k\ell s}^{(1)}Z_i
   294	\right)
   295	X_{ik}^{\ell}d_{ts}.
   296	\end{aligned}
   297	\tag{1}
   298	\]
   299	
   300	Here:
   301	
   302	- \(H_i\) is the full Chamberlain intercept projection from separate
   303	  pre-period histories and mean/trend summaries;
   304	- \(\widetilde W_{r,h}\) is a standardized element of the complete
   305	  2011–2022 AEWR-change history;
   306	- \(X_{ik}^{\ell}\) is baseline covariate \(k\)'s component at hierarchy
   307	  level \(\ell\); and
   308	- the allowed history set is
   309	
   310	\[
   311	\mathcal A_s
   312	=\{2011,\ldots,2022\}\setminus\{s,s-1,s-2\}.
   313	\tag{2}
   314	\]
   315	
   316	Equation (1) contains:
   317	
   318	- 120 separately parameterized causal columns:
   319	  \(3\) horizons × \(2\) powers × \(10\) years × baseline/\(Z\) slope;
   320	- the complete non-focal treatment vector in every nonreference year,
   321	  both alone and in a triple interaction with \(Z_i\);
   322	- 33 county/market/state baseline mean components, each interacted with
   323	  all nine nonreference years and again with \(Z_i\), for 594 baseline
   324	  trend columns;
   325	- nine unrestricted \(Z_i\times\)year trends;
   326	- 99 candidate Chamberlain intercept terms;
   327	- unrestricted year indicators; and
   328	- unrestricted AEWR-region indicators.
   329	
   330	The principal full-sample models retain 922 coefficients after 89 purely
   331	algebraic redundancies are removed. The code fails if any current or lagged
   332	causal basis column is removed.
   333	
   334	## Why the literal full equation cannot be estimated
   335	
   336	The researcher's unrestricted equation places both
   337	
   338	\[
   339	W_{i,t-p}d_{ts}
   340	\]
   341	
   342	in the causal block and
   343	
   344	\[
   345	W_{ir}d_{ts}
   346	\]
   347	
   348	in the Chamberlain history block for every \(r\). When \(r=s-p\), these are
   349	the same regressor. If the history term is standardized, it remains an affine
   350	transformation of the same regressor; the year indicator absorbs the
   351	constant. Likewise,
   352	
   353	\[
   354	W_{i,t-p}Z_id_{ts}
   355	\]
   356	
   357	and the corresponding \(r=s-p\) triple interaction are collinear after
   358	\(Z_i\times d_{ts}\) is included.
   359	
   360	Therefore \(\beta_{p,1,s}\) and \(\rho_{s,s-p}\) cannot be separately
   361	estimated. No software, sample size, or delta-method routine can recover both
   362	from the same column. The implementation removes the focal current and lag
   363	coordinates from the nuisance history set in (2). It retains every non-focal
   364	history coordinate.
   365	
   366	There is a second assignment-support constraint. In a given year, the literal
   367	non-\(Z\) equation requests:
   368	
   369	\[
   370	1+3\times3+12=22
   371	\]
   372	
   373	region-level columns from only 17 AEWR regions. Merely removing the three
   374	exact focal duplicates leaves
   375	
   376	\[
   377	1+3\times3+9=19>17.
   378	\]
   379	
   380	The richest cellwise polynomial compatible with the full non-focal history
   381	projection is quadratic:
   382	
   383	\[
   384	1+3\times2+9=16<17.
   385	\]
   386	
   387	Accordingly, the primary master model uses a quadratic in every
   388	lag-by-calendar-year cell. Cubic treatment columns remain constructed and
   389	documented for sensitivity work, but a cellwise cubic is not labeled as
   390	identified. The exact count and duplicate audit is retained in
   391	`mc_identification_rank_audit.csv`.
   392	
   393	## Outcomes
   394	
   395	The master equation is estimated separately for:
   396	
   397	| ID | Outcome | Sample |
   398	| --- | --- | --- |
   399	| `applications` | Applications per 1,000 workers in 2011 farm employment | All eligible county-years |
   400	| `employers` | Raw balanced-linkage H-2A employer count | All |

| AEWR bite | `aewr_cz_p25` | level |
| Population | `ln_pop_census` | log already supplied |
| Farm-employment share | `farm_emp_share` | level |
| Employment/population | `emp_pop_ratio` | level |
| Crop-income share | `share_farm_crop_cashandinc` | level |
| Animal-income share | `share_farm_animal_cashandinc` | level |
| Hired-labor cost share | `share_farm_laborexp_prodexp` | level |
| Low wage | `wage_p25` | log |
| Cropland intensity | `cropland_acr` | \(\log(1+\text{acres}/\max(\text{farm employment},1))\) |
| Predicted H-2A intensity | `h2a_predicted_share_2011` | inverse hyperbolic sine |

Predicted H-2A intensity is the selected cutoff's static county propensity,
based on fixed 2011 farm-employment exposure. It is repeated unchanged over
panel years; repeated pre-period entries therefore carry no annual-score
interpretation.

Finite missing baseline values are imputed first by AEWR-region median and
then, if necessary, by the national median. Missingness indicators are
retained in the constructed panel. Scaling constants and the complete term
inventory are written to the intermediate-data directory.

For the nine variables most closely related to H-2A selection, farm
structure, local binding, and untreated outcome paths, the Chamberlain
intercept projection retains the separate 2008, 2009, and 2010 values. The
remaining variables enter through their three-year mean and linear trend.

## Implemented master conditional-mean model

Let \(d_{ts}=1[t=s]\), let \(s_0=2013\) be the reference year, and define the
scaled polynomial basis

\[
b_1(w)=w,\qquad b_2(w)=w^2/25.
\]

For outcome \(j\), the primary identity-link conditional mean is

\[
\begin{aligned}
E[Y_{it}^{j}\mid\mathcal H_i]
&=
\theta_t+\alpha_{r(i)}
+H_i'\lambda
+\sum_{s\ne s_0}\psi_s Z_i d_{ts}\\
&\quad+
\sum_{p=0}^{2}
\sum_{m=1}^{2}
\sum_{s=2013}^{2022}
\left(
  \beta_{pms}^{(0)}
  +\beta_{pms}^{(1)}Z_i
\right)
b_m(W_{r(i),t-p})d_{ts}\\
&\quad+
\sum_{s\ne s_0}
\sum_{h\in\mathcal A_s}
\left(
  \rho_{sh}^{(0)}
  +\rho_{sh}^{(1)}Z_i
\right)
\widetilde W_{r(i),h}d_{ts}\\
&\quad+
\sum_{\ell\in\{C,M,S\}}
\sum_{k=1}^{K}
\sum_{s\ne s_0}
\left(
  \delta_{k\ell s}^{(0)}
  +\delta_{k\ell s}^{(1)}Z_i
\right)
X_{ik}^{\ell}d_{ts}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]

Here:

- \(H_i\) is the full Chamberlain intercept projection from separate
  pre-period histories and mean/trend summaries;
- \(\widetilde W_{r,h}\) is a standardized element of the complete
  2011–2022 AEWR-change history;
- \(X_{ik}^{\ell}\) is baseline covariate \(k\)'s component at hierarchy
  level \(\ell\); and
- the allowed history set is

\[
\mathcal A_s
=\{2011,\ldots,2022\}\setminus\{s,s-1,s-2\}.
\tag{2}
\]

Equation (1) contains:

- 120 separately parameterized causal columns:
  \(3\) horizons × \(2\) powers × \(10\) years × baseline/\(Z\) slope;
- the complete non-focal treatment vector in every nonreference year,
  both alone and in a triple interaction with \(Z_i\);
- 33 county/market/state baseline mean components, each interacted with
  all nine nonreference years and again with \(Z_i\), for 594 baseline
  trend columns;
- nine unrestricted \(Z_i\times\)year trends;
- 99 candidate Chamberlain intercept terms;
- unrestricted year indicators; and
- unrestricted AEWR-region indicators.

The principal full-sample models retain 922 coefficients after 89 purely
algebraic redundancies are removed. The code fails if any current or lagged
causal basis column is removed.

## Why the literal full equation cannot be estimated

The researcher's unrestricted equation places both

\[
W_{i,t-p}d_{ts}
\]

in the causal block and

\[
W_{ir}d_{ts}
\]

in the Chamberlain history block for every \(r\). When \(r=s-p\), these are
the same regressor. If the history term is standardized, it remains an affine
transformation of the same regressor; the year indicator absorbs the
constant. Likewise,

\[
W_{i,t-p}Z_id_{ts}
\]

and the corresponding \(r=s-p\) triple interaction are collinear after
\(Z_i\times d_{ts}\) is included.

Therefore \(\beta_{p,1,s}\) and \(\rho_{s,s-p}\) cannot be separately
estimated. No software, sample size, or delta-method routine can recover both
from the same column. The implementation removes the focal current and lag
coordinates from the nuisance history set in (2). It retains every non-focal
history coordinate.

There is a second assignment-support constraint. In a given year, the literal
non-\(Z\) equation requests:

\[
1+3\times3+12=22
\]

region-level columns from only 17 AEWR regions. Merely removing the three
exact focal duplicates leaves

\[
1+3\times3+9=19>17.
\]

The richest cellwise polynomial compatible with the full non-focal history
projection is quadratic:

\[
1+3\times2+9=16<17.
\]

Accordingly, the primary master model uses a quadratic in every
lag-by-calendar-year cell. Cubic treatment columns remain constructed and
documented for sensitivity work, but a cellwise cubic is not labeled as
identified. The exact count and duplicate audit is retained in
`mc_identification_rank_audit.csv`.

## Outcomes

The master equation is estimated separately for:

| ID | Outcome | Sample |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `applications` | Applications per 1,000 workers in 2011 farm employment | All eligible county-years |
| `employers` | Raw balanced-linkage H-2A employer count | All |

   412	
   413	## Model ladder
   414	
   415	Every outcome is estimated under four declared specifications:
   416	
   417	1. `twfe_benchmark`: current and two lagged AEWR changes with county and year
   418	   fixed effects;
   419	2. `mundlak_multilevel`: the nested mean/trend projection, heterogeneous

   429	
   430	## Potential-outcome interpretation
   431	
   432	For a focal horizon \(p\), define the dose-response contrast while holding the
   433	observed type and all nuisance-history coordinates fixed:
   434	
   435	\[
   436	\Delta_{p,it}(\delta)
   437	=
   438	Y_{it}\!\left(
   439	  W_{r,t-p}+\delta;
   440	  \mathbf W_{r,-(t-p)}
   441	\right)
   442	-
   443	Y_{it}\!\left(
   444	  W_{r,t-p};
   445	  \mathbf W_{r,-(t-p)}
   446	\right).
   447	\tag{3}
   448	\]
   449	
   450	Holding the Chamberlain projection fixed is deliberate. It treats the
   451	projection as a description of the unit's latent type and selection history,
   452	not as a structural causal channel that should be redrawn when a focal dose
   453	is perturbed.
   454	
   455	The primary standardized estimand is
   456	
   457	\[
   458	\operatorname{ASF}_{p}(\delta)
   459	=
   460	\frac{\sum_{it}\omega_{it}
   461	E[\Delta_{p,it}(\delta)\mid\mathcal H_i]}
   462	{\sum_{it}\omega_{it}}.
   463	\tag{4}
   464	\]
   465	
   466	The retained standardizations are:
   467	
   468	- equal county-year weight;
   469	- equal region-year weight, implemented by weighting each county by the
   470	  inverse number of estimation-sample counties in its region-year;
   471	- baseline-farm-employment weight for the four farm-employment-normalized
   472	  program-volume outcomes; and
   473	- application or certified-position exposure weights for the conditional
   474	  ratio outcomes.
   475	
   476	Sample-period total effects are also reported for the five volume outcomes.
   477	Employer-count effects are summed directly; the other fitted rates are
   478	converted back to application, position, or hour totals.

   481	
   482	Under the quadratic identity-link model, the unit-level marginal effect at
   483	horizon \(p\), year \(s\), dose \(w\), and moderator \(z\) is

   487	=
   488	\beta_{p,1,s}^{(0)}
   489	+\beta_{p,1,s}^{(1)}z
   490	+\frac{2w}{25}
   491	\left(
   492	  \beta_{p,2,s}^{(0)}
   493	  +\beta_{p,2,s}^{(1)}z
   494	\right).

   496	\]

   502	\Delta_{p,s}(w,z;\delta)
   503	&=
   504	\delta
   505	\left(
   506	  \beta_{p,1,s}^{(0)}

   529	\]

   535	=
   536	\widehat{\mathbf g}'
   537	\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{dcCCV}}
   538	\widehat{\mathbf g}.
   539	\tag{7}

1	# Reading the Mundlak–Chamberlain specification and its delta-method effects
     2	
     3	This note is a guided reading of the implemented multilevel
     4	Mundlak–Chamberlain design. Its two goals are to make the regression
     5	specification visually legible and to show exactly how the fitted regression
     6	is converted into average treatment effects and standard errors.
     7	
     8	The central idea is:
     9	
    10	\[
    11	\underbrace{\text{estimate a rich conditional mean}}_{\text{regression step}}
    12	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    13	\overbrace{\text{change one AEWR-growth coordinate}}^{\text{counterfactual step}}
    14	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    15	\underbrace{\text{average fitted changes}}_{\text{causal estimand}}
    16	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    17	\overbrace{\text{propagate coefficient uncertainty}}^{\text{delta method}}.
    18	\]
    19	
    20	The primary model is Gaussian with an identity link. Consequently, the
    21	reported effects are linear combinations of the estimated coefficients once
    22	the observed doses, moderators, sample, and counterfactual change are fixed.
    23	The delta-method variance calculation is therefore exact with respect to the
    24	estimated coefficient vector for this implemented model. It would become a
    25	first-order approximation under a nonlinear link.
    26	
    27	## 1. What varies, and at what level?
    28	
    29	Counties are indexed by \(i\), calendar years by \(t\), and AEWR regions by
    30	\(r\). County \(i\) belongs to AEWR region \(r(i)\). The annual treatment is
    31	
    32	\[
    33	\underbrace{W_{r,t}}_{\substack{\text{AEWR-growth dose}\\
    34	\text{in log percentage points}}}
    35	=
    36	\overbrace{100}^{\text{percentage-point scale}}
    37	\left[
    38	  \underbrace{\log(\operatorname{AEWR}_{r,t})}_{\text{current log AEWR}}
    39	  -
    40	  \underbrace{\log(\operatorname{AEWR}_{r,t-1})}_{\text{lagged log AEWR}}
    41	\right].
    42	\]
    43	
    44	Thus treatment varies at the **AEWR-region-by-year** level even though the
    45	outcome is observed at the **county-by-year** level. Thousands of counties do
    46	not create thousands of independent AEWR policy paths: there are 17 regional
    47	paths.
    48	
    49	The three causal horizons are
    50	
    51	\[
    52	\underbrace{W_{r(i),t}}_{p=0:\ \text{current growth}},
    53	\qquad
    54	\overbrace{W_{r(i),t-1}}^{p=1:\ \text{one-year lag}},
    55	\qquad
    56	\underbrace{W_{r(i),t-2}}_{p=2:\ \text{two-year lag}}.
    57	\]
    58	
    59	The primary treatment basis is quadratic:
    60	
    61	\[
    62	\underbrace{b_1(w)=w}_{\text{linear response}}
    63	\qquad\text{and}\qquad
    64	\overbrace{b_2(w)=\frac{w^2}{25}}^{\substack{\text{curvature}\\
    65	\text{scaled around a 5-point change}}}.
    66	\]
    67	
    68	Dividing the quadratic by \(25=5^2\) improves numerical conditioning. It does
    69	**not** scale an outcome. In particular, the employer outcome remains the raw
    70	balanced-linkage count:
    71	
    72	\[
    73	\underbrace{Y_{it}^{\text{employers}}}_{\text{modeled outcome}}
    74	=
    75	\overbrace{\operatorname{nbr\_employers\_balanced\_start\_year}_{it}}
    76	^{\text{raw integer count}},
    77	\qquad
    78	\underbrace{\frac{Y_{it}^{\text{employers}}}
    79	{\operatorname{farm\ employment}_{i,2011}}}_{\text{not used}}.
    80	\]
    81	
    82	## 2. A brace map of the complete conditional mean
    83	
    84	Let \(d_{ts}=1[t=s]\), let \(s_0=2013\) be the reference year, and let \(Z_i\)
    85	be the standardized pre-policy AEWR bite. For outcome \(j\), the implemented
    86	primary conditional mean is
    87	
    88	\[
    89	\begin{aligned}
    90	E[Y_{it}^{j}\mid\mathcal H_i]
    91	&=
    92	\underbrace{\theta_t}_{\text{unrestricted year effect}}
    93	+
    94	\overbrace{\alpha_{r(i)}}^{\text{AEWR-region intercept}}
    95	+
    96	\underbrace{H_i'\lambda}_{\substack{\text{Chamberlain intercept projection}\\
    97	\text{from predetermined histories}}}
    98	\\[3pt]
    99	&\quad+
   100	\overbrace{
   101	\sum_{s\ne s_0}\psi_s Z_i d_{ts}
   102	}^{\substack{\text{baseline bite}\\\times\ \text{calendar-year trend}}}
   103	\\[3pt]
   104	&\quad+
   105	\underbrace{
   106	\sum_{p=0}^{2}\sum_{m=1}^{2}\sum_{s=2013}^{2022}
   107	\left[
   108	  \overbrace{\beta_{pms}^{(0)}}^{\text{effect at }Z_i=0}
   109	  +
   110	  \underbrace{\beta_{pms}^{(1)}Z_i}_{\text{effect heterogeneity}}
   111	\right]
   112	\overbrace{b_m(W_{r(i),t-p})}^{\text{dose basis}}
   113	\underbrace{d_{ts}}_{\text{year cell}}
   114	}_{\textbf{causal current-and-lag dose-response block}}
   115	\\[3pt]
   116	&\quad+
   117	\overbrace{
   118	\sum_{s\ne s_0}\sum_{h\in\mathcal A_s}
   119	\left[
   120	  \underbrace{\rho_{sh}^{(0)}}_{\text{history main effect}}
   121	  +
   122	  \overbrace{\rho_{sh}^{(1)}Z_i}^{\text{history}\times\text{bite}}
   123	\right]
   124	\underbrace{\widetilde W_{r(i),h}}_{\text{non-focal AEWR history}}
   125	d_{ts}
   126	}^{\substack{\text{Chamberlain treatment-history projection}\\
   127	\text{held fixed in a focal counterfactual}}}
   128	\\[3pt]
   129	&\quad+
   130	\underbrace{
   131	\sum_{\ell\in\{C,M,S\}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{s\ne s_0}
   132	\left[
   133	  \overbrace{\delta_{k\ell s}^{(0)}}^{\text{baseline trend}}
   134	  +
   135	  \underbrace{\delta_{k\ell s}^{(1)}Z_i}_{\text{trend}\times\text{bite}}
   136	\right]
   137	\overbrace{X_{ik}^{\ell}}^{\substack{\text{county, market, or state}\\
   138	\text{baseline component}}}
   139	d_{ts}
   140	}_{\textbf{hierarchical predetermined-trend projection}}.
   141	\end{aligned}
   142	\tag{1}
   143	\]
   144	
   145	This looks forbidding because it protects the causal block from several forms
   146	of selection. Reading one line at a time makes its role clearer.
   147	
   148	### Fixed time and place
   149	
   150	\[
   151	\underbrace{\theta_t}_{\substack{\text{common shocks}\\
   152	\text{in calendar year }t}}
   153	+
   154	\overbrace{\alpha_{r(i)}}^{\substack{\text{persistent differences}\\
   155	\text{across AEWR regions}}}.
   156	\]
   157	
   158	These terms absorb common calendar shocks and time-invariant differences
   159	across the 17 treatment-assignment regions.
   160	
   161	### Predetermined latent type
   162	
   163	\[
   164	\underbrace{H_i'\lambda}_{\text{county latent-type projection}}
   165	=
   166	\overbrace{
   167	\text{separate 2008, 2009, and 2010 histories}
   168	}^{\text{Chamberlain components}}
   169	+
   170	\underbrace{
   171	\text{pre-period means and trends}
   172	}_{\text{Mundlak summaries}}.
   173	\]
   174	
   175	The hierarchy decomposes baseline variables into county, market, state, and
   176	region pieces. This permits, for example, a county to differ from its local
   177	market while the local market differs from its state.
   178	
   179	### Heterogeneous causal response
   180	
   181	For a particular horizon \(p\), polynomial degree \(m\), and outcome year
   182	\(s\), the causal coefficient is
   183	
   184	\[
   185	\underbrace{
   186	\beta_{pms}^{(0)}+\beta_{pms}^{(1)}Z_i
   187	}_{\substack{\text{county-specific response}\\
   188	\text{indexed by predetermined AEWR bite}}}
   189	=
   190	\overbrace{\beta_{pms}^{(0)}}^{\text{response at mean bite}}
   191	+
   192	\underbrace{\beta_{pms}^{(1)}Z_i}_{\text{bite-gradient in response}}.
   193	\]
   194	
   195	The response may therefore differ by horizon, calendar year, dose level, and
   196	predetermined local binding intensity.
   197	
   198	## 3. Why focal treatment histories are excluded
   199	
   200	The nuisance history set for outcome year \(s\) is
   201	
   202	\[
   203	\underbrace{\mathcal A_s}_{\text{allowed nuisance histories}}
   204	=
   205	\overbrace{\{2011,\ldots,2022\}}^{\text{complete treatment history}}
   206	\setminus
   207	\underbrace{\{s,s-1,s-2\}}_{\text{current and two focal lags}}.
   208	\tag{2}
   209	\]
   210	
   211	This exclusion is an identification requirement, not a convenience. Within
   212	year \(s\), \(d_{ts}\) forces \(t=s\), so
   213	
   214	\[
   215	\underbrace{W_{r(i),t-p}d_{ts}}_{\text{causal regressor}}
   216	=
   217	\overbrace{W_{r(i),s-p}d_{ts}}^{\text{same numerical column}}
   218	=
   219	\underbrace{
   220	\left.\widetilde W_{r(i),h}d_{ts}\right|_{h=s-p}
   221	}_{\substack{\text{focal nuisance-history regressor}\\
   222	\text{up to standardization and a year constant}}}.
   223	\]
   224	
   225	Including both would ask the data to distinguish two coefficients multiplying
   226	the same column. The same problem occurs after interacting each copy with
   227	\(Z_i\):
   228	
   229	\[
   230	\underbrace{W_{r(i),t-p}Z_i d_{ts}}_{\text{causal heterogeneity}}
   231	=
   232	\overbrace{
   233	\left.\widetilde W_{r(i),h}Z_i d_{ts}\right|_{h=s-p}
   234	}^{\text{duplicated nuisance heterogeneity}}.
   235	\]
   236	
   237	No estimator, sample-size increase, covariance correction, or delta method
   238	can separately identify coefficients on duplicated columns.
   239	
   240	The 17-region assignment support also disciplines polynomial complexity:
   241	
   242	\[
   243	\underbrace{1}_{\text{intercept}}
   244	+
   245	\overbrace{3\times2}^{\substack{\text{three horizons}\\\times\text{two powers}}}
   246	+
   247	\underbrace{9}_{\text{non-focal histories}}
   248	=
   249	\overbrace{16}^{\text{region-level columns per year}}
   250	<
   251	\underbrace{17}_{\text{AEWR regions}}.
   252	\]
   253	
   254	A cellwise cubic would instead exceed the available region-level rank once
   255	the non-focal history projection is retained.
   256	
   257	## 4. What is held fixed in a treatment contrast?
   258	
	< truncated lines 259-489 >
   490	\overbrace{
   491	a_{it}^{(2)}(\delta)
   492	=\frac{2W_{r(i),t-p}\delta+\delta^2}{25}
   493	}^{\text{quadratic-basis change}}.
   494	\]
   495	
   496	Then the gradient entries are weighted sample moments:
   497	
   498	\[
   499	\underbrace{g_{p,m,s}^{(0)}}_{\text{gradient for }\beta_{pms}^{(0)}}
   500	=
   501	\overbrace{
   502	\frac{\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal S}
   503	\omega_{it}d_{ts}a_{it}^{(m)}(\delta)}
   504	{\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal S}\omega_{it}}
   505	}^{\text{average basis change in year }s},
   506	\]
   507	
   508	\[
   509	\underbrace{g_{p,m,s}^{(1)}}_{\text{gradient for }\beta_{pms}^{(1)}}
   510	=
   511	\overbrace{
   512	\frac{\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal S}
   513	\omega_{it}d_{ts}a_{it}^{(m)}(\delta)Z_i}
   514	{\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal S}\omega_{it}}
   515	}^{\text{moderator-weighted average basis change}}.
   516	\]
   517	
   518	For an AME, replace the finite-change basis terms with derivatives:
   519	
   520	\[
   521	\underbrace{a_{it}^{(1)}}_{\text{linear derivative}}=1,
   522	\qquad
   523	\overbrace{a_{it}^{(2)}}^{\text{quadratic derivative}}
   524	=\frac{2W_{r(i),t-p}}{25}.
   525	\]
   526	
   527	All nuisance-coordinate entries are zero in the direct effect gradient:
   528	
   529	\[
   530	\underbrace{
   531	\frac{\partial h}{\partial(\theta,\alpha,\lambda,\psi,\rho,\delta)}
   532	}_{\substack{\text{direct gradient entries for fixed}\\
   533	\text{nuisance histories and baseline type}}}
   534	=
   535	\overbrace{\mathbf 0}^{\text{held fixed in the counterfactual}}.
   536	\]
   537	
   538	Those nuisance regressors still matter: estimating them changes the covariance
   539	of the relevant \(\widehat\beta\) coefficients.
   540	
   541	## 8. Delta-method variance with design-covariance CCV
   542	
   543	Let \(\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{dcCCV}}\) be the covariance matrix of the
   544	complete identified coefficient vector. The reported variance is
   545	
   546	\[
   547	\underbrace{
   548	\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat q)
   549	}_{\text{uncertainty in the reported treatment effect}}
   550	=
   551	\overbrace{\widehat{\mathbf g}'}^{\text{left sensitivity}}
   552	\underbrace{\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{dcCCV}}}
   553	_{\substack{\text{coefficient covariance from}\\
   554	\text{17 balanced path assignments}}}
   555	\overbrace{\widehat{\mathbf g}}^{\text{right sensitivity}}.
   556	\tag{9}
   557	\]
   558	
   559	Thus
   560	
   561	\[
   562	\underbrace{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat q)}_{\text{reported CCV SE}}
   563	=
   564	\overbrace{
   565	\sqrt{
   566	\widehat{\mathbf g}'
   567	\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{dcCCV}}
   568	\widehat{\mathbf g}}
   569	}^{\text{delta-method standard error}},
   570	\]
   571	
   572	and the 95 percent interval is
   573	
   574	\[
   575	\underbrace{\widehat q}_{\text{point estimate}}
   576	\ \pm\
   577	\overbrace{t_{0.975,16}}^{\substack{\text{critical value based on}\\
   578	\text{17 independent policy paths}}}
   579	\underbrace{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat q)}_{\text{delta-method CCV SE}}.
   580	\tag{10}
   581	\]
   582	
   583	The covariance itself is formed by cyclically assigning the 17 observed AEWR
   584	paths to the 17 region labels. If \(a=0,\ldots,16\) indexes these equally likely
   585	assignment states, then
   586	
   587	\[
   588	\underbrace{\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{dcCCV}}}_{\text{reporting covariance}}
   589	=
   590	\overbrace{\frac{1}{17}}^{\text{finite-design probability weight}}
   591	\sum_{a=0}^{16}
   592	\underbrace{
   593	\left(\widehat{\mathbf b}_{e,a}-\overline{\mathbf b}_e\right)
   594	\left(\widehat{\mathbf b}_{e,a}-\overline{\mathbf b}_e\right)'
   595	}_{\text{state-specific coefficient-error outer product}}.
   596	\tag{11}
   597	\]
   598	
   599	The delta method and the design covariance perform different jobs:
   600	
   601	\[
   602	\underbrace{\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{dcCCV}}}
   603	_{\text{How uncertain are the regression coefficients?}}
   604	\qquad+qquad
   605	\overbrace{\widehat{\mathbf g}}^{\text{How does the estimand use them?}}
   606	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
   607	\underbrace{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat q)}
   608	_{\text{How uncertain is the ATE or AME?}}.
   609	\]
   610	
   611	## 9. A two-coefficient miniature example
   612	
   613	Suppose, only for illustration, that the fitted response were linear:
   614	
   615	\[
   616	\underbrace{\widehat Y_i(w)}_{\text{fitted raw employer count}}
   617	=
   618	\overbrace{\widehat\beta_0}^{\text{baseline}}
   619	+
   620	\underbrace{\widehat\beta_1 w}_{\text{dose response}}.
   621	\]
   622	
   623	A \(\delta=5\) change gives every row
   624	
   625	\[
   626	\underbrace{\widehat Y_i(w+5)-\widehat Y_i(w)}_{\text{finite treatment effect}}
   627	=
   628	\overbrace{5\widehat\beta_1}^{\text{coefficient combination}}.
   629	\]
   630	
   631	Therefore
   632	
   633	\[
   634	\underbrace{\widehat q}_{\text{average effect}}=5\widehat\beta_1,
   635	\qquad
   636	\overbrace{\widehat{\mathbf g}}^{\text{gradient}}
   637	=
   638	\underbrace{(0,5)'}_{\substack{\text{zero sensitivity to }\beta_0\\
   639	\text{five-unit sensitivity to }\beta_1}},
   640	\]
   641	
   642	and
   643	
   644	\[
   645	\underbrace{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat q)}_{\text{effect variance}}
   646	=
   647	\overbrace{(0,5)}^{\text{left gradient}}
   648	\underbrace{
   649	\begin{pmatrix}
   650	V_{00}&V_{01}\\V_{10}&V_{11}
   651	\end{pmatrix}
   652	}_{\text{coefficient covariance}}
   653	\overbrace{(0,5)'}^{\text{right gradient}}
   654	=
   655	\underbrace{25V_{11}}_{\text{propagated variance}}.
   656	\]
   657	
   658	The implemented model follows exactly this logic with hundreds of nuisance
   659	coefficients and year-specific linear and quadratic treatment coefficients.
   660	
   661	## 10. How the implementation checks the algebra
   662	
   663	The production code constructs a sparse named gradient by placing the sample
   664	moments from (8) into the appropriate year-by-horizon coefficient coordinates.
   665	As a validation, it also builds the complete observed and counterfactual model
   666	matrices:
   667	
   668	\[
   669	\underbrace{\mathbf X_0}_{\text{observed design matrix}}
   670	=
   671	\overbrace{\mathbf X(W)}^{\text{observed focal dose}},
   672	\qquad
   673	\underbrace{\mathbf X_1}_{\text{counterfactual design matrix}}
   674	=
   675	\overbrace{\mathbf X(W+\delta)}^{\text{shifted focal dose}}.
   676	\]
   677	
   678	For an equally weighted average, the direct formula-matrix gradient is
   679	
   680	\[
   681	\underbrace{\widehat{\mathbf g}_{\mathrm{direct}}}_{\text{full-matrix check}}
   682	=
   683	\overbrace{
   684	\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i,t}
   685	\left(\mathbf x_{1,it}-\mathbf x_{0,it}\right)
   686	}^{\text{average counterfactual change in every regressor}}.
   687	\]
   688	
   689	The employer-outcome validation requires
   690	
   691	\[
   692	\underbrace{
   693	\max_k\left|
   694	\widehat g_{\mathrm{named},k}
   695	-
   696	\widehat g_{\mathrm{direct},k}
   697	\right|
   698	}_{\text{largest delta-gradient discrepancy}}
   699	\approx
   700	\overbrace{5.55\times10^{-17}}^{\text{observed numerical error}}.
   701	\]
   702	
   703	This check is especially useful because it jointly tests the year cells,
   704	quadratic rescaling, \(Z_i\) interactions, counterfactual basis refresh, and
   705	coefficient-name alignment.
   706	
   707	## 11. Interpretation checklist
   708	
   709	Before interpreting an employer-count effect, verify each layer:
   710	
   711	\[
   712	\underbrace{Y_{it}}_{\text{raw balanced employer count}}
   713	\quad\xleftarrow{\text{modeled by}}\quad
   714	\overbrace{E[Y_{it}\mid\mathcal H_i]}^{\text{rich identity-link projection}}
   715	\quad\xrightarrow{W_{t-p}\mapsto W_{t-p}+\delta}\quad
   716	\underbrace{\Delta_{it}(\delta)}_{\text{county-year fitted effect}}
   717	\quad\xrightarrow{\text{average}}\quad
   718	\overbrace{\widehat{\operatorname{ATE}}(\delta)}^{\text{reported estimand}}
   719	\quad\xrightarrow{\text{delta method}}\quad
   720	\underbrace{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}}_{\text{dcCCV uncertainty}}.
   721	\]
   722	
   723	In words:
   724	
   725	1. The employer outcome is a raw count, not divided by farm employment.
   726	2. Treatment is annual AEWR growth measured in log percentage points.
   727	3. A counterfactual shifts one current-or-lag dose coordinate while holding
   728	   predetermined type and non-focal history fixed.
   729	4. County-year fitted changes are averaged using a declared standardization.
   730	5. A named gradient maps coefficient covariance into ATE or AME covariance.
   731	6. The causal interpretation still requires the conditional parallel-trends
   732	   and treatment-history assumptions described in the main design README.
   733	
   734	## 12. Code map
   735	
   736	| Mathematical object | Implementation |
   737	| --- | --- |
   738	| Outcomes, horizons, basis, and design version | [`design.R`](design.R) |
   739	| Baseline histories, hierarchy, treatment columns, raw employer outcome | [`01_build_panel.R`](01_build_panel.R) |
   740	| Formula assembly | [`helpers.R`](helpers.R), especially `mc_build_formula()` |
   741	| Four-model estimation ladder and coefficient covariance | [`02_estimate_models.R`](02_estimate_models.R) |
   742	| Named finite-change and AME gradients | [`helpers.R`](helpers.R), especially `mc_master_sample_effect()` |
   743	| Standardizations and sample-period totals | [`03_postestimation.R`](03_postestimation.R) |
   744	| Raw-count and direct delta-gradient checks | [`05_validate.R`](05_validate.R) |
   745	
   746	The main design assumptions, rank argument, CCV reference law, and artifact
   747	inventory remain documented in [`README.md`](README.md).
   748

258	
   259	Choose a horizon \(p\) and change its dose by \(\delta\) log percentage points.
   260	Here, the unsubscripted \(\delta\) denotes a treatment change. It is unrelated
   261	to the nuisance-trend coefficients \(\delta_{k\ell s}^{(0)}\) and
   262	\(\delta_{k\ell s}^{(1)}\) in equation (1):
   263	
   264	\[
   265	\underbrace{W_{r(i),t-p}}_{\text{observed focal coordinate}}
   266	\quad\longrightarrow\quad
   267	\overbrace{W_{r(i),t-p}+\delta}^{\text{counterfactual focal coordinate}}.
   268	\]
   269	
   270	The contrast changes the focal dose basis and its \(Z_i\) interaction while
   271	holding fixed
   272	
   273	\[
   274	\underbrace{H_i}_{\text{predetermined type}},\quad
   275	\overbrace{Z_i}^{\text{baseline moderator}},\quad
   276	\underbrace{\widetilde W_{r,h},\ h\in\mathcal A_s}_{\text{non-focal history}},
   277	\quad
   278	\overbrace{X_{ik}^{\ell}}^{\text{baseline hierarchy}},\quad
   279	\underbrace{\theta_t,\alpha_{r(i)}}_{\text{time and region}}.
   280	\]
   281	
   282	This is a **coordinate intervention** on a continuous treatment history. It
   283	is not a claim that all elements of the historical AEWR path change together.
   284	
   285	## 5. From the quadratic regression to a unit-level effect
   286	
   287	For brevity, fix \(p\) and \(s\), write the observed focal dose as \(w\), and
   288	write the county's moderator as \(z\). The relevant fitted causal response is
   289	
   290	\[
   291	\underbrace{
   292	\left(\beta_{p,1,s}^{(0)}+\beta_{p,1,s}^{(1)}z\right)w
   293	}_{\text{linear dose contribution}}
   294	+
   295	\overbrace{
   296	\left(\beta_{p,2,s}^{(0)}+\beta_{p,2,s}^{(1)}z\right)
   297	\frac{w^2}{25}
   298	}^{\text{quadratic dose contribution}}.
   299	\]
   300	
   301	### Finite treatment change
   302	
   303	Replacing \(w\) with \(w+\delta\) and subtracting the observed prediction gives
   304	
   305	\[
   306	\begin{aligned}
   307	\Delta_{p,s}(w,z;\delta)
   308	&=
   309	\underbrace{
   310	\delta
   311	\left(\beta_{p,1,s}^{(0)}+\beta_{p,1,s}^{(1)}z\right)
   312	}_{\text{linear-basis change}}
   313	\\[3pt]
   314	&\quad+
   315	\overbrace{
   316	\frac{2w\delta+\delta^2}{25}
   317	\left(\beta_{p,2,s}^{(0)}+\beta_{p,2,s}^{(1)}z\right)
   318	}^{\text{quadratic-basis change}}.
   319	\end{aligned}
   320	\tag{3}
   321	\]
   322	
   323	The factor \(2w\delta+\delta^2\) comes from
   324	
   325	\[
   326	\underbrace{(w+\delta)^2}_{\text{counterfactual square}}
   327	-
   328	\overbrace{w^2}^{\text{observed square}}
   329	=
   330	\underbrace{2w\delta+\delta^2}_{\text{change in the square}}.
   331	\]
   332	
   333	### Marginal treatment effect
   334	
   335	Taking the derivative with respect to the focal dose gives
   336	
   337	\[
   338	\operatorname{ME}_{p,s}(w,z)
   339	=
   340	\underbrace{
   341	\beta_{p,1,s}^{(0)}+\beta_{p,1,s}^{(1)}z
   342	}_{\text{linear-basis slope}}
   343	+
   344	\overbrace{
   345	\frac{2w}{25}
   346	\left(\beta_{p,2,s}^{(0)}+\beta_{p,2,s}^{(1)}z\right)
   347	}^{\text{dose-dependent curvature slope}}.
   348	\tag{4}
   349	\]
   350	
   351	The marginal effect changes with \(w\), \(z\), \(s\), and \(p\). A single raw
   352	regression coefficient is therefore not the design's average treatment
   353	effect.
   354	
   355	## 6. Averaging unit-level effects
   356	
   357	Let \(\mathcal S\) denote the requested estimation subset and let
   358	\(\omega_{it}\ge0\) be its standardization weight. The average finite treatment
   359	effect is
   360	
   361	\[
   362	\widehat{\operatorname{ATE}}_{p}(\delta)
   363	=
   364	\underbrace{
   365	\frac{1}{\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal S}\omega_{it}}
   366	}_{\text{normalization}}
   367	\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal S}
   368	\overbrace{\omega_{it}}^{\text{standardization weight}}
   369	\underbrace{
   370	\widehat\Delta_{p,t}
   371	\left(W_{r(i),t-p},Z_i;\delta\right)
   372	}_{\text{county-year fitted treatment effect}}.
   373	\tag{5}
   374	\]
   375	
   376	Here “ATE” means the average effect of a common \(\delta\)-point shift in one
   377	continuous-treatment coordinate. It is not a binary treated-versus-control
   378	contrast.
   379	
   380	The corresponding average marginal effect is
   381	
   382	\[
   383	\widehat{\operatorname{AME}}_{p}
   384	=
   385	\overbrace{
   386	\frac{1}{\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal S}\omega_{it}}
   387	}^{\text{average rather than total}}
   388	\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal S}
   389	\underbrace{\omega_{it}}_{\text{chosen target population}}
   390	\overbrace{
   391	\widehat{\operatorname{ME}}_{p,t}
   392	\left(W_{r(i),t-p},Z_i\right)
   393	}^{\text{effect evaluated at the observed dose}}.
   394	\tag{6}
   395	\]
   396	
   397	The retained employer-count standardizations are:
   398	
   399	\[
   400	\underbrace{\omega_{it}=1}_{\text{equal county-year average}},
   401	\qquad
   402	\overbrace{
   403	\omega_{it}=\frac{1}{n_{r(i),t}}
   404	}^{\text{equal region-year average}}.
   405	\]
   406	
   407	There is no farm-employment weight or farm-employment divisor for the employer
   408	outcome. The sample-period employer total instead uses
   409	
   410	\[
   411	\underbrace{\omega_{it}=1}_{\text{one raw employer-count effect per row}},
   412	\qquad
   413	\overbrace{\text{normalization}=1}^{\text{sum, do not average}},
   414	\]
   415	
   416	so that
   417	
   418	\[
   419	\underbrace{
   420	\widehat{\operatorname{TotalEffect}}_{p}^{\text{employers}}(\delta)
   421	}_{\text{employer units over the sample period}}
   422	=
   423	\overbrace{
   424	\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal S}
   425	\widehat\Delta_{p,t}^{\text{employers}}(\delta)
   426	}^{\text{direct sum of raw-count effects}}.
   427	\]
   428	
   429	## 7. Why a delta method is needed
   430	
   431	The regression returns a coefficient vector, not an ATE:
   432	
   433	\[
   434	\underbrace{\widehat{\boldsymbol\gamma}}_{\text{all fitted coefficients}}
   435	=
   436	\overbrace{
   437	\left(\widehat\theta,\widehat\alpha,\widehat\lambda,

   446	\text{year effect, or subgroup effect}}}

   449	\]
   450	
   451	The delta method asks how sensitive \(h\) is to every coefficient:
   452	
   453	\[
   454	\underbrace{\widehat{\mathbf g}}_{\text{named gradient}}

   456	\overbrace{
   457	\frac{\partial h(\widehat{\boldsymbol\gamma})}
   458	{\partial\widehat{\boldsymbol\gamma}'}

   460	\tag{7}
   461	\]
