content.text:
1	# Saturation, rank budgets, and a specification program for Mundlak–Chamberlain
     2	
     3	## Status and purpose
     4	
     5	This is the design and implementation note for the version-3
     6	Mundlak–Chamberlain specification program. The program is implemented in
     7	`specification_program.R` and the numbered `*_01_*.R` drivers in this
     8	directory. The frozen version-2.3 design remains available as a compatibility
     9	benchmark; the selected version-3 primary replaces its `chamberlain_rich`
    10	result in the reporting layer.
    11	
    12	The current version-2.3 design is one admissible point in the implemented
    13	specification space:
    14	
    15	\[
    16	\underbrace{2008\text{--}2010}_{\text{baseline window}},
    17	\qquad
    18	\underbrace{p\in\{0,1,2\}}_{\text{three dose horizons}},
    19	\qquad
    20	\underbrace{d\in\{1,2\}}_{\text{linear and quadratic basis}},
    21	\qquad
    22	\underbrace{Z_i=\text{baseline AEWR bite}}_{\text{causal moderator}}.
    23	\]
    24	
    25	Version 3 turns those fixed choices into a program whose input is a
    26	specification record and whose output is an average treatment effect, its
    27	delta-method uncertainty, and a complete audit trail. The organizing
    28	principle is
    29	
    30	\[
    31	\overbrace{\text{add flexibility in county and market space}}^{
    32	  \text{large rank budgets}
    33	}
    34	\quad\text{while}\quad
    35	\underbrace{\text{rationing region-by-year coordinates}}_{
    36	  \text{only 17 policy paths}
    37	}.
    38	\]
    39	
    40	This architecture applies to every outcome, including the raw balanced
    41	employer count. Employer count remains measured in employers; it is not divided
    42	by farm employment. Its average effects are nevertheless calculated by the
    43	same delta-method contract as every other outcome.
    44	
    45	## 1. The estimand does not change when the dictionary grows
    46	
    47	Let \(W_{r,t}\) be annual AEWR growth in log percentage points for region \(r\)
    48	and year \(t\). County \(i\) belongs to region \(r(i)\). For a dose change
    49	\(h\), the sample average finite-change effect under specification \(s\) is
    50	
    51	\[
    52	\widehat{\tau}_s(h)
    53	=
    54	\underbrace{
    55	  \frac{1}{\sum_i\omega_i}
    56	  \sum_i\omega_i
    57	  \left[
    58	    \widehat{\mu}_s\!\left\{W_{r(i),t-p}+h,X_i\right\}
    59	    -
    60	    \widehat{\mu}_s\!\left\{W_{r(i),t-p},X_i\right\}
    61	  \right]
    62	}_{\text{average fitted treatment contrast}}
    63	=
    64	\overbrace{\mathbf g_s(h)^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_s}^{
    65	  \text{reported causal quantity}
    66	}.
    67	\]
    68	
    69	For an average marginal effect,
    70	
    71	\[
    72	\widehat{\operatorname{AME}}_s
    73	=
    74	\underbrace{
    75	  \frac{1}{\sum_i\omega_i}
    76	  \sum_i\omega_i
    77	  \frac{\partial\widehat{\mu}_s(W,X_i)}{\partial W}
    78	}_{\text{average slope at observed doses}}
    79	=
    80	\overbrace{\mathbf g_s^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_s}^{
    81	  \text{another named aggregation, not a raw coefficient}
    82	}.
    83	\]
    84	
    85	Thus the coefficient vector may contain hundreds or thousands of entries
    86	without changing the object reported to the reader. The dictionary expands
    87	the conditional mean; the estimand remains a weighted average of factual and
    88	counterfactual predictions.
    89	
    90	This distinction is especially important for employer count:
    91	
    92	\[
    93	\underbrace{Y_{it}^{\mathrm{emp}}}_{\text{raw number of linked employers}}
    94	\neq
    95	\overbrace{
    96	  Y_{it}^{\mathrm{emp}}/\text{farm employment}_i
    97	}^{\text{not an outcome in this design}}.
    98	\]
    99	
   100	## 2. The geometry: four different rank budgets
   101	
   102	Within an outcome year, the coarsest unit among the factors in an interaction
   103	determines the space in which the resulting column can vary. In the current
   104	balanced panel, the relevant ceilings are
   105	
   106	\[
   107	\underbrace{3{,}041}_{\text{county cells}}
   108	\;>\;
   109	\underbrace{745}_{\text{market cells}}
   110	\;>\;
   111	\underbrace{48}_{\text{state cells}}
   112	\;>\;
   113	\underbrace{17}_{\text{AEWR-region cells}}.
   114	\]
   115	
   116	For a year indicator \(D_t\), a dose basis \(b_d(W_{r(i),t-p})\), and a
   117	predetermined moderator \(Z_{ik}^{(\ell)}\) measured at hierarchy level
   118	\(\ell\),
   119	
   120	\[
   121	\underbrace{
   122	  D_t\,b_d(W_{r(i),t-p})Z_{ik}^{(c)}
   123	}_{\text{county-level causal heterogeneity}}
   124	\in\mathbb R^{3{,}041},
   125	\]
   126	
   127	\[
   128	\underbrace{
   129	  D_t\,b_d(W_{r(i),t-p})Z_{ik}^{(m)}
   130	}_{\text{market-level causal heterogeneity}}
   131	\in\mathbb R^{745},
   132	\]
   133	
   134	\[
   135	\underbrace{
   136	  D_t\,b_d(W_{r(i),t-p})Z_{ik}^{(q)}
   137	}_{\text{state-level causal heterogeneity}}
   138	\in\mathbb R^{48},
   139	\]
   140	
   141	\[
   142	\underbrace{
   143	  D_t\,b_d(W_{r(i),t-p})Z_{ik}^{(r)}
   144	}_{\text{region-level causal heterogeneity}}
   145	\in\mathbb R^{17}.
   146	\]
   147	
   148	“Cheap” below means cheap in assignment-cell rank. It does not mean free in
   149	memory, run time, residual degrees of freedom, or numerical conditioning.
   150	Every accepted specification must therefore pass both
   151	
   152	\[
   153	\underbrace{\text{blockwise rank guards}}_{\text{identification}}
   154	\quad\text{and}\quad
   155	\overbrace{\text{parameter-to-row and conditioning guards}}^{
   156	  \text{estimation stability}
   157	}.
   158	\]
   159	
   160	## 3. The region-by-year budget is the binding constraint
   161	
   162	Let a specification have
   163	
   164	- \(H_s\) dose horizons;
   165	- \(D_s^{(0)}\) unmoderated dose-basis degrees;
   166	- \(J_{st}\) admitted leave-focal-out treatment-history coordinates in year
   167	  \(t\);
   168	- \(U_{st}^{(r)}\) year-specific region-level untreated-mean coordinates;
   169	- \(M_{st}^{(r)}\) region-level dose-moderator coordinates; and
   170	- \(C_{st}^{(r)}\) cross-horizon or other region-level causal coordinates.
   171	
   172	The raw region-cell demand in year \(t\) is
   173	
   174	\[
   175	\underbrace{B_{st}^{(r)}}_{\text{region-cell demand}}
   176	=
   177	\underbrace{1}_{\text{year cell}}
   178	+
   179	\underbrace{H_sD_s^{(0)}}_{\text{unmoderated dose bases}}
   180	+
   181	\underbrace{J_{st}}_{\text{history projection}}
   182	+
   183	\underbrace{U_{st}^{(r)}}_{\text{region-level untreated mean}}
   184	+
   185	\underbrace{M_{st}^{(r)}}_{\text{region moderators}}
   186	+
   187	\underbrace{C_{st}^{(r)}}_{\text{cross-horizon terms}}.
   188	\]
   189	
   190	The current specification reaches
   191	
   192	\[
   193	\underbrace{1}_{\text{year cell}}
   194	+
   195	\underbrace{3\times2}_{\substack{\text{current, lag 1, lag 2}\\
   196	                                  \text{linear and quadratic}}}
   197	+
   198	\underbrace{(12-3)}_{\text{leave-focal-out history}}
   199	=
   200	\overbrace{16}^{\text{coordinates used}}
   201	<
   202	\underbrace{17}_{\text{region cells}}.
   203	\]
   204	
   205	The terminal year drops one additional nuisance-history coordinate so that
   206	all cyclic reference-design states retain a common identified coefficient
   207	basis. The version-3 compiler preserves that safety margin:
   208	
   209	\[
   210	\boxed{\max_t B_{st}^{(r)}\le 16}
   211	\qquad
   212	\underbrace{\text{followed by a global rank test in every one of 17 states}}_{
   213	  \text{the arithmetic guard is necessary, not sufficient}
   214	}.
   215	\]
   216	
   217	This inequality makes the expensive choices transparent. A third
   218	unmoderated polynomial degree costs \(H_s\) region coordinates per year.
   219	Another lag has a gross cost of \(D_s^{(0)}\); when leave-focal-out also
   220	removes that lag's corresponding linear history coordinate, its net cost is
   221	\(D_s^{(0)}-1\). A cross-horizon dose product costs another coordinate. A
   222	year-specific region trend costs one. A region-level moderator crossed with
   223	every basis may cost \(H_sD_s^{(0)}\). These choices must trade against the
   224	history projection, not enter by accident.
   225	
   226	The state budget needs its own assertion. A raw column count is not enough
   227	because the region span is nested inside the state span. The relevant
   228	quantity is the incremental rank after projecting out previously admitted
   229	columns:
   230	
   231	\[
   232	\underbrace{B_{st}^{(q)}}_{\text{incremental state demand}}
   233	=
   234	\operatorname{rank}
   235	\left[
   236	  \underbrace{
   237	    M_{\mathcal A_{st}}\mathbf X_{st}^{(q)}
   238	  }_{\substack{\text{state block residualized on year,}\\
   239	                \text{region, history, and earlier blocks}}}
   240	\right]
   241	\le
   242	\underbrace{
   243	  48-\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal A_{st}\text{ within state space})
   244	}_{\text{remaining state capacity}}.
   245	\]
	< truncated lines 246-799 >
   800	or CCV state 07 lost basis. This prevents the reported curve from looking like
   801	a hand-selected subset.
   802	
   803	Declaration is intentionally separated from execution. The default execution
   804	registry contains 16 predeclared records rather than evaluating all 648
   805	Cartesian cells: the four H3-D2 primary-family richness tiers, an R1 lag/basis
   806	ladder on the target calendar, and four R1 calendar perturbations. The full
   807	declaration grid remains available only through an explicit `exhaustive`
   808	stage. Before a fit begins, the compiler also requires
   809	
   810	\[
   811	\underbrace{8N_sK_s/2^{30}}_{\text{one dense design matrix in GiB}}
   812	\le 1.25
   813	\quad\text{and}\quad
   814	\overbrace{
   815	  4(8N_sK_s)+3(8K_s^2)
   816	}^{\text{conservative matrix working-set proxy}}
   817	/2^{30}
   818	\le 6.
   819	\]
   820	
   821	These are computational admissibility conditions, distinct from the
   822	statistical parameter-to-row guard.
   823	
   824	Cross-horizon products should be a separate, expensive grid field. They
   825	should not be bundled into “cubic” because
   826	
   827	\[
   828	\underbrace{W_{t}^{3}}_{\text{within-horizon curvature}}
   829	\quad\text{and}\quad
   830	\overbrace{W_tW_{t-1}}^{\text{cross-horizon complementarity}}
   831	\]
   832	
   833	encode different response surfaces and spend different ledger entries.
   834	
   835	## 12. Diagnostics that make saturation interpretable
   836	
   837	### Within-year treatment alignment
   838	
   839	For a candidate moderator block \(\mathbf M_{st}\), let
   840	\(\mathbf A_{st}\) be the already admitted design and
   841	\(\mathbf D_{st}\) the focal dose-basis block. Residualize both:
   842	
   843	\[
   844	\underbrace{\widetilde{\mathbf D}_{st}}_{\text{remaining dose coordinates}}
   845	=
   846	M_{\mathbf A_{st}}\mathbf D_{st},
   847	\qquad
   848	\overbrace{\widetilde{\mathbf M}_{st}}^{\text{new moderator block}}
   849	=
   850	M_{\mathbf A_{st}}\mathbf M_{st}.
   851	\]
   852	
   853	Report the largest canonical correlation
   854	
   855	\[
   856	\underbrace{\rho_{st}^{\max}}_{\text{block alignment}}
   857	=
   858	\sigma_{\max}
   859	\left[
   860	  (\widetilde{\mathbf D}_{st}^{\top}\widetilde{\mathbf D}_{st})^{-1/2}
   861	  \widetilde{\mathbf D}_{st}^{\top}\widetilde{\mathbf M}_{st}
   862	  (\widetilde{\mathbf M}_{st}^{\top}\widetilde{\mathbf M}_{st})^{-1/2}
   863	\right].
   864	\]
   865	
   866	A nearly orthogonal block may add conditional-mean flexibility while doing
   867	little to distinguish dose responses and potentially worsening conditioning.
   868	This diagnostic should be reported, not used to delete a block after observing
   869	the outcome estimate unless a deletion rule was preregistered.
   870	
   871	Also store each block's incremental rank, smallest singular value, and
   872	condition number. A formula can be technically full rank and still be
   873	numerically unusable.
   874	
   875	### Leave-one-reference-state-out influence
   876	
   877	For each reference state \(a\), form
   878	
   879	\[
   880	\underbrace{
   881	  \widehat{\mathbf V}_{s,-a}
   882	}_{\text{covariance without state }a}
   883	=
   884	\frac{1}{16}
   885	\sum_{b\ne a}
   886	\overbrace{
   887	  (\widehat{\mathbf e}_{s,b}-\bar{\mathbf e}_{s,-a})
   888	  (\widehat{\mathbf e}_{s,b}-\bar{\mathbf e}_{s,-a})^\top
   889	}^{\text{remaining-state contribution}}.
   890	\]
   891	
   892	For the same gradient, report
   893	
   894	\[
   895	\underbrace{
   896	  \operatorname{se}_{s,-a}
   897	}_{\text{leave-one-state-out uncertainty}}
   898	=
   899	\overbrace{
   900	  \sqrt{\mathbf g_s^\top
   901	  \widehat{\mathbf V}_{s,-a}
   902	  \mathbf g_s}
   903	}^{\text{projection onto the estimand}}.
   904	\]
   905	
   906	The point estimate need not be redefined for this diagnostic. The useful
   907	influence summaries are the largest proportional change in standard error,
   908	the state producing it, and whether the interval conclusion changes when the
   909	diagnostic uses \(t_{15}\). This reveals whether one cyclic reassignment is
   910	carrying the uncertainty calculation.
   911	
   912	## 13. Required program outputs
   913	
   914	Every run should write:
   915	
   916	| Output | Contents |
   917	| --- | --- |
   918	| mc_specification_registry.csv | Every declared candidate and its design fields |
   919	| mc_specification_model_diagnostics.csv | Outcome-specific estimate/rejection status, row guard, and rank fields |
   920	| mc_rank_budget_audit.csv | Region-coordinate ledger by specification and year |
   921	| mc_common_basis_audit.csv | Identified coefficient basis in all 17 states |
   922	| mc_delta_gradient_audit.csv | Formula, counterfactual, and named-gradient equality plus matrix error |
   923	| mc_moderator_alignment.csv | Within-year marginal and partial multiple correlations with each dose basis |
   924	| mc_reference_state_influence.csv | Leave-one-state-out uncertainty changes |
   925	| mc_specification_effects.csv | Effect, standard error, interval, and all specification fields |
   926	
   927	The headline figure is a specification curve:
   928	
   929	\[
   930	\underbrace{
   931	  \left\{\widehat{\tau}_s:s\in\mathcal S_{\mathrm{admissible}}\right\}
   932	}_{\text{effects ordered by magnitude}}
   933	\quad+\quad
   934	\overbrace{
   935	  \left\{
   936	  H_s,D_s,\text{moderator tier},\text{pre-period},\text{history rule}
   937	  \right\}
   938	}^{\text{annotations explaining each point}}.
   939	\]
   940	
   941	Raw employer-count effects should be labeled “employers per county-year” for
   942	an average effect and “employers over the sample period” only when the
   943	post-estimation weights are intentionally summed rather than normalized.
   944	
   945	## 14. Implemented sequence
   946	
   947	### Phase A: architecture and compatibility record
   948	
   949	1. Use the version-2.3 bite channel as the bite-only richness tier R0 while
   950	   retaining version 2.3 itself as a separate frozen compatibility path.
   951	2. Make the version-3 formula builder read only a specification record.
   952	3. Generate causal terms and counterfactual gradients from one moderator
   953	   dictionary.
   954	4. Retain the version-2.3 estimator and its benchmarks as a frozen
   955	   compatibility path.
   956	5. Add region/state rank ledgers and all-17-state common-basis assertions.
   957	
   958	This phase is complete only if
   959	
   960	\[
   961	\underbrace{
   962	  \widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{record}}
   963	  -\widehat{\tau}_{\mathrm{current}}
   964	}_{\text{architecture-only change}}
   965	\approx 0
   966	\quad\text{and}\quad
   967	\overbrace{
   968	  \widehat{\operatorname{se}}_{\mathrm{record}}
   969	  -\widehat{\operatorname{se}}_{\mathrm{current}}
   970	}^{\text{same covariance contract}}
   971	\approx 0.
   972	\]
   973	
   974	### Phase B: cheap-rank saturation — implemented
   975	
   976	Add county and market first-order moderators, trajectory coordinates, and
   977	declared untreated-mean pairs. Introduce blocks one tier at a time so failures
   978	can be attributed to a dictionary choice rather than to one enormous formula.
   979	
   980	### Phase C: expensive-coordinate sweep — implemented
   981	
   982	Sweep lag count, unmoderated polynomial degree, cross-horizon products, and
   983	admissible state terms. Compile the rank budget before any model fit and run
   984	the common-basis test before computing a CCV.
   985	
   986	### Phase D: calendar sweep — implemented
   987	
   988	Generate admissible pre-period and analysis-window records from actual data
   989	support. Keep the causal and history rules fixed within a comparison unless
   990	the changed rule is itself the labeled specification dimension.
   991	
   992	### Phase E: specification-curve reporting — implemented
   993	
   994	Estimate all outcomes under every admissible record, apply the same
   995	delta-method and covariance conventions, and render the effect distribution
   996	with design annotations and state-influence diagnostics.
   997	
   998	## 15. A defensible primary-specification rule
   999	
  1000	The primary specification is named before outcome estimates are inspected.
  1001	The implemented rule is:
  1002	
  1003	> Choose the richest strong-heredity specification with three dynamic
  1004	> horizons, a quadratic unmoderated dose basis, the full admissible
  1005	> leave-focal-out history projection, county/market trajectory moderators,
  1006	> no region-level dose moderators, and all predeclared rank, common-basis,
  1007	> conditioning, and parameter-to-row guards satisfied.
  1008	
  1009	This rule spends abundant county/market rank before trading away scarce
  1010	region-level history coordinates. If the richest declared tier fails a row,
  1011	rank, or common-basis guard for an outcome, the selector promotes the next
  1012	richest admissible tier. The complete admissible grid remains the substance
  1013	of the result:
  1014	
  1015	\[
  1016	\underbrace{\text{one preregistered primary estimate}}_{\text{headline}}
  1017	\quad\text{inside}\quad
  1018	\overbrace{\text{the full specification distribution}}^{
  1019	  \text{robustness argument}
  1020	}.
  1021	\]
  1022	
  1023	## 16. What this program can and cannot accomplish
  1024	
  1025	Richer conditioning can make the conditional parallel-trends restriction
  1026	more credible and the response surface less brittle. It cannot manufacture
  1027	new independent AEWR paths:
  1028	
  1029	\[
  1030	\underbrace{
  1031	  \text{more flexible point-estimate model}
  1032	}_{\text{bias and credibility}}
  1033	\;\not\Rightarrow\;
  1034	\overbrace{
  1035	  \text{more than 16 covariance directions}
  1036	}^{\text{inferential resolution}}.
  1037	\]
  1038	
  1039	The program succeeds if it makes every modeling convention visible, every
  1040	rank trade explicit, and every reported effect an audited delta-method
  1041	aggregation. It fails if “saturation” becomes a long formula assembled in one
  1042	place while the counterfactual, gradient, covariance, or reporting code still
  1043	assumes the old bite-only design.
  1044

   281	\end{aligned}
   282	\]
   283	
   284	where \(B_i\) is the baseline AEWR bite and all moderators are centered before
   285	interactions are constructed.
   286	
   287	This equation supports a ladder rather than a single jump:
   288	
   289	| Tier | Causal dictionary | Purpose |
   290	| --- | --- | --- |
   291	| 0 | Bite only | Reproduces the current primary causal block |
   292	| 1 | County and market predetermined means | Rich level heterogeneity |
   293	| 2 | Tier 1 plus separate pre-period values or an equivalent full-rank trajectory transform | Conditions response on path shape |
   294	| 3 | Tier 2 plus dose × bite × county/market moderators | Heterogeneity of the bite gradient |
   295	| 4 | Tier 3 plus selected state moderators that pass the state-rank audit | Adds higher-level heterogeneity cautiously |
   296	
   297	Region-level moderators are excluded from the causal dictionary by default.
   298	They may remain in the untreated-mean or correlated-effects projection when
   299	identified, but crossing them with dose spends the scarce 17-cell budget.
   300	
   301	### Pre-period trajectory rather than pre-period mean alone
   302	
   303	For a baseline variable \(X\), a mean-only moderator treats these histories as
   304	equivalent:
   305	
   306	\[
   307	\underbrace{(-1,0,1)}_{\text{rising path}}
   308	\quad\text{and}\quad
   309	\overbrace{(1,0,-1)}^{\text{falling path}},
   310	\qquad
   311	\underbrace{\bar X=0}_{\text{same mean}}.
   312	\]
   313	
   314	The trajectory tier instead admits
   315	
   316	\[
   317	\underbrace{
   318	  \left(X_{i,t_0},X_{i,t_0+1},\ldots,X_{i,t_1}\right)
   319	}_{\text{separate predetermined positions}}
   320	\quad\text{or an equivalent full-rank transform}\quad
   321	\overbrace{
   322	  \left(\bar X_i,\operatorname{slope}_i,\operatorname{curvature}_i,\ldots\right)
   323	}^{\text{trajectory coordinates}}.
   324	\]
   325	
   326	An orthogonal transform is acceptable for conditioning and numerical
   327	stability, but the transformation matrix must be stored so that factual and
   328	counterfactual design matrices use exactly the same coordinates.
   329	
   330	### Curvature and heredity
   331	
   332	County-level cubic heterogeneity can be rank-cheap even when an unmoderated
   333	cubic is unaffordable:
   334	
   335	\[
   336	\underbrace{
   337	  D_t\,W_{r(i),t-p}^{3}Z_{ik}^{(c)}
   338	}_{\text{county-varying column}}
   339	\quad\text{does not occupy only region space, whereas}\quad
   340	\overbrace{
   341	  D_t\,W_{r(i),t-p}^{3}
   342	}^{\text{region-only column}}
   343	\quad\text{does}.
   344	\]
   345	
   346	That is coherent under **weak heredity**, but it makes the response at
   347	\(Z=0\) lower-order than the response away from \(Z=0\). The specification
   348	record must state one of
   349	
   350	\[
   351	\underbrace{
   352	  D_s^{(\mathrm{moderated})}\le D_s^{(0)}
   353	}_{\text{strong heredity}}
   354	\qquad\text{or}\qquad
   355	\overbrace{
   356	  D_s^{(\mathrm{moderated})}>D_s^{(0)}
   357	}^{\text{weak-heredity sensitivity}}.
   358	\]
   359	
   360	Strong heredity is the safer primary convention. Weak heredity belongs in the
   361	grid because it uses the geometry efficiently, but it should never arise
   362	silently from a formula builder.
   363	
   364	## 5. Preventing an invisible region interaction
   365	
   366	For an unstandardized hierarchical decomposition,
   367	
   368	\[
   369	\underbrace{X_i-\bar X_{m(i)}}_{\text{county component}}
   370	+
   371	\underbrace{\bar X_{m(i)}-\bar X_{q(i)}}_{\text{market component}}
   372	+
   373	\underbrace{\bar X_{q(i)}-\bar X_{r(i)}}_{\text{state component}}
   374	+
   375	\underbrace{\bar X_{r(i)}}_{\text{region component}}
   376	=
   377	\overbrace{X_i}^{\text{level}}.
   378	\]
   379	
   380	After componentwise standardization, the same identity holds with known scale
   381	coefficients. Consequently, admitting the standardized level and every
   382	sub-regional component to a dose interaction can implicitly span the omitted
   383	region interaction:
   384	
   385	\[
   386	\underbrace{W X_i}_{\text{level interaction}}
   387	-
   388	\overbrace{
   389	  \left(a_cWZ_i^{(c)}+a_mWZ_i^{(m)}+a_qWZ_i^{(q)}\right)
   390	}^{\text{sub-regional interactions}}
   391	=
   392	\underbrace{a_rWZ_i^{(r)}}_{\text{region interaction recovered implicitly}}.
   393	\]
   394	
   395	This is not merely redundant notation; it spends region rank invisibly.
   396	
   397	The dictionary therefore needs a representation rule for every source
   398	variable:
   399	
   400	1. use the level alone;
   401	2. use an explicitly declared subset of hierarchical components; or
   402	3. use a full decomposition and charge the implied region coordinate.
   403	
   404	For AEWR bite, use the level as the interpretive channel and exclude its
   405	hierarchical components from the **causal dose dictionary**. The components
   406	may still be used in the untreated-mean projection if the formula and rank
   407	audits keep the roles separate.
   408	
   409	## 6. Saturating the untreated mean
   410	
   411	Let \(\mathbf H_i\) collect predetermined histories and hierarchical
   412	components. A rich untreated mean can be written
   413	
   414	\[
   415	\mu_{it,s}^{0}
   416	=
   417	\underbrace{\alpha_t+a_{r(i)}}_{\text{calendar and persistent region terms}}
   418	+
   419	\underbrace{
   420	  \mathbf H_i^\top\boldsymbol\lambda_{t,s}
   421	}_{\text{unrestricted year-specific first-order projection}}
   422	+
   423	\overbrace{
   424	  \sum_{j<k}H_{ij}H_{ik}\lambda_{jk,t,s}
   425	}^{\text{selected second-order county/market projection}}
   426	+
   427	\underbrace{
   428	  \mathbf L_{r(i)}^\top\boldsymbol\rho_{t,s}
   429	}_{\text{leave-focal-out treatment history}}.
   430	\]
   431	
   432	No dose factor appears in the pairwise \(\mathbf H_i\) terms, so county- and
   433	market-level pairs do not spend the region-only causal budget. They can still
   434	create severe computational and residual-degrees-of-freedom costs. The
   435	program should therefore add second-order terms in declared blocks, not emit
   436	every possible pair in one opaque formula.
   437	
   438	Recommended nuisance ladder:
   439	
   440	| Tier | Untreated-mean projection |
   441	| --- | --- |
   442	| U0 | Current first-order hierarchy and history controls |
   443	| U1 | All predetermined county/market first-order terms by year |
   444	| U2 | U1 plus separate pre-period trajectory coordinates by year |
   445	| U3 | U2 plus within-source and substantively declared cross-source pairs |
   446	| U4 | U3 plus admissible state trends after the state-rank audit |
   447	
   448	The causal and nuisance ladders should be separate specification fields. This
   449	allows the grid to distinguish a change in conditional parallel trends from a
   450	change in treatment-effect heterogeneity.
   451	
   452	## 7. Calendar conventions become specification fields
   453	
   454	### Symmetric coding
   455	
   456	The current implementation uses a reference-year parameterization. The
   457	proposed symmetric form is
   458	
   459	\[
   460	\underbrace{
   461	  \sum_{t\in\mathcal T_s}D_t\alpha_t
   462	}_{\text{one intercept for every calendar year}}
   463	+
   464	\overbrace{a_{r(i)}}^{\text{absorbed region effect}},
   465	\qquad
   466	\underbrace{\text{no global intercept}}_{\text{no omitted calendar year}}.
   467	\]
   468	
   469	This should span the same space as the current intercept-plus-omitted-year
   470	coding. Before it becomes the default, an equivalence test must show, for the
   471	current specification, that
   472	
   473	\[
   474	\underbrace{
   475	  \max_i|\widehat\mu_i^{\mathrm{reference}}
   476	          -\widehat\mu_i^{\mathrm{symmetric}}|
   477	}_{\text{fitted-value discrepancy}}
   478	\le\varepsilon,
   479	\qquad
   480	\overbrace{
   481	  |\widehat\tau^{\mathrm{reference}}
   482	   -\widehat\tau^{\mathrm{symmetric}}|
   483	}^{\text{estimand discrepancy}}
   484	\le\varepsilon.
   485	\]
   486	
   487	The change is then a coding simplification, not a robustness specification.
   488	
   489	### Pre-period and analysis windows
   490	
   491	The calendar record should contain
   492	
   493	\[
   494	\underbrace{t_{\mathrm{pre,start}}}_{\text{where histories begin}},
   495	\qquad
   496	\underbrace{t_{\mathrm{pre,end}}}_{\text{where they end}},
   497	\qquad
   498	\underbrace{t_{\mathrm{analysis,start}}}_{\text{first outcome year}},
   499	\qquad
   500	\underbrace{t_{\mathrm{analysis,end}}}_{\text{last outcome year}}.
   501	\]
   502	
   503	For a maximum lag \(P_s\), a clean predetermined-history rule is
   504	
   505	\[
   506	\underbrace{t_{\mathrm{pre,end}}}_{\text{last moderator year}}
   507	<
   508	\overbrace{
   509	  t_{\mathrm{analysis,start}}-P_s
   510	}^{\text{earliest focal dose year}}.
   511	\]
   512	
   513	The treatment-history window must cover every focal dose year and every
   514	non-focal history coordinate admitted by the specification. Candidate
   515	calendar records should be generated from observed support and rejected if
   516	they violate either rule; years should not be inserted merely to complete a
   517	rectangular grid.
   518	
   519	## 8. One specification record, no global design constants
   520	
   521	Conceptually, one record should look like:
   522	
   523	~~~r
   524	mc_spec <- list(
   525	  spec_id = "pre_2008_2010__h3_d2__cm_traj__bite3",
   526	  calendar = list(
   527	    pre_years = 2008:2010,
   528	    history_years = 2011:2022,
   529	    analysis_years = 2013:2022,
   530	    coding = "symmetric"
   531	  ),
   532	  dynamics = list(
   533	    lags = 0:2,
   534	    unmoderated_degrees = 1:2,
   535	    moderated_degrees = 1:2,
   536	    cross_horizon = "none",
   537	    heredity = "strong"
   538	  ),
   539	  moderators = list(
   540	    tier = "county_market_trajectory",
   541	    bite_interactions = TRUE,
   542	    region_dose_moderators = character()
   543	  ),
   544	  untreated_mean = list(
   545	    tier = "trajectory_first_order",
   546	    pair_dictionary = character()
   547	  ),
   548	  history = list(rule = "leave_focal_out"),
   549	  guards = list(
   550	    reserve_region_coordinates = 1L,
   551	    max_parameter_row_ratio = "predeclared",
   552	    require_common_ccv_basis = TRUE
   553	  ),
   554	  covariance = list(
   555	    method = "finite_design_covariance_ccv",
   556	    residual_df_adjustment = "N_over_N_minus_K"
   557	  )
   558	)
   559	~~~

content.thinking:
I'm planning how to structure the answer: start by identifying the core flaw in the first sentence, then walk through the specific issues with the markdown file and its broken references to papers that aren't actually included in the archive due to gitignore rules.

Then I'll pivot to what I actually did—pulling the two primary sources directly and summarizing their content to show where the current design sits relative to them. The key tension I'm seeing is that the 2025 Stata talk's framework assumes cohorts with well-defined treatment timing and never-treated units, but the H-2A design has neither: every region experiences an AEWR change annually with no zero-dose periods or comparison group. Wooldridge touches on this briefly in one slide about non-zero treatment levels, but the mismatch between the theoretical setup and the actual data structure is substantial and needs to be addressed head-on.

The design is really a distributed-lag continuous-dose conditional-mean model using Chamberlain projection, not an instance of the ETWFE nonbinary framework—so the README's invocation of Wooldridge lineage should be traced through CRE and Mundlak, not through the heterogeneous-slopes cohort logic. The moderation through Z_i is doing the work of conditioning on observables to allow selection-on-gains, but without cohorts, the entire identifying assumption rests on Z_i plus the Chamberlain history projection, and that's the load-bearing assumption that needs to be made explicit rather than left implicit.

The TWM equivalence result shows that TWFE equals pooled OLS with unit and period cross-sectional averages, and the design uses pooled OLS with region and year indicators plus a Chamberlain projection—which sits on the TWM side of that equivalence. But Theorem 3.1 requires both unit time averages and period cross-sectional averages, and here the period-specific cross-sectional averages of the treatment are collinear with year dummies since the treatment is constant within region-year cells in a balanced panel.

So the unit time-average of the treatment across time is a region-level constant absorbed by the region intercepts, and the year-specific cross-sectional average is absorbed by the year dummies—meaning the TWM correspondence actually holds here, which is a useful validation that the pooled OLS design with region and year effects is indeed the correct TWM regression for this treatment structure. Though I need to be careful about the mechanics: for each county, the time average of the region's treatment path is a region constant, and the year-t cross-sectional average across counties is a weighted mean of the region-level treatment paths.

This raises a question about whether adding county fixed effects instead of region fixed effects would change the treatment coefficients. The county time-average of the treatment is still region-constant, so the TWM regression would still need region-level constants to capture it. That suggests county fixed effects wouldn't add anything beyond what region fixed effects plus the Chamberlain projection already provides. This equivalence holds precisely when the panel is balanced within each region and there are no other county-level regressors varying over time, but once I add interactions like Z_i×year or county trends, the equivalence breaks down. I should state this cleanly for the twfe_benchmark model where it applies. There's also a real issue with the design's reliance on the 2025 slides — Wooldridge's case requires an intervention date, which this setup doesn't have, so I need to find the closest legitimate anchor in his framework.

The honest citation here isn't ETWFE at all but Wooldridge (2005) on correlated random coefficients, which the Stata talk explicitly references — that's about when fixed-effects estimators recover population-averaged slopes when unit-specific slopes correlate with covariates. On the exogeneity claim in the README, I should push back: under Callaway, Goodman-Bacon, and Sant'Anna's framework, saying treatment doesn't need random assignment because parallel trends suffices is too loose for continuous doses. With continuous treatment, parallel trends alone doesn't eliminate selection bias across dose levels; you need the stronger condition of parallel trends holding at every dose level.

The real problem is that the estimands under standard and strong parallel trends are identical, so the lead-placebo pre-tests the README relies on can't actually distinguish between them — they can't diagnose the identification failure. The README's counterfactual is a coordinate shift in dose, which is exactly the kind of causal-response object that CGS say requires the stronger assumption. This is a specific, citable vulnerability that a referee will exploit, and it's worth laying out clearly and substantively without turning it into a full essay.

I need to cite the web sources properly where I reference what Wooldridge's papers say, and keep the prose clean — no headers, no bullets, em-dashes kept tight. The opening should land the answer directly: there's only one markdown file in that designs folder, the README, and the Wooldridge sources it cites aren't actually in the archive. The papers directory is gitignored, and three specific files are referenced but missing.…

content.text:
There is exactly one markdown in `code/designs/mundlak_chamberlain` — `README.md` — and the three Wooldridge files it points to are not in the archive. Line 35 of `.gitignore` is `papers/`, so `papers/metrics/wooldridge/deep-research-report-wooldridge.md`, `wooldridge_stata-conf_2025_nonbinary_treatments.md`, and `wooldridge_empiricalecon_2025_twfe_twmundlak_did.md` never made it into the repo. Two of the README's other relative links are also broken: `specification_and_delta_method.md` and `saturation_budgets_and_specification_program.md` resolve to the design directory but actually live in top-level `markdowns/`. I've read those two, the README, and the version-3 program note in full, and I went and pulled the two named Wooldridge primaries directly rather than working from a summary I can't see.

The Stata talk is the nonbinary/continuous piece. Its core is a heterogeneous random-slopes model, explicitly borrowed from Wooldridge (2005, REStat), with dose-response function `Y_it(w) = wB_it + θ_t + C_i + U_it`. The identifying restriction is `E[B_it | W_i1,...,W_iT] = E[B_it | D_iq,...,D_iT]`, and Wooldridge states its content sharply: treatment timing may be related to the per-unit gain, but the treatment level may not. Adding controls relaxes this to `E[B_it|W,X_i] = E[B_it|D,X_i]`, which is where covariate moderation earns its keep. He also handles the case where treatment is never zero — you define W_it = 0 before the intervention, and a stronger selection assumption is needed because every unit is treated at some level. The Empirical Economics paper is the algebraic backbone: adding unit-specific time averages and period-specific cross-sectional averages to pooled OLS reproduces the two-way fixed effects estimates, and in the staggered-intervention setting cohort imputation, POLS on cohort dummies, TWFE, RE, and BJS imputation are all the same estimator.

The gap you should be braced for is that this design is not an instance of the ETWFE nonbinary framework, and the README implies it is. Every construct in the Stata talk — `D_ig`, a well-defined first treatment period, `W_it = 0` for `t < g`, the never-treated or last-treated comparison — is absent here. There are no cohorts, no never-treated regions, and no pre-intervention period in which the dose is zero: all 17 regions get an AEWR change every year, and 2011 is a window boundary rather than an intervention date. That means Wooldridge's one escape hatch for always-treated units doesn't apply, because it requires an intervention date to define the zero. The honest lineage for what `chamberlain_rich` actually is runs through Chamberlain's correlated-effects projection and Wooldridge (2005), on when fixed-effects-type estimators recover population-averaged slopes with unit-specific slopes correlated with the covariates, not through ETWFE. A referee who knows the 2025 talk will look for `dg·fs_t` and won't find it.

There is a compensating result worth exploiting. Because `W` varies only at region-year, every two-way Mundlak term for the treatment basis is degenerate: the county time-average of `W_{r(i),t-p}` is a region-level constant absorbed by `α_r`, and the year cross-sectional average is a year constant absorbed by `θ_t`. Theorem 3.1 then says the dose coefficients in `twfe_benchmark` should be numerically identical whether you absorb county or region fixed effects, in the balanced 3,041 × 10 panel. That's a free executable assertion for `05_validate.R` and `06_01_validate_specification_program.R`, and it's a cleaner demonstration of the Wooldridge lineage than any of the current rank audits.

Where I'd push back hardest is the README's central identification statement, specifically the sentence claiming this is the same sense in which DiD doesn't require exogenous assignment. For a continuous dose that isn't right, and Callaway, Goodman-Bacon, and Sant'Anna are the ones to cite against it: treatment-on-the-treated parameters are identified under a generalized parallel trends assumption analogous to the binary case, but comparing them across doses is challenging because parallel trends does not rule out selection bias. The design's reported object is a δ-point coordinate shift from the observed dose — an ACRT-type derivative, exactly the parameter they flag as complicated to interpret under the commonly invoked parallel trends assumption. Removing that selection-bias term requires strong parallel trends, and the diagnostic consequence is the sharp one: the estimands under standard and strong parallel trends coincide, so pre-tests cannot distinguish between them. Your one-year-lead placebo therefore cannot certify the assumption the ASF and AME estimands actually rest on. The README currently treats the placebo failures as evidence of weak support or overparameterization; that list should include a fourth possibility it can't rule out by construction.

The upside for you is that CGS also supply the argument the design needs: with a continuous dose you can still run DiD with no never-treated units, because cross-dose comparisons cancel the untreated path under either version of parallel trends. That is the correct citation for why 17 always-treated regions are not fatal — stronger than anything currently in the README, which defends the point on its own authority.

Practically, I'd add `strong_parallel_trends` as an explicit named field in the specification record alongside `heredity`, since assuming it is what licenses interpreting `ME_{p,s}(w,z)` as a causal response rather than a fitted slope, and right now that assumption is implicit in the delta-method contract rather than declared in it. If you can get me the missing `papers/metrics/wooldridge/` directory I'll reconcile against whatever the deep-research report actually claimed; absent that, the two primaries above are what I'm working from.

1	# Jeffrey M. Wooldridge on Difference-in-Differences from 2021 through 2026
     2	
     3	## Executive summary
     4	
     5	I identified **13 qualifying items** from 2021 through 2026 that are authored or coauthored by Jeffrey M. Wooldridge and whose main subject is difference-in-differences: **2 journal articles, 3 NBER/SSRN-style working papers, 5 formal conference papers/proceedings records, 2 additional 2026 preprints/working papers, and 1 AEA conference preview paper**. I found **no qualifying book chapters** in this window. The research arc is clear: Wooldridge first reframed modern staggered-adoption DiD through the two-way Mundlak/extended two-way fixed-effects equivalence, then extended DiD to nonlinear outcomes, repeated cross-sections, nonbinary treatments, and small-cross-section inference, while coauthors extended the framework to rolling transformations and aggregation of cohort-time effects. Every year from 2021 through 2026 has at least one qualifying item. citeturn37view0turn4view0turn25view0turn20view0turn32view0turn32view1turn17view0turn30search1turn31search0
     6	
     7	The highest-confidence backbone of this corpus comes from official records at entity["organization","SSRN","elsevier research network"], entity["organization","National Bureau of Economic Research","cambridge, ma, us"], entity["organization","IDEAS/RePEc","economics bibliography"], journal publisher pages, the entity["organization","American Economic Association","economics association"] program, and Jeffrey M. Wooldridge’s June 2024 CV from entity["organization","Michigan State University","east lansing, mi, us"]. A few 2026 metadata points remain slightly messy, especially one SSRN identifier conflict for the small-sample-inference paper; I flag that explicitly below instead of smoothing it over. citeturn3search0turn25view0turn32view0turn32view1turn17view0turn13view0turn30search1turn30search7
     8	
     9	The timeline below uses the **first public appearance** I could verify for each substantive item. Published-journal versions are recorded in the table and version notes. citeturn15view1turn25view0turn16view0turn20view0turn26view0turn41view3turn32view0turn42search5turn41view1turn32view1turn17view0turn30search1turn31search0
    10	
    11	```mermaid
    12	timeline
    13	    title Jeffrey M. Wooldridge diff-in-diff papers and formal conference papers 2021-2026
    14	    2021 : Nonlinear difference in differences with panel data
    15	         : Two-Way Fixed Effects, the Two-Way Mundlak Regression, and Difference-in-Differences Estimators
    16	    2022 : Using Stata to implement simple difference-in-differences estimators for staggered interventions
    17	         : Simple Approaches to Nonlinear Difference-in-Differences with Panel Data
    18	    2023 : A Simple Transformation Approach to Difference-in-Differences Estimation for Panel Data
    19	    2024 : Relationships among recent difference-in-differences estimators and how to compute them in Stata
    20	         : A Flexible, Heterogeneous Treatment Effects Difference-in-Differences Estimator for Repeated Cross-Sections
    21	         : Difference-in-Differences Estimator of Quantile Treatment Effect on the Treated
    22	    2025 : Difference in difference for nonbinary treatments in Stata
    23	         : Aggregating Average Treatment Effects on the Treated in Difference-in-Differences Models
    24	    2026 : Nonlinear Difference-in-Differences with Repeated Cross Sections
    25	         : Simple Approaches to Inference with Difference-in-Differences Estimators with Small Cross-Sectional Sample Sizes
    26	         : Rolling Difference-in-Differences Estimation for Small and Moderately Sized Data Sets
    27	```
    28	
    29	## Scope and inclusion rules
    30	
    31	I included an item when all of the following were true: Jeffrey M. Wooldridge was an author or coauthor; the item was publicly posted, published, or listed as a formal conference paper during 2021 through 2026; and the **primary topic or a substantial share of the content** was DiD methodology or a DiD application. I prioritized official records from Wooldridge’s CV, author pages, journal pages, NBER, SSRN, and IDEAS/RePEc. I excluded software components from the main table because the brief asked for papers, chapters, preprints, and conference papers; I still note directly related code or software where I found it. citeturn3search0turn37view0turn25view0turn32view0turn32view1turn17view0turn42search2turn42search4turn42search9
    32	
    33	One judgment call matters. Several Stata conference records are not merely talks in a loose sense; they are formal conference-paper records indexed by RePEc/IDEAS with stable handles, abstracts, and often downloadable PDFs. I therefore include them. By contrast, I did **not** promote informal workshop pages or videos into the main corpus unless they had a formal conference-paper or preview-paper record. citeturn15view0turn16view0turn38view1turn38view0turn17view0
    34	
    35	## Chronological table
    36	
    37	| Year | Citation | Type | Link | PDF | Summary | Versions and notes |
    38	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
    39	| 2021 | Wooldridge, Jeffrey M. “Nonlinear difference in differences with panel data.” *Economics Virtual Symposium 2021*, paper 4, entity["organization","Stata Users Group","stata conferences"]. | Conference paper | IDEAS/RePEc handle RePEc:boc:econ21:4. citeturn15view0turn15view1 | Zip of presentation materials linked from IDEAS/RePEc. citeturn15view0 | Earliest formal conference record in this window for Wooldridge’s nonlinear DiD program; it is the visible precursor to the 2022 SSRN preprint and 2023 journal article on nonlinear DiD with panel data. citeturn15view0turn20view0turn23search1 | Official record has **no abstract**. Series page dates the symposium to **10 Nov. 2021**. Materials are distributed as a zip, not a standalone PDF. citeturn15view0turn15view1 |
	< truncated lines 40-62 >
    63	**A Simple Transformation Approach to Difference-in-Differences Estimation for Panel Data.** The SSRN record shows a 2023 posting and a 2025 revision, with coauthorship by Lee and Wooldridge. The paper’s abstract is unusually clear: transform outcomes using pre-treatment averages, carefully select controls period by period, and then apply familiar treatment-effect estimators, including doubly robust ones. The July 2023 PDF shows both authors at Michigan State University, while the revised SSRN page shows Lee at Southern Illinois University Carbondale; that is a normal affiliation drift across versions, not a bibliographic conflict. citeturn26view0turn31search23
    64	
    65	**Relationships among recent difference-in-differences estimators and how to compute them in Stata.** This 2024 UK Stata conference paper is a synthesis piece rather than a paper with a new theorem. Its value is practical and interpretive: it compares popular modern DiD estimators for panel staggered-adoption settings and shows how to compute and interpret them in Stata. For lawyers, consultants, and policy analysts trying to choose among estimators in real work, that sort of synthesis matters more than it sounds. citeturn38view1turn41view2turn41view3
    66	
    67	**A Flexible, Heterogeneous Treatment Effects Difference-in-Differences Estimator for Repeated Cross-Sections.** This is one of the most important coauthored Wooldridge DiD papers in the period because it tackles repeated cross-sections, which are everywhere in public-policy data. The first-page PDF gives the affiliations explicitly: Hunter College/NBER, University of Michigan/NBER, Michigan State, and Tufts. The paper also has the cleanest author-linked software tie-in I found: `flexdid` is explicitly described as implementing the FLEX framework in Stata. citeturn32view0turn33view0turn42search4turn42search8
    68	
    69	**Difference-in-Differences Estimator of Quantile Treatment Effect on the Treated.** This article pushes Wooldridge’s DiD program beyond mean effects into distributional treatment effects. The official abstract says the identifying assumption is a common time effect on the CDF of untreated potential outcomes, allowing covariates and remaining compatible with usual mean DiD logic. It also has unusually good practical extras: a Stata ado file is hosted on Doosoo Kim’s site, and a Taylor & Francis Figshare record exists for the article materials. citeturn18view1turn42search5turn42search9turn19search6
    70	
    71	**Difference in difference for nonbinary treatments in Stata.** This 2025 Stata conference paper is not just a narrow software note. The abstract shows that Wooldridge is generalizing ETWFE-style DiD to continuous or multi-level treatments while preserving standard regression-based aggregation, inference, pretrend checks, and heterogeneous trends. That matters because modern DiD debates increasingly involve intensity or dose rather than a simple treated/untreated split. citeturn38view0turn41view0turn41view1
    72	
    73	**Aggregating Average Treatment Effects on the Treated in Difference-in-Differences Models.** This paper is more important than the title may suggest. Once modern DiD methods give a menu of cohort-time effects, the next fight is always about which average is being reported. Deb, Norton, Wooldridge, and Zabel show that aggregation weights used in common software are often not the naive treated-years weights users assume, and they explain why that can change interpretation. The SSRN page and NBER page line up on the paper’s October 2025 circulation. citeturn32view1turn35search3turn35search0
    74	
    75	**Nonlinear Difference-in-Differences with Repeated Cross Sections.** The 2026 AEA preview paper makes the research arc obvious: take the 2023 nonlinear panel-data paper, then transplant it to repeated cross-sections. The preview PDF is substantive enough to count as a real conference paper, not just a one-paragraph abstract, and the AEA program page provides a stable official source. If the repeated-cross-section FLEX paper is the linear backbone, this AEA paper is the nonlinear counterpart. citeturn17view0turn39view0turn40view0
    76	
    77	**Simple Approaches to Inference with Difference-in-Differences Estimators with Small Cross-Sectional Sample Sizes.** This paper goes after one of the nastiest practical DiD problems: one treated state, two control states, or similarly tiny cross-sectional samples. The sources I found agree on the content but disagree on the SSRN identifier, so I am deliberately not pretending the metadata are perfectly clean. Substantively, though, the paper is easy to classify: it is a genuine 2026 Wooldridge DiD preprint focused on exact or near-exact inference after a transformation to cross-sectional regression. citeturn27search0turn29search2turn30search1turn30search7
    78	
    79	**Rolling Difference-in-Differences Estimation for Small and Moderately Sized Data Sets.** This 2026 paper looks like the operational sequel to the 2023 transformation paper and the 2026 small-sample inference paper. The sources consistently describe it as introducing `lwdid`, and the official RePEc software page states directly that `lwdid` implements Lee and Wooldridge’s 2025 and 2026 rolling DiD estimators. In plain English, this is the point where the methodological sequence becomes a usable estimation ecosystem. citeturn31search0turn31search1turn42search2turn31search18
    80	
    81	## Analytical synthesis
    82	
    83	The corpus breaks into five substantive waves. The first wave is **identification and estimator equivalence**: the 2021 TWFE/TWM paper is Wooldridge’s central intervention in the staggered-adoption DiD literature, because it shows that what many users treat as a specialized TWFE object can instead be understood as flexible pooled regression with the right interactions. That move is powerful because it makes heterogeneity, pretrend diagnostics, cohort-specific effects, and nonlinear extensions much more transparent. citeturn25view0turn25view2
    84	
    85	The second wave is **nonlinear DiD**. The 2021 symposium paper, 2022 SSRN preprint, and 2023 *Econometrics Journal* article develop a coherent answer to a practical question applied work often dodges: what if the outcome is binary, fractional, or a count, so that the linear model is a bad mean-function approximation? Wooldridge’s answer is not to abandon DiD, but to shift parallel-trends restrictions to an appropriate index of the conditional mean and estimate treatment effects through pooled QMLE and average partial effects. citeturn15view0turn20view0
    86	
    87	The third wave is **generalization beyond balanced panels and binary treatment**. The 2024 repeated-cross-section FLEX paper extends heterogeneity-robust DiD to repeated cross-sections; the 2025 conference paper extends it to nonbinary treatments; and the 2026 AEA preview extends the nonlinear version to repeated cross-sections. This is the cleanest sign that Wooldridge’s DiD program is not a one-off estimator paper but a general regression architecture for modern policy evaluation. citeturn32view0turn38view0turn17view0
    88	
    89	The fourth wave is **post-estimation interpretation**. The 2025 ATT-aggregation paper is basically about what people report after they estimate a modern DiD model. That sounds secondary, but it is not. A lot of disagreement in empirical DiD work is really disagreement about which weighted average of cohort-time effects is economically meaningful, and this paper squarely addresses that. citeturn32view1
    90	
    91	The fifth wave is **small-sample inference and software implementation**. Lee and Wooldridge’s 2023 transformation paper, 2026 small-sample inference paper, and 2026 rolling-estimation paper together push the agenda toward settings where the number of treated or control units is tiny and classical cluster-asymptotics are weak. The related software trail is unusually visible: `flexdid` for FLEX, `lwdid` for rolling estimators, and a Stata ado file for the QTT paper. That makes this corpus unusually useful for actual applied work, not just reading. citeturn26view0turn42search4turn42search2turn42search9
    92	
    93	The blunt bottom line is that Wooldridge’s 2021-2026 DiD work is not a scatter of unrelated papers. It is a **single evolving research program**: start from regression equivalence and heterogeneity-robust staggered DiD, then extend to nonlinear outcomes, repeated cross-sections, nonbinary treatments, aggregation, and small-sample inference, while building usable Stata implementations around the theory. citeturn25view0turn20view0turn32view0turn32view1turn38view0turn17view0turn30search1turn31search0
    94	
    95	## Open questions and limitations
    96	
    97	The one real bibliographic ambiguity I found concerns **“Simple Approaches to Inference with Difference-in-Differences Estimators with Small Cross-Sectional Sample Sizes.”** SSRN search results expose one identifier, while secondary references and package documentation cite another. I therefore treat the paper as definitely public and relevant, but I would verify the canonical SSRN record directly before importing it into a formal bibliography manager. citeturn29search0turn30search1turn30search7turn29search2
    98	
    99	A smaller limitation is that the official 2021 symposium record for **“Nonlinear difference in differences with panel data”** contains **no abstract**, and the 2022 French Stata conference record does not expose a downloadable paper file on IDEAS/RePEc. I handled those cases conservatively by using the official record for bibliographic facts and a separate short analytical summary based on the title, series context, and later versions. citeturn15view0turn16view0
   100	
   101	I also did **not** find official author-issued replication archives for every item. Where I found code, I reported it; where I did not, I said so. The strongest code links in the corpus are the QTT ado file on Doosoo Kim’s site, `flexdid` for the repeated-cross-sections FLEX framework, and `lwdid` for the rolling/small-sample Lee-Wooldridge line. citeturn42search9turn42search4turn42search2

I included an item when all of the following were true: Jeffrey M. ## Analytical synthesis

The corpus breaks into five substantive waves. The first wave is **identification and estimator equivalence**: the 2021 TWFE/TWM paper is Wooldridge’s central intervention in the staggered-adoption DiD literature, because it shows that what many users treat as a specialized TWFE object can instead be understood as flexible pooled regression with the right interactions. That move is powerful because it makes heterogeneity, pretrend diagnostics, cohort-specific effects, and nonlinear extensions much more transparent. citeturn25view0turn25view2

The second wave is **nonlinear DiD**. The 2021 symposium paper, 2022 SSRN preprint, and 2023 *Econometrics Journal* article develop a coherent answer to a practical question applied work often dodges: what if the outcome is binary, fractional, or a count, so that the linear model is a bad mean-function approximation? Wooldridge’s answer is not to abandon DiD, but to shift parallel-trends restrictions to an appropriate index of the conditional mean and estimate treatment effects through pooled QMLE and average partial effects. citeturn15view0turn20view0

The third wave is **generalization beyond balanced panels and binary treatment**. The 2024 repeated-cross-section FLEX paper extends heterogeneity-robust DiD to repeated cross-sections; the 2025 conference paper extends it to nonbinary treatments; and the 2026 AEA preview extends the nonlinear version to repeated cross-sections. This is the cleanest sign that Wooldridge’s DiD program is not a one-off estimator paper but a general regression architecture for modern policy evaluation. citeturn32view0turn38view0turn17view0

The fourth wave is **post-estimation interpretation**. The 2025 ATT-aggregation paper is basically about what people report after they estimate a modern DiD model. That sounds secondary, but it is not. A lot of disagreement in empirical DiD work is really disagreement about which weighted average of cohort-time effects is economically meaningful, and this paper squarely addresses that. citeturn32view1

The fifth wave is **small-sample inference and software implementation**. Lee and Wooldridge’s 2023 transformation paper, 2026 small-sample inference paper, and 2026 rolling-estimation paper together push the agenda toward settings where the number of treated or control units is tiny and classical cluster-asymptotics are weak. The related software trail is unusually visible: `flexdid` for FLEX, `lwdid` for rolling estimators, and a Stata ado file for the QTT paper. That makes this corpus unusually useful for actual applied work, not just reading. citeturn26view0turn42search4turn42search2turn42search9

The blunt bottom line is that Wooldridge’s 2021-2026 DiD work is not a scatter of unrelated papers. It is a **single evolving research program**: start from regression equivalence and heterogeneity-robust staggered DiD, then extend to nonlinear outcomes, repeated cross-sections, nonbinary treatments, aggregation, and small-sample inference, while building usable Stata implementations around the theory. citeturn25view0turn20view0turn32view0turn32view1turn38view0turn17view0turn30search1turn31search0

## Open questions and limitations

The one real bibliographic ambiguity I found concerns **“Simple Approaches to Inference with Difference-in-Differences Estimators with Small Cross-Sectional Sample Sizes.”** SSRN search results expose one identifier, while secondary references and package documentation cite another. I therefore treat the paper as definitely public and relevant, but I would verify the canonical SSRN record directly before importing it into a formal bibliography manager. citeturn29search0turn30search1turn30search7turn29search2

A smaller limitation is that the official 2021 symposium record for **“Nonlinear difference in differences with panel data”** contains **no abstract**, and the 2022 French Stata conference record does not expose a downloadable paper file on IDEAS/RePEc. I handled those cases conservatively by using the official record for bibliographic facts and a separate short analytical summary based on the title, series context, and later versions. citeturn15view0turn16view0

# Two-way fixed effects, the two-way mundlak regression, and difference-in-differences estimators

Jeffrey M. Wooldridge

Received: 27 December 2024 / Accepted: 30 July 2025 / Published online: 27 August 2025 © The Author(s) 2025, corrected publication 2025

## Abstract

I derive a result on the equivalence between the two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimator and an estimator obtained from a pooled ordinary least squares regression that includes unit-specific time averages and time-period-specific cross-sectional averages—the two-way Mundlak (TWM) regression. The equivalence between TWFE and TWM implies that various estimators used for intervention analysis can be computed using pooled OLS that controls for time-constant treatment cohort indicators, time-period indicators, covariates, and interactions among them—allowing for considerable treatment effect heterogeneity. An extended version of TWFE (ETWFE) is equivalent to the POLS approach. I show that an imputation estimator, derived under no anticipation and parallel trends assumptions, is also equivalent to the POLS ETWFE estimator. The equivalence among various estimators shows that average treatment effects on the treated are identified by flexible regression. The framework allows for event study estimators, which can be used to test for pre-trends, and flexible estimation that allows for cohort-specific trends.

**Keywords** Panel data · Two-way fixed effects · Two-way mundlak regression · Staggered interventions · Heterogeneous treatment effects · Heterogeneous trends

## 1 Introduction

Panel data structures are used routinely across many fields in attempts to determine causality and estimate the effects of policy interventions. At the micro level, panels are often characterized by a small number of time periods ( *T* ) and a large cross-sectional sample size ( *N* ). At more aggregated levels, the number of time periods may be substantial, possibly even larger than the cross-sectional dimension.

# Two-way fixed effects, the two-way mundlak regression, and difference-in-differences estimators

Jeffrey M. Wooldridge

Received: 27 December 2024 / Accepted: 30 July 2025 / Published online: 27 August 2025 © The Author(s) 2025, corrected publication 2025

## Abstract

I derive a result on the equivalence between the two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimator and an estimator obtained from a pooled ordinary least squares regression that includes unit-specific time averages and time-period-specific cross-sectional averages—the two-way Mundlak (TWM) regression. The equivalence between TWFE and TWM implies that various estimators used for intervention analysis can be computed using pooled OLS that controls for time-constant treatment cohort indicators, time-period indicators, covariates, and interactions among them—allowing for considerable treatment effect heterogeneity. An extended version of TWFE (ETWFE) is equivalent to the POLS approach. I show that an imputation estimator, derived under no anticipation and parallel trends assumptions, is also equivalent to the POLS ETWFE estimator. The equivalence among various estimators shows that average treatment effects on the treated are identified by flexible regression. The framework allows for event study estimators, which can be used to test for pre-trends, and flexible estimation that allows for cohort-specific trends.

**Keywords** Panel data · Two-way fixed effects · Two-way mundlak regression · Staggered interventions · Heterogeneous treatment effects · Heterogeneous trends

## 1 Introduction

Panel data structures are used routinely across many fields in attempts to determine causality and estimate the effects of policy interventions. At the micro level, panels are often characterized by a small number of time periods ( *T* ) and a large cross-sectional sample size ( *N* ). At more aggregated levels, the number of time periods may be substantial, possibly even larger than the cross-sectional dimension.

    68	- *T* time periods with no units treated in *t* = 1.

    79	    - $Y\_t(T)$ is the outcome treated in only the final period.
    80	    - Adopt Athey and Imbens (2021, Journal of Econometrics): $Y\_t(\infty)$ is the outcome if a unit is never treated in $ { q,\ldots,T } $.

{"language": "markdown", "code": "## 2. Staggered Interventions: Notation and Assumptions

- *T* time periods with no units treated in *t* = 1.
- First unit is treated at *t* = *q* < *T* .
- Initially, no reversibility: once a unit is subjected to the intervention, it stays in place.
- Treated units are added up through *t* = *T* .
- Is there a never treated group?
    - Determines whether certain ATTs are identified; assume so here.

8

- For $g \in { q,\ldots,T } $, $Y\_t(g)$ is the outcome if the unit is first subjected to the intervention at time g.
    - In $Y\_t(g)$, the number of treated periods decreases with g.
    - $Y\_t(T)$ is the outcome treated in only the final period.
    - Adopt Athey and Imbens (2021, Journal of Econometrics): $Y\_t(\infty)$ is the outcome if a unit is never treated in $ { q,\ldots,T } $.
    - $Y\_t(0)$ is common but more confusing in this context.

9

- Treatment effects of primary focus:
$$TE\_{gt}=Y\_t(g)-Y\_t(\infty), \quad g=q,\ldots,T;\ t=g,\ldots,T$$
▸ For any $t$, $Y\_t(\infty)$ is the outcome in the control state.
- Exhaustive and mutually exclusive dummy variables:$$D\_g=1 \text{ if unit is first subjected to intervention at } g \in { q,\ldots,T } $$
$$D\_\infty=1-(D\_q+D\_{q+1}+\cdots+D\_T)$$
▸ $D\_{i\infty}=1$ means unit $i$ is never treated (up through $T$).
▸ $D\_{i\infty}=0$ for all $i$ means that all units are treated by time $T$.

10

- Goal is to estimate[ \tau\_{gt}=E[Y\_t(g)-Y\_t(\infty)\mid D\_g=1],\ t=g,g+1,\ldots,T ]▸ Sometimes the focus is on the instantaneous effects, ( \tau\_{gg} ) .▸ ( \tau\_{gt}, t>g ) allows us to estimate persistence.

11

**Assumption NA (No Anticipation):** All pre-intervention treatment effects are zero:

[ E[Y\_t(g)-Y\_t(\infty)\mid D\_g,\ldots,D\_T]=0,\ t\in { 1,2,\ldots,g-1 } ,\ g\in { q,\ldots,T } . \square ]

▸ Implies ( \tau\_{gt}=0,\ t<g ) .

**Assumption PT (Parallel Trends):** For ( t=2,\ldots,T ) ,

[ E[Y\_t(\infty)-Y\_1(\infty)\mid D\_g,\ldots,D\_T]=E[Y\_t(\infty)-Y\_1(\infty)]. \square ]

▸ Allows the ( D\_g ) to be correlated with ( Y\_1(\infty) ) ; selection into treatment.

12

- We observe $ { D\_{i0}, D\_{iq}, D\_{i,q+1}, \ldots, D\_{iT} } $ and the outcome$$ Y\_{it}=D\_{i0}\cdot Y\_i(\infty)+D\_{iq}\cdot Y\_{it}(q)+\cdots+D\_{iT}\cdot Y\_{it}(T) $$
    - If $D\_{ig}=0$ for all $i$, simply drop that dummy: no units in cohort $g$.
- Often start with $W\_{it}$, the time-varying treatment indicator.
    - $W\_{i,t-1}=1 \Rightarrow W\_{it}=1$.
- Define post-treatment time dummies by cohort:$$ p\_{gt}=f\_{gt}+\cdots+f\_{Tt};\quad p\_{gt}=1 \text{ if } t\ge g $$
- Then$$ W\_{it}=D\_{iq}\cdot p\_{qt}+D\_{i,q+1}\cdot p(q+1)t+\cdots+D\_{iT}\cdot pTt $$

13

## 3. Estimators without Controls

- Simplest pooled OLS regression estimates a single coefficient:
    - $D\_{iq}, \ldots, D\_{iT}, f2\_t, \ldots, fT\_t$ act as controls.
$Y\_{it}$ on $W\_{it}, 1, D\_{iq}, \ldots, D\_{iT}, f2\_t, \ldots, fT\_t$
- Algebraically the same as replacing $1, D\_{iq}, \ldots, D\_{iT}$ with unit fixed effects:
    - Equivalence very useful to simply computation; extends to nonlinear models.
$Y\_{it}$ on $W\_{it}, C\_{i1}, \ldots, C\_{iN}, f2\_t, \ldots, fT\_t$

Do NOT use this skill for PDF creation, form filling, merging, splitting, watermarking, or encryption — use the pdf skill instead."
