content.text:
Yes. The organizing principle is Chamberlain wherever rank is abundant and Mundlak only where it's scarce, and since the only scarce dimension is region-by-year, the maximal specification is the one that saturates county, market, and state space completely while spending the sixteen region coordinates deliberately rather than by accident.

Start with the calendar coding, since that's what "no special year" means concretely. Drop the reference year and the global intercept: `Σ_{t∈T} D_t α_t` with all ten year dummies, and every block interacted with all ten rather than with nine. Your saturation note already proposes this and correctly requires an equivalence test first, that fitted values and `τ̂` match the reference-year parameterization to within tolerance, so it lands as a coding change rather than a robustness specification. Under symmetric coding the `ψ_s Z_i D_t` trends become ten rather than nine, and the same for every baseline-by-year block. Nothing about identification changes; what changes is that no year is silently the baseline against which heterogeneity is reported.

The region ledger is where the real work is, and the move that buys the most is applying your own Chamberlain-versus-Mundlak logic to the treatment history instead of only to the covariate history. You already give nine baseline variables separate 2008, 2009, and 2010 values while the rest enter as three-year mean and trend. Do the same to the AEWR path: keep separate coordinates for the most recent admissible history years and summarize the distant tail by its mean and slope. Combine that with the leave-future-out rule and the terminal year, which is the binding one, goes from nine nuisance coordinates to five — three recent separate plus two summary. The budget becomes `1 + 3D + 5 ≤ 16`, so `D = 3`. A cellwise cubic dose response, which the current design explicitly declines to call identified, becomes affordable at every year including 2022.

That gain forces a choice you should make explicitly rather than by default. Adding a region-specific linear trend costs one coordinate, leaving `1 + 3D + 5 + 1 ≤ 16` and still permitting the cubic. Adding all three cross-horizon products, `W_t W_{t-1}`, `W_t W_{t-2}`, and `W_{t-1} W_{t-2}`, costs three more, and `1 + 9 + 5 + 1 + 3 = 19` does not fit. At quadratic it fits exactly at sixteen. So the maximal specification is cubic-with-region-trends-and-no-cross-horizon, or quadratic-with-region-trends-and-full-cross-horizon, and these are two distinct maxima rather than one. Your note is right that cross-horizon belongs in its own grid field precisely because it competes with curvature for the same ledger; this is the arithmetic that shows the competition is binding rather than notional.

Everything moderated is close to free, so saturate it. Every baseline covariate enters the causal dictionary through its county and market components at the full moderated degree under strong heredity, `D^(moderated) = D^(0)`, so cubic-by-county and cubic-by-market interactions with all three horizons in all ten years. Replace mean-and-trend moderators with full trajectory coordinates, the separate 2008, 2009, and 2010 values or a stored orthogonal transform, since the mean-only version cannot distinguish a rising from a falling pre-path. Add the bite-gradient tier, dose by bite by county-or-market moderator. Exclude region-level components from the causal dose dictionary entirely, and enforce the representation rule per source variable, because admitting the standardized level alongside all three sub-regional components spans the omitted region interaction and spends region rank invisibly — that identity is the one way this specification can blow its budget without any line of the ledger showing it.

The untreated mean saturates the same way and for the same reason. Year-specific first-order projection of every predetermined county and market coordinate, trajectory coordinates rather than summaries, and declared within-source second-order pairs, all of which live in 3,041- and 745-dimensional space and cost nothing at region level. What they do cost is residual degrees of freedom and memory, so this is where your parameter-to-row guard binds, and it binds hardest on `positions_per_application` and `hours_per_position` because those run on restricted samples. Expect the selector to promote a lower tier for those two outcomes, and predeclare which tier rather than discovering it.

What stays genuinely special is exactly the two years you named, for mechanical reasons. The first analysis year has no admissible leave-future-out history at all, since every candidate coordinate is either focal or later, so its region budget is `1 + 3D + 0` and it carries the loosest constraint in the panel. The last year is the reverse: it binds the ledger, it carries the common-basis safeguard that keeps all seventeen cyclic states full rank, and it has no lead available. Every year in between should be treated identically by construction, and the rank ledger CSV should show that — a ledger where interior years differ from each other is a bug, not a design choice.

Two caveats I'd hold onto. The claim that a region trend costs exactly one coordinate is your note's arithmetic, and region trends and region intercepts both project onto the same seventeen-dimensional space, so I would confirm it through the residualized QR audit before treating the cubic-plus-trend combination as admissible; the arithmetic guard is necessary and not sufficient, as you already say. And none of this touches inference. Saturating the conditional mean buys identification and functional-form credibility, the covariance still has rank at most sixteen, and the critical value is still `t_16` no matter how rich the point-estimate model gets.

separate 2008, 2009, and 2010 values is a no-no actually as is forcing linear trends or some such thing, and no cubic or quadratic should be included for now; I don't even get the strong heredity thing

content.thinking:
He's pushing back on three points and raising a fourth question. The core issue with separating 2008, 2009, and 2010 as distinct values is that it's imposing a specific parameterization—treating each pre-period year as its own coordinate. With only three pre-period years, I'm essentially using up all the degrees of freedom (three values = three df), whereas a mean-plus-trend approach would use just two. His objection seems to be that separate values force assumptions about linear trends or similar constraints, so he's objecting to both approaches as currently framed.

The real insight is that any choice among separate years, mean-plus-trend, or mean-only is arbitrary special treatment of the pre-period structure. The clean, non-arbitrary solution is the Mundlak device: unit-specific time averages and period cross-sectional averages. That's what the Wooldridge-Mundlak-Chamberlain equivalence actually specifies—just the means, nothing more. Theorem 3.1 shows that adding unit time averages and period averages reproduces TWFE exactly. Adding trends or separate-year coordinates goes beyond that equivalence and introduces extra parametric assumptions that aren't justified by the theory.

For this application, I'm keeping the dose linear only—no quadratic or cubic terms—which dramatically simplifies the budget and avoids the heredity constraint entirely. Since heredity only becomes relevant once you have polynomial degrees to manage, it's not a concern here, and I should clarify that distinction rather than carry it forward as a field.

Now I'm thinking through what the maximally rich specification looks like under these constraints: symmetric year coding with no reference year, linear dose across three horizons, pre-period as Mundlak averages rather than separate years, and leave-future-out history. The key tension is whether to use the full Chamberlain approach—projecting on the entire vector of period-specific coefficients—or stick with Mundlak-style time averages, which is what he's leaning toward.

The resolution is that Chamberlain applies to the treatment path itself, where each year's AEWR coordinates get their own unrestricted coefficients, while Mundlak applies to the covariates through their time averages. The hierarchical decomposition across county, market, state, and region levels then provides the multilevel Mundlak structure.

For the region budget with linear dose, I'm checking whether the degrees of freedom work out: one intercept plus three horizon terms plus the history coordinates needs to stay under 16. With leave-future-out limiting the history to at most 9 coordinates by 2022, that gives me 13 total, leaving three degrees of freedom to allocate. The question is whether to use one of those for a region-specific trend, though there was pushback against forcing linear trends in the pre-period covariates.

If I'm refusing parametric time structure there, I should be consistent and refuse it for regions too — the non-parametric alternative would be full region-by-year saturation, but that's prohibitively expensive at 17×10 and competes directly with treatment effects. So region trends are off the table on principle, which means accepting that the pre-trend problem won't get an easy parametric fix.

With three free coordinates available, the question becomes what's worth spending them on. Cross-horizon products like W_t·W_{t-1} are interactions rather than polynomials and represent a different response surface, but he said no quadratic terms, and these would be second-order in W anyway. The cleaner move is to leave those coordinates as slack — a safety margin — rather than fill them speculatively.

For "maximally rich" specification without adding degrees of freedom, richness shifts entirely into the county and market space where it's essentially free at the region level: baseline covariates decomposed into their county and market components, Mundlak-averaged over 2008-2010, then interacted with year dummies to capture year-specific projections of the untreated mean, and the same components interacted with dose-by-year to identify causal moderators, plus state-level components as well.

I should also clarify the two-way Mundlak requirement: Theorem 3.1 needs both the cross-sectional mean x̄_i· and the time mean x̄_·t, but in a balanced region-year panel those are already absorbed by region and year fixed effects. And since the pre-period covariates are time-constant, measured only in 2008-2010, their "time average" is computed over that pre-period window, not across the full panel — that's how the Mundlak device works in this design.

The real issue is that the current approach uses a hierarchical decomposition of covariates at each nesting level (county, market, state, region), which is the multilevel Mundlak approach and it's mean-based without trends or separate years — that part is already correct. What needs fixing is the separate retention of 2008, 2009, and 2010 values for those nine variables in H_i, plus the linear trend summaries. The fix is to drop both the separate-year values and the trend terms, keeping only the three-year mean at each hierarchy level in the panel-building code. That leaves just the mean, which he seems comfortable with.

I initially pushed back on this because I thought losing the trajectory information was wasteful — you could have rising versus falling paths with the same mean. But he's right to reject that: distinguishing trajectories requires imposing a trend parameterization, which treats time as special. The Mundlak device is fundamentally about the mean, so I should acknowledge that reverses my earlier recommendation.

Now for heredity: it's a principle from factorial and polynomial model building where if you include a higher-order or interaction term, you must include its lower-order constituents. For the moderated polynomial, strong heredity means the moderated degree never exceeds the unmoderated degree — you don't fit a Z-interacted cubic without the plain cubic. Weak heredity is more permissive.

Why this matters is the real issue: with weak heredity, the response at Z=0 becomes lower-order than the response elsewhere, so you're parameterizing the average and the heterogeneity inconsistently, and the shape at your reference point becomes an artifact. In his case, county-level cubic moderators are cheap to fit while an unmoderated cubic is expensive, creating temptation to buy the cheap version. But if everything is degree 1, the whole thing collapses — you might as well drop the field or hardcode it.

I should also walk through the region ledger arithmetic explicitly and clarify how the first and last year mechanics work.

Now I'm drafting a response to his question about strong heredity. I'll keep it moderate in length, lead…

content.text:
Heredity first, since it's a model-building convention rather than an econometric result. If a model contains a higher-order or interaction term, heredity says it must also contain that term's lower-order constituents: no `W²` without `W`, no `W×Z` without `W` and `Z`. Strong heredity in your saturation note is the polynomial version applied to moderated versus unmoderated dose degrees, `D^(moderated) ≤ D^(0)`, meaning you never carry a `Z`-interacted cubic without a plain cubic. It's in the note because county-level cubic interactions are rank-cheap while an unmoderated cubic costs three region coordinates, which creates a standing temptation to buy the cheap one alone. The cost of yielding to it is that the response at `Z = 0` is lower-order than the response away from it, so the reported average shape is a parameterization artifact. With a linear dose everywhere the constraint is vacuous, since moderated and unmoderated degrees are both one. Hardcode it or drop the field.

The other three corrections I take, and the second one reverses advice I gave two turns ago about trajectory coordinates. Mundlak's device is the time average. Separate 2008, 2009, and 2010 coordinates are Chamberlain applied to the covariates, and a fitted pre-period slope is a third parameterization, and choosing among mean, separate values, and mean-plus-trend is precisely the special-casing of the time dimension you're ruling out. The consistent position is means only, at each hierarchy level, which is what the four telescoping components already are. That does forfeit distinguishing a rising from a falling pre-path with the same mean, and I think you're right to pay it rather than smuggle a trend in to recover it.

That leaves a clean division of labor, and it's the one that earns the compound name. Chamberlain governs the treatment path: every admissible history year gets its own unrestricted `ρ_sh`, applied by rule rather than by selection, which is exactly what "no special treatment of any year" means operationally. Mundlak governs the covariates: hierarchical means at county-within-market, market-within-state, state-within-region, and region-within-nation, with no time structure imposed on them at all. The Wooldridge layer is the algebraic one, and here it's degenerate in a useful way, since the unit time average and the period cross-sectional average of a region-year dose are a region constant and a year constant, absorbed by the region dummies and the symmetric year set.

The ledger becomes comfortable. Symmetric coding with all ten year dummies and no intercept, linear dose at three horizons, leave-future-out history so year `s` carries `s − 2013` coordinates. The demand is `1 + 3 + J_s`, which is 4 in 2013 and 13 in 2022. That sits three under your 16 guard and four under the 17 ceiling, and I'd leave it as reserve rather than spend it. Worth knowing for later: restoring the quadratic costs three more and lands the terminal year at exactly 16, so the quadratic is still available with the full uniform history and leave-future-out, at precisely zero margin. Dropping it now is a modeling choice, not a rank-forced one, and the ledger tells you what reinstating it costs.

Richness therefore lives entirely in county and market space, where it is free at region level and constrained only by rows and conditioning. Year-specific first-order projection of every predetermined county and market component across all ten years rather than nine, the same crossed with `Z_i`, declared within-source second-order pairs in the untreated mean, and on the causal side the dose interacted with county and market components at all three horizons in all ten years. State components enter only after the residualized incremental-rank audit, since the region span is nested inside the state span and a raw column count won't catch it. The representation rule still binds and is still the way this specification can overspend without any ledger line showing it: admitting a standardized level alongside all three sub-regional components spans the omitted region interaction exactly.

Two years stay special for mechanical reasons rather than by choice, which I think is what you meant by the exception. Under leave-future-out, 2013 has no admissible history coordinates at all, so its untreated mean rests entirely on the hierarchy and `Z`, with no AEWR-path projection; it is also the cheapest year in the ledger. The terminal year binds the ledger, carries the common-basis safeguard that keeps all seventeen cyclic states full rank, and has no lead available. Every interior year should be identical by construction, and `mc_rank_budget_audit.csv` showing any interior-year variation other than the monotone history count is then a bug rather than a design feature.

One consistency point to settle rather than let drift. If imposed linear trends are out for the pre-period, region-specific linear trends are out on the same principle, and I should retract the recommendation I made twice. The honest consequence is that the pre-trend evidence loses its cheap parametric fix, and the remaining diagnostics are the history-rule contrast from last turn and the reference-state influence audit. Inference is unchanged either way, since none of this adds policy paths.

Interaction terms are fine and good. Three years before current year should also be dropped. It's arbitrary and wack. Also having standard errors on every regression term is actually unnecessary since what we care about is post-fit delta method inference on constructed combinations anyway.

content.thinking:
He's clarifying that interaction terms are perfectly valid—cross-horizon products like lagged variable pairs don't need to be treated with suspicion the way I was worried about heredity effects. So including interactions between time periods is fine, which actually undermines my earlier concern about needing quadratic terms to justify the model structure.

On the focal exclusion set, he's pushing back on the arbitrary three-year window I'm using to exclude collinear terms from the nuisance block. He's questioning whether dropping exactly {s, s-1, s-2} makes sense or if the whole lag structure needs rethinking. So maybe the real insight is to abandon the focal window distinction altogether and treat the entire admissible history uniformly—every coordinate gets a causal interpretation with year-specific coefficients, no artificial separation between "dose" and "nuisance." That's actually the cleanest approach: the focal window itself is just another arbitrary parameterization choice, and if you're eliminating those elsewhere, why keep it here?

The delta method then handles all effect construction post-fit, which means you don't need exclusion restrictions or arbitrary lag counts at all. And that directly supports his third point—individual coefficient standard errors become irrelevant because inference happens on the constructed combinations afterward, not on the raw parameters.

So points two and three collapse into one: fit a single saturated model without the causal-versus-nuisance distinction, then build everything you need from the full coefficient vector and covariance matrix using delta method gradients. That elegantly sidesteps the collinearity problem I was treating as fundamental—it was actually self-imposed by the coordinate split. Now I need to recalculate the rank budget: instead of 1 + 3 + J_s, it's just 1 plus however many history coordinates are actually admitted in year s.

For a leave-future-out rule where h ≤ s-3, that's 1 + (s-2013) parameters per year—only 10 for 2022, well below the 16 I was worried about. But wait, that exclusion rule would also drop the contemporaneous dose W_{r,s} itself, which defeats the purpose since I need it to estimate the current effect. I need to separate the leave-future-out logic for the nuisance block from what applies to the focal causal term.

Actually, if I drop the focal/nuisance distinction entirely, the admissible set for year s becomes simply all realized doses through the current year—{2011, ..., s}—with nothing after. That's cleaner and aligns with sequential exogeneity: condition on the full policy history up to now, nothing forward-looking. For 2013 that's 3 coordinates, for 2022 it's 12, which is manageable.

The budget works out nicely too: 1 + (s - 2010) parameters, so 4 for 2013 and 13 for 2022, both well under 16. And because all lags carry their own coefficients, the dynamics are flexible—I can construct any horizon-specific effect after fitting. If I add cross-horizon interactions like adjacent-year products, I'm still within the constraint even for 2022. It's monotone, uniform, no arbitrary windows, and it fits cleanly.

Now for the computational side: I don't actually need to store standard errors for every coefficient or form the full K×K covariance matrix from the 17 state-level regressions. What matters is projecting that covariance onto the specific gradients I care about—so instead of computing and storing an 810k-entry matrix, I can work directly with the state-specific coefficient vectors projected onto each gradient direction.

This is the key insight: keep the 17×K matrix of centered coefficient errors and compute variance as a simple 17-vector norm per gradient, never materializing the K×K covariance. That directly addresses the memory constraints flagged in the README and lets me handle much richer models without hitting the dense matrix limits.

The rank constraint is automatic and exact this way, and the delta-method standard errors reduce to just 17 scalars. The clustered covariance becomes optional—only needed for the coefficient comparison table. Dropping the focal/nuisance split doesn't break the delta method either; the gradient entries are nonzero only on the perturbed history coordinate. I need to keep the coefficient names and the common basis across all 17 states, but I can drop the per-term standard errors and avoid materializing the full K×K matrix. Removing the focal window also means the entire section explaining why the literal full equation can't be estimated becomes unnecessary, along with all that rank arithmetic. Let me write this up cleanly in prose and document these design decisions—…

content.text:
Dropping the focal window dissolves the collinearity the README spends a whole section on, because that collinearity was self-inflicted. The exclusion set exists only because the design declares `{s, s-1, s-2}` causal and everything else nuisance, then discovers that `W_{r,t-p} d_ts` and `W̃_{r,h} d_ts` at `h = s-p` are the same column. Stop labeling coordinates and the problem evaporates: one history block, every admissible dose coordinate gets one year-specific coefficient, and nothing is excluded to protect a distinction that has no estimation content. The section titled "Why the literal full equation cannot be estimated" becomes obsolete, along with its 22-versus-19-versus-16 arithmetic, which was counting the cost of a carve-out rather than a real constraint.

The admissible set then has one rule with no free parameters: for outcome year `s`, condition on `{2011, ..., s}` and nothing later. Sequential exogeneity supplies the upper limit, and there is no lag count to choose. Dynamics are not lost, they're just no longer hardcoded — every lag is present with its own coefficient, and any horizon-specific effect is a gradient over the coordinate you perturb. The region demand is `1 + (s − 2010)`, which is 4 in 2013 rising monotonically to 13 in 2022, under the 16 guard with room to spare. That room is where cross-horizon interactions go, and since they're interactions rather than polynomial degrees, they satisfy heredity with a linear basis and my earlier caution doesn't apply to them. Three adjacent-pair products at region level put the terminal year at exactly 16.

Your point about standard errors is the one with the largest implementation payoff, and it inverts what the model bundle currently keeps. The delta-method variance is `g' V g` where `V = (1/17) Σ_a (b_a − b̄)(b_a − b̄)'`. You never need `V`. Stack the seventeen centered coefficient-error vectors into a `17 × K` matrix `E` and the variance is `(1/17) ‖E g‖²`, seventeen inner products per reported quantity. The README says the bundle retains the complete CCV covariance and discards the state-specific error matrices once the covariance is formed. That's exactly backwards: the `K × K` object is the expensive one and the only one you can throw away. At `K = 5000` the covariance is 200 MB and `E` is under a megabyte.

This is what unbinds your resource guards. `MC_SPEC_MAX_DENSE_GIB` at 1.25 and `MC_SPEC_MAX_PEAK_GIB` at 6 are rejecting saturated specifications before fitting, and the working-set proxy `4(8NK) + 3(8K²)` carries a `K²` term that is entirely the covariance you no longer form. Drop that term and the ceiling on county and market saturation rises by roughly an order of magnitude in `K`. Rank at most 16 also stops being a claim you assert and becomes arithmetic you can't violate, since `E` has seventeen rows and is centered.

What still has to survive the change: coefficient names, the identified-basis assertion across all seventeen states, and the analytic-versus-model-matrix gradient check. Those need the basis to be common and stably ordered, not the per-term standard errors. So `mc_parameter_estimates.csv` keeps estimates and names and loses the SE column, `mc_ccv_coefficients` as a reported table goes away, and `05_validate.R` keeps its gradient contract unchanged. The comparison clustered covariance has no consumer left once the coefficient table is gone.

One thing to state deliberately rather than inherit. With no causal-versus-nuisance labels, the estimand has to carry the whole interpretive load, and the README already writes it correctly as a coordinate intervention: perturb `W_{r,s-p}` by `δ`, hold the remaining path fixed, average fitted changes. The gradient is nonzero on that coordinate's column in year `s` plus any cross-horizon product containing it, and zero everywhere else, which is mechanical rather than a claim about which parameters are structural. That's a cleaner story than the current one, where holding the projection fixed is justified by calling it a description of latent type.
There is a twist; you do still have to use the continuous CCV standard errors to do stuff properly (and in this case everything is observed) using the methodology in the CCV repo

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"To convert your document to standard, clean Markdown, I have replaced the non-standard block equations with valid LaTeX math blocks (using `$$`), corrected the formatting of lists, and applied consistent header levels.

---

# Formalizing the Continuous-Dose CCV Estimator

Here is the formal version. The punchline is:

$$
\widehat V_{\text{CCV},D} = \widehat\lambda_D \widehat V_{\text{cluster}} + (1-\widehat\lambda_D)\widehat V_{\text{robust}}
$$

where $D$ is the continuous AEWR-bite treatment after residualizing covariates and fixed effects, and

$$
\widehat\lambda_D = 1 - q \frac{\left(G^{-1}\sum_{g=1}^G \widehat\Omega_g\right)^2}{G^{-1}\sum_{g=1}^G \widehat\Omega_g^2}, \qquad \widehat\Omega_g = \frac{1}{n_g} \sum_{i\in g} \widetilde D_{gi}^2
$$

This is the clean continuous-dose analog of the AAIW fixed-effect CCV formula. AAIW’s published fixed-effect CCV is explicitly a convex combination of robust and clustered variance estimators, with the weight based on within-cluster treatment variation ($\bar W_g(1-\bar W_g)$). They also emphasize that the fixed-effect estimator and this variance estimator require within-cluster treatment variation.

## 1. Setup

Let $g=1,\dots,G$ index counties or county-like clusters, and let $i=1,\dots,n_g$ index observations within county $g$. Let $Y_{gi}$ be the outcome, and let $D_{gi}$ be the continuous AEWR treatment intensity, for example:

$$
D_{gi} = \max\{0, \log(\text{AEWR}_{gi})-\log(w^0_{gi})\}
$$

Let $Z_{gi}$ collect all controls and fixed effects other than $D_{gi}$. The regression is:

$$
Y_{gi} = \beta D_{gi} + Z_{gi}'\theta + u_{gi}
$$

Stack the data and write $Y = D\beta + Z\theta + u$. Let $M_Z = I - Z(Z'Z)^{-1}Z'$ be the residual-maker. Define:

$$
\widetilde Y = M_ZY, \quad \widetilde D = M_ZD, \quad \widetilde u = M_Zu
$$

By Frisch–Waugh–Lovell:

$$
\widehat\beta = \frac{\widetilde D'\widetilde Y}{\widetilde D'\widetilde D}
$$

Let $S = \sum_{g=1}^G \sum_{i=1}^{n_g} \widetilde D_{gi}^2$. Then:

$$
\widehat\beta - \beta = S^{-1} \sum_{g=1}^G \sum_{i=1}^{n_g} \widetilde D_{gi}\widetilde u_{gi}
$$

Define the observation-level score $\psi_{gi} = \widetilde D_{gi}\widetilde u_{gi}$, and the county-level score $\Psi_g = \sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\psi_{gi}$. Thus:

$$
\widehat\beta - \beta = S^{-1}\sum_{g=1}^G \Psi_g
$$

## 2. Robust and clustered variance estimators

The Eicker–Huber–White variance estimator is:

$$
\widehat V_{\text{robust}} = S^{-2} \sum_{g=1}^G \sum_{i=1}^{n_g} \widehat\psi_{gi}^2
$$

The usual Liang–Zeger county-clustered estimator is:

$$
\widehat V_{\text{cluster}} = S^{-2} \sum_{g=1}^G \left( \sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\widehat\psi_{gi} \right)^2
$$

Expanding the cluster estimator shows the difference:

$$
\widehat V_{\text{cluster}} - \widehat V_{\text{robust}} = S^{-2} \sum_{g=1}^G \sum_{i \neq j} \widehat\psi_{gi}\widehat\psi_{gj}
$$

## 3. Continuous-treatment analog of the AAIW fixed-effect weight

For continuous treatment $D_{gi}$, the exact analog of $\bar W_g(1-\bar W_g)$ is the within-county residualized treatment variance $\widehat\Omega_g = \frac{1}{n_g} \sum_{i=1}^{n_g} \widetilde D_{gi}^2$.

Defining $\widehat\lambda_D$ as above, the continuous-treatment CCV estimator is:

$$
\widehat V_{\text{CCV},D} = \widehat\lambda_D \widehat V_{\text{cluster}} + (1-\widehat\lambda_D) \widehat V_{\text{robust}}
$$

If panel lengths $n_g$ are highly unequal and your estimand is unit-weighted, replace $\widehat\Omega_g$ with $\widehat S_g = \sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\widetilde D_{gi}^2$ and use the corresponding unit-weighted $\widehat\lambda_D^{\text{unit}}$.

## 4. Proof that this reduces to AAIW in the binary case

Setting $D_{gi} = W_{gi} \in \{0,1\}$, we have $\widetilde D_{gi} = W_{gi} - \bar W_g$. Since $W_{gi}^2 = W_{gi}$ for binary variables:

$$
\widehat\Omega_g = \frac{1}{n_g} \sum_i (W_{gi} - \bar W_g)^2 = \bar W_g(1 - \bar W_g)
$$

Plugging this into the continuous formula yields the AAIW fixed-effect CCV weight, confirming it is a strict extension.

## 5. Proof that the CCV estimator is a convex combination

Assuming $0 \leq q \leq 1$ and non-zero variation, Cauchy–Schwarz implies:

$$
\left( G^{-1}\sum_g \widehat\Omega_g \right)^2 \leq G^{-1}\sum_g \widehat\Omega_g^2
$$

It follows that $0 \leq \widehat\lambda_D \leq 1$, confirming that $\widehat V_{\text{CCV},D}$ is a convex combination of the clustered and robust variance estimators.

## 6. Consistency argument

As $G \to \infty$ and $\max_g \frac{S_g}{S} \to 0$, under standard regularity conditions and the assumption that the residualized treatment has non-zero limiting variation:

$$
\widehat\lambda_D \to_p \lambda_D = 1 - q \frac{\Omega_1^2}{\Omega_2}
$$

By Slutsky’s theorem, $\widehat V_{\text{CCV},D}$ consistently estimates the corresponding continuous-dose CCV asymptotic variance.

## 7. Limitations

This formula is exact under a continuous-dose assignment model where the cluster-level identifying-variation object $\Omega_g$ is sufficient (e.g., a common-shape location-scale assignment process). For arbitrary continuous treatments, higher moments and slope heterogeneity may affect the variance.

\widehat V_{\text{CCV},D} = \widehat\lambda_D \widehat V_{\text{cluster}} + (1-\widehat\lambda_D) \widehat V_{\text{robust}}
$$

## 4. Proof that this reduces to AAIW in the binary case

Setting $D_{gi} = W_{gi} \in \{0,1\}$, we have $\widetilde D_{gi} = W_{gi} - \bar W_g$. Since $W_{gi}^2 = W_{gi}$ for binary variables:

$$
\widehat\Omega_g = \frac{1}{n_g} \sum_i (W_{gi} - \bar W_g)^2 = \bar W_g(1 - \bar W_g)
$$

Plugging this into the continuous formula yields the AAIW fixed-effect CCV weight, confirming it is a strict extension.

## 5. Proof that the CCV estimator is a convex combination

Assuming $0 \leq q \leq 1$ and non-zero variation, Cauchy–Schwarz implies:

$$
\left( G^{-1}\sum_g \widehat\Omega_g \right)^2 \leq G^{-1}\sum_g \widehat\Omega_g^2
$$

It follows that $0 \leq \widehat\lambda_D \leq 1$, confirming that $\widehat V_{\text{CCV},D}$ is a convex combination of the clustered and robust variance estimators.

## 6. Consistency argument

As $G \to \infty$ and $\max_g \frac{S_g}{S} \to 0$, under standard regularity conditions and the assumption that the residualized treatment has non-zero limiting variation:

$$
\widehat\lambda_D \to_p \lambda_D = 1 - q \frac{\Omega_1^2}{\Omega_2}
$$

By Slutsky’s theorem, $\widehat V_{\text{CCV},D}$ consistently estimates the corresponding continuous-dose CCV asymptotic variance.

## 7. Limitations

This formula is exact under a continuous-dose assignment model where the cluster-level identifying-variation object $\Omega_g$ is sufficient (e.g., a common-shape location-scale assignment process). For arbitrary continuous treatments, higher moments and slope heterogeneity may affect the variance.

This document compares the proof idea behind the original binary-treatment CCV
argument with the continuous-treatment extension. It is written to be readable
without consulting the Lean formalization.

The main message is simple:

- In the binary case, treatment algebra collapses because `W_i^2 = W_i`.
- In the continuous case, that collapse is unavailable, so the proof keeps the
  full treatment-assignment covariance kernel.

The binary proof is therefore a treatment-share and cluster-sum proof. The
continuous proof is a quadratic-form and covariance-kernel proof.

## 1. Common Setup

Think of a residualized regression after applying fixed effects or other
controls. For observation or cell `i`, write:

```text
Ytilde_i = beta * Dtilde_i + u_i.
```

Here:

- `Ytilde_i` is the residualized outcome;
- `Dtilde_i` is the residualized treatment;
- `beta` is the scalar treatment coefficient;
- `u_i` is the residualized structural error or potential-outcome residual.

The scalar FWL/OLS coefficient is:

```text
betaHat = (sum_i Dtilde_i Ytilde_i) / (sum_i Dtilde_i^2).
```

Let:

```text
S = sum_i Dtilde_i^2.
```

If `S != 0`, substituting `Ytilde_i = beta * Dtilde_i + u_i` gives the finite
sample score expansion:

```text
betaHat - beta
  = (sum_i Dtilde_i u_i) / S.
```

This identity is common to both the binary and continuous cases. The difference
between the two proofs is how they handle the variance of the score:

```text
sum_i Dtilde_i u_i.
```

## 2. Original Binary-Treatment Proof

### 2.1 Binary Treatment Algebra

In the binary case, treatment is an indicator:

```text
W_i in {0, 1}.
```

The decisive algebraic fact is:

```text
W_i^2 = W_i.
```

This means that second moments of treatment can often be rewritten as first
moments. If `Wbar` is the average treatment share in a finite group,

```text
Wbar = (1 / n) * sum_i W_i,
```

then the within-group residualized treatment second moment is:

```text
(1 / n) * sum_i (W_i - Wbar)^2 = Wbar * (1 - Wbar).
```

The calculation is:

```text
sum_i (W_i - Wbar)^2
  = sum_i (W_i^2 - 2 W_i Wbar + Wbar^2)
  = sum_i W_i - 2 Wbar sum_i W_i + n Wbar^2
  = n Wbar - 2 n Wbar^2 + n Wbar^2
  = n Wbar (1 - Wbar).
```

Dividing by `n` gives:

```text
mean((W_i - Wbar)^2) = Wbar * (1 - Wbar).
```

This identity is the key simplification in the original binary proof. The
within-group treatment variation can be described by the scalar treatment share
`Wbar`, not by a full covariance matrix.

### 2.2 Clustered Score Algebra

Now suppose observations are grouped into clusters `g`. Let `psi_gi` be the
score contribution for observation `i` inside cluster `g`.

The cluster score is:

```text
Psi_g = sum_i psi_gi.
```

The clustered variance estimator uses squared cluster scores:

```text
V_cluster = S^(-2) * sum_g Psi_g^2
          = S^(-2) * sum_g (sum_i psi_gi)^2.
```

The square of the cluster sum expands as:

```text
(sum_i psi_gi)^2
  = sum_i sum_j psi_gi psi_gj
  = sum_i psi_gi^2 + sum_{i != j} psi_gi psi_gj.
```

Therefore:

```text
V_cluster
  = S^(-2) * sum_g sum_i psi_gi^2
    + S^(-2) * sum_g sum_{i != j} psi_gi psi_gj.
```

The first term is the Eicker-Huber-White or robust diagonal part. The second
term is the within-cluster cross-product correction. The clustered variance
estimator is exactly what you get when you allow arbitrary within-cluster score
correlation and no across-cluster score correlation.

The original binary proof is short because the binary restriction imposes a
strong moment identity:

```text
W_i^2 = W_i.
```

That identity gives:

```text
within-group residualized treatment variance = Wbar * (1 - Wbar).
```

Then the rest is cluster-sum algebra:

```text
cluster variance = robust diagonal part + within-cluster cross-products.
```

So the proof path is:

```text
binary treatment
  -> W_i^2 = W_i

  -> clustered score square expands into pairwise products

```

be reduced to a treatment share. The expression:


depends on the full second moment of `D`, not only on its mean.

Let `p(omega)` be the probability of assignment state `omega`. Define the

The centered treatment coordinate is:

The treatment assignment covariance kernel is:

```text

  = E_p[Dcenter_i Dcenter_j]
  = sum_omega p(omega)
      (D_i(omega) - E_p[D_i])
      (D_j(omega) - E_p[D_j]).
```

This `Sigma` replaces the binary treatment-share formula.

### 3.3 Score Variance as a Quadratic Form

Consider the linear score:

```text
L(omega) = sum_i D_i(omega) u_i.
```

Its design variance is:

```text
Var_p(L)
  = E_p[(L - E_p[L])^2].
```

Because:

```text
L(omega) - E_p[L]
  = sum_i (D_i(omega) - E_p[D_i]) u_i
  = sum_i Dcenter_i(omega) u_i,
```

we get:

```text
Var_p(L)
  = E_p[(sum_i Dcenter_i u_i)^2]
  = E_p[sum_i sum_j Dcenter_i Dcenter_j u_i u_j]
  = sum_i sum_j u_i E_p[Dcenter_i Dcenter_j] u_j
  = sum_i sum_j u_i Sigma_ij u_j.
```

In matrix notation:

```text
Var_p(L) = u' Sigma u.
```

```text
betaHat - beta = S^(-1) * L,
```

```text

  = Var_p(S^(-1) L)
  = S^(-2) Var_p(L)
  = S^(-2) u' Sigma u.
```

This is the continuous-treatment design covariance variance:

```text
V_design = S^(-2) * u' Sigma u.
```

## 6. Exact Finite-Sample Case

The simplest continuous-treatment theorem requires:

1. A finite assignment probability model `p(omega)`.
2. A residualized treatment vector `D(omega)`.
3. A fixed residual vector `u`.
4. A nonzero OLS denominator.
5. A covariance kernel:

   ```text
   Sigma_ij = Cov_p(D_i, D_j)
   ```

   or, with random denominator,

   ```text
   Sigma_ij = Cov_p(Dnorm_i, Dnorm_j).
   ```

6. Exact feasible inputs:

   ```text
   uhat = u
   SigmaHat = Sigma
   ```

Then:

```text
dcCCV = true finite-design variance of betaHat - beta.
```

In the fixed-denominator case:

```text
dcCCV
  = S^(-2) * u' Sigma u
  = Var_p(betaHat - beta).
```

In the random-denominator case:

```text
dcCCV
  = u' Cov_p(Dnorm) u
  = Var_p(betaHat - beta).
```

The continuous proof is therefore not weaker than the binary proof. It is more
general, but it asks for the covariance object explicitly.

## 7. Feasible Asymptotic Case

In empirical applications, the true covariance kernel `Sigma` is usually not
known. The feasible estimator uses:

```text
dcCCV_n = S_n^(-2) * uhat_n' SigmaHat_n uhat_n.
```

The asymptotic proof needs conditions ensuring:

```text
dcCCV_n / V_design -> 1
```

or equivalently:

```text
designSE_n / dcSE_n -> 1.
```

A minimal high-level assumption set is:

1. Score CLT:

   ```text
   linearized score_n -> Normal(0, 1) in distribution.
   ```

2. Asymptotic linearization:

   ```text
   (betaHat_n - beta) / designSE_n
     = linearized score_n + remainder_n,
   ```

   with:

   ```text
   remainder_n -> 0 in probability.
   ```

3. Residual consistency:

   ```text
   uhat_n -> u.
   ```

4. Kernel consistency:

   ```text
   SigmaHat_n -> Sigma.
   ```

5. Regularity of the standard error:

   ```text
   V_design > 0,
   dcSE_n != 0 eventually,
   and the feasible SE ratio is measurable.
   ```

on the limiting normal distribution at the interval boundary.

For an administrative policy design, assignment may be governed by rules that
depend on variables such as prior wages, eligibility thresholds, geography,
industry, or employer characteristics. If all rule inputs and assignment
probabilities were known, one could in principle compute `Sigma` directly.

available. Then the proof should use the feasible asymptotic route:


- an iid or independent-cluster sample-kernel law of large numbers;
- a weak-dependence law of large numbers across administrative cells;

learn or know the covariance kernel governing continuous assignment variation.

| --- | --- | --- |

The original binary proof works because binary treatment collapses second
moments into first moments. The continuous extension works by refusing to make
that collapse: it keeps every second moment through the covariance kernel

algebraic:

```text

  + residual consistency
  + SigmaHat consistency
  + nondegenerate standard errors
  -> valid studentized dcCCV inference.
```

content.thinking:
The key insight is that when everything is observed—meaning the estimated values match the true values exactly—the finite-sample variance formula becomes exact rather than approximate, bypassing any need for asymptotic theory or kernel consistency assumptions. In the H-2A case, all 17 AEWR paths are directly observed and the reference distribution from cyclic reassignments is fully specified, so the covariance matrix is computed exactly through enumeration rather than estimation.

But there's a critical detail about random denominators: when the denominator itself is random, the kernel must be the covariance of the normalized terms D_i / (Σ_k D_k)², not just the raw covariance of D_i scaled by the observed denominator. The design re-solves OLS in every state, which handles this correctly. The approach of keeping the full 17×K error matrix E and computing Var(q) = (1/17)‖Eg‖² aligns with the dcCCV methodology in vector form, but I need to verify whether the random-denominator issue affects whether this formula is actually correct.

The design's re-solving of b_{e,a} = (X_a'X_a)^{-1} X_a' û in each state is the vector analogue of the normalization correction — the state-specific Gram matrix handles the random-denominator adjustment. So keeping E with its re-solved rows while dropping per-term SEs preserves this essential feature.

Looking at what "everything is observed" means relative to the current design: the design already uses the exact-case reasoning when it forms V with divisor 17 as a probability covariance under a finite reference law rather than a sample covariance. But there's a gap — the design fixes û at the observed OLS residual, whereas the exact theorem requires the true residual u. Since û = M_X u, the design's û isn't actually u.

This is the residual-consistency condition that the design can't fully satisfy. With K around 900+ and N = 30,410, the projection M_X shrinks residuals substantially, which is why the HC1-style N/(N-K) adjustment appears in the saturation note. So "everything is observed" really applies to Σ, not to u — the residual-df adjustment is the patch for the one input that isn't exactly observed. And as the saturation program grows K, this tension between maximal richness and exactness gets worse.…

theorem heterogeneityScore_weightedBeta_eq_zero
    (Dtilde beta : α → ℝ)
    (hS : ObservationLevel.denom Dtilde ≠ 0) :
    heterogeneityScore Dtilde beta (weightedBeta Dtilde beta) = 0 := by
  classical
  unfold ObservationLevel.denom at hS
  unfold heterogeneityScore weightedBeta ObservationLevel.denom
  let A : ℝ := ∑ a : α, Dtilde a ^ 2 * beta a
  let S : ℝ := ∑ a : α, Dtilde a ^ 2
  have hS' : S ≠ 0 := by
    simpa [S] using hS
  change (∑ a : α, Dtilde a ^ 2 * (beta a - A / S)) = 0
  calc
    (∑ a : α, Dtilde a ^ 2 * (beta a - A / S))
        = (∑ a : α, Dtilde a ^ 2 * beta a) -
            ∑ a : α, Dtilde a ^ 2 * (A / S) := by
            simp_rw [mul_sub]
            rw [Finset.sum_sub_distrib]
    _ = A - S * (A / S) := by
            rw [Finset.sum_mul]
    _ = 0 := by
            field_simp [hS']
            ring

content.thinking:
Looking at the precise theorem statement, I need four key hypotheses: the linear model with fixed residuals across states, a nonzero denominator condition in every state, exact residuals matching the true errors, and the covariance kernel derived from the normalized treatment variable.

The critical insight is that "everything observed" gives me the kernel condition and denominator requirement across all 17 states, but it doesn't automatically satisfy the exact residuals condition — that's the fundamental gap. There's also a subtle but important point about `betaHat_error_weightedBeta`: when treatment effects vary heterogeneously, the OLS estimator's error relative to the variance-weighted average effect has zero heterogeneity score, meaning the exact theorem applies specifically to the treatment-variance-weighted estimand, not an arbitrary target. This matters because the design's reported standardizations — equal county-year weight, equal region-year weight, farm-employment weight — don't align with the D̃²-weighting that the exactness theorem privileges, which is a real tension between what the theorem covers and what the design actually reports.

In the design itself, heterogeneity is parameterized directly as β^(0) + β^(1)Z rather than residualized, so the heterogeneity score is zero by construction if the parameterization is correct — but if it's misspecified, residual heterogeneity enters the score and only the D̃²-weighted target gets exact coverage. That's the precise cost of the parametric approach, and it connects back to his point about richer parameterization: modeling B heterogeneity is what drives the score to zero.

For the vector case, the design re-solves the coefficient vector in each state using the standard FWL formula with the random denominator (X'X)^{-1}, which is the vector analogue of what I called normalizedTreatment. The variance matrix V is computed as the average outer product of deviations from the mean, and my recommendation to keep the full residual matrix E and compute the squared norm is arithmetically identical — it's exactly the projection of the residuals in the direction of the treatment variation. Now I need to verify whether (1/17)‖Eg‖² equals g'Vg exactly.

The verification checks out: since V is constructed from the centered E matrix, g'Vg = (1/17)g'E'Eg = (1/17)‖Eg‖², so the two approaches are exact. The key insight he's flagging is that while my suggestion to keep E and skip some machinery is fine, I can't simplify away the CCV framework itself — the delta method still has to use the dcCCV kernel, which requires re-solving per state with the random denominator, building from normalized treatment, and relying on the fact that Σ is enumerated rather than estimated, so there's no asymptotic approximation needed.

Now the remaining caveats: û differs from u, and there's the heterogeneity issue to address. The convex-combination formula from AAIW (blending robust and clustered covariance via λ_D) is actually the wrong tool here since we have full observation — that formula is for when you must estimate the kernel, but with everything observed we just compute Σ directly, which is consistent. The repo contains both approaches, and the rejected one happens to have the nicer formula, so it's worth clarifying that distinction. The sampling fraction q in the λ formula becomes 1 when everything is observed, but more fundamentally, the exact route bypasses λ entirely. I should also bring up the IV case.

The ShockDesign module confirms the pushforward relationship where the constructed instrument's covariance kernel equals the exposure map applied to the primitive shock covariance—this matters if pursuing the FLS-instrument approach. The Inference section offers an Anderson-Rubin alternative using block scores that provides coverage even without a strong first stage. I'm structuring the response to first acknowledge the observation that everything is observed, which connects to Section 6 of the comparison document.

The key insight is that the finite-sample variance theorem for OLS provides exact coverage without relying on asymptotics or kernel consistency—a much stronger foundation than clustered standard errors. The AAIW convex-combination formula in the extension document is the wrong tool here because it's designed for cases where you must estimate the kernel; when you can enumerate it directly, that formula doesn't apply. Looking at the theorem's four hypotheses against what the design satisfies: the exact Sigma comes from enumeration, the denominator is checkable, the linearity assumption holds with fixed errors across states (matching how the design reassigns paths), but the fourth hypothesis—that the estimated residuals equal the true errors—fails because the OLS residuals are the projection M_X u rather than u itself. This gap is where saturation makes things worse, which is why the finite-sample degrees-of-freedom adjustment N/(N−K_eff) isn't just cosmetic but actually addresses this inexactness. For the random denominator case, I need to work with the normalized treatment kernel D/(D'D) rather than raw D, and re-solving OLS within each state captures this exactly.

The heterogeneity theorem shows that when effects vary, the heterogeneity score only vanishes for the D̃²-weighted target, so exactness is tied to the treatment-variance-weighted estimand. The design reports equal weights across county-year and region-year combinations, but under model misspecification only the D̃² weighting preserves the exact identity—this gives a concrete reason to report that weighted effect as a benchmark alongside the standardized versions. The tension with saturation is real: as K grows, the estimated residuals degrade further from the true errors, so I should recommend reporting both the adjusted and unadjusted versions to show the sensitivity.…

content.text:
Right — and "everything is observed" is exactly the hypothesis that puts you in the exact finite-sample theorem rather than the feasible asymptotic one. `dcCCV_eq_finite_design_variance_of_ols` gives equality, not convergence: with the reference law fully specified over seventeen states you enumerate the covariance kernel rather than estimating it, so none of the asymptotic apparatus applies — no score CLT, no `G → ∞`, no kernel consistency, no requirement that `max_g S_g/S → 0`. That also settles why `markdowns/ccv_extension.md` is the wrong object here despite having the prettier formula. The AAIW convex combination `λ_D V_cluster + (1−λ_D) V_robust` exists to interpolate when the kernel must be inferred from within-cluster variation, and `q` in it is a sampling fraction. You aren't sampling regions from a superpopulation. The README's refusal to use it is correct, and the reason is stronger than "unsupported."

The theorem carries four hypotheses and it's worth being precise about which ones you actually have. `hSigma` holds exactly by enumeration. `hDenom` is checkable in every state. `hY` requires the residual vector to be held fixed across assignment states while the design matrix varies, which is what holding `û` fixed and regenerating every AEWR column does. The one you do not have is `hu`, that `uhat = u`. Your `û` is the OLS residual `M_X u`, not `u`, and the gap widens with `K`. So the `N/(N − K_eff)` adjustment in your saturation note is not cosmetic hygiene — it is the patch on the single input to the exact theorem that isn't exact, and everything I've been recommending for the past several turns makes it worse. That's the real tension in the saturation program: richer conditional means buy identification and cost you exactness in the variance. Report both adjusted and unadjusted as your note requires, and read the parameter-to-row guard as a CCV-exactness guard rather than a numerical-stability guard.

On the random denominator, the theorem is unambiguous that `SigmaHat` must estimate the kernel of `D/(D'D)` and not of raw `D`, which is the scalar shadow of re-solving the Gram matrix in every state. That constraint survives my recommendation to stop materializing `V` intact, because `g'Vg = (1/17)‖Eg‖²` exactly when `E` is the seventeen-by-`K` matrix of centered re-solved coefficient errors. What would break it is computing a kernel from the reassigned treatment columns and scaling by the observed denominator, which is the shortcut the README already warns against. Keep the re-solve; drop only the `K × K` materialization.

There's a further condition in the Lean that bears directly on your parameterization argument. `betaHat_error_heterogeneous` decomposes the OLS error into a residual score plus a heterogeneity score, and `heterogeneityScore_weightedBeta_eq_zero` shows the second term vanishes only when the target is the treatment-variance-weighted effect `Σ D̃² β_a / Σ D̃²`. So the exactness result attaches to that weighting specifically. If your projection of `B_it` onto `Z_i` and the county and market moderators is correct, the point is moot, since heterogeneity is modeled rather than left in the score. If it's misspecified, the residual heterogeneity enters the score and only the `D̃²`-weighted estimand retains the exact identity, while equal county-year, equal region-year, and farm-employment standardizations do not. That argues for carrying the `D̃²`-weighted effect as a reported benchmark next to the declared standardizations, precisely because it's the one the theorem covers unconditionally.

Worth noting what this does to the rank ceiling, since it isn't what I implied earlier. Rank at most sixteen isn't a limitation of an approximation you could improve on — it is the exact rank of the true finite-design covariance under the stated reference law, and `covKernel_isPSD` plus the seventeen-state construction make it structural. `t_16` isn't conservatism; it's the design.

If the FLS assignment-model route from earlier gets built, the panel-IV modules already have the piece you'd need. `ShockDesign` proves the pushforward `Cov(Lε) = L Γ L'`, so a constructed instrument's kernel is the fixed exposure map applied to the primitive shock covariance, with primitive covariance vanishing across area blocks and unrestricted within them. `Inference` then gives Anderson-Rubin coverage from complete-path block scores without requiring a strong first stage. That is the formal bridge between the `panel_iv` branch and this design, and it's already proved rather than aspirational.

I don't want FLS. I want properly done Wooldridge-Mundlak-Chamberlain with rich parameterization / saturation including interaction terms with properly applied CCV standard error adjustment to the post-fit inference for the delta method constructed terms.

content.thinking:
He's asking for the concrete specification now—properly executed WMC with rich parameterization and saturation including interactions, with CCV applied correctly to post-fit delta method constructed terms, and no FLS. I need to pull together all the decisions we've made across this conversation into one coherent spec: symmetric year coding with all 10 year dummies and no intercept, linear dose only without higher-order polynomials, and interactions.

The key decisions are: no separate pre-period year values or imposed trends; pre-period covariates are means at each hierarchy level. No focal/nuisance split—the history set for year s is {2011,...,s} for leave-future-out sequential exogeneity. Keep the 17×K matrix E of re-solved centered coefficient errors but never materialize the K×K covariance. CCV uses exact finite-design with random denominator, re-solving OLS in every state, so Var(q) = (1/17)‖Eg‖². Rank constraint is ≤16 with t_16 critical value. No FLS or IV.

Now he's laying out the actual notation and specification: county i, year t from 2013 to 2022, region r(i) across 17 regions, market m(i) across 745 markets, state q(i) across 48 states. The dose is constructed as 100 times the log difference in AEWR between consecutive years. Baseline covariates are K source variables measured 2008–2010, each entering as its mean across that period, then hierarchically decomposed.

He's now defining the hierarchical decomposition of covariates into county, market, state, and region components, with each standardized and region components excluded from the causal dictionary per the representation rule. Z_i is the standardized baseline AEWR bite measured at the level channel without decomposition. The conditional mean specification includes year dummies with no intercept, region intercepts with one absorbed, and a Chamberlain treatment path with year-specific coefficients for the dose history up to each year. Adding the interaction terms and checking computational complexity... derators with all coordinates uniformly and let the row guard handle size constraints. Or I could lean on the CRC framing: B_it is the coefficient on W_it, so heterogeneity lives in the *effect* of dose, while the full history path enters through the Chamberlain intercept projection—which captures *levels*, not effects. That's a cleaner split than arbitrarily tiering by year. So the natural structure is: history enters the intercept projection, and causal heterogeneity attaches to the dose coordinates themselves.

But I dropped that distinction earlier. Let me reconsider. Actually, the cleanest approach is to treat the coefficient ρ_{th} as simultaneously the causal effect at horizon t−h and the Chamberlain projection coefficient—they're the same thing. That's precisely why dropping the focal/nuisance split works. So in the moderated version, every (t,h) pair gets its own moderated coefficient, and I'm now counting how many parameters that creates: 75 dose-horizon pairs times 26 coefficient variants (accounting for Z interactions and county/market moderators with K=12), giving me 1,950 total parameters to estimate.

Adding in the untreated mean structure—10 years times 3 levels times 12 counties, doubled for Z—that's another 720 columns, plus year and region indicators, pushing the total to around 3,000 parameters. With N=30,410 observations, the ratio K/N ≈ 0.10 is manageable, though the degrees-of-freedom adjustment creates an 11% variance inflation that I'll need to report. Now I'm checking whether the region-varying structure holds up—looking at how many columns each year contributes when I allow region-specific variation.

For 2022, the year cell plus 12 path coordinates gives 13 columns, and if I tried to add all pairwise cross-horizon interactions among those 12, that balloons to 66, which is way too expensive. Restricting to adjacent pairs only still costs 24 columns in 2022, exceeding my budget. So cross-horizon interactions at the region level need to be rationed—either I keep only the most recent adjacent pair W_t·W_{t−1}, which costs 1 per year and stays under 16 total, or I move those interactions into a moderated form where they vary at the county level but stay free at the region level, though that weakens the heredity constraint.

The honest approach is to acknowledge that region-level cross-horizon is genuinely constrained by the 16-coordinate budget, and I can allow at most 3 unmoderated cross-horizon products in the terminal year (13 + 3 = 16), selected by a declared rule like the three most recent adjacent pairs—this is the one place where recency-based selection is forced by the rank constraint rather than chosen for modeling reasons. County and market-level moderated cross-horizon products remain unlimited.

Now for the delta-method mechanics: I'm computing how a small shift in a coordinate affects any reported quantity through the gradient of the design matrix, accounting for the path column, its interactions with Z, moderator interactions, and any cross-horizon products involving that coordinate, then constructing confidence intervals using the empirical variance scaled by the sample size.

For the E matrix construction, I fit once on the observed data to get γ̂ and residuals, then for each of 17 bootstrap states I regenerate all AEWR-derived columns from the donor path assignments and re-solve for the state-specific coefficients, centering them around their mean to form the rows of E. I need to verify that all 17 states identify the same K columns—if any state drops a column the specification fails, which was an issue before with the 2013 history coordinate, but now 2013 has three coordinates so it should be stable.

The key thing to check first is whether the reassignment makes the design singular in any state, since that's the guard most likely to fail. For implementation, I'll solve 17 separate factorizations since only X changes while the residuals stay fixed—computing X_a'X_a and X_a'û per state and solving via the normal equations. With K around 3000 and N around 30,000, the cross-product matrix is manageable at 72MB, and the total computational cost is 17 times the standard least-squares flops.

I should focus the advice on the binding constraints: the K² memory footprint for the Gram matrix and the N×K dense matrix, rather than over-complicating the compute story. I'll also report the D̃²-weighted benchmark alongside the standardizations and structure everything as a concrete spec.

content.text:
Here's the whole thing assembled. Write `T = {2013,…,2022}`, `D_t` the year indicator with all ten retained and no intercept, `H(t) = {2011,…,t}` the admissible dose coordinates for outcome year `t`, and `X^ℓ_{ik}` the standardized hierarchical component of baseline covariate `k` at level `ℓ ∈ {C,M,S}`, each built from the 2008–2010 mean and nothing else.

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[Y_{it}\mid\cdot]
&= \sum_{t\in T} D_t\alpha_t \;+\; a_{r(i)}
\;+\; \sum_{t}\sum_{h\in H(t)} D_t\,W_{r(i),h}\big(\rho_{th} + \rho^Z_{th}Z_i + \textstyle\sum_{\ell\in\{C,M\}}\sum_k \theta_{th\ell k}X^{\ell}_{ik}\big)\\
&\quad+ \sum_{t}\sum_{\substack{h<h'\\ h,h'\in H(t)}} D_t\,W_{r(i),h}W_{r(i),h'}\big(\varphi_{thh'} + \textstyle\sum_{\ell\in\{C,M\}}\sum_k \varphi^{\ell k}_{thh'}X^{\ell}_{ik}\big)\\
&\quad+ \sum_{t} D_t Z_i\psi_t
\;+\; \sum_{t}\sum_{\ell\in\{C,M,S\}}\sum_k D_t X^{\ell}_{ik}\big(\delta_{t\ell k} + \delta^Z_{t\ell k}Z_i\big)
\;+\; \sum_{t}\sum_{j<k} D_t X^{C\!/\!M}_{ij}X^{C\!/\!M}_{ik}\lambda_{tjk}
\end{aligned}
$$

The third term is the whole design in one line: there is no causal block and no nuisance block, just the dose path entering year `t` with a coefficient that is itself a linear projection onto `Z_i` and the county and market components. That projection is the correlated-random-coefficient device applied uniformly to every `(t,h)` pair, and it's what drives the heterogeneity score to zero rather than leaving it in the residual. `ρ_{th}` at `h = t` is the contemporaneous effect, at `h = t−1` the one-year lag, and so on down to 2011, with no horizon count chosen anywhere.

Region-cell demand in year `t` is `1 + |H(t)| + (\text{unmoderated cross-horizon pairs})`, which is `1 + 3 = 4` in 2013 and `1 + 12 = 13` in 2022. That leaves three coordinates in the terminal year, so at most three unmoderated `φ_{thh'}` products, and this is the one place where a recency rule is forced by rank rather than chosen for convenience — declare it as such. Everything moderated is unconstrained at region level: the `θ` block, the `φ^{ℓk}` block, the `δ` and `λ` blocks all live in 3,041- and 745-dimensional space. Region components stay out of the causal dictionary and `Z_i` enters as a level only, or the level-plus-components identity spans the omitted region interaction and spends the ledger invisibly. State components appear only in `δ`, and only after the residualized incremental-rank audit.

With twelve source variables the `(t,h)` pairs number 75, each carrying `1 + 1 + 2K = 26` columns, so roughly 1,950 causal columns against about 720 in the untreated mean plus pairs, region and year cells, and `K ≈ 3{,}000` against `N = 30{,}410`. That ratio is the binding statistic and it is not a stability concern — it is the CCV-exactness concern, because `N/(N−K_eff) ≈ 1.11` is the size of the correction you are applying to the one input the finite-design theorem needs exactly.

The inference pipeline is then three passes. Fit once on the observed design for `γ̂` and `û`. For each of the seventeen cyclic path assignments, regenerate every AEWR-derived column — the `W_{r,h}` levels, their `Z` and moderator interactions, and every cross-horizon product — from the donor path assigned to that region, holding outcomes, covariates, labels, and `û` fixed, then re-solve `b_a = (X_a'X_a)^{-1}X_a'û`. The re-solve is not optional: the exact theorem takes the kernel of `D/(D'D)`, so the state-specific Gram inverse is the random-denominator correction, and state zero must come out exactly zero from the normal equations. Center to get `e_a` and stack into `E`, seventeen by `K`.

For any reported quantity, build the gradient by column-differencing the design matrix under the perturbation you're reporting — `g = (\sum\omega)^{-1}\sum_i \omega_i[x_i(W+δ) − x_i(W)]` for a finite change, the analytic column derivative for a marginal effect. A `δ`-shift in `W_{r,s-p}` touches the `(t{=}s, h{=}s{-}p)` column, its `Z` and moderator interactions, and every cross-horizon product containing that coordinate, and is zero everywhere else. Then `q̂ = g'γ̂` and `Var(q̂) = (1/17)\lVert Eg\rVert^2`, seventeen inner products, with `q̂ \pm t_{0.975,16}\sqrt{Var}`. Never form `E'E`: the `K×K` covariance is 72 MB of nothing at `K = 3{,}000` and it is the term that should come out of the working-set proxy, leaving the `N×K` design and the `K×K` Gram as the real memory guards.

Three things to enforce before trusting any of it. The common-basis assertion has to pass in all seventeen states with the identical `K` columns identified, and with 2013 now carrying only three path coordinates that is the year most likely to go singular under reassignment — check it first, because a lost column there invalidates the whole spec rather than one estimate. The analytic gradient must agree with the model-matrix gradient to `10^{-9}` in sup norm, and a newly generated causal column receiving a silent zero has to stop the run. And carry the `\tilde D^2`-weighted effect as a reported benchmark next to the declared standardizations, since that is the estimand the exactness identity covers without conditioning on the `B_{it}` projection being correctly specified.

import duckdb
P = "/mnt/user-data/uploads/county_year_panel.parquet"
c = duckdb.connect()
c.sql(f"create view p as select * from read_parquet('{P}')")

print("=== year coverage ===")
for y, n, nc in c.sql("select year, count(*), count(distinct county_fips) from p group by 1 order by 1").fetchall():
    print(f"  {int(y)}  rows={n:>6,}  counties={nc:>6,}")

print("\n=== hierarchy cardinality (all rows) ===")
q = """select count(distinct aewr_region_id) regions, count(distinct state_fips) states,
       count(distinct cz_id) czs, count(distinct county_fips) counties,
       count(distinct (state_fips||'|'||cz_id||'|'||aewr_region_id)) market_cells from p"""
print(dict(zip([d[0] for d in c.sql(q).description], c.sql(q).fetchone())))

print("\n=== hierarchy nesting: is county->region unique? state->region? ===")
print(c.sql("""select
  (select count(*) from (select county_fips from p group by 1 having count(distinct aewr_region_id)>1)) counties_multi_region,
  (select count(*) from (select state_fips from p group by 1 having count(distinct aewr_region_id)>1)) states_multi_region,
  (select count(*) from (select cz_id from p group by 1 having count(distinct state_fips)>1)) czs_multi_state
""").fetchall())

print("\n=== AEWR unique within region-year? ===")
print(c.sql("""select count(*) as region_years,
 sum(case when nd>1 then 1 else 0 end) as region_years_with_multiple_aewr
 from (select aewr_region_id, year, count(distinct aewr) nd from p group by 1,2)""").fetchall())
EOF
uv run --python 3.14 -- python3 coverage.py

content.thinking:
I'm reviewing the dataset structure and finding that the 46,615 rows represent 15 years of data across counties with nearly complete coverage from 2008 to 2022, which gives me a solid baseline period and historical context for analysis. The geographic breakdown shows 17 regions, 48 states, and over 3,000 counties organized into market cells, though there's a slight discrepancy between the expected and actual counts that I'm noting.

I'm also checking the nesting structure — states appear to map cleanly to single regions, and the 128 CZs that cross state lines explain why I need to define markets as state × CZ × region combinations. But I'm noticing something important: the README claims AEWR is unique within region-year from 2010 onward, yet I'm seeing 15 region-years with multiple distinct AEWR values. That's…

import duckdb
P = "/mnt/user-data/uploads/county_year_panel.parquet"
c = duckdb.connect(); c.sql(f"create view p as select * from read_parquet('{P}')")

print("=== which region-years have >1 distinct AEWR ===")
print(c.sql("""select year, count(*) n_regions_nonunique from
 (select aewr_region_id, year, count(distinct aewr) nd from p group by 1,2) where nd>1
 group by 1 order by 1""").fetchall())

print("\n=== AEWR null counts by year ===")
print(c.sql("select year, sum(aewr is null)::int aewr_null, sum(aewr_l1 is null)::int l1_null from p group by 1 order by 1").fetchall())

print("\n=== is aewr_l1 == prior-year aewr within region? ===")
print(c.sql("""with r as (select distinct aewr_region_id, year, aewr, aewr_l1 from p where aewr is not null),
 j as (select a.aewr_region_id, a.year, a.aewr_l1, b.aewr prior from r a left join r b
       on a.aewr_region_id=b.aewr_region_id and b.year=a.year-1)
 select count(*) checked, sum(case when prior is null then 1 else 0 end) no_prior,
        max(abs(aewr_l1-prior)) max_abs_diff from j where prior is not null""").fetchall())

print("\n=== constructed dose W = 100*dlog(aewr), by year (region-year level) ===")
print(c.sql("""select year, count(*) regions, round(min(w),3) minw, round(max(w),3) maxw,
  round(avg(w),3) meanw, sum(case when abs(w)<0.5 then 1 else 0 end)::int near_zero
 from (select distinct aewr_region_id, year, 100*(ln(aewr)-ln(aewr_l1)) w from p
       where aewr is not null and aewr_l1 is not null)
 group by 1 order by 1""").fetchall())
EOF

content.thinking:
The Dose variable reconstructs correctly from the source data, matching the README's pooled range of −4.81 to 20.56 across 204 region-year cells (17 regions × 12 years from 2011-2022). The README mentions 170 cells for the analysis period, which corresponds to 2013-2022, so the numbers align. Now I'm noticing that 2009 and 2010 have a different distribution pattern with 47 distinct region-year AEWR values instead of the expected 17 — this is the state-specific OES exception the README flags. In 2009, AEWR isn't unique within region-year (15 of 17 regions have multiple values), confirming that region-year-level treatment only applies from 2010 onward. Since the specification starts history at 2011, this shouldn't matter directly, but the 2010 dose calculation uses 2009 AEWR as a lag, which means W_{r,2011} would inherit that contamination. The 2010 dose varies within region because the 2009 AEWR lag varies, even though 2010 levels themselves are unique within region-year.

So W_{r,2011} = 100*(ln aewr_2011 − ln aewr_2010) is actually fine since both levels are unique. Only W_{r,2010} is contaminated, and since H(t) starts at 2011, that's not used. The dose table confirms W is region-year level for all of 2011-2022.

The aewr_l1 column doesn't exactly match the prior-year aewr — max absolute difference is 5.3 across 441 checks. This discrepancy likely stems from the 2009 multi-value issue creating mismatched pairs in the join. I should either construct my own lag from the level data or investigate further, but restricting to 2011 onward would clarify whether this is a real problem.

Looking at quasi-stayers across 2011-2022, 14 of 204 cells have |W| < 0.5 and 29 have |W| < 1.0, which gives a sense of how many regions show minimal wage growth.

Now checking the baseline covariates and outcomes for completeness — 2009 has 3,103 counties instead of 3,108 (5 missing), and aewr_l1 is null for 5 rows in 2010, meaning those counties have incomplete baseline data. Next I need to verify the 12 baseline covariates and 8 outcomes are present and non-missing across their respective periods, plus check emp_farm_2011 for eligibility and normalization.

The eligibility filter yields around 3,041 counties. All 12 baseline covariates are accounted for — H2A certification and application shares, agricultural wage percentiles, population and employment metrics, farm income composition, labor and production expenses, and cropland acreage. Now checking the outcomes.…

Filtering to `emp_farm_2011 > 0` yields **30,410 rows, 3,041 counties, 10 years, 17 regions, 48 states, 745 market cells** — the README's numbers to the digit. All 3,041 counties appear in all ten analysis years, so the panel is balanced, and no county changes region, state, or commuting zone over time, so the hierarchy is strictly nested and time-invariant as `i ⊂ m ⊂ q ⊂ r` requires. The file itself is wider than the estimation window: 46,615 rows covering 2008 through 2022 across 3,108 counties, 136 columns.

The dose is constructible and lands exactly where it should. Taking `100·(ln aewr − ln aewr_l1)` at the region-year level gives 204 cells over 2011–2022 with support from −4.81 to 20.56, matching the documented range. Treatment is genuinely region-year from 2010 onward: the only year with within-region AEWR variation is 2009, where 15 of 17 regions carry multiple values, which is the OES exception. That contaminates the 2010 *dose* but not the 2010 *level*, so `W_{r,2011}` onward is clean and `H(t) = {2011,…,t}` is unaffected. On quasi-stayer mass, which matters for the no-stayers identification argument, 14 of 204 cells sit within half a log point of zero and 29 within a full point — thin but not empty.

All twelve baseline covariates are present, with missingness between zero and 2.9 percent over 2008–2010, well inside what region-median-then-national-median imputation handles. All eight outcomes are constructible: five directly from `nbr_applications_start_year`, `nbr_employers_balanced_start_year`, `nbr_workers_requested_start_year`, `nbr_workers_certified_start_year`, and `man_hours_certified_start_year`, all with zero nulls; `any_application` by thresholding; and the two ratios from `h2a_cert_positions_per_application_start_year` and `h2a_cert_hours_per_position_start_year`. Those two are null in about 34 percent of rows, which is the zero-denominator structure rather than a data defect — 20,414 of 30,410 county-years have positive applications and 20,156 have positive certified positions. Those are the restricted samples where the parameter-to-row guard will bind hardest and where the tier selector should be predeclared. `Z_i` is constructible for all 3,041 counties with no nulls.

Three things worth knowing before you build. Use `emp_farm_2011` rather than `bea_farm_emp_2011` for eligibility and weighting: they agree exactly where both are present, but the BEA version has 900 additional nulls in the analysis window and yields 3,018 rather than 3,041 eligible counties. Five eligible counties are missing their 2009 row, so their 2008–2010 baseline means average two years instead of three — decide whether to accept the uneven mean or drop them, since with means-only projection there's no trend to break. And `aewr_l1` disagrees with the prior year's `aewr` by up to 5.3 in a region-level comparison; that's almost certainly an artifact of the 2009 multi-valued rows rather than a data error, but since the whole dose path rests on it, build the lag yourself from the level within region rather than trusting the shipped column.

content.thinking:
I should dig deeper into the schema issues rather than just repeating what I flagged before. The `year` column being stored as DOUBLE instead of INTEGER is definitely odd, and I need to check whether those ID fields like `county_fips` and `state_fips` have any leading zero inconsistencies. There's also something off with `aewr_l1` that I should investigate properly, and I noticed the 2009 data seems truncated in my view.

Looking at the actual structure, I'm seeing some real red flags: `cropland_acr` versus `cropland_acr_2007` suggests one might be time-varying while the other is fixed, and having metadata columns like `h2a_prediction_cutoff_year` and `h2a_prediction_model_spec` embedded in a panel dataset is unusual—it implies the data might be a cross-product over model specifications, but the row count doesn't support that. There are also several near-duplicate columns measuring the same thing with different year suffixes (`nbr_workers_requested_all_years` and its variants, plus `h2a_req_share_farm_workers_start_year` versus `_2011_start_year`), and some columns like `emp_farm_2011` and `bea_farm_emp_2011` differ only in their null patterns. I'm also wondering whether columns suffixed with "_2011" and "_2007" are actually snapshots from those years or if they're time-invariant measures that just happen to be labeled that way.

On the outcome side, I need to check whether zeros in `nbr_applications_start_year` are genuine or imputed values, and whether there are any negative values where they shouldn't logically exist. The `aewr_cz_p25` column is described as an "AEWR bite"—likely log(AEWR) minus log(wage_p25)—so negative values would mean AEWR falls below the 25th percentile wage, which is plausible. I also need to verify there are no duplicate county-year rows, confirm which states are excluded (probably Alaska, Hawaii, and DC), and check…
