content.text:
The unit-level ratio estimands are in, and they close the last gap on the "every margin" list.

Year-specific Grams work as expected — 170 matrices instead of 17, the county side still shared across all seventeen reassignment states, state-zero invariants at `2.1e-12` and `3.7e-13`. On the restricted samples of 20,414 and 20,156 county-years:

```
certified positions per application       +1.023  (SE 0.360)
certified hours per certified position    -9.228  (SE 5.226)
```

Both under equal region-year weighting, at `h=0`, per one log point of AEWR. So a permanent one-percent AEWR lift raises certified positions per application by about one position — against a mean of roughly 19 — and the effect on hours per position is indistinguishable from zero.

That is worth putting next to the aggregate version. Two turns ago the `E[num]/E[den]` construction gave `−0.545` (SE 2.06) for positions per application; the unit-level `E[num/den]` gives `+1.023` (SE 0.360), opposite sign and six times more precise. They are different estimands and both are legitimate, but the divergence is large enough that the design record has to name which one the paper reports. The unit-level version weights every participating county-year equally; the ratio-of-means version weights by application volume, so it is dominated by large filers. Given the consolidation story the other outcomes point to, that distinction is substantive rather than technical — the two answers differ precisely because the response varies across the size distribution.

The one caution on these: region-year cell sizes fall to 15 and 14 at the minimum, so the smallest cells are thin and the equal region-year weighting gives them full weight. Weighting by application exposure, which the README also declares, would be the natural companion.

That leaves the audit results as the binding statement on what's reportable: `+1` log point only, with the design-space leverage at 1.14–1.20 times observed maximum flagged as modest extrapolation; `+5` and `+10` off the table. Everything at `h ≥ 1` still has intervals covering zero on the volume outcomes, and the participation and per-application results are the two that separate.

I need to figure out what's most valuable to tackle next. The elasticity estimate of around 9 seems implausible and I haven't fully investigated it—that's the biggest substantive question still open. My working theory is that the moderator block might be capturing region-year variation that's skewing the results, but I haven't confirmed this yet.

The real test would be running a specification curve: varying the moderator tier and lag-profile order to see if the elasticity holds steady across different specifications or swings around. If it's stable, the estimate is genuine; if it moves, it's just absorption bias. That's actually the saturation note's headline figure and I haven't produced it yet.

The other critical piece is the strict exogeneity test—the history-rule contrast between leaving future doses out versus including them is the cleanest feedback diagnostic, and it's a proper identification test that the parametric approach can't relax. I haven't run that either, though it's straightforward now: just modify the lag structure to include future years and compare the results.

For the extrapolation problem in design space, I could report a perturbation that stays within observed regions—swapping one region's path for another observed path, which is the path-contrast estimand I mentioned but never built. Both endpoints would be observed, so it's fully supported by construction and actually aligns with what the reference law itself contemplates.

I should also look at the other design documents in the repo and the 2023 rule change,…

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"# Predetermined AEWR-bite design

## Question and estimand

Estimate whether the same regional AEWR change has a larger effect on H-2A demand in local labor markets where the wage floor was more likely to bind.

The design identifies a differential response to predetermined AEWR exposure. It does not, without additional structure, identify the aggregate elasticity to the region-wide AEWR level.

## Why the earlier bite design was discarded

The earlier treatment,

\[
AEWR_{rt}-w^{25}_{ct},
\]

used a time-varying local wage quantile. That wage is itself affected by local labor-demand shocks and may respond to the AEWR. The resulting bite therefore combines the policy with an endogenous outcome. Interacting it with a post-2011 indicator does not create an external policy shock.

## Revised exposure

Freeze the local wage distribution \(F_c^0(w)\) using a pooled pre-period, preferably 2007--2008. Never update it using post-treatment wages.

Construct predicted per-worker exposure:

\[
B^0_{ct}
=
\int
\left[
AEWR_{rt}-\max\{w,M_{ct}\}
\right]_+
dF_c^0(w),
\]

where \(M_{ct}\) is the other applicable wage floor. Simpler alternatives are the fixed baseline share below each year's AEWR, or the baseline gap interacted with the annual AEWR change. Use the full distribution as the preferred measure.

The baseline distribution can use all wage-and-salary workers, matching the old design, with agricultural and low-wage-worker distributions as sensitivity analyses.

## Empirical design

Estimate

\[
\log E[Y_{ct}]
=
\alpha_c+\lambda_{st}
+\beta B^0_{ct}
+X_{ct}'\gamma+\varepsilon_{ct},
\]

where \(\lambda_{st}\) is a state-by-year fixed effect. Identification therefore compares counties or CZs facing the same AEWR and state-level shocks in the same year but having different frozen baseline exposure. AEWR-region-by-year effects are a less restrictive alternative.

An equivalent specification interacts a fixed baseline exposure measure with annual changes in \(\log AEWR_{rt}\). Use a zero-filled county- or CZ-year panel and PPML for applications and requested positions.

## Identifying assumption

Conditional on state-by-year effects and controls, locations with different baseline exposure would have followed parallel H-2A demand trends absent the AEWR change. The main threat is that initially low-wage agricultural areas have different secular changes in crops, technology, labor supply, or H-2A adoption.

## Required controls and diagnostics

- Baseline-exposure-bin trends or baseline covariates interacted with year.
- Crop-by-year and harvest-calendar-by-year effects.
- Event-study coefficients by baseline exposure.
- Placebo interactions using pre-period AEWR changes.
- Alternative frozen baseline years and wage distributions.
- No specifications using contemporaneous local wages.
- AEWR-region wild-bootstrap and few-cluster-robust inference.
- Results excluding border areas and large shared employer/FLC networks.
- Reweighting high- and low-exposure places to common baseline support.
- Employer-level estimates among continuing employers, alongside local-market entry and exit.

Interpret \(\beta\) as the response to predicted relative wage-cost exposure. Translating it into an overall AEWR elasticity requires an explicit assumption about how this exposure maps into each employer's marginal H-2A cost.
==================== 2023 RULE ====================
# 2023 AEWR rule-change design

## Question and estimand

Estimate how H-2A demand responds when a regulatory formula changes the wage floor for non-field-and-livestock occupations.

This identifies an elasticity for the relatively small group of occupations moved to occupation-specific OEWS AEWRs. It does not directly identify the response of the main field-and-livestock workforce.

## Policy variation

The 2023 rule took effect on March 30, 2023. Six field-and-livestock SOC codes retained the state or regional FLS AEWR. Other non-range occupations became subject to statewide occupation-specific OEWS AEWRs. A job containing multiple SOCs is subject to the highest applicable AEWR.

The new methodology applies according to the ETA-790/790A job-order submission date. [DOL implementation guidance](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/ETA/oflc/pdfs/2023-AEWR-Final-Rule-FAQs_implementation_FINAL.pdf) provides the cutoff and wage rules.

## Predicted wage shock

For job type \(j\), state \(s\), occupation \(o\), and AEWR region \(r\), construct

\[
Shock^0_{jso}
=
\log W^{new}_{so}
-
\log W^{old}_{r},
\]

where both terms incorporate other applicable wage floors. Set the shock to zero for jobs remaining under the FLS formula.

Classify occupation using a pre-rule employer-job cell or a task-text classifier trained only on pre-rule cases. Do not define treatment from the post-rule SOC, because employers may change task descriptions or occupation coding in response to the rule.

## Empirical design

Create a balanced employer-by-worksite-by-pre-rule-job-type monthly panel, including zero-application months. Let

\[
Post_{jt}
=
\mathbf 1\{\text{job order submitted on or after March 30, 2023}\}.
\]

Use \(Post_{jt}\times Shock^0_{jso}\) as an instrument for the log applicable wage floor. Include:

- employer-worksite-job-type fixed effects;
- state-by-month or AEWR-region-by-month fixed effects;
- SOC-by-month effects;
- intended-start-month and crop-season controls.

Estimate requested positions and applications with a zero-preserving count model. Report certified positions as a secondary outcome.

Base inference on the state-by-pre-rule-SOC shock cells. Report state-clustered and employer-clustered sensitivity estimates.

## Identifying assumption

Absent the rule, high- and low-shock job cells would have followed parallel relative trends after conditioning on local-time and occupation-time shocks. The mechanical formula difference must be unrelated to occupation-specific demand changes except through the wage floor.

## Main outcomes

- Applications and requested positions.
- Employer entry, exit, and contract size.
- Withdrawals and amendments.
- SOC recoding, task relabeling, and job bundling.
- Offered wage and the first-stage pass-through.

Avoidance responses are part of the policy effect, but stable pre-rule job cells should be the main elasticity sample.

## Required diagnostics

- Event-study coefficients before March 2023.
- Filing-date density and bunching around the announced cutoff.
- Results excluding a narrow cutoff window.
- Comparisons with both unchanged FLS occupations and low-shock OEWS occupations.
- Stable-employer and stable-task samples.
- Placebos using March 30 in earlier years.
- Alternative occupation classifications and highest-SOC treatment rules.

DOL reported that roughly 97% of initially certified positions remained under the FLS rate, so power and external validity are the central limitations. Public OFLC files through FY2025 are available from the [DOL performance-data page](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/eta/foreign-labor/performance).

==================== 2023 RULE ====================
# 2023 AEWR rule-change design

## Question and estimand

Estimate how H-2A demand responds when a regulatory formula changes the wage floor for non-field-and-livestock occupations.

This identifies an elasticity for the relatively small group of occupations moved to occupation-specific OEWS AEWRs. It does not directly identify the response of the main field-and-livestock workforce.

## Policy variation

The 2023 rule took effect on March 30, 2023. Six field-and-livestock SOC codes retained the state or regional FLS AEWR. Other non-range occupations became subject to statewide occupation-specific OEWS AEWRs. A job containing multiple SOCs is subject to the highest applicable AEWR.

The new methodology applies according to the ETA-790/790A job-order submission date. [DOL implementation guidance](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/ETA/oflc/pdfs/2023-AEWR-Final-Rule-FAQs_implementation_FINAL.pdf) provides the cutoff and wage rules.

## Predicted wage shock

For job type \(j\), state \(s\), occupation \(o\), and AEWR region \(r\), construct

\[
Shock^0_{jso}
=
\log W^{new}_{so}
-
\log W^{old}_{r},
\]

where both terms incorporate other applicable wage floors. Set the shock to zero for jobs remaining under the FLS formula.

Classify occupation using a pre-rule employer-job cell or a task-text classifier trained only on pre-rule cases. Do not define treatment from the post-rule SOC, because employers may change task descriptions or occupation coding in response to the rule.

## Empirical design

Create a balanced employer-by-worksite-by-pre-rule-job-type monthly panel, including zero-application months. Let

\[
Post_{jt}
=
\mathbf 1\{\text{job order submitted on or after March 30, 2023}\}.
\]

Use \(Post_{jt}\times Shock^0_{jso}\) as an instrument for the log applicable wage floor. Include:

- employer-worksite-job-type fixed effects;
- state-by-month or AEWR-region-by-month fixed effects;
- SOC-by-month effects;
- intended-start-month and crop-season controls.

Estimate requested positions and applications with a zero-preserving count model. Report certified positions as a secondary outcome.

Base inference on the state-by-pre-rule-SOC shock cells. Report state-clustered and employer-clustered sensitivity estimates.

## Identifying assumption

Absent the rule, high- and low-shock job cells would have followed parallel relative trends after conditioning on local-time and occupation-time shocks. The mechanical formula difference must be unrelated to occupation-specific demand changes except through the wage floor.

## Main outcomes

- Applications and requested positions.
- Employer entry, exit, and contract size.
- Withdrawals and amendments.
- SOC recoding, task relabeling, and job bundling.
- Offered wage and the first-stage pass-through.

Avoidance responses are part of the policy effect, but stable pre-rule job cells should be the main elasticity sample.

## Required diagnostics

- Event-study coefficients before March 2023.
- Filing-date density and bunching around the announced cutoff.
- Results excluding a narrow cutoff window.
- Comparisons with both unchanged FLS occupations and low-shock OEWS occupations.
- Stable-employer and stable-task samples.
- Placebos using March 30 in earlier years.
- Alternative occupation classifications and highest-SOC treatment rules.

DOL reported that roughly 97% of initially certified positions remained under the FLS rate, so power and external validity are the central limitations. Public OFLC files through FY2025 are available from the [DOL performance-data page](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/eta/foreign-labor/performance).

Reading the two design notes I'd skipped changed my ranking, and one of them speaks directly to the elasticity problem.

`predetermined_aewr_bite_design.md` says outright that the bite design identifies a differential response to predetermined exposure and "does not, without additional structure, identify the aggregate elasticity to the region-wide AEWR level." That is exactly the object I've been reporting at around 9, off seventeen region paths, and it's the note's own stated limitation. It also warns that translating an exposure response into an overall AEWR elasticity "requires an explicit assumption about how this exposure maps into each employer's marginal H-2A cost" — which is the missing structure. So the implausible magnitude probably isn't a bug in my pipeline; it's the design being asked for a parameter it isn't built to deliver. Worth saying before more effort goes into refining that number.

What I want to do first is the strict-exogeneity test, because it's the one assumption the parametric route can't relax by adding terms, and we established the right diagnostic two turns ago without ever running it. AEWRs are set from prior-year FLS regional wages, so outcome innovations can enter future doses; the test is the contrast between the current leave-future-out history and one that admits `h > t`. Under no feedback both projections are consistent and the estimates should agree; a systematic gap localizes the problem to the future-dose coordinates. It's cheap — one change to `slots()` and a refit — and it's cleaner than the lead placebo, which is a poor anticipation test when the dose is this persistent. If that fails, the elasticity question is moot.

The runner-up is the specification curve the saturation note calls its headline figure: sweep the moderator tier and the lag-profile order and see whether the elasticity is stable or swings. The deciding tradeoff is that the feedback test can invalidate everything while the curve only calibrates confidence in a number I already suspect is the wrong parameter.

One thing I'd fold in either way, because it fixes the leverage finding for free: report path-contrast estimands alongside dose perturbations. Replacing region `r`'s realized path with region `r'`'s is a move between two observed points, so it's inside the design region by construction with no extrapolation, and it's the exact vocabulary the seventeen-state reference law already uses. That's the estimand this design can support cleanly, as opposed to a coordinate shift that always leaves the observed hull.

Two smaller things I'd note rather than do: my `Z` uses a 2008–2010 frozen baseline while that note prefers 2007–2008, which is a checkable sensitivity; and the 2023 rule-change design is a genuinely separate identification strategy with its own data requirements — employer-by-worksite monthly panels, ETA-790 submission dates — that this parquet doesn't contain.

content.text:
The test ran, and it's uninformative rather than reassuring — the full-window specification has no power.

Look at the standard errors. Admitting future doses inflates them by one to two orders of magnitude: applications at `h=0` goes from `SE 0.76` to `SE 69.05`, certified positions from `38.6` to `1351`. The lead coefficients are all statistically zero (`|t| ≤ 0.87`), but with standard errors that large they would be zero against almost any alternative, so failing to reject tells us nothing about feedback. The gap-over-SE column reads as large multiples only because the denominator is the *tight* leave-future-out standard error; measured against the full-window standard errors the two specifications are statistically indistinguishable at every horizon.

The reason is structural and I should have anticipated it. Under the full window the cubic Almon profile spans all twelve years for every outcome year, so the same four dose coordinates are being asked to separate past from future response using seventeen region paths that are strongly serially correlated. The lead and lag directions become nearly collinear within the compressed basis, and the design simply cannot tell them apart. The polynomial compression that made the leave-future-out specification well-conditioned is what destroys the contrast here — the lead test needs the lead coordinates to be separately free, which is exactly what the Almon restriction removes.

So the honest state is that strict exogeneity remains untested, not that it passed. Two ways to get a real test, and I'd take the first: fit the full window with the lead block *unrestricted* while keeping the cubic profile on the lags only, so leads get their own coordinates rather than sharing a polynomial with the lags. That costs one or two extra region coordinates out of the eleven currently spare in the ledger, and it makes the lead coefficients genuinely free. The alternative is a single-lead specification — add only `W_{r,t+1}`, which is Wooldridge's own strict-exogeneity check — cheapest of all at one coordinate, though with a persistent dose it tests less than the block version.

Worth noting what the run does confirm: the leave-future-out estimates are stable and precise across a specification change that alters the entire nuisance projection, and the sign structure holds — participation down, volume up, effects building through `h=3`. That's not nothing, but it isn't the identification test I set out to run.

def blocks(t,perm,Mu):

    return A,rhs,B

    As={};Bs={};Ai={};us={}

content.text:
Now the test has power, and it fails for the participation outcome.

With free lead coordinates — cubic Almon on the lags, unrestricted coefficients on `W_{r,t+1}` and `W_{r,t+2}`, seven of sixteen region coordinates — `cond(R_t)` stays at 110 and the state-zero invariant at `6.8e-12`, so the specification is well behaved. The leads:

```
outcome            lead h=-1          lead h=-2       joint F(2,15)
applications      +3.27 (4.37)      +0.38 (1.58)          0.61
certified       +160.74 (164.92)   +52.27 (79.61)         0.84
any_app          -0.49 (0.17)      -0.05 (0.08)           8.48
```

Applications and certified positions pass cleanly — leads indistinguishable from zero, joint statistics well under one. `P(any application)` does not: the one-year lead is `−0.49` with a standard error of `0.17`, roughly `t = −2.9`, and the joint statistic is `8.48` against an `F(2,15)` five-percent critical value near `3.68`. Next year's AEWR growth predicts this year's participation, which is what strict exogeneity forbids.

Two readings, and they have different consequences. Either counties anticipate announced AEWR changes and adjust filing before the rate takes effect — plausible, since AEWRs are published in advance of the filing season — or outcome innovations feed into the FLS wages that set next year's AEWR, which is the feedback channel we identified from the assignment mechanism. Anticipation would be a no-anticipation violation, addressable by redefining the treatment date to the announcement; feedback is the harder one, and neither is fixable by adding terms.

The lag effects in this specification are also worth noting: the point estimates roughly quintuple against the leave-future-out benchmark and the standard errors grow proportionately, so the volume outcomes stay statistically silent while `P(any application)` remains significant throughout at a magnitude that is now clearly too large to take literally. That inflation is the cost of asking seventeen serially correlated paths to separate leads from lags, and it means this specification is a diagnostic rather than a reporting specification.

So the state of play: the volume results survive their identification test, the participation result — the one estimand that was cleanly significant — does not. That's an uncomfortable but genuine finding, and it's the one that most needs resolving before anything gets written up. The natural next step is to distinguish anticipation from feedback by dating treatment to the AEWR publication date rather than the effective year, since the two hypotheses make different predictions once the timing is corrected.

"""Full history, every lag freely estimated. No polynomial restriction on the lag profile.
Linear in the dose; interactions retained (full 42-term moderator dictionary x every lag).
CCV applied properly: finite-design covariance with the declared residual-df adjustment."""
import duckdb, numpy as np, polars as pl, time
exec(open("almon42.py").read().split('def legend(')[0])
nm=len(cmod); ne=len(cext)
Cz=np.linalg.qr(np.eye(R)-np.ones((R,R))/R)[0][:,:R-1]
LAGH={t:list(range(2011,t+1)) for t in YEARS}                 # every lag, free
def Am(t,Wd):
    A=np.ones((R,1+len(LAGH[t])))
    for ri,r in enumerate(regions): A[ri,1:]=[Wd[(r,h)] for h in LAGH[t]]
    return A
Ad={t:Am(t,W) for t in YEARS}; Qd={};Rd={};kt={}
for t in YEARS:
    U,s_,Vt=np.linalg.svd(Ad[t],full_matrices=False); k=int((s_>s_.max()*1e-10).sum())
    Qd[t]=U[:,:k]; Rd[t]=np.diag(s_[:k])@Vt[:k]; kt[t]=k
dim={t:kt[t]*nm+ne for t in YEARS}; offs={}; o=0
for t in YEARS: offs[t]=o; o+=dim[t]
nD=o; K=nD+R-1
print(f"free lags p_t={[Ad[t].shape[1] for t in YEARS]}  k_t={[kt[t] for t in YEARS]}  K={K}")
def blocks(t,perm,Mu):
    k=kt[t]; A=np.zeros((dim[t],dim[t])); rhs=np.zeros(dim[t]); B=np.zeros((dim[t],R-1))
    for ri in range(R):
        av=Qd[t][perm[ri]]; Sr=S[ri]; mm=Mu[ri,t-2013]
        A[:k*nm,:k*nm]+=np.kron(np.outer(av,av),Sr[np.ix_(cmod,cmod)])
        blk=np.kron(av.reshape(-1,1),Sr[np.ix_(cmod,cext)])
        A[:k*nm,k*nm:]+=blk; A[k*nm:,:k*nm]+=blk.T; A[k*nm:,k*nm:]+=Sr[np.ix_(cext,cext)]
        rhs[:k*nm]+=np.kron(av,mm[cmod]); rhs[k*nm:]+=mm[cext]
        B+=np.outer(np.concatenate([np.kron(av,Sr[cmod,0]),Sr[cext,0]]),Cz[ri])
    return A,rhs,B
def fit(perm,Mu,refine=3):
    As={};Bs={};Ai={};us={}
    for t in YEARS:
        A,rhs,B=blocks(t,perm,Mu); As[t]=A;Bs[t]=B;us[t]=rhs
        Ai[t]=np.linalg.pinv(A,rcond=1e-11,hermitian=True)
    Sc=(Cz.T*(n_r*NY))@Cz
    for t in YEARS: Sc=Sc-Bs[t].T@(Ai[t]@Bs[t])
    v=Cz.T@np.array([Mu[i,:,0].sum() for i in range(R)])
    def sv(rD,rR):
        scr=rR.copy()
        for t in YEARS: scr=scr-Bs[t].T@(Ai[t]@rD[t])
        g=np.linalg.solve(Sc,scr); return {t:Ai[t]@(rD[t]-Bs[t]@g) for t in YEARS},g
    bD,gam=sv(us,v)
    for _ in range(refine):
        pD={t:As[t]@bD[t]+Bs[t]@gam for t in YEARS}
        pR=(Cz.T*(n_r*NY))@Cz@gam+sum(Bs[t].T@bD[t] for t in YEARS)
        dD,dg=sv({t:us[t]-pD[t] for t in YEARS}, v-pR)
        for t in YEARS: bD[t]=bD[t]+dD[t]
        gam=gam+dg
    b=np.zeros(K); b[nD:]=gam
    for t in YEARS: b[offs[t]:offs[t]+dim[t]]=bD[t]
    return b
KEYS=["applications","employers","certified","any_app"]
beta={k:fit(np.arange(R),M[k]) for k in KEYS}
Mu={}
for k in KEYS:
    U_=np.zeros_like(M[k])
    for t in YEARS:
        kk=kt[t]; b=beta[k][offs[t]:offs[t]+dim[t]]; Phi=b[:kk*nm].reshape(kk,nm); be=b[kk*nm:]
        for ri in range(R):
            co=np.zeros(L); co[cmod]+=Phi.T@Qd[t][ri]; co[cext]+=be
            U_[ri,t-2013]=M[k][ri,t-2013]-S[ri]@co-(Cz[ri]@beta[k][nD:])*S[ri][:,0]
    Mu[k]=U_
print("state-0:", f"{np.abs(fit(np.arange(R),Mu['certified'])).max()/np.abs(beta['certified']).max():.1e}")
E={k:np.array([fit((np.arange(R)+s)%R,Mu[k]) for s in range(R)]) for k in KEYS}
for k in KEYS: E[k]=E[k]-E[k].mean(0)
# --- CCV applied properly: K_eff = rank of the fitted design; HC1-style residual-df multiplier
Keff=sum(np.linalg.matrix_rank(blocks(t,np.arange(R),M["certified"])[0],
         tol=1e-11*np.abs(blocks(t,np.arange(R),M["certified"])[0]).max()) for t in YEARS)+(R-1)
N=int(n_r.sum()*NY); dfadj=N/(N-Keff)
print(f"CCV: N={N:,}  K_eff={Keff:,}  residual-df multiplier N/(N-K_eff)={dfadj:.4f}"
      f"  -> SE inflation {100*(np.sqrt(dfadj)-1):.2f}%   rank(V)=16, t_16 critical value 2.1199")
def grad(p):
    g=np.zeros(K); nrm=0.0
    for t in YEARS:
        if (t-p) not in LAGH[t]: continue
        dv=np.zeros(Ad[t].shape[1]); dv[1+LAGH[t].index(t-p)]=1.0
        lam=np.linalg.solve(Rd[t].T,np.tile(dv,(R,1)).T).T
        for ri in range(R):
            g[offs[t]:offs[t]+kt[t]*nm]+=np.outer(lam[ri],S[ri][cmod,0]/n_r[ri]).ravel()
        nrm+=1
    return g/max(nrm,1e-30)
print("\n=== AME, all lags free, equal region-year, +1 log pt  [SE unadjusted | df-adjusted] ===")
print(f"{'outcome':<16}"+"".join(f"{'h='+str(p):>26}" for p in range(4)))
for k in KEYS:
    cells=[]
    for p in range(4):
        g=grad(p); q=g@beta[k]; se=np.sqrt(((E[k]@g)**2).sum()/R)
        cells.append(f"{q:>+10.4f}({se:.4f}|{se*np.sqrt(dfadj):.4f})")
    print(f"{k:<16}"+"".join(cells))
con.close()

content.text:
You were right about the cubic — it was a smooth three-lag window wearing a polynomial. Removing it and freeing every lag, the CCV correction is now applied properly and the estimates are unusable, which is informative in itself.

The residual-df adjustment I'd been omitting: `N = 30,410`, `K_eff = 5,875`, multiplier `1.2395`, so standard errors were understated by 11.3 percent throughout everything I've reported. That's now applied and reported both ways per your saturation note. Rank of `V` is 16 and the critical value is `t₁₆ = 2.1199` regardless.

With all thirteen lags free, `P(any application)` comes out at `+95.3` at `h=0` and `−186.6` at `h=3`. Those are probabilities. The model is fitting, the state-zero invariant is `6e-6` — consistent with roundoff at this conditioning but two orders worse than the restricted runs — and the estimates are meaningless.

This is the same wall as before and I don't think it's an implementation failure I can code around. The arithmetic: in 2022 the dose block asks for 13 region-level coordinates out of 17, plus a year cell and the region contrasts. After the untreated-mean projection and the region effects absorb what they absorb, the dose coefficients are identified off whatever region variation is left, which is close to nothing — so they take enormous compensating values that cancel in fitted values but explode in any single-coordinate contrast. The estimability gate passes because `R_t` is invertible; the functional is estimable and simultaneously worthless, which is exactly the distinction between "identified" and "identified with useful precision."

Your instruction was full history or one lag. I have now run full history properly and it does not produce reportable per-lag effects. So the honest recommendation is one lag: `H(t) = {t}`, contemporaneous dose only, spending two region coordinates instead of thirteen, with the full 42-term moderator dictionary and all its interactions intact. That respects both constraints in your rule, keeps every term linear, and puts the region budget where you wanted it — on interactions rather than on lag structure.

The thing I'd want to check before accepting that: whether the full-history blowup is genuine or whether the untreated-mean block is stealing region-year variation the dose should own. The `c_extra` block carries 230 columns per year including the state components, and state nests inside region, so `1 ⊗ X^S_k` lives in 48-dimensional state space with the region-level part supposedly netted out by construction. If that netting is imperfect the state block is absorbing region-year signal. That's a rank test on the residualized state block against the region indicators, and it's cheap.
Okay yeah figure that out first and make sure you keep using CCV corrected HC3 and proper, methodologically valid delta method stuff

content.thinking:
I need to tackle two things here: first, checking whether the state components block is capturing variation that should belong to the dose variable across regions and years, and second, switching to HC3-corrected covariance and validating whether the delta method still holds up methodologically. For the HC3 correction, I'm thinking through how leverage-adjusted residuals work—dividing by one minus the leverage term instead of using raw residuals—and whether that's compatible with the CCV framework, which requires the residuals to match the true errors exactly.

The key insight is that HC3 gives observation-specific corrections rather than a uniform scaling, which is more precise. I can compute leverage for each county-year pair using the block structure of the design matrix: the leverage depends on the year-specific information matrix inverse and the county-specific component vectors. Since I have around 3,000 counties and 10 years, I'd need to calculate roughly 30,000 leverage values, but the structure of the problem—with the Kronecker product and block-diagonal pieces—makes this computationally feasible. For the residual moment I need in the CCV calculation, I'd weight each residual by one over one minus its leverage, which requires pulling out the per-county leverage from the year-specific inverse. I realize I need row-level residuals to compute HC3 properly — that means pulling per-county y values from the panel table and calculating û_it = y_it - fitted values. Then I can form the weights 1/(1-h_it) and aggregate the weighted moments Σ_i c_i û/(1-h) per region-year in DuckDB, which is all doable with the block inverses and county matrices I already have.…

"""One-lag spec (contemporaneous dose), full 42-term moderator dictionary with interactions,
HC3-corrected finite-design CCV, estimability-gated delta method.

HC3: the exact-CCV theorem wants uhat = u.  uhat = M_X u shrinks, and the HC1 scalar N/(N-K)
corrects it only on average.  HC3 divides each residual by its own leverage, 1 - h_it, which is
observation-specific and is the right correction when leverage is uneven -- it is here, because
region sizes run 47 to 331.  Leverage comes from the year-block inverse in closed form.
"""
import duckdb, numpy as np, polars as pl, time
exec(open("almon42.py").read().split('def legend(')[0])
nm=len(cmod); ne=len(cext); Cz=np.linalg.qr(np.eye(R)-np.ones((R,R))/R)[0][:,:R-1]
def Am(t,Wd): return np.column_stack([np.ones(R), [Wd[(r,t)] for r in regions]])
Ad={t:Am(t,W) for t in YEARS}; Qd={};Rd={};kt={}
for t in YEARS:
    U,s_,Vt=np.linalg.svd(Ad[t],full_matrices=False); k=int((s_>s_.max()*1e-10).sum())
    Qd[t]=U[:,:k]; Rd[t]=np.diag(s_[:k])@Vt[:k]; kt[t]=k
dim={t:kt[t]*nm+ne for t in YEARS}; offs={}; o=0
for t in YEARS: offs[t]=o; o+=dim[t]
nD=o; K=nD+R-1
print(f"one lag: p_t=2 k_t={[kt[t] for t in YEARS]} dim={[dim[t] for t in YEARS][0]} K={K}"
      f"  region ledger 2 of 16  cond(R_t) max={max(np.linalg.cond(Rd[t]) for t in YEARS):.1f}")
# county matrix for leverage
cw=con.sql("select county_fips,j,v from clong").pl()
cf=con.sql("select county_fips from county2 order by county_fips").pl()["county_fips"].to_list()
ci={c:i for i,c in enumerate(cf)}; C=np.zeros((len(cf),L))
C[cw["county_fips"].replace_strict(ci).to_numpy(), cw["j"].to_numpy()]=cw["v"].to_numpy()
rof=np.array([rix[r] for r in con.sql("select region from county2 order by county_fips").pl()["region"]])
pan=con.sql("select county_fips,t,y_applications,y_employers,y_certified,y_any_app from panelm").pl()
pi=pan["county_fips"].replace_strict(ci).to_numpy(); pt=pan["t"].to_numpy()-2013
Y={k:np.zeros((len(cf),NY)) for k in ["applications","employers","certified","any_app"]}
for k in Y: Y[k][pi,pt]=pan["y_"+k].to_numpy()
def blocks(t,perm,Mu):
    k=kt[t]; A=np.zeros((dim[t],dim[t])); rhs=np.zeros(dim[t]); B=np.zeros((dim[t],R-1))
    for ri in range(R):
        av=Qd[t][perm[ri]]; Sr=S[ri]; mm=Mu[ri,t-2013]
        A[:k*nm,:k*nm]+=np.kron(np.outer(av,av),Sr[np.ix_(cmod,cmod)])
        blk=np.kron(av.reshape(-1,1),Sr[np.ix_(cmod,cext)])
        A[:k*nm,k*nm:]+=blk; A[k*nm:,:k*nm]+=blk.T; A[k*nm:,k*nm:]+=Sr[np.ix_(cext,cext)]
        rhs[:k*nm]+=np.kron(av,mm[cmod]); rhs[k*nm:]+=mm[cext]
        B+=np.outer(np.concatenate([np.kron(av,Sr[cmod,0]),Sr[cext,0]]),Cz[ri])
    return A,rhs,B
def fit(perm,Mu,refine=3):
    As={};Bs={};Ai={};us={}
    for t in YEARS:
        A,rhs,B=blocks(t,perm,Mu); As[t]=A;Bs[t]=B;us[t]=rhs; Ai[t]=np.linalg.pinv(A,rcond=1e-12,hermitian=True)
    Sc=(Cz.T*(n_r*NY))@Cz
    for t in YEARS: Sc=Sc-Bs[t].T@(Ai[t]@Bs[t])
    v=Cz.T@np.array([Mu[i,:,0].sum() for i in range(R)])
    def sv(rD,rR):
        scr=rR.copy()
        for t in YEARS: scr=scr-Bs[t].T@(Ai[t]@rD[t])
        g=np.linalg.solve(Sc,scr); return {t:Ai[t]@(rD[t]-Bs[t]@g) for t in YEARS},g
    bD,gam=sv(us,v)
    for _ in range(refine):
        pD={t:As[t]@bD[t]+Bs[t]@gam for t in YEARS}
        pR=(Cz.T*(n_r*NY))@Cz@gam+sum(Bs[t].T@bD[t] for t in YEARS)
        dD,dg=sv({t:us[t]-pD[t] for t in YEARS}, v-pR)
        for t in YEARS: bD[t]=bD[t]+dD[t]
        gam=gam+dg
    b=np.zeros(K); b[nD:]=gam
    for t in YEARS: b[offs[t]:offs[t]+dim[t]]=bD[t]
    return b,{t:Ai[t] for t in YEARS},Sc
KEYS=["applications","employers","certified","any_app"]
beta={}; Ainv=None; Scm=None
for k in KEYS:
    beta[k],Ainv,Scm=fit(np.arange(R),M[k])
# ---- exact leverage from the year-block inverse, then HC3 residual moments ----
lev=np.zeros((len(cf),NY))
for t in YEARS:
    ti=t-2013; k=kt[t]; Ai=Ainv[t]
    for ri in range(R):
        a=Qd[t][ri]; sel=np.where(rof==ri)[0]
        T=np.zeros((nm,nm)); X=np.zeros((nm,ne))
        for q in range(k):
            for qq in range(k): T+=a[q]*a[qq]*Ai[q*nm:(q+1)*nm, qq*nm:(qq+1)*nm]
            X+=a[q]*Ai[q*nm:(q+1)*nm, k*nm:]
        Ecc=Ai[k*nm:,k*nm:]
        Cm=C[sel][:,cmod]; Ce=C[sel][:,cext]
        lev[sel,ti]=(Cm@T*Cm).sum(1)+2*(Cm@X*Ce).sum(1)+(Ce@Ecc*Ce).sum(1)+Cz[ri]@np.linalg.solve(Scm,Cz[ri])
print(f"leverage: mean {lev.mean():.4f}  max {lev.max():.4f}  frac>0.5 {100*(lev>0.5).mean():.2f}%"
      f"   HC3 weight 1/(1-h): mean {np.mean(1/(1-np.clip(lev,0,0.999))):.4f}")
hw=1.0/(1.0-np.clip(lev,0,0.999))
E={}
for k in KEYS:
    fitv=np.zeros((len(cf),NY))
    for t in YEARS:
        ti=t-2013; kk=kt[t]; b=beta[k][offs[t]:offs[t]+dim[t]]; Phi=b[:kk*nm].reshape(kk,nm); be=b[kk*nm:]
        for ri in range(R):
            sel=np.where(rof==ri)[0]; a=Qd[t][ri]
            fitv[sel,ti]=C[sel][:,cmod]@(Phi.T@a)+C[sel][:,cext]@be+Cz[ri]@beta[k][nD:]
    u=(Y[k]-fitv)*hw                                   # HC3-corrected residuals
    Mu=np.zeros((R,NY,L))
    for ri in range(R):
        sel=np.where(rof==ri)[0]
        for ti in range(NY): Mu[ri,ti]=C[sel].T@u[sel,ti]
    Em=np.array([fit((np.arange(R)+s)%R,Mu)[0] for s in range(R)]); E[k]=Em-Em.mean(0)
def grad(wk="regionyear"):
    g=np.zeros(K); nrm=0.0
    for t in YEARS:
        dv=np.array([0.0,1.0]); lam=np.linalg.solve(Rd[t].T,np.tile(dv,(R,1)).T).T
        for ri in range(R):
            w=S[ri][cmod,0]/n_r[ri] if wk=="regionyear" else (S[ri][cmod,0] if wk=="county" else S[ri][cmod,1])
            g[offs[t]:offs[t]+kt[t]*nm]+=np.outer(lam[ri],w).ravel()
        nrm+= R if wk=="regionyear" else n_r.sum()
    return g/nrm
print("\n=== contemporaneous AME of +1 log pt, HC3-corrected dcCCV, t_16 ===")
print(f"{'outcome':<14}{'equal region-year':>26}{'equal county-year':>26}{'per 1 SD of Z':>26}")
for k in KEYS:
    row=[]
    for wk in ("regionyear","county","zint"):
        g=grad(wk); q=g@beta[k]; se=np.sqrt(((E[k]@g)**2).sum()/R)
        row.append(f"{q:>+13.4f}({se:.4f})")
    print(f"{k:<14}"+"".join(row))
con.close()

Structurally it can't be the culprit anyway: it enters with `a = 1` only, so it spans one region direction per year rather than seventeen, and cannot reach region-year dose variation. The one-lag specification is well behaved throughout. Two region coordinates of sixteen, `cond(R_t)` at most 15.3, and the full 42-term moderator dictionary with all its `Z` and county/market interactions retained — the interactions cost nothing at region level, which was the whole point of freeing the ledger.

HC3 is now doing real work rather than the HC1 scalar. Leverage computed exactly from the year-block inverse averages 0.105 with 1.27 percent of observations above 0.5 and a maximum touching 1.0, so the correction is genuinely uneven — the mean HC3 weight is 1.54 against the uniform HC1 multiplier of 1.24 I'd been applying. content.text:
The delta method is right — I checked it rather than asserting it. Computing the average of unit-level marginal effects row by row from the fitted coefficients and the county matrix reproduces `g'β̂` to `8.9e-16` at lag 0 and `2.7e-15` at lag 1. So the heterogeneous effects are being combined correctly: the gradient's county-side weights are exactly `Σ_{i∈r} c_i`, which recovers `(1/N) Σ_{i,t} ME_it` including the `Z` and county/market moderator contributions to each unit's own slope. The aggregation isn't the problem.

Which means the positive sign is what the specification is actually saying, and you should push back on it rather than on the arithmetic. The lag-1 dose — arguably the decision-relevant one, since job orders are filed months ahead of the start date — gives the same picture: applications `+0.056` (SE `0.046`), employers `+0.364` (SE `0.427`), certified positions `+1.941` (SE `1.993`). All positive, none distinguishable from zero.

Two things worth separating here. First, none of those level effects is significant, so the design isn't asserting a positive labor-demand response — it's asserting nothing about the level, which is exactly what the bite design note says to expect. The only estimand that separates from zero is the heterogeneity: `−0.086` (SE `0.040`) for applications and `−2.33` (SE `1.88`) for certified positions per standard deviation of baseline bite, both negative and consistent at both lags. Counties where the floor binds harder respond more negatively, which is the sign economics predicts, and it's the differential the design is built to identify.

Second, if the level effect genuinely should be negative and the point estimate is stubbornly positive, the most likely culprit is not the estimator. Seventeen regions with strongly trending AEWRs over a decade when H-2A use was growing rapidly nationally means the region-year variation available after year effects and region contrasts is thin and possibly confounded with the secular expansion. The year cells absorb the common trend, but any residual correlation between which regions raised AEWRs faster and which regions were expanding H-2A fastest goes straight into the dose coefficient with the wrong sign.

The check I'd run next is the one the bite design proposes and this specification doesn't do: state-by-year fixed effects instead of region contrasts plus year cells. That forces identification off within-state, within-year variation in predetermined exposure, which is the design's own stated identifying comparison, and it would tell you whether the positive level effect survives conditioning that the current spec is too coarse to impose.

This means the level effect of the dose drops out entirely under state-by-year saturation—only the dose interactions with county or market-level moderators remain identified, since those vary within state-year cells. C=np.zeros((len(cf),L)); C[cw["county_fips"].replace_strict(ci).to_numpy(), cw["j"].to_numpy()]=cw["v"].to_numpy()
st=cf["state"].to_list(); su={s:i for i,s in enumerate(sorted(set(st)))}; sof=np.array([su[s] for s in st])
rg=cf["region"].to_list(); regions=sorted(set(rg)); rix={r:i for i,r in enumerate(regions)}
rof=np.array([rix[r] for r in rg]); R=len(regions)
Cw=C.copy()                                            # FWL: demean within state
for s in range(len(su)):
    m=sof==s; Cw[m]-=Cw[m].mean(0)
cols=np.array(causal+nuis); nc=len(causal); nu=len(nuis)
d=con.sql("select region,h,W from dose").pl(); W={(r,int(h)):w for r,h,w in d.iter_rows()}
pan=con.sql("select county_fips,t,y_applications,y_employers,y_certified,y_any_app from panelm").pl()
pi=pan["county_fips"].replace_strict(ci).to_numpy(); pt=pan["t"].to_numpy()-2013
KEYS=["applications","employers","certified","any_app"]
Y={k:np.zeros((len(cf),NY)) for k in KEYS}
for k in KEYS: Y[k][pi,pt]=pan["y_"+k].to_numpy()
Yd={k:Y[k].copy() for k in KEYS}                       # outcome demeaned within state-year
for k in KEYS:
    for t in range(NY):

    """rows = counties; cols = [W_perm(r) * c_causal , c_nuis]  (within-state demeaned)"""
    w=np.array([W[(regions[perm[rof[i]]],t)] for i in range(len(cf))])
    return np.column_stack([Cw[:,causal]*w[:,None], Cw[:,nuis]])

    XX=np.zeros((nc+nu,nc+nu)); XY={k:np.zeros(nc+nu) for k in KEYS}

        X=design(t,perm); XX+=X.T@X
        for k in KEYS: XY[k]+=X.T@Yuse[k][:,t-2013]

    return {k:Ai@XY[k] for k in KEYS}, Ai, XX

# HC3 leverage (design part; the absorbed FE contribute 1/n_{s,t} each)
lev=np.zeros((len(cf),NY))
for t in YEARS:

for t in range(NY):

U={k:np.zeros((len(cf),NY)) for k in KEYS}
for t in YEARS:

content.thinking:
I'm spotting an issue with my state-0 validation—the check is giving me 55.8 when it should be near zero. The problem is that I'm fitting on HC3-weighted residuals, but HC3 weighting breaks the orthogonality condition where X'U should equal zero, so my intercept calculation is off.

The state-0 identity only holds for raw OLS residuals, not HC3-adjusted ones. I should be checking the invariant on unweighted residuals first, then applying HC3 weighting to the meat of the covariance matrix afterward. This means I need to report both the raw and HC3-weighted versions to see what's happening.

On the second issue, the level effects are coming out exactly zero as expected—the state-by-year interactions are absorbing all the dose variation, which confirms the theory. But my gradient calculation for the level term is hitting zeros because the design matrix doesn't have a constant column.

The heterogeneity estimates are now showing the negative relationship he predicted: higher AEWR correlates with less H-2A usage in counties where the wage floor binds. But the standard errors have shrunk dramatically—about 4.5 times smaller than before—which seems suspicious given the degrees of freedom. The state-by-year absorption is likely reducing variation in the reassignment, or the HC3 weighting is doing something unexpected. I need to investigate whether this is a genuine tightening or a computational artifact.…

content.text:
The state-by-year specification produces the sign you expected, and it's the design's own identifying comparison rather than a fix I imposed.

Since states nest strictly inside AEWR regions, state×year effects span region×year and absorb the dose level completely — the level estimates come back as exact zeros, which confirms the algebra rather than failing. Absorbing them by FWL means demeaning within state, and the telescoping identity makes that free: `x_i − x̄_state = X^C + X^M` exactly, so the within-state design *is* the county-plus-market block that was already there. The saturation survives intact — 41 dose-by-moderator interactions plus 210 second-order county/market pairs, `K = 251` after absorption, full rank.

```
per 1 SD of baseline AEWR bite         estimate      SE      95% CI
applications                            -0.0891   0.0074   [-0.105, -0.074]
employers                               -0.2642   0.0395   [-0.348, -0.180]
certified positions                     -0.4994   0.4541   [-1.462, +0.463]
P(any application)                      -0.0033   0.0004   [-0.004, -0.002]
```

All four negative, three of them decisively so. Counties where the wage floor binds harder cut applications, employers, and participation when the AEWR rises — labor demand sloping down, identified off within-state, within-year variation in predetermined exposure, exactly as `predetermined_aewr_bite_design.md` specifies.

Two methodological notes on the standard errors. The state-zero invariant no longer applies once HC3 is in the meat: dividing each residual by `1 − h_it` deliberately breaks `X'û = 0`, so state zero returns `4.35` rather than zero. I checked this properly by rerunning with raw OLS residuals, where state zero comes back at `7.4e-11` and the estimates are unchanged with standard errors of `0.0072` against HC3's `0.0074`. So the invariant is intact where it should hold, and HC3 is contributing a modest and correctly-signed inflation. Leverage is much better behaved here than in the unabsorbed spec — mean `0.024`, max `0.34`, mean HC3 weight `1.025` — because absorbing state×year removes the high-leverage directions.

The standard errors are far tighter than in the region-contrast specification, which deserves scrutiny rather than celebration. Some of that is real: absorbing state×year removes a large amount of nuisance variation from the residual. But the reassignment law still permutes only seventeen paths, so I'd want to confirm the leave-one-state-out influence diagnostic on this specification before treating intervals this narrow as final.

content.text:
The influence audit clears the specification and the decomposition explains where the result comes from.

Leave-one-reference-state-out moves the standard errors by 8.7 to 18.3 percent at worst, and no significance conclusion flips under `t₁₅` on the reduced state set. So the tight intervals aren't an artifact of one favourable path assignment — they're the genuine consequence of absorbing state×year variation, which removes a large amount of nuisance noise from the residual without touching the seventeen-path covariance rank.

The family decomposition needed fixing first, and the reason is worth stating because it's a real property of this specification rather than a coding slip. Under state×year absorption every moderator is demeaned within state, so the unweighted average of any moderator across counties is exactly zero — which is why the level effects came back as exact zeros. The identified object isn't an average effect at all; it's a differential, the response of a county relative to its own state's mean. Once the decomposition uses the same second-moment construction as the reported estimand:

```
dose x moderator family        contribution to the applications differential
Z (baseline bite)                    +0.428  (SE 0.118)
county components                    -0.002  (SE 0.001)
market components                    -0.476  (SE 0.109)
Z x county                           +0.002  (SE 0.002)
Z x market                           -0.040  (SE 0.009)
```

The net `−0.089` is a near-cancellation of two large opposing pieces: the bite moderator alone contributes `+0.428` while the market-level covariate components contribute `−0.476`. That is a substantively important finding and a fragility warning at once. It means the headline differential is not a clean bite effect — it's what survives after market-level composition pulls hard in the opposite direction, and the county-level components contribute essentially nothing. Whatever is driving it lives at the commuting-zone-by-state level, not at the county level.

Two consequences. The saturation is earning its keep here rather than decorating: a bite-only causal dictionary would have reported roughly `+0.43` with the opposite sign, and only the market components reveal that as compositional. And the near-cancellation means the result is sensitive to which market-level covariates are in the dictionary, so the specification curve over moderator tiers is now the most informative robustness check available, not an optional extra.

"""Specification curve over the causal moderator tier and the untreated-mean pair block.
The headline differential is a near-cancellation of a large +bite and a large -market term,
so its stability across the dictionary is the load-bearing robustness check."""
import duckdb, numpy as np, polars as pl, os
src=open("stateyear.py").read().split('beta,Ai,XX=fityr')[0]
G={}; exec(compile(src,"<s>","exec"),G)
kk=G['kk']; kinds=G['kinds']; L=G['L']; Cw=G['Cw']; rof=G['rof']; R=G['R']; YEARS=G['YEARS']
NY=G['NY']; Yd=G['Yd']; KEYS=G['KEYS']; W=G['W']; regions=G['regions']; cf=G['cf']; sof=G['sof']; su=G['su']
names=kk['name'].to_list()
byk=lambda kd,suf=None:[j for j in range(L) if kinds[j]==kd and (suf is None or names[j].endswith(suf))]
TIERS=[("T0 bite only",             byk("Z")),
       ("T1 +county comps",         byk("Z")+byk("CM","_C")),
       ("T2 +market comps",         byk("Z")+byk("CM","_C")+byk("CM","_M")),
       ("T3 +Z x county",           byk("Z")+byk("CM","_C")+byk("CM","_M")+byk("ZCM","_C")),
       ("T4 full (+Z x market)",    byk("Z")+byk("CM","_C")+byk("CM","_M")+byk("ZCM","_C")+byk("ZCM","_M"))]
PAIRS=byk("PAIR"); jZ=byk("Z")[0]
def run(causal,nuis):
    nc=len(causal); Kd=nc+len(nuis)
    def design(t,perm):
        w=np.array([W[(regions[perm[rof[i]]],t)] for i in range(len(cf))])
        return np.column_stack([Cw[:,causal]*w[:,None], Cw[:,nuis]]) if nuis else Cw[:,causal]*w[:,None]
    def fitall(perm,Yuse):
        XX=np.zeros((Kd,Kd)); XY={k:np.zeros(Kd) for k in KEYS}
        for t in YEARS:
            X=design(t,perm); XX+=X.T@X
            for k in KEYS: XY[k]+=X.T@Yuse[k][:,t-2013]
        Ai=np.linalg.pinv(XX,rcond=1e-12,hermitian=True)
        return {k:Ai@XY[k] for k in KEYS}, Ai
    beta,Ai=fitall(np.arange(R),Yd)
    lev=np.zeros((len(cf),NY))
    for t in YEARS:
        X=design(t,np.arange(R)); lev[:,t-2013]=(X@Ai*X).sum(1)
    for t in range(NY):
        for s in range(len(su)):
            m=sof==s; lev[m,t]+=1.0/m.sum()
    hw=1.0/(1.0-np.clip(lev,0,0.999))
    U={k:np.zeros((len(cf),NY)) for k in KEYS}
    for t in YEARS:
        X=design(t,np.arange(R))
        for k in KEYS: U[k][:,t-2013]=(Yd[k][:,t-2013]-X@beta[k])*hw[:,t-2013]
    E={k:[] for k in KEYS}
    for s in range(R):
        bs,_=fitall((np.arange(R)+s)%R,U)
        for k in KEYS: E[k].append(bs[k])
    for k in KEYS: E[k]=np.array(E[k])-np.array(E[k]).mean(0)
    gz=np.zeros(Kd); nrm=0.0
    for t in YEARS:
        for ri in range(R):
            sel=rof==ri
            gz[:nc]+=(Cw[sel][:,causal]*Cw[sel][:,[jZ]]).mean(0); nrm+=1
    gz/=nrm
    return {k:(gz@beta[k], np.sqrt(((E[k]@gz)**2).sum()/R)) for k in KEYS}, Kd
print("=== specification curve: dose x moderator differential per 1 SD of baseline bite ===")
print(f"{'tier':<24}{'pairs':>7}{'K':>6}"+"".join(f"{k:>22}" for k in ["applications","employers","any_app"]))
for lab,cau in TIERS:
    for pl_ in (False,True):
        res,Kd=run(cau, PAIRS if pl_ else [])
        cells="".join(f"{res[k][0]:>+13.4f}({res[k][1]:.4f})" for k in ["applications","employers","any_app"])
        print(f"{lab:<24}{'yes' if pl_ else 'no':>7}{Kd:>6}"+cells)

The specification curve is stable in sign and ordered in magnitude across all ten cells.

Every configuration gives a negative differential for all three outcomes, and none of the intervals covers zero. That retires my worry from last turn: the near-cancellation of `+0.428` bite against `−0.476` market components is a decomposition of the full-dictionary estimate, not a fragility — the estimate itself doesn't flip when you remove the market block, it just shrinks.

```

T0 bite only             no     -0.033 (0.007)   -0.043 (0.014)   -0.0040 (0.0004)
T2 +market comps         no     -0.037 (0.007)   -0.092 (0.028)   -0.0045 (0.0003)

T4 full                 yes     -0.089 (0.007)   -0.264 (0.040)   -0.0033 (0.0004)
```

Two patterns run through it. Enriching the causal dictionary monotonically strengthens the applications and employers differentials — bite-only understates by a factor of two to six against the full tier. And adding the 210 second-order untreated-mean pairs roughly doubles both again, independently of the causal tier. So the saturation is not decorative on either side of the model: the sparse specification is the one that would have understated the effect, which is the opposite of the usual worry about rich conditioning manufacturing results.

`P(any application)` behaves differently and that's worth noting rather than smoothing over. It is the one outcome where adding the pair block *attenuates* the differential, from `−0.0045` to `−0.0033`, and where the causal tier barely matters. Participation is a bounded outcome and the pairs are absorbing composition that the volume outcomes leave in, so the two margins are not simply scaled versions of each other.

Reading the full-dictionary numbers substantively: a county one standard deviation above its state's mean baseline bite responds to a one-log-point AEWR increase with about 0.09 fewer applications per 1,000 baseline workers, 0.26 fewer linked employers, and a 0.33 percentage point lower probability of participating at all. All identified off within-state, within-year variation in predetermined exposure, with HC3-corrected finite-design standard errors and `t₁₆`.

The remaining hole is the one the design note names and this cannot close: these are differentials, and converting them to an aggregate AEWR elasticity needs an explicit assumption about how predicted exposure maps into each employer's marginal H-2A cost. Nothing in the current specification supplies it.

content.text:
Both diagnostics come back badly, and one of them is a bug in my code rather than a finding.

The event-study "profile" is identical across all ten years, which is not a result — it's the specification. The dose coefficients are constant over time in this model, so a per-year gradient just reweights the same coefficients by the same moderator moments and returns the same number. To get a real event-study profile the dose-by-moderator interactions have to be year-specific, which is a different design: `W_t × Z × D_t`, spending ten times the coefficients. My gradient was never going to produce year variation from a model that doesn't have any. That's a straightforward error on my part and the table should be discarded.

The lead placebo is a genuine result and it fails. Next year's dose interacted with baseline bite predicts this year's outcome at essentially the same magnitude as the contemporaneous term — applications `−0.052` against `−0.053`, employers `−0.133` against `−0.164`, participation `−0.0019` against `−0.0020`, with `t` statistics of `−5.5`, `−3.3` and `−4.4`. The placebo is indistinguishable from the effect it's supposed to falsify.

That is the same failure I found earlier at the region level for participation, now appearing on the differential for every outcome once state×year absorption tightens the standard errors enough to see it. Two readings remain available and they are not equally comfortable. Anticipation is plausible — AEWRs are published ahead of the filing season, so a county facing next year's announced rate may adjust this year's filings, and the fix is to date treatment to publication rather than effective year. Feedback is the harder one: outcome innovations entering the FLS wages that set next year's AEWR, which no amount of conditioning repairs.

There is also a third possibility that the near-identical magnitudes point to directly. AEWR growth is strongly serially correlated at the region level, so `W_{r,t+1}` and `W_{r,t}` are close substitutes, and a placebo that loads identically on both may simply be unable to separate them rather than detecting anticipation. The discriminating test is the correlation structure: if `corr(W_{r,t}, W_{r,t+1})` is high, the placebo has no power and this tells us nothing; if it's low, the placebo is informative and the design has a real problem.

That correlation is one line to compute and it decides whether the headline differential survives. I'd run it before anything else.

content.text:
The collinearity escape route is closed. `W_{r,t}` and `W_{r,t+1}` are essentially uncorrelated — `−0.08` raw, `−0.19` after removing year means — with a condition number of 1.18, a singular-value ratio of 1.18, and a variance inflation factor of 1.03. Ninety-seven percent of next year's dose is orthogonal to this year's. The design can separate them cleanly, so the lead placebo has full power and its failure is real.

That is the decisive negative result of this session. Next year's AEWR growth, interacted with predetermined baseline bite, predicts this year's H-2A outcomes at essentially the same magnitude as the contemporaneous term, with `t` statistics between `−3.3` and `−5.5`, and it does so using variation that is nearly orthogonal to the contemporaneous dose. Conditional no-anticipation and strict exogeneity cannot both hold.

Worth noting the sign of the serial correlation, because it inverts an assumption I made repeatedly. I had been attributing the full-history blowup and the growing lag profile to a persistent, serially correlated dose path. It isn't persistent — annual AEWR growth is close to serially independent, even mildly negative at one and two years. So that diagnosis was wrong, and the earlier collapse under thirteen free lags was purely the region-coordinate scarcity, not collinearity across horizons.

Where that leaves the result. The differential is stable across the whole specification curve, robust to leave-one-state-out, precisely estimated, and correctly signed — and it fails the identification test the design's own note lists as required. The two live explanations are anticipation, since AEWRs are published before the filing season and the ETA-790 job order is submitted months ahead of the start date, and feedback through the FLS wages that set the next rate. Anticipation is testable and fixable: redate treatment to the AEWR publication date rather than the effective year, which the `mean_receipt_to_start_days_start_year` and `mean_decision_to_start_days_start_year` columns in the parquet can help calibrate. Feedback is not fixable within this design.

That redating is what I would do next, and it's the cleanest discriminating test available: if the lead effect collapses once the dose is aligned to when employers actually observe it, the story is anticipation and the estimates survive with a corrected timing convention. If it persists, the differential is not identified here and the panel-IV branch with the FLS instrument becomes the necessary route rather than an alternative one.

If H-2A activity in year t affects those surveyed wages — either because H-2A workers are included in the survey or because H-2A demand influences local wages — then next year's wage floor is correlated with current-year outcomes through reverse causality, not anticipation. content.text:
The timing data undercuts the anticipation explanation and points at feedback.

Filing lead time is only about 33 days on average — a job order is received roughly one month before the start date, `p90` at 64 days. So an employer filing for a spring or summer start in year `t` faces the year-`t` AEWR, and the start-year convention the panel uses is approximately correct. Redating to publication would shift things by weeks, not a year, so misdating cannot explain a lead effect as large as the contemporaneous one.

That variable also has its own defect worth adding to the parquet list: `mean_receipt_to_start_days_start_year` runs 52, 54, 41 in 2013–2015, then `−3.6, −4.6, −3.5, +4.8` in 2016–2019, then 58, 59, 60 in 2020–2022. Negative days-to-start means orders received after the job began, which is implausible; the pattern is a clean break in construction across two boundaries rather than a behavioural change.

With anticipation weakened, the mechanism that fits is the one built into the assignment rule. The year `t+1` AEWR is set from the FLS survey conducted during year `t`. If county H-2A activity in year `t` moves the regional farm wages that survey measures, then `W_{r,t+1}` is mechanically a function of year-`t` outcomes. That is not anticipation — it is reverse causality through the policy formula, and it predicts exactly what we see: a lead coefficient matching the contemporaneous one in magnitude because the same underlying activity drives both.

That mechanism makes a sharp, falsifiable prediction the data can adjudicate. Feedback through the FLS is one step: year-`t` outcomes enter the year-`t+1` rate. Since annual dose growth is nearly serially independent, contamination should not propagate to `W_{r,t+2}`. So if the `t+1` lead loads and the `t+2` lead does not, the signature is one-step policy feedback. If both load, the problem is a common trend in bite-correlated regions and the differential is not identified at all.

That is a two-line change to the lead block in the state×year specification, and it distinguishes the two remaining explanations cleanly. I'll run it next.

content.text:
The test splits the outcomes rather than giving one answer, which is more informative than either clean result would have been.

```
differential per 1 SD of bite      W_t        W_t+1      W_t+2      (t-stats)
applications                    -0.038     -0.032     -0.042     -7.4  -5.3  -5.3
employers                       -0.158     -0.139     -0.003     -4.3  -3.5  -0.1
certified positions             -0.202     +0.067     +0.357     -0.7   0.2   1.0
P(any application)              -0.0017    -0.0014    -0.0011    -3.9  -3.0  -1.8
```

Employers shows the one-step feedback signature exactly: contemporaneous and one-year lead both strongly negative, two-year lead dead at `t = −0.10`. That is what FLS reverse causality predicts — year-`t` activity enters the year-`t+1` rate and, with annual dose growth nearly serially independent, cannot reach `t+2`. Participation behaves the same way, decaying monotonically from `−3.9` to `−3.0` to `−1.8`.

Applications does not. All three horizons load at essentially identical magnitude, with the two-year lead if anything the largest. One-step feedback cannot produce that, and neither can anticipation at a one-month filing lead. The remaining explanation is a common trend: regions whose baseline bite is high were on a differentially declining application path over the whole sample, and the dose is picking that up regardless of which year's dose you use. Certified positions is uninformative throughout — nothing separates from zero at any horizon.

So the honest verdict differs by margin. The employer-count and participation differentials are contaminated by policy feedback, which is a specific, mechanism-identified problem with a known route out: the FLS instrument in the `panel_iv` branch, which is designed precisely to strip the endogenous component out of the AEWR. The applications differential fails a stricter test — it looks like differential trends by baseline exposure, which is the main threat the bite design note names and which the note's own remedy list addresses with baseline-exposure-bin trends and covariates interacted with year.

That gives a concrete next specification rather than a general worry: add baseline-bite-bin trends to the untreated-mean block and see whether the applications differential survives. If it collapses, it was a trend; if it survives while the two-year lead disappears, the trend was the contaminant and the effect is real. Either way that is a cheap addition to the existing state×year design, since bite-bin-by-year terms are county-level and cost nothing in the region ledger.

Equation (1) = random-coefficients panel model Y = W*B_it + gamma_t + C_i + U_it with Chamberlain projection on C_i and a correlated-random-coefficient projection on B_it
- Position: richer parameterization handles the strict-exogeneity/feedback problem (AEWR set from FLS regional wages, so outcome innovations can enter future doses)
- Design decisions for the maximal MCW spec: NO separate pre-period year values (2008/2009/2010) in the projection, NO imposed linear trends, NO quadratic or cubic dose basis for now (linear dose only). Pre-period covariates enter as means at each hierarchy level
- More MCW spec decisions: interaction terms are fine and good; drop the arbitrary 3-year focal window {s, s-1, s-2} entirely (no causal-vs-nuisance split in the history block); per-term standard errors on every regression coefficient are unnecessary since inference is post-fit delta method on constructed combinations

Said interpretability degrading under full history means the implementation isn't being done properly, not that the spec is wrong
- REJECTED the cubic Almon lag profile as "some bullshit way to hide a three-lag window". No quadratic or cubic terms anywhere, including polynomial restrictions on the lag profile. Full history with every lag freely estimated; interaction terms remain fine and good
- CCV corrections to the standard errors must be applied properly (the residual-df adjustment was missing)
- The FLS-instrument / panel-IV route is NOT necessary for this work (said he would explain why later)

"""Add (a) a fully year-specific untreated mean and (b) baseline-bite-bin trends.
If the applications differential is a differential trend by baseline exposure, these kill it.
Bite-bin-by-year and county-by-year terms are county-level, so they cost nothing in the
17-coordinate region ledger -- this is the MCW saturation working as intended."""
import numpy as np
src=open("stateyear.py").read().split('beta,Ai,XX=fityr')[0]
G={}; exec(compile(src,"<s>","exec"),G)
kinds=G['kinds'];L=G['L'];Cw=G['Cw'];rof=G['rof'];R=G['R'];YEARS=G['YEARS'];NY=G['NY']
Yd=G['Yd'];KEYS=G['KEYS'];W=G['W'];regions=G['regions'];cf=G['cf'];sof=G['sof'];su=G['su'];C=G['C']
causal=G['causal']; pairs=G['nuis']; jZ=[j for j in range(L) if kinds[j]=="Z"][0]
nc=len(causal)
Z=C[:,jZ]
qs=np.quantile(Z,[.2,.4,.6,.8]); bins=np.digitize(Z,qs)          # 5 bite bins
Bin=np.zeros((len(cf),5)); Bin[np.arange(len(cf)),bins]=1.0
def wsdemean(Xa):
    Y=Xa.copy()
    for s in range(len(su)):
        m=sof==s; Y[m]-=Y[m].mean(0)
    return Y
Binw=wsdemean(Bin)
NUIS=np.column_stack([Cw[:,causal], Cw[:,pairs], Binw])          # year-specific block, per year
nn=NUIS.shape[1]
SH=[0,1,2]
def design(t,perm):
    bl=[]
    for s in SH:
        h=min(t+s,2022)
        w=np.array([W[(regions[perm[rof[i]]],h)] for i in range(len(cf))])
        bl.append(Cw[:,causal]*w[:,None])
    bl.append(NUIS)                                              # own coefficients each year
    return np.column_stack(bl)
Kc=nc*len(SH)
def fitall(perm,Yuse):
    """causal coefficients shared across years; nuisance block year-specific (FWL by year)."""
    XcXc=np.zeros((Kc,Kc)); XcY={k:np.zeros(Kc) for k in KEYS}
    P={}
    Nn=NUIS.T@NUIS; Ninv=np.linalg.pinv(Nn,rcond=1e-12,hermitian=True)
    for t in YEARS:
        X=design(t,perm)[:,:Kc]
        Xr=X-NUIS@(Ninv@(NUIS.T@X))                              # residualize on year-t nuisance
        XcXc+=Xr.T@Xr
        for k in KEYS:
            y=Yd[k][:,t-2013]; yr=y-NUIS@(Ninv@(NUIS.T@y)); XcY[k]+=Xr.T@yr
        P[t]=(Xr,)
    Ai=np.linalg.pinv(XcXc,rcond=1e-12,hermitian=True)
    return {k:Ai@XcY[k] for k in KEYS}, Ai, Ninv
beta,Ai,Ninv=fitall(np.arange(R),Yd)
print(f"causal K={Kc}  year-specific nuisance {nn} x {NY} = {nn*NY} absorbed by FWL"
      f"  effective K ~ {Kc+nn*NY+len(su)*NY:,} of N=30,410")
lev=np.zeros((len(cf),NY))
for t in YEARS:
    X=design(t,np.arange(R))[:,:Kc]; Xr=X-NUIS@(Ninv@(NUIS.T@X))
    lev[:,t-2013]=(Xr@Ai*Xr).sum(1)+(NUIS@Ninv*NUIS).sum(1)
    for s in range(len(su)):
        m=sof==s; lev[m,t-2013]+=1.0/m.sum()
hw=1.0/(1.0-np.clip(lev,0,0.999))
print(f"leverage mean {lev.mean():.4f} max {lev.max():.4f}  HC3 weight mean {hw.mean():.4f}")
U={k:np.zeros((len(cf),NY)) for k in KEYS}
for t in YEARS:
    X=design(t,np.arange(R))[:,:Kc]; Xr=X-NUIS@(Ninv@(NUIS.T@X))
    for k in KEYS:
        y=Yd[k][:,t-2013]; yr=y-NUIS@(Ninv@(NUIS.T@y))
        U[k][:,t-2013]=(yr-Xr@beta[k])*hw[:,t-2013]
E={k:[] for k in KEYS}
for s in range(R):
    bs,_,_=fitall((np.arange(R)+s)%R,U)
    for k in KEYS: E[k].append(bs[k])
for k in KEYS: E[k]=np.array(E[k])-np.array(E[k]).mean(0)
def gz(slot):
    g=np.zeros(Kc); n=0.0
    for t in YEARS:
        for ri in range(R):
            sel=rof==ri; g[slot*nc:(slot+1)*nc]+=(Cw[sel][:,causal]*Cw[sel][:,[jZ]]).mean(0); n+=1
    return g/n
print("\n=== with year-specific untreated mean + bite-bin trends ===")
print(f"{'outcome':<14}{'W_t':>22}{'W_t+1':>22}{'W_t+2':>22}")
for k in ["applications","employers","any_app"]:
    row=""
    for s in range(3):
        g=gz(s); q=g@beta[k]; se=np.sqrt(((E[k]@g)**2).sum()/R)
        row+=f"{q:>+13.4f}({se:.4f})"
    print(f"{k:<14}"+row)

That settles the applications question, and not in the effect's favour.

With a fully year-specific untreated mean plus baseline-bite-bin trends — 2,560 nuisance columns absorbed by FWL, effective `K ≈ 3,163` against `N = 30,410` — the applications differential collapses from `−0.038` (SE `0.005`) to `−0.004` (SE `0.020`). It loses an order of magnitude and its standard error quadruples. The two-year lead, which was the anomaly at `t = −5.3`, also vanishes to `+0.006` (SE `0.026`). Both moving together is the signature of a differential trend: the bite-bin trends absorbed a common path that the dose was previously picking up regardless of which year's dose you used. So the applications result was a trend, exactly as the failed lead-2 test suggested, and the note's own remedy identified it.

Participation goes the same way — `−0.0005` (SE `0.0013`), gone.

Employers is the one that survives with its structure intact: `−0.358` (SE `0.143`) contemporaneous, `−0.241` (SE `0.181`) at the one-year lead, `−0.098` (SE `0.168`) at two years. The point estimate actually strengthens against the `−0.158` from the sparser specification rather than attenuating, and the decay across horizons is preserved with the two-year lead firmly dead. That is the pattern a real effect contaminated by one-step policy feedback would show, and it is not the pattern a trend would show — a trend would have flattened all three, as it did for applications.

So after saturating both sides properly, one differential is left standing: counties one standard deviation above their state's mean baseline bite lose about 0.36 linked H-2A employers per county-year for each log point of AEWR growth. The extensive margin measured by participation and the volume margin measured by applications do not survive; the employer-count margin does, and it is the outcome least sensitive to the apportionment and zero-inflation issues that afflict the others.

The remaining problem on that survivor is the one-year lead at `t = −1.33` — not significant, but not clean either, and the mechanism story says it shouldn't be zero if FLS feedback is operating. You've said the IV route isn't necessary and you'll explain why, so I'll stop short of proposing it and note only that the surviving estimate carries that caveat until whatever you have in mind resolves it.

So what you didn't realize about Mundlak-Chamberlain-Wooldridge is that when there is an issue like the one you see, you can fix it ***by adjusting the specification to control for it by construction***

When I removed future years to enforce sequential exogeneity, I actually stripped away the very device that handles this feedback — the full treatment path projection is what allows the unobserved component to correlate freely with the doses. Projecting onto the complete path is precisely what makes `Cov(W_r, c_i)` unrestricted, so if the differential response correlates with future doses, including them absorbs that correlation and the contemporaneous coefficient comes out purged. I imposed leave-future-out on sequential-exogeneity grounds and thereby deleted the machinery that handles the problem, then spent several turns treating the lead coefficients as failed placebos when they were nuisance projection terms doing their job.

The complete-path projection runs — 492 causal columns, twelve path coordinates crossed with the full 41-term moderator dictionary, all identified off within-state variation because state×year absorption frees the interactions from the region ledger. But the output says the projection is now too rich to separate the coordinates.

Every horizon returns essentially the same number. Applications gives `−0.53, −0.46, −0.46, −0.52, −0.56` across lag 2 through lead 2; employers `−2.21, −2.15, −1.99, −2.07, −1.78`. Only applications separates from zero at all, and barely.

The rank tells the story: 483 of 492. So nine columns are exactly collinear, and the rest are nearly so. With twelve path coordinates all interacted with the same 41 moderators, the columns differ only through `W_{r,h}` varying across seventeen regions — and since annual dose growth is nearly serially independent, each coordinate contributes genuine but *thin* variation, seventeen values per year, spread across 41 moderator directions. The interactions escaped the region ledger in the sense that they are county-level columns, but the *dose factor* in each of them still takes only seventeen distinct values, so twelve of them cannot be told apart.

So the by-construction fix is right in principle and this is not the way to implement it. Conditioning on the full path is what absorbs the feedback, but the full path times the full moderator dictionary is 492 columns of near-duplicate information. The version that should work is the projection restricted on the *moderator* side rather than the path side: let every path coordinate enter, crossed only with the bite `Z`, while the richer county and market moderators are reserved for the contemporaneous dose. That gives twelve lead-and-lag projection terms carrying the correlated-effects work and one saturated causal block carrying the effect, which is the actual shape of Chamberlain's device — a rich projection of the nuisance onto the path, not a rich causal dictionary replicated at every horizon.
