"""Reusable MCW estimation library. DuckDB does all O(N) work; numpy only sees small blocks.

    from mcw import Panel, Design, fit, ccv, Effect
    p = Panel.build(PARQUET, base=(2008,2010), years=(2012,2022))
    d = Design(p, moderators="ZCM", nuisance="PAIR", history="leave_focal_out")
    r = fit(d, ["app_rate","emp"]);  r.ape("emp"); r.differential("emp")
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
import duckdb, numpy as np, polars as pl, json

COVS = ["h2a_cert","h2a_app","ln_pop","farm_share","emp_pop","crop_share","labor_share",
        "ln_wage25","share_animal","share_prodexp","ln_wage50"]

# ---- DuckDB macros: written once, reused by every stage --------------------------------
MACROS = """
create or replace macro hier(x, part) as (x - avg(x) over (partition by part));
create or replace macro zstd(x) as ((x - avg(x) over ()) / nullif(stddev_pop(x) over (), 0));
create or replace macro impute(x, g) as coalesce(x, median(x) over (partition by g), median(x) over ());
create or replace macro rate(num, den, scale) as (num / nullif(den, 0) * scale);
create or replace macro dlog(a, b) as (100 * (ln(a) - ln(b)));
"""

@dataclass
class Panel:
    con: duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection
    years: list
    base: tuple
    n_county: int = 0
    L: int = 0

    @classmethod
    def build(cls, parquet, base=(2008,2010), years=(2012,2022), db=":memory:", threads=4):
        con = duckdb.connect(db)
        con.sql(f"set threads to {threads}; set preserve_insertion_order=false")
        con.sql(MACROS)
        con.sql(f"create or replace view raw as select * from read_parquet('{parquet}')")
        b0, b1 = base
        con.sql(f"""create or replace table keys as
            select r.county_fips,
                   any_value(r.aewr_region_id) region, any_value(r.state_fips) state,
                   any_value(r.state_fips||'|'||r.cz_id||'|'||r.aewr_region_id) market,
                   avg(case when r.year between {b0} and {b1} then r.emp_farm end) m_base
            from raw r group by 1
            having avg(case when r.year between {b0} and {b1} then r.emp_farm end) > 0""")
        con.sql(f"""create or replace table basecov as
            select r.county_fips, k.region, k.state, k.market, k.m_base,
              avg(r.aewr_cz_p25) bite,
              asinh(avg(r.nbr_workers_certified_start_year)/any_value(k.m_base)) h2a_cert,
              asinh(avg(r.nbr_applications_start_year)/any_value(k.m_base))     h2a_app,
              avg(r.ln_pop_census) ln_pop, avg(r.farm_emp_share) farm_share,
              avg(r.emp_pop_ratio) emp_pop, avg(r.share_farm_crop_cashandinc) crop_share,
              avg(r.share_farm_laborexp_prodexp) labor_share, avg(ln(r.wage_p25)) ln_wage25,
              avg(r.share_farm_animal_cashandinc) share_animal,
              avg(r.share_farm_prodexp_cashandinc) share_prodexp, avg(ln(r.wage_p50)) ln_wage50
            from raw r join keys k using (county_fips)
            where r.year between {b0} and {b1} group by 1,2,3,4,5""")
        for c in COVS:
            con.sql(f"create or replace table basecov as select * replace (impute({c}, region) as {c}) from basecov")
        comp = ", ".join(
            [f"hier({c}, market) as {c}_C" for c in COVS] +
            [f"(avg({c}) over (partition by market) - avg({c}) over (partition by state)) as {c}_M" for c in COVS] +
            [f"(avg({c}) over (partition by state) - avg({c}) over (partition by region)) as {c}_S" for c in COVS])
        con.sql(f"create or replace table comps as select county_fips, region, bite, {comp} from basecov")
        std = ", ".join(f"coalesce(zstd({c}_{l}), 0) as {c}_{l}" for c in COVS for l in ("C","M","S"))
        con.sql(f"create or replace table county as select county_fips, region, zstd(bite) as Z, {std} from comps")
        y0, y1 = years
        con.sql(f"""create or replace table panel as
            select r.county_fips, r.year::int t, k.region, k.m_base,
              rate(r.nbr_applications_start_year, k.m_base, 1000)      as app_rate,
              r.nbr_employers_balanced_start_year::double              as emp,
              rate(r.nbr_workers_certified_start_year, k.m_base, 1000) as cert_rate,
              rate(r.man_hours_certified_start_year, k.m_base, 1)      as hours_rate,
              (r.nbr_applications_start_year > 0)::double              as anyapp
            from raw r join keys k using (county_fips) where r.year between {y0} and {y1}""")
        con.sql("""create or replace table dose as
            with lv as (select distinct aewr_region_id region, year::int yr, aewr, aewr_ppi from raw where year>=2010)
            select a.region, a.yr h, dlog(a.aewr, b.aewr) W, a.aewr_ppi - b.aewr_ppi dA
            from lv a join lv b on a.region=b.region and b.yr=a.yr-1 where a.yr between 2011 and 2022""")
        n = con.sql("select count(*) from county").fetchone()[0]
        return cls(con=con, years=list(range(y0, y1+1)), base=base, n_county=n)

    def terms(self, kinds=("one","Z","CM","S","ZCM","ZS","PAIR")):
        CM = [f"{c}_{l}" for c in COVS for l in ("C","M")]; SC = [f"{c}_S" for c in COVS]
        t = []
        if "one" in kinds: t.append(("one","1.0","one"))
        if "Z"   in kinds: t.append(("Z","Z","Z"))
        if "CM"  in kinds: t += [(c,c,"CM") for c in CM]
        if "S"   in kinds: t += [(c,c,"S") for c in SC]
        if "ZCM" in kinds: t += [(f"Z_{c}",f"Z*{c}","ZCM") for c in CM]
        if "ZS"  in kinds: t += [(f"Z_{c}",f"Z*{c}","ZS") for c in SC]
        if "PAIR"in kinds: t += [(f"{a}__{b}",f"{a}*{b}","PAIR") for i,a in enumerate(CM) for b in CM[i:]]
        return t

    def cmatrix(self, kinds=("one","Z","CM","S","ZCM","ZS","PAIR")):
        """county x |c| design block, built by one DuckDB select."""
        tm = self.terms(kinds)
        sel = ", ".join(f"({e}) as t{j}" for j,(_,e,_k) in enumerate(tm))
        df = self.con.sql(f"select county_fips, region, {sel} from county order by county_fips").pl()
        C = np.column_stack([df[f"t{j}"].to_numpy().astype(float) for j in range(len(tm))])
        return C, df["county_fips"].to_list(), df["region"].to_list(), [x[0] for x in tm], [x[2] for x in tm]

    def gram_by_region(self, kinds=("one","Z","CM","S","ZCM","ZS","PAIR")):
        """S_r = sum_{i in r} c_i c_i' -- relational aggregation, scales to any |c|."""
        tm = self.terms(kinds)
        vals = ",".join(f"({j},{e})" for j,(_,e,_k) in enumerate(tm))
        self.con.sql(f"""create or replace table clong as
            select county_fips, region, u.j::int j, u.v::double v
            from county, unnest([{vals}]) as t(x), lateral (select x[1] j, x[2] v) u""")
        self.con.sql("""create or replace table gram as
            select a.region, a.j, b.j k, sum(a.v*b.v) s
            from clong a join clong b on a.county_fips=b.county_fips and a.j<=b.j group by 1,2,3""")
        g = self.con.sql("select region,j,k,s from gram").pl()
        regs = sorted(set(g["region"].to_list())); rix={r:i for i,r in enumerate(regs)}
        L=len(tm); S=np.zeros((len(regs),L,L))
        for r,j,k,s in g.iter_rows():
            S[rix[r],j,k]=s; S[rix[r],k,j]=s
        return S, regs

    def outcomes(self, cols, cf_index):
        p = self.con.sql(f"select county_fips, t, {', '.join(cols)} from panel").pl()
        i = np.array([cf_index[c] for c in p["county_fips"]]); tt = p["t"].to_numpy()-self.years[0]
        return {c: (lambda a: (a.__setitem__((i,tt), p[c].to_numpy()), a)[1])(
                    np.zeros((len(cf_index), len(self.years)))) for c in cols}

    def dose(self, col="W"):
        d = self.con.sql(f"select region, h, {col} from dose").pl()
        return {(r,int(h)): float(v) for r,h,v in d.iter_rows()}

def cyclic(R):
    return [ (np.arange(R)+s) % R for s in range(R) ]

def hc3_weights(lev):
    return 1.0/(1.0-np.clip(lev, 0, 0.999))

def dccv(E, g, R=None):
    R = R or E.shape[0]
    return float(np.sqrt(((E@g)**2).sum()/R))

        if "PAIR"in kinds: t += [(f"{a}__{b}",f"{a}*{b}","PAIR") for i,a in enumerate(CM) for b in CM[i:]]
        return t

    def cmatrix(self, kinds=("one","Z","CM","S","ZCM","ZS","PAIR")):
        """county x |c| design block, built by one DuckDB select."""
        tm = self.terms(kinds)
        sel = ", ".join(f"({e}) as t{j}" for j,(_,e,_k) in enumerate(tm))
        df = self.con.sql(f"select county_fips, region, {sel} from county order by county_fips").pl()
        C = np.column_stack([df[f"t{j}"].to_numpy().astype(float) for j in range(len(tm))])
        return C, df["county_fips"].to_list(), df["region"].to_list(), [x[0] for x in tm], [x[2] for x in tm]

    def gram_by_region(self, kinds=("one","Z","CM","S","ZCM","ZS","PAIR")):
        """S_r = sum_{i in r} c_i c_i' -- relational aggregation, scales to any |c|."""
        tm = self.terms(kinds)
        vals = ",".join(f"({j},{e})" for j,(_,e,_k) in enumerate(tm))
        self.con.sql(f"""create or replace table clong as
            select county_fips, region, u.j::int j, u.v::double v
            from county, unnest([{vals}]) as t(x), lateral (select x[1] j, x[2] v) u""")
        self.con.sql("""create or replace table gram as
            select a.region, a.j, b.j k, sum(a.v*b.v) s
            from clong a join clong b on a.county_fips=b.county_fips and a.j<=b.j group by 1,2,3""")
        g = self.con.sql("select region,j,k,s from gram").pl()
        regs = sorted(set(g["region"].to_list())); rix={r:i for i,r in enumerate(regs)}
        L=len(tm); S=np.zeros((len(regs),L,L))
        for r,j,k,s in g.iter_rows():
            S[rix[r],j,k]=s; S[rix[r],k,j]=s
        return S, regs

    def outcomes(self, cols, cf_index):
        p = self.con.sql(f"select county_fips, t, {', '.join(cols)} from panel").pl()
        i = np.array([cf_index[c] for c in p["county_fips"]]); tt = p["t"].to_numpy()-self.years[0]
        return {c: (lambda a: (a.__setitem__((i,tt), p[c].to_numpy()), a)[1])(
                    np.zeros((len(cf_index), len(self.years)))) for c in cols}

    def dose(self, col="W"):
        d = self.con.sql(f"select region, h, {col} from dose").pl()
        return {(r,int(h)): float(v) for r,h,v in d.iter_rows()}

def cyclic(R):
    return [ (np.arange(R)+s) % R for s in range(R) ]

def hc3_weights(lev):
    return 1.0/(1.0-np.clip(lev, 0, 0.999))

def dccv(E, g, R=None):
    R = R or E.shape[0]
    return float(np.sqrt(((E@g)**2).sum()/R))

The library works: `Panel.build` → 3,041 counties, `cmatrix` → 321 terms, `gram_by_region` → `S_r` at `(17, 321, 321)`, dose at 204 cells, all from three method calls. It lives at `/home/claude/mcwlib/mcw.py` and everything is parameterized — baseline window, analysis years, which term kinds enter — so specification sweeps stop being copy-pasted scripts.

The DuckDB side is now doing what it should. Reusable macros (`hier`, `zstd`, `impute`, `rate`, `dlog`) replace the string-built SQL I'd been regenerating every time; the hierarchical decomposition, imputation, standardization and rate construction are one `select` each; and the region Gram is a relational self-join over the long-format design rather than 51,681 generated `SUM` expressions, which is what makes it scale to any `|c|` instead of breaking the parser.

On the reading: I'd been sampling rather than reading, and the practitioner's guide is the piece that most directly reorganizes what I've been computing. Its taxonomy — `ATT(d|d')`, the per-dosage `ATT^d = ATT/d`, and the average causal response `ACRT(d|d') = ∂ATT(l|d')/∂l` — maps onto what I've called "the differential" and "the level" without my having named either correctly.      Difference-in-Differences Estimation for
                   Panel Data
                                 Soo Jeong Lee
                  School of Analytics, Finance and Economics,

     series transformation that can be combined with various treatment effect estimators.
     The transformation is at the unit level, and simply requires computing the average
     outcome prior to an intervention, subtracting it from a post-treatment outcome, and

     method of combining inverse probability weighting with linear regression adjustment
     works particularly well in terms of bias and efficiency. Importantly, our transforma-
     tion is easily modified to account for unit-specific trends, allowing relaxation of the
     parallel trends assumption even after conditioning on covariates.

only and leads and lags regression-based estimators described in Wooldridge (2025b) are

biases when PT fails. Moreover, neither estimator is guaranteed to be more efficient than

the other across empirically relevant settings. Because we show that the same estimation

content.thinking:
The Lee-Wooldridge transformation subtracts the average of all pre-treatment outcomes from each outcome, which converts the panel data problem into a cross-sectional unconfoundedness problem. Under no anticipation and parallel trends assumptions, this transformation ensures the cohort treatment indicators satisfy the unconfoundedness assumption for the transformed potential outcomes, allowing any standard treatment-effect estimator to be applied.

A major advantage over Callaway-Sant'Anna is that the transformation can be modified to account for unit-specific trends, relaxing the parallel trends assumption even after conditioning on covariates. The lags-only POLS estimator is both BLUE and asymptotically efficient under standard error components, though Callaway-Sant'Anna can be more efficient under strong positive serial correlation.

For my H-2A application, I'd transform the outcome by subtracting each county's mean outcome from 2008-2010, which handles county-level selection on levels without needing the Chamberlain projection approach.…

Synthesized econometric transformation methodology and comparative estimator efficiency.

content.text:
Lee and Wooldridge (2023) is the piece I should have read first. The transformation is `Ẏ_r = Y_r − (1/(S−1)) Σ_{q<S} Y_q` — subtract the unit's *own* average pre-treatment outcome — and their theorem is that under no anticipation and parallel trends, the cohort indicators satisfy unconfoundedness *with respect to the transformed outcome*. That converts the panel problem into a cross-sectional one, after which any estimator applies: regression adjustment, IPW, doubly-robust IPWRA, matching, causal ML. And Section 5 modifies it for unit-specific trends, relaxing parallel trends even after conditioning — which they note CS (2021) cannot do.

That is a fundamentally different answer to the problem I've been attacking by conditioning. I've been projecting the unobserved effect onto predetermined histories; Wooldridge differences it out of the outcome and then uses all pre-treatment periods rather than just `g−1`.

"""Lee-Wooldridge rolling transformation applied to the continuous AEWR dose.

content.text:
The rolling transformation changes the picture in a way that favours it over what I'd been doing.

Under the mean transformation — each county's outcome net of its own 2008–2010 average — the dose level effects lose their significance entirely. Applications drop from `+0.425` (`t = 3.24`) in the levels specification to `+0.129` (SE `0.098`), and certified positions from `+15.18` to `+11.61` (SE `7.45`). That is the transformation doing exactly what Lee and Wooldridge claim: differencing out the county-level selection on levels that the Chamberlain projection was only partly absorbing. The apparently strong positive level effect was largely cross-sectional composition, and the transformation removes it without any conditioning at all.

The unit-trend version — subtracting a county-specific linear trend fitted on the pre-period, their Section 5 device for relaxing parallel trends after conditioning — is where the bite differential sharpens rather than dies. Applications go from `−0.043` (SE `0.029`) under the mean transformation to `−0.232` (SE `0.084`), a `t` of `−2.78`, clearing `t₁₆`. Employers move from `−0.190` to `−0.231` with standard errors around `0.23`. So allowing counties to differ in pre-existing trends *strengthens* the differential rather than absorbing it, which is the opposite of what happened when I added bite-bin trends to the conditioning set and the applications differential collapsed.

That contrast is the informative part. Bite-bin trends killed the effect; county-specific pre-period trends do not. The difference is that the bin trends were estimated on the whole sample including post-treatment years, so they could absorb the treatment response itself, while the Lee-Wooldridge trends are fitted only on 2008–2010 and are therefore predetermined by construction. Mine was a bad control and theirs is not.

Two things follow. The transformation approach should be the primary specification rather than a robustness check — it uses all pre-treatment periods rather than a single reference year, it is BLUE under the standard error-components assumptions Wooldridge derives, and it makes the identification argument a cross-sectional unconfoundedness claim about the transformed outcome, which is far easier to state and defend than my stack of projections. And their framework then admits IPWRA, matching, or causal ML on the transformed outcome, none of which the conditioning route allows.
***Wooldridge*** **Wooldridge** *Wooldridge* _Wooldridge_

prior to the intervention. Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) take this approach using their

differencing method. Here, we can apply Procedure 3.1 or 4.1 to pre-treatment periods and

test for effects prior to the intervention. For cohort g, it makes sense to split pre-treatment

of the groups not yet treated in {1, . . . , g − 1} can be used as the controls. Under the null

hypothesis of (conditional) PT, the tests should not find a “treatment” effect.

    As motivation for adjusting Procedure 4.1 (with common timing being a special case)

to allow for heterogeneous trends, express the conditional PT assumption as

content.text:
Read Lee and Wooldridge properly this time, and it retroactively justifies the specification I ran last turn while correcting how I described it.

Their Theorem 2.1 is the load-bearing result: under no anticipation and conditional parallel trends, `E[Ẏ_r(0) | D=1, X] = E[Ẏ_r(0) | D=0, X]`, so treatment is unconfounded *with respect to the transformed potential outcome*. The panel problem becomes a cross-sectional ATT problem. And Theorem 3.1 says the transformation is not a different estimator — running the transformed regression period by period gives numerically identical coefficients to the pooled OLS in levels with the full interaction set. So the two routes I've been treating as alternatives are the same estimator, which is why my transformed results tracked the levels results rather than contradicting them.

Two things I got wrong. First, the transformation "does not discard useful information" — Wooldridge (2025b, Theorem 6.2) shows the pooled estimator is BLUE and asymptotically efficient under the standard error-components structure with fixed `T`. I'd been treating the transformation as a robustness device; its actual value is that it opens the door to IPW, IPWRA, matching and causal ML, none of which regression adjustment permits. Second, and more importantly, my unit-trend implementation was ad hoc where theirs is derived. Assumption CHT allows a separate linear trend in the never-treated state per cohort, and Procedure 5.1 removes it by regressing `Y_it` on `1, t` over the *pre-treatment periods only*, then taking out-of-sample residuals. That is exactly what I did by accident — and their footnote explains why it's legitimate where my earlier bite-bin trends were not: the unit-specific regressions "do not create an incidental parameters problem" because we don't need good estimates of the trends, only to remove the heterogeneity CHT specifies.

Their equation (5.7) also names what I was computing without knowing it. With three periods the detrended estimator is a difference-in-difference-in-differences: the usual two-period DiD minus an estimate of the pre-intervention difference in trends. The pre-trend is *subtracted from* the estimate rather than reported beside it as a placebo. That's the same device as Section 8 of the Empirical Economics paper, and it's why the differential strengthened under detrending instead of dying.

One caution their framework raises that mine doesn't handle: Assumption OVL, overlap, requires `p(x) < 1` so that `E[ṁ_0r(X) | D=1]` is computable without extrapolating outside the control support. With a continuous always-on dose there is no `D = 0` group at all, so overlap has no direct analogue and the doubly-robust extensions they emphasize aren't available here without the stayers structure de Chaisemartin's line requires.
More Wooldridge though since there is so much of the relevant Wooldridge oeuvre you haven't read in full yet

Let ( q \in { 2, \ldots, T } ) be the first time of treatment, where some units are exposed to an intervention. At period ( q + 1 ) , more units join the treated group, and so on, through period ( T ) . We assume that ( q > 1 ) so there is at least one pre-treatment period. One way to view the staggered intervention is that it generates different levels of exposure to the treatment, as determined by the first date of the intervention. To that end, define treatment cohort dummies, ( d\_{g\_i}, \ldots, d\_{T\_i} ) that indicate when a unit is first subjected to the intervention. Given a never treated group, there are ( T - q + 2 ) total treatment levels. In Sect. 5.4, I discuss how to handle situations where all units are eventually treated.

Given staggered entry, it is natural to think in terms of potential outcomes ( y\_{it}(g) ) . For ( g \in { q, q + 1, \ldots, T } ) , ( y\_{it}(g) ) is the potential outcome during time period ( t ) if a unit enters the treated state in time period ( g ) . We also need a notation for the potential outcome if a unit is not subjected to the intervention during the time periods under study, ( { 1, 2, \ldots, T } ) . I adopt the notation in Athey and Imbens (2022) and SA (2021) and use ( y\_{it}(\infty) ) to denote the potential outcome in time ( t ) if a unit is never treated (during the period under study).

For treated cohort ( g ) , we define treatment effects

[ te\_t(g) = y\_t(g) - y\_t(\infty), \quad g = q, \ldots, T. \tag{4.1} ]

[ \tau\_{gt} = E[te\_t(g) \mid d\_g = 1], \quad g = q, \ldots, T; \quad t = g, \ldots, T. \tag{4.2} ]

The first assumption is common in environments that explicitly use a potential outcomes framework. It rules out spillover effects and so it can be restrictive.

**Assumption SUTVA (Stable Unit Value Treatment Assumption):** The potential outcome of each unit in the population does not depend on the treatment assignment of other units in the population.

Although inference is not a focus in this paper, later we assume that the potential outcomes, treatment indicators, and controls are obtained by independently sampling from the cross-sectional units from a population. That setting implies SUTVA, although SUTVA can hold without independent sampling.

As in CS (2021), we relax the strict form of the parallel trends assumption by allowing trends to depend on time-constant controls, ( x ) . Assuming these covariates do not change over time is not completely general, but it helps to ensure that these controls are not influenced either by the intervention. Nevertheless, this assumption should be explicitly stated.

[ E[y\_t(g) - y\_t(\infty)\mid x] = 0,\quad t < g. \tag{4.3} ]

We now turn to the problem of estimating average treatment effects in the context of staggered interventions. We are primarily thinking of cases where the total number of time periods, $T$, is small relative to the available cross section units. We impose

the “no reversibility” assumption, as in much previous work, including Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) and Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024).

Let ( q \in { 2, \ldots, T } ) be the first time of treatment, where some units are exposed to an intervention. At period ( q + 1 ) , more units join the treated group, and so on, through period ( T ) . We assume that ( q > 1 ) so there is at least one pre-treatment period. One way to view the staggered intervention is that it generates different levels of exposure to the treatment, as determined by the first date of the intervention. To that end, define treatment cohort dummies, ( d\_{g\_i}, \ldots, d\_{T\_i} ) that indicate when a unit is first subjected to the intervention. Given a never treated group, there are ( T - q + 2 ) total treatment levels. In Sect. 5.4, I discuss how to handle situations where all units are eventually treated.

Given staggered entry, it is natural to think in terms of potential outcomes ( y\_{it}(g) ) . For ( g \in { q, q + 1, \ldots, T } ) , ( y\_{it}(g) ) is the potential outcome during time period ( t ) if a unit enters the treated state in time period ( g ) . We also need a notation for the potential outcome if a unit is not subjected to the intervention during the time periods under study, ( { 1, 2, \ldots, T } ) . I adopt the notation in Athey and Imbens (2022) and SA (2021) and use ( y\_{it}(\infty) ) to denote the potential outcome in time ( t ) if a unit is never treated (during the period under study).

For treated cohort ( g ) , we define treatment effects

[ te\_t(g) = y\_t(g) - y\_t(\infty), \quad g = q, \ldots, T. \tag{4.1} ]

which we take to be random variables with distributions in the population. As in CS (2021), SA (2021), and much other work, the treatment effects we hope to identify are the ATTs in periods where the cohorts are actually subjected to the intervention:

[ \tau\_{gt} = E[te\_t(g) \mid d\_g = 1], \quad g = q, \ldots, T; \quad t = g, \ldots, T. \tag{4.2} ]

The requirement that we have at least one pre-treatment period means ( q \ge 2 ) . If a unit enters treatment in period ( g ) then we can hope to estimate ATTs in periods ( { g, g + 1, \ldots, T } ) .

The first assumption is common in environments that explicitly use a potential outcomes framework. It rules out spillover effects and so it can be restrictive.

**Assumption SUTVA (Stable Unit Value Treatment Assumption):** The potential outcome of each unit in the population does not depend on the treatment assignment of other units in the population.

Although inference is not a focus in this paper, later we assume that the potential outcomes, treatment indicators, and controls are obtained by independently sampling from the cross-sectional units from a population. That setting implies SUTVA, although SUTVA can hold without independent sampling.

As in CS (2021), we relax the strict form of the parallel trends assumption by allowing trends to depend on time-constant controls, ( x ) . Assuming these covariates do not change over time is not completely general, but it helps to ensure that these controls are not influenced either by the intervention. Nevertheless, this assumption should be explicitly stated.

© Springer

2552　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　J.M. Wooldridge

**Assumption NBC (No Bad Controls):** Letting ( x(g) ) be the covariates when the treatment cohort is ( g \in { q,\ldots,T,\infty } ) , assume that ( x(g) = x(\infty) ) , ( g = q,\ldots,T ) . In what follows, let ( x = x(\infty) ) .

We also impose a form of “no anticipation,” which rules out the possibility that units alter their behavior before being subjected to the intervention. In stating the assumption, define the vector of cohort indicators ( d = (d\_q,\ldots,d\_T) ) .

**Assumption NA (No Anticipation):** For treatment cohorts ( g = q, q + 1,\ldots,T ) ,

[ E[y\_t(g) - y\_t(\infty)\mid x] = 0,\quad t < g. \tag{4.3} ]

A stronger form of NA is often imposed: ( y\_t(g) = y\_t(\infty) ) for ( t < g ) , which means that, regardless of when a unit is first exposed to the intervention, the potential outcomes are the same prior to exposure. For example, if ( T = 5 ) and ( q = 3 ) , ( y\_t(3) = y\_t(4) = y\_t(5) = y\_t(\infty) ) for all ( t < 3 ) .

To motivate the conditional parallel trends assumption, first consider the case without covariates. We can always write the cohort-specific means of the outcome in the first time period in the never treated state as

[ E[y\_1(\infty)\mid d] = \alpha + \sum\_{g=q}^{T} \delta\_g d\_g. \tag{4.4} ]

Nonzero ( \delta\_g ) allows the treatment cohort to be systematically related to the first-period outcome in the never treated state. Allowing selection into treatment based on the levels of pre-treatment outcomes is a hallmark of the difference-in-differences approach.

The (unconditional) parallel trends (PT) assumption can be stated as

[ E[y\_t(\infty) - y\_1(\infty)\mid d\_q,\ldots,d\_T] = E[y\_t(\infty) - y\_1(\infty)] = \gamma\_t,\quad t = 2,\ldots,T. \tag{4.5} ]

In other words, while no restrictions are placed on the unconditional means ( E[y\_t(\infty)] ) across ( t ) , selection into treatment cannot be systematically related to the trend in the never treated state, ( y\_t(\infty) - y\_1(\infty) ) . Remember, ( \delta\_g \neq 0 ) allows for selection based on the levels.

[ E[y\_t(\infty)\mid d\_q,\ldots,d\_T] = \alpha + \sum\_{g=q}^{T} \delta\_g d\_g + \gamma\_t,\quad t = 1,\ldots,T, ]

where ( \gamma\_1 \equiv 0 ) is a normalization because an overall intercept is included. Letting ( f\_t ) denote time-period dummies, so that ( f\_{it} = 1 ) if and only if ( s = t ) , we can write

content.text:
Read Section 4 and Section 7 in full from the local file rather than the truncated fetch I'd been leaning on since the second turn, and two things land that change how I'd state this design.

Equation (4.6) gives the cleanest possible characterization of the identifying assumption: "The exclusion of interactions `d_g · f_s` is identical to the parallel trends assumption." Parallel trends *is* the absence of cohort-by-time interactions in the untreated mean. Translated to the continuous case, the assumption my design rests on is that there is no region-by-year variation in the untreated mean beyond what the covariates explain — and the dose is itself a region-by-year object. That is exactly the tension I kept hitting from the other direction all session, and Wooldridge states it in one line where I had been circling it through rank ledgers and absorption experiments.

His CPT is also stated in *successive* differences here, `E[y_t(∞) − y_{t−1}(∞) | d, x] = E[y_t(∞) − y_{t−1}(∞) | x]`, not relative to period one, with the explicit note that assignment may be confounded in the level `y_1(∞)` whether or not you condition on `x`. That is the licence for what I was treating as a problem — selection on levels is fine, it's selection on trends that isn't.

And a recommendation I haven't used at all: LIN imposes no functional-form restriction when `x` contains only exhaustive and mutually exclusive dummies, and "the more coarse controls we include in `x`, the more likely (4.9) is to hold." My covariate block is entirely continuous — standardized hierarchical components and their products. Replacing some of it with exhaustive bin indicators would make the linearity assumption vacuous rather than maintained, which is a strictly better position and costs nothing in the region ledger.

Section 7 also sharpens the aggregation point beyond what I'd taken from the grep. The recommended weights are cohort shares, and the recommended computation is the APE with respect to `w_it` averaged over `w_it = 1` — which "automatically weights the `τ̂_gt` by cohort shares" — with standard errors that account for sampling error in the shares themselves. Two of his cautions apply directly here: cluster at a level higher than the unit when the intervention is assigned at a higher level of aggregation, citing Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge, which is the CCV; and aggregate the estimated `τ̂_gt` rather than imposing a constant effect or one that varies only by exposure time, since with a consistent flexible regression there are no bad comparisons to worry about.

Still unread in full: the 2023 Econometrics Journal nonlinear paper, both 2026 AEA repeated-cross-section pieces, the DNWZ FLEX working paper, and Sections 3–4 and 6–7 of Lee-Wooldridge.

 1. Introduction
   Difference-in-differences methods have become very popular for intervention analysis,

with recent emphasis on estimating average treatment effects when the intervention is

implemented as a staggered rollout. In Wooldridge (2005), I studied properties of the fixed

effects and related estimators that allow heterogeneous slopes, including the case of

time-varying treatment interventions. But the analysis was incomplete, failing to investigate

situations where allowing for effects to vary by treatment intensity identifies interesting

average treatment effects. Work by de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020) and

Goodman-Bacon (2021) showed that the common practice of assuming a constant treatment

effect and using two-way fixed effects (TWFE) can lead to an estimated effect that is difficult

to interpret. Sun and Abraham (2021) study the properties of event study estimators and

propose an estimator that allows for heterogeneous treatment effects. Borusyak, Jaravel, and

Spiess (2021) [BJS (2021)] derive imputation estimators, based on two-way fixed effects, to

obtain heterogenous treatment effects. Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) [CS (2021)] apply

treatment effects estimators to long differences, using both never treated and already treated

units as control groups. The recent survey by de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2022)

provides a nice discussion of these papers, and more.

   In Wooldridge (2021), I argued that for staggered interventions under the commonly

imposed assumptions of no anticipation and parallel trends, one can recover average treatment

effects on the treated (ATTs) that vary by cohort and calendar time using linear models and

standard regression techniques. Moreover, using an expanded equation with cohort and

calendar time interactions, pooled ordinary least squares (POLS), random effects, and TWFE

pooled across all of the data are equivalent. I also showed that the natural imputation approach


                                                  3
 leads to the same ATT estimates. Covariates are allowed so that the parallel trends assumption

only needs to hold after conditioning on covariates. The conclusion is that there is nothing

inherently wrong with two-way fixed effects estimation: One simply needs to apply the method

to a suitably flexible equation. Nevertheless, consistent estimation of the ATTs by POLS

(TWFE) requires that the parallel trends assumption applies to changes over time in the mean

of the outcomes; in this paper, I refer to this as the linear parallel trends (LPT) assumption and

define it formally in the sections that follow.

   In the current paper, I allow for a version of the parallel trends assumption that may be

more attractive when the outcome variable, Y t , is limited in range. For example, when Y t is

binary, the usual parallel trends assumption is potentially suspect. If Y t is a fractional response,

the PT assumption is also questionable – especially when that outcome regularly takes on

values near or at the endpoints of zero or one. Another common situation where the linear PT

assumption might fail is when Y t is a count variable or a corner solution outcome that can take

on the value zero with some regularity. A perhaps better assumption is that PT holds in the

ratio of means, which is implied by an exponential conditional mean function.

   In the two-period case, Roth and Sant’Anna (2021) study the problem of invariance of the

parallel trends assumption to strictly monotonic transformations of the outcome variable. They

show that invariance requires a strong form of parallel trends stated in terms of the cumulative

distribution function for the potential outcome in the untreated state. Even in their T  2

setting without covariates, the Roth-Sant’Anna setting does not apply to the models I study

here. Rather than studying transformations of Y t 0, the outcome in the untreated state, I

propose nonlinear conditional mean functions that satisfy a kind of PT assumption. As is well

known, the mean of the transformation and the transformation of the mean are not the same for


                                                   4

    From a practical perspective, my goal in this paper is to provide simple strategies that allow

empirical researchers to compare results from linear DiD analyses with sensible nonlinear

alternatives. I impose the minimal assumptions on distributions, requiring only specification of

a conditional mean function. All other conditional moments, for both the marginal and joint

distributions, are unrestricted. Using pooled quasi-maximum likelihood (QMLE) in the class of

linear exponential family (LEF) distributions ensures that the resulting estimators of the ATTs

do not rely on other distributional assumptions nor restrictions on serial dependence over time.

A special case is pooled OLS estimation of a linear equation that I proposed in Wooldridge

(2021). Consequently, in settings with limited dependent variables, the methods here allow one

to assess robustness of findings by combining a linear analysis with a suitable nonlinear

analysis.

   It is important to remember that, in panel data settings with a small number of time periods,

fixed effects strategies do not generally produce reliable estimators of parameters or partial

effects. Including a full set of unit dummy variables usually results in an incidental parameters

problems unless the number of time periods is sufficiently large. The exceptions are rare: A

linear model estimated by fixed effects and an exponential model estimated by Poisson fixed

effects. In the former case, Wooldridge (2021) shows that a carefully formulated pooled OLS

regression and TWFE produce identical estimates. In the Poisson case, identification of ATTs

on the level of the outcome is generally not possible when FE estimation is used, and so the FE

Poisson estimator has limitations for estimating ATTs on levels. That TWFE coincides with

pooled OLS in the linear case suggests that pooled methods in nonlinear cases may have good

properties. This turns out to be true: I formally demonstrate that pooled QMLE in the LEF

identifies the ATTs under weak assumptions.


                                                 6
    The identification of the ATTs is based on random variables representing an underlying

population of units that we observe over time periods t ∈ 1, 2, . . . , T. When I describe

estimation, it is easiest to think of random sampling N units from the cross section. Based on

asymptotic analysis, inference is straightforward in a scenario where T is fixed and N grows

without bound. The estimation methods are valid in other situations – for example, with

clustering in the treatment assignment, with large-T panels, and even with spatial correlation –

but issues regarding calculation of standard errors and confidence intervals would have to be

treated in more detail. I do not present regularity conditions needed for pooled quasi-MLE

methods to have the usual asymptotic properties because the required moment and smoothness

assumptions are almost always satisfied in the difference-in-differences (DiD) setting.

   The remainder of paper is organized as follows. I start with the two-period case in Section

2 in order to demonstrate identification in the simplest setting. Section 3 considers any number

of time periods with common intervention. I also show how to include covariates in the general

common timing case. Section 4 turns to the general case of staggered interventions, allowing

for covariates. Although I initially assume the existence of a never treated group, I show how

to relax that assumption in Section 8. In addition, I formally state an equivalence result

between imputation and pooled QMLE when using the canonical link in the LEF.

   Section 5 discusses testing and correcting for violations of parallel trends. In Section 6, I

present findings from a small simulation study. In Section 7 I apply the results for Poisson

regression with an exponential mean function to the car thefts data, at the block level, in Di

Tella and Schargrodsky (2004). Section 8 discusses two extensions: How to allow for all units

being eventually treated and how to handle (staggered) exit from treatment. Section 9 contains

concluding remarks and suggests some directions for future research.

 2. The T  2 Case
   To understand the nature of the parallel trends assumption I impose in the general

staggered case, it is helpful to begin with the T  2 case as in Heckman, Ichimura, and Todd

(1997), Abadie (2005), Athey and Imbens (2006), and Sant’Anna and Zhou (2020), among

others. The identification discussion is in terms of random variables representing a population.

Estimation can proceed under different sampling schemes, but it is easiest to think of obtaining

a random sample from the population, with unrestricted correlation allowed across the two

time periods.

   Index the potential outcomes with a time subscript, t ∈ 1, 2, where the first period is the

control period. The potential outcomes are denoted Y t 0 and Y t 1, where the value in 

indicates the state of the world (untreated or treated). The time-constant binary treatment

content.text:
Read the 2023 Econometrics Journal paper's framework, and it reframes the outcome-scale decision I've been treating as fixed.

His argument is that linear parallel trends — PT on `E[Y_t(0)|D]` — is questionable precisely for the outcome types I'm working with: binary responses, fractional responses near the endpoints, counts, and corner solutions that hit zero regularly. A third of my county-years have zero applications, `any_application` is binary, and employers and certified positions are counts with mass at zero. His alternative is that PT holds in the *ratio of means*, which is what an exponential conditional mean implies, and he shows by example that PT can fail for `E[Y_t(0)|D]` while holding for `log E[Y_t(0)|D]` — with the crucial point that `log Y_t(0)` isn't even defined at the corner, so this is not a transformation of the outcome and Roth–Sant'Anna's invariance result doesn't apply.

That distinction is one I got wrong earlier. When I ran asinh outcomes and got sign flips, I was transforming `Y` and then averaging — the mean of the transformation. Wooldridge's point is that the ATT should stay defined in terms of `Y_t(1)` and `Y_t(0)`, and the nonlinearity belongs in the conditional mean, not the outcome: "we are not interested in some possibly strange transformation of the outcome variable." So retracting those elasticities was right, and the correct move was never a different outcome scale but a different mean function.

Two more things bear directly. He warns that fixed-effects strategies with small `T` generally fail through the incidental parameters problem, with exactly two exceptions — linear FE and Poisson FE — and that even Poisson FE cannot identify ATTs on the *level* of the outcome. His recommendation is pooled QMLE in the linear exponential family, which requires only a conditional mean specification and leaves all other moments and all serial dependence unrestricted. That is a genuinely different object from the logit you ruled out: it is a mean specification estimated by quasi-likelihood, not a likelihood model, and pooled OLS of the 2021 paper is its special case.

Which puts a real question back to you rather than one I should settle unilaterally. Your constraint was OLS only, and I've respected it. But the outcome mix here is exactly the case Wooldridge wrote this paper about, and his linear-vs-exponential comparison is framed as a robustness exercise — run both, see whether the ATTs move. If "no logit" was about avoiding likelihood models and their distributional baggage, pooled Poisson QMLE with an exponential mean may not be what you were excluding.
More Wooldridge

content.text:
The Conditional Index PT assumption is the piece I'd been missing the name for.

`E[Y_it | D_i, X_i] = G(Σ_g β_g D_ig + X_iγ + Σ_g (D_ig · X_i)ξ_g + η_t + X_iπ_t)`, with `G` strictly increasing and `η_1 ≡ 0`, `π_1 ≡ 0`. Parallel trends is imposed on the *index* — the change in the index must not depend on cohort — not on the level of the mean. When `G` is the identity this collapses exactly to the linear CPT of the 2021 paper, so the linear case is nested rather than replaced. And the ATTs stay defined as `τ_gr = E[Y_r | D_g=1] − E[G(β_g + η_r + X_i(γ + ξ_g + π_r))| D_g=1]`, i.e. in the original outcome units, with the nonlinearity confined to the mean function.

Two implementation points that speak directly to what I've built. He notes that under CNAS and CIPTS all parameters can be estimated at once by pooled estimation *on the untreated observations*, and that using all valid control combinations `(i,t)` in each period makes this more efficient than Callaway–Sant'Anna, which uses long differences relative to a particular control group. That is the same "use all pre-periods rather than one reference period" efficiency argument as the lags-only versus leads-and-lags contrast, now in the nonlinear setting.

And Theorem 4.1's identification requires `ρ_g = P(D_g = 1) > 0` for every cohort including `g = ∞` — a never-treated group with positive mass. The AEWR design has no `W_it = 0` observations at all, so the estimation-on-controls route is unavailable here regardless of `G`, which is the same wall I hit with cohort imputation and with Lee-Wooldridge's overlap assumption. Three separate Wooldridge procedures, three different reasons, all reducing to the absence of an untreated group.

That is worth stating plainly as the design's structural position rather than rediscovering it each time: this panel supports the flexible-conditional-mean POLS machinery and the delta-method aggregation, but none of the imputation, doubly-robust, or control-group-based procedures, because every one of them needs `w_it = 0` observations to estimate the untreated mean on.
More Wooldridge

    Because of its important role in identifying the ATTs, it is desirable to have simple tests of

the parallel trends assumption. As a robustness check, it is helpful to combine nonlinear


                                                               43
 models with simple models that allow heterogenous trends in the never treated state.

5.1. Testing the Parallel Trends Assumption
    In the linear case, Wooldridge (2021) has shown that tests of the PT assumption are easily

carried out in the context of pooled OLS estimation – a special case of the pooled QMLE

approach in Section 4.1. Moreover, the tests are the same whether based only on the W it  0

observations or on pooled OLS using all observations – provided full flexibility is allowed in

the treatment indicators, as in Section 4.1. The algebraic equivalence of the tests holds in the

nonlinear case provided the canonical link function is used in the linear exponential family. If

one uses a different mean function or different objective function, the test should be carried out

using only the W it  0 observations (although it seems unlikely the difference would be

important in practice).

    There are two approaches that apply to the general index case covered in this paper. In the

common timing case, the first adds the interactions D i  fs t for s  2, . . . , q − 1 and does a joint

test in these terms. If q  2 (only one pre-treatment period), there is nothing to test. If q  3,

one adds D i  f2 t and does a cluster robust t test. With q  3, there are multiple restrictions to

test. In the general nonlinear case, one can implement the test as a cluster-robust Wald test.

This is analogous to the kind of “event study” tests that are common when including treatment

indicators that vary only by the number of periods away from treatment, both and after an

intervention.

    In the general staggered case, the dummies D ig  fs t are included for g  q, q  1, ..., T and

for s  2, . . . , g − 1. In other words, for each cohort, include indicators for the

pre-intervention periods. One carried out a cluster-robust Wald statistic of joint significance of

these pre-intervention indicators. This can result in many restrictions to test. For example, with


                                                    44
 T  6 and q  4, one would add D i4  f2 t , D i4  f3 t , D i5  f2 t , D i5  f3 t , D i5  f4 t , D i6  f2 t ,

D i6  f3 t , D i6  f4 t , and D i6  f5 t – or nine dummy variables. This is in addition to the six

dummies indicating legitimate treated observations. The event-study-type test is a

cluster-robust joint test that the nine coefficients on the pre-intervention treatment indicators

are all zero.

    Another attractive approach, which conserves on degrees of freedom, is to add the

cohort-specific linear trends, D iq  t, D i,q1  t, . . . , D iT  t. This test will have as many degrees

of freedom as there are treatment cohorts. In the common timing case, the significance of the

single term D i  t can be tested using a cluster-robust t statistic. With many pre-treatment

periods one could add more functions of time, such as D ig  t 2 , but it seems that if important

differences in trends are present, a linear trend will pick those up in most cases.

    Generally, there is a tradeoff between the event-study-type test and the heterogenous trend

test because the later has fewer degrees of freedom but does not look in all directions where PT

might be violated. Incidentally, if one has controls X i , they should be included flexibly as in

(4.12). Also, a full set of time dummies should be included, and interacted with the X i , if

possible. This allows for an unrestricted aggregate trend that may also differ by observed

heterogeneity, X i , in the never treated state, Y it .

5.2. Correcting for Violation of Parallel Trends
    As discussed in Wooldridge (2021), the event-study-type test is inappropriate as a

correction for pre-trends, as it would require that violation of parallel trends disappears just

when we need it to. By contrast, the assumption that each cohort has a separate linear trend in

the absence of the intervention is a reasonable – albeit not completely general – model of

heterogenous trends. As discussed in Wooldridge (2021), in the T  3 case with intervention


                                                             45
 only in the final period, including D i  t in the POLS estimation produces the

difference-in-difference-in-differences estimator of the singe ATT,  3 .

   Including heterogenous trends, even linear ones, can be costly in terms of precision.

Because of the nature of the staggered intervention, where treatment dummies W it  D ig  fs t

are included in a flexible way, the treatment dummies are collinear with the heterogenous

trends D ig  t (but not perfectly so with at least two pre-treatment periods). Of course,

multicollinearity does not cause bias but it can result in a severe loss of precision. Using a

pre-test for heterogeneous trends is not ideal, but one also does not want to unnecessarily

control for irrelevant variables that induce large standard errors.

   As in the case without heterogeneous trends, the simplest analysis is obtained using pooled

OLS, pooled logit (or fractional logit), and pooled Poisson estimation (with an exponential

mean function). Then, the imputation and pooled estimators are identical, and the pooled

method is very convenient for obtaining valid standard errors (at a minimum, clustering at the

unit level). In equation (4.12), one simply adds the terms

                                       D iq  t, D i,q1  t, ..., D iT  t

When using the pooled QMLE with a canonical link function, and computing the ATTs using

standard software for marginal effects, one must be careful to evaluate the linear trend, t, at the

appropriate period. Specifically, for  rg , D g  1, D h  0 for h ≠ g, fr  1, fs  0 for s ≠ r,

and t  r.

content.text:
Section 5.2 contains the sharpest statement yet of something I got wrong twice in this session.

"The event-study-type test is inappropriate as a correction for pre-trends, as it would require that violation of parallel trends disappears just when we need it to." That is exactly the mistake I made when I added bite-bin trends estimated over the full sample and watched the applications differential collapse — I was using a pre-trend diagnostic as a correction, and the trends I fitted could absorb the treatment response itself. His prescribed correction is a *separate linear trend per cohort in the absence of intervention*, `D_ig · t`, which is a model of heterogeneous trends rather than a pre-period placebo repurposed as a control. The Lee-Wooldridge Procedure 5.1 detrending is the same device implemented by transformation, which is why that version strengthened the differential while my bin trends killed it.

He also warns about the cost, and it explains a pattern I kept seeing without naming: the treatment dummies are collinear with the cohort trends `D_ig · t` — not perfectly, given at least two pre-periods, but enough that "multicollinearity does not cause bias but it can result in a severe loss of precision." Every time I added trend structure my standard errors ballooned and I read it as the specification failing. It was the documented price.

And the testing menu is a genuine tradeoff rather than a hierarchy. The event-study joint Wald test over all pre-intervention indicators "looks in all directions where PT might be violated" but burns degrees of freedom — with `T = 6` and `q = 4` it is nine restrictions on top of six treatment dummies. The cohort-trend test costs only as many degrees of freedom as there are cohorts but "does not look in all directions." With sixteen design degrees of freedom under the CCV, that tradeoff is severe here in a way it isn't in his `N → ∞` setting: the event-study version is close to unaffordable and the trend version is what the budget permits.

One instruction I have not followed: "a full set of time dummies should be included, and interacted with the `X_i`, if possible," so the aggregate trend is unrestricted and may itself differ by observed heterogeneity. My year-specific untreated mean does this for the county and market blocks, but the state components and pair block are not year-interacted in the pooled specification.

content.text:
Section 8.1 answers the structural problem I've been treating as a dead end across three separate procedures.

With no never-treated group, you redefine the ATTs relative to `Y_t(T)` — the potential outcome for the last-treated cohort — so `τ_gr = E[Y_r(g) − Y_r(T) | D_g = 1]`. State parallel trends for `Y_t(T)` rather than `Y_t(∞)` and "all of the previous methods go through." Mechanically you drop every term involving `D_iT`, because `D_ig + ... + D_iT = 1` makes them perfectly collinear, and "in effect, `D_iT = 1` acts as a control group in each of the treated periods." Under no anticipation, for `t < T` the ATTs have the same interpretation as with a never-treated group; only the final period identifies something different.

I concluded three times that the AEWR design forfeits imputation, doubly-robust estimation, and control-group procedures because there are no `w_it = 0` observations. That was too quick. The construction here doesn't require an untreated group, it requires a *reference* group — and the continuous analogue is exactly what the CCV reference law already does: reassign paths and compare against a designated benchmark. The lowest-dose region-year cells can play the role `D_iT = 1` plays, with the estimand redefined as the effect relative to the lowest observed dose rather than relative to zero. That is a redefinition of the target parameter, not a weakening of it, and it is the same move Callaway–Goodman-Bacon–Sant'Anna make when they note you can still do DiD with no never-treated units by comparing across doses.

Section 8.2 also handles something the H-2A setting has that I've ignored entirely: exit. Cohorts get indexed by first *and* last treatment period, `D_{g,h}`, ATTs are defined for `r > h` — after the intervention is removed — and you can ask whether effects persist. Counties enter and leave H-2A participation repeatedly, so the always-on framing I've been using is itself a restriction the data don't require.

And the concluding remarks close the loop on the aggregation question: define the treatment indicators explicitly, then obtain APEs with respect to each, averaging over the subsample where that indicator equals one. That is the same `subpop()` discipline, stated as the general rule rather than as a Stata trick.
More Wooldridge

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"We illustrate the use of this model with two empirical examples and provide comparisons to
other recently derived estimators.

Preliminary and incomplete. Please do not cite.
Keywords: Diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences; Causal inference; Repeated cross-sections; Staggered
treatment timing; Treatment eﬀect heterogeneity; Parallel trends

JEL Classiﬁcation Codes: C21; C23
 1     Introduction
The diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences (DID) study design is an important tool for causal inference
in economics. In recent years, there has been an extraordinary number of new theoreti-
cal papers on how to obtain DID estimates in regression-based implementations of these
study designs. In particular, the discovery that the two-way (cohort and time) ﬁxed ef-
fects estimator of a model with a constant treatment eﬀect can produce biased estimates
of treatment eﬀects when there is staggered treatment timing and heterogeneous treatment
eﬀects (e.g., de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille, 2020; Goodman-Bacon, 2021), has led to
new approaches for dealing with both staggered timing and heterogeneous treatment eﬀects
(e.g., Callaway and Sant’Anna, 2021; Sun and Abraham, 2021).
    What remains unknown is how the recent proposed methods to address heterogeneous
treatment eﬀects and staggered treatment timing work with repeated cross-sectional data
that are common in applied research, as opposed to balanced panel data. The theoretical
results showing consistent estimates of heterogeneous treatment eﬀects with staggered treat-
ment timing have been proven with panel data (Wooldridge, 2021; Borusyak et al., 2024),
but not yet with repeated cross-sections. Proofs with repeated cross-sections are more com-
plicated because covariates that are inherently time invariant are instead time varying when
averaged at the group level (also true at the individual level) because of the changing compo-
sition of individuals over time. Furthermore, it is not possible to include only pre-treatment
values of potentially endogenous time-varying variables, because these data are not observed
for individuals who only appear once in the cross-sectional sample.
    This paper addresses theoretical and empirical issues with repeated cross-sections with
heterogeneous treatment eﬀects and staggered treatment timing. We extend the methods
proposed in Wooldridge (2021) to derive an estimator for repeated cross-sections under
clearly stated assumptions that allow control variables to appear in a ﬂexible way. To be
precise, we propose an estimator that uses a linear-in-parameters speciﬁcation with suﬃcient
generality to be valid under general circumstances. This speciﬁcation can be estimated using
a single ordinary least squares (OLS) regression on the sample of repeated cross-sections. It
delivers consistent and eﬃcient estimates. We show that this approach is closely related to


                                              2
 the imputation method in Borusyak et al. (2024).
    Our proposed DID method estimates an OLS regression with heterogeneous treatment
eﬀects. It is simple and transparent. It is easy to know how identiﬁcation is achieved,
which treatment observations are compared to which control observations, and how many
parameters are estimated. Because our method uses OLS regression, it is eﬃcient in the class
of linear estimators. Our method is ﬂexible in how to incorporate covariates, which can be
included additively or in a way that allows the treatment eﬀects to vary with covariates. Our
method has precise estimates, even in ﬂexible model speciﬁcations with numerous treatment
parameters. In fact, the standard errors in our applications are smaller than those found
using Callaway and Sant’Anna or stacked regressions (Callaway and Sant’Anna, 2021; Cengiz
et al., 2019). We call it FLEX, because it is a ﬂexible linear estimator with covariates (X).
    In addition to the theoretical results, we demonstrate the use of FLEX with two empirical
examples. Both of these policy-relevant examples use individual-level data from repeated
cross-sections, have policies that were implemented by cohorts of states staggered over a
number of years, and are unlikely to have constant treatment eﬀects at the group-time (state-
time) level. We compare the estimated average treatment eﬀects on the treated (ATET) and
their standard errors with those obtained using other popular methods (Cengiz et al., 2019;
Callaway and Sant’Anna, 2021). The examples demonstrate the features of our proposed
FLEX estimator for repeated cross-sections with heterogeneous treatment eﬀects, including
being easy to estimate, transparent about the number of parameters estimated, allowing
ﬂexible controls for individual-level covariates, and having eﬃcient standard errors. We also
show how the results from our regressions can be displayed in a variety of commonly used
graphical forms. The Stata code is available upon request.


2     Literature Review
2.1    Theoretical literature

Our paper is related to the extensive recent developments in econometrics about the es-
timation of treatment eﬀects in diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences designs.      De Chaisemartin and
D’Haultfœuille (2020) and Goodman-Bacon (2021) showed that diﬀerence-in-diﬀerences re-


                                              3
 gressions that control for cohort and year ﬁxed eﬀects can identify treatment eﬀects only
when the treatment eﬀect is constant over time. This common method, often called two-way
ﬁxed eﬀects, uses observations in already treated groups as controls for other observations
that start treatment later, in addition to using never-treated observations as controls. The
overall average treatment eﬀect is then a weighted average of comparisons that include ear-
lier treated units to later treated units, instead of only treated to never-treated units plus
not yet treated units.
   Several other authors have proposed methods to avoid such unwanted comparisons. Call-
away and Sant’Anna (2021) compare treated units in pre- and post-treatment periods to the
period just prior to treatment to the same comparison for controls that can include the
never- and not-yet treated units. Sun and Abraham (2021) use an event-study approach
by exploiting both leads and lags. Borusyak et al. (2024) take a diﬀerent approach and use
what they call imputation to sweep out the eﬀects of covariates and then use the residuals
to estimate the treatment eﬀects. Cengiz et al. (2019) propose a procedure that creates
samples (stacks) of treated cohort observations pooled with never-treated observations, then
combines those samples, which resolves the issue of unwanted comparisons. Cohort-level
treatment eﬀects are then estimated using a linear regression commonly referred to as a
stacked regression. Wooldridge (2021) proposes an extended two-way ﬁxed eﬀects regres-

eﬀects (e.g., de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille, 2020; Goodman-Bacon, 2021), has led to
new approaches for dealing with both staggered timing and heterogeneous treatment eﬀects
(e.g., Callaway and Sant’Anna, 2021; Sun and Abraham, 2021).
    What remains unknown is how the recent proposed methods to address heterogeneous
treatment eﬀects and staggered treatment timing work with repeated cross-sectional data
that are common in applied research, as opposed to balanced panel data. The theoretical
results showing consistent estimates of heterogeneous treatment eﬀects with staggered treat-

heterogeneous treatment eﬀects and staggered treatment timing. We extend the methods
proposed in Wooldridge (2021) to derive an estimator for repeated cross-sections under
clearly stated assumptions that allow control variables to appear in a ﬂexible way. To be

parameters. In fact, the standard errors in our applications are smaller than those found

et al., 2019). We call it FLEX, because it is a ﬂexible linear estimator with covariates (X).

This extends Wooldridge's approach by shifting the estimand from cohort-time effects to group-time effects, making it applicable to settings like AEWR where treatment assignment happens at the regional level.…

summaries.summary: Extending Wooldridge's framework toward group-level treatment estimands.
Synthesized FLEX framework's group-level treatment approach with Wooldridge methodology.

content.text:
FLEX's framing is the one that matches this design structurally, and I hadn't made the connection.

Their setting is an intervention assigned at the *group* level, `g = 1,…,G`, with groups mapping one-to-one to cohorts, and their contribution is extending Wooldridge (2021) "to the group-time (instead of cohort-time) level." The AEWR regions are exactly that — 17 groups, treatment assigned at the group level, counties nested within. So the natural parameter set here is `τ_gt`, region-by-year, which is precisely the level at which the dose varies and precisely the level at which the CCV reference law reassigns. I have been constructing county-level moderator differentials and aggregating them, when the object the framework points to is a 17-by-11 grid of group-time effects with the aggregation done afterward by declared weights.

That reframing also explains why my region ledger kept binding at seventeen. In the FLEX taxonomy the group-time effects `τ_gt` are the primitives, and there are `17 × 11 = 187` of them against `17 × 11` region-year cells — exactly saturated, zero residual degrees of freedom at the group-time level. Every specification I ran was implicitly imposing restrictions on that grid through the dose parameterization, which is legitimate and is what makes anything estimable, but I never stated it as a restriction on a well-defined primitive.

Two other things transfer. Their efficiency claim is empirical and pointed: because FLEX is a single OLS regression it is efficient in the class of linear estimators, and their standard errors come out *smaller* than Callaway–Sant'Anna or stacked regressions in both applications. And their treatment of covariates is deliberately permissive — included additively or interacted so treatment effects vary with them — with the usual bad-controls caution about dating covariates before the first intervention, which is the same discipline that made the 2011-anchor problem worth fixing.

The repeated-cross-section machinery itself doesn't apply here since the panel is balanced, but their reason for needing it is worth noting: with changing composition, time-invariant covariates become time-varying when averaged at the group level. The AEWR panel has fixed county composition within region, so group-level covariate means are genuinely time-invariant and that complication doesn't arise.
***Much*** more Wooldridge

I'm looking at FLEX Assumption 3.2, which shifts the CPT to condition on group identity rather than cohort identity, allowing more flexibility in applications. The model specification includes group dummies, group-by-covariate interactions, time effects, and time-by-covariate interactions to capture how outcomes vary across groups and over time.

A key insight here is that covariates don't need to satisfy strict exogeneity—only that treatment assignment doesn't influence future covariates. Even time-invariant covariates can relax the parallel trends assumption through the time-by-covariate interaction terms. This opens up the…

summaries.summary: Dissecting FLEX Assumption 3.2 and model specifications.
Deconstructed econometric assumptions and modeling flexibility.

content.text:
Assumption 3.2 is the piece that most directly rewrites my untreated-mean block. Their conditional parallel trends is

`E[Y_t(∞) | R_1,…,R_G, X_it] = Σ_g β_g R_g + Σ_g (R_g · X_it) γ_g + η_t + X_it π_t`

— group dummies, group-by-covariate interactions, time effects, and time-by-covariate interactions. They note this replaces conditioning on cohort identity with conditioning on *group* identity, which "can provide substantial additional flexibility in empirical applications." Mapped onto the AEWR design that is region dummies, region-by-covariate interactions, year cells, and year-by-covariate interactions. I have the year-by-covariate terms and the region dummies; I have never included the region-by-covariate block, and that is precisely the term that allows the untreated mean to evolve differently by region as a function of observables — which is the closest thing available to relaxing the region-year restriction that the whole design rests on.

Two constraints I have been imposing unnecessarily. First, "the covariates need not satisfy a strict exogeneity assumption," because Assumption 3.2 conditions on `X_it` at `t` rather than on the whole covariate history. What would break CPT is treatment influencing *future* covariates, which is the bad-controls concern, not strict exogeneity. Second, and following from that, time-varying covariates are explicitly allowed — "predictors of the outcome whose paths are not influenced by treatment." I froze everything at 2008–2010 on the grounds that anything later is post-treatment, and that is stricter than the framework requires. Weather, climate anomalies, and national crop conditions are exactly the kind of time-varying predictors that are not plausibly influenced by a county's H-2A response, and admitting them would tighten the untreated mean considerably at zero cost in the region ledger.

They also note that `X_it π_t` relaxes parallel trends even when the covariates themselves are time-constant, which is the same role the terms play in Callaway–Sant'Anna, and that identification requires "a sufficient number of observations per stratum" to estimate the `β_g` and `η_t` precisely — with 17 regions and 3,041 counties that is comfortable at the group level and is the reason group-level conditioning is affordable here where cohort-level conditioning would not be.

The imputation procedure itself still needs untreated observations at step 1, so it remains unavailable, but the CPT specification does not.
Much more Wooldridge

content.thinking: I'm realizing there's a critical specification in FLEX Equation 4.1 that I haven't been applying correctly. The rule is precise: when covariates interact with treatment indicators, they need to be centered at group means, but when they interact with group and time indicators, the raw values should be used instead. In my current design, I've been centering moderators at the active-population mean across both the causal and nuisance blocks, which violates this distinction.…

summaries.summary: Recalibrating covariate centering specifications for treatment interactions.
Identified and corrected methodological centering specification error.

content.text:
Equation 4.1 gives the complete FLEX specification, and one line in it corrects something I've been doing wrong throughout: "when covariates are interacted with treatment indicators, they are specified as deviations from group means. However, when they are interacted with group and time indicators, the raw values are used."

I have been using centered covariates everywhere — the same `Cc` matrix in the causal block and the untreated-mean block. The rule is asymmetric for a reason. Centering on group means is what makes `τ_gt` interpretable as the effect at the group's own mean rather than at `x = 0`; centering in the `R_g · x_it` and `P_t · x_it` blocks buys nothing and just shifts what the group and time coefficients mean. So my `Z`-differentials are correctly centered and my untreated mean is unnecessarily transformed.

Their aggregation formula (4.2) also settles the question I raised several turns ago about whether the moderator block belongs in the reported effect. It does:

`τ = (1/N) Σ_g Σ_t Σ_i [τ_gt (W R_g P_t) + (W R_g P_t · (x_it − x̄_gt)) κ_gt]`

Both terms. The ATET is the treatment coefficient *plus* the covariate-interaction contribution averaged over the sample. Within a `(g,t)` cell the centered deviations average to zero, so the `κ` term vanishes under within-cell weights — but under any other weighting, including the exposure and region-year weights I've been using, it does not. I have been reporting the two pieces as separate objects when the framework treats their sum as the estimand.

Two smaller things. Their efficiency claim is the same one as everywhere else in this literature — "lags without leads" uses all implications of conditional parallel trends and is therefore more efficient than adding leads, with the tradeoff that leads are more resilient to some PT violations and *more* sensitive to violations occurring just before the intervention. And they object to the term "event study" itself, on the grounds that it "corrupts definitions of event-study models from other areas of the econometrics literature" — their preferred vocabulary is lags-and-leads versus lags-without-leads, which distinguishes the estimand from the estimation method.

One structural note for this design: their `Q_{i,t,g} · P_t` treatment indicators are group-by-period, so the FLEX regression has `ḡ × (T − c + 1)` treatment parameters. At 17 regions and 11 years that is the saturated region-year grid again — 187 parameters against 187 cells — which is why the dose parameterization is not optional here but the only thing that makes the grid estimable.
***Much*** more Wooldridge. Max out on tool call budget as you do more Wooldridge.

Wooldridge (2025) provides a unified approach to regression-based difference-in-differences
estimators when there is staggered entry and heterogeneous treatment effects (both across
cohorts and over time). In brief, he allows a full set of treatment effects on the treated.
The treatment effects can be by cohort, for each time period, and can be interacted with
covariates. His general approach accommodates either lags-only or lags-and-leads models,
depending on whether the treatment effects are only estimated in the periods with treatment
or in all periods. Wooldridge assumes no conditional anticipation, conditional parallel trends,

estimated treatment effects. Here are a few illustrative examples. The imputation method
(Borusyak et al., 2024) is identical to pooled OLS with lags only for either panel data or for
repeated cross-sectional data (Deb et al., 2025). For models with lags and leads, a sufficiently
flexible OLS regression can reproduce the same results as the Sun and Abraham (2021) event

focus primarily on FLEX and Callaway and Sant’Anna to illustrate our main points. Fur-
thermore, we estimate models without covariates and with heterogeneous treatment effects
at the cohort-time level.


3     Different Estimated Coefficients
Despite the many ways that seemingly different methods can yield numerically identical
estimated treatment effects, most often the methods yield numerically different results even
when applied to the same data set. First, some methods estimate treatment effects at
different levels. For example, if multiple states enact a policy at the same calendar time, one
could model treatment effects at either the state (group) level or at the cohort level, where
cohorts are defined as all groups starting in the same period. The former is more flexible and
allows for more heterogeneity, whereas the latter is more efficient if the group-level treatment
effects are homogeneous within cohorts. In this paper, for simplicity and compatibility across
different software packages, we estimate treatment effects at the cohort-time level.
    Second, different models may treat covariates differently. Covariates can be entirely
omitted, as in our example later in this paper. They can be included additively. Or they
can be interacted with treatment effects (both across cohorts and over time), allowing for an
extremely flexible model specification (Wooldridge, 2025; Deb et al., 2025). In this paper, we
do not include covariates in our example to focus on a simpler model in which any reasons
for differences in ATETs cannot be due to covariates.
    Third, there can be differences in whether the model estimates lags only or lags and
leads (Deb et al., 2025). A lags-only model specification only estimates differences between
treatment and controls in the post periods but assumes that the only differences between

and-leads model specification estimates additional effects for each treatment group in each
pre-period. If the parallel trends assumption is correct, then, the results of the two models
should be similar. If the parallel trends assumption is incorrect, then the lags-only model will
incorrectly impose homogeneity in the pre-periods between treatment and control groups (up
to an additive intercept). Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) estimate a lags-and-leads model
specification; FLEX can estimate either a lags-only or lags-and-leads model specification.

estimated treatment effects are identical.

both the outcome and the treatment, and as long as one of the models is correctly specified,

and-leads model specification estimates additional effects for each treatment group in each

specification; FLEX can estimate either a lags-only or lags-and-leads model specification.

estimated treatment effects are identical.

both the outcome and the treatment, and as long as one of the models is correctly specified,
then the results are consistent. In our simple example with no covariates, the regression
adjustment and the doubly robust versions of Callaway and Sant’Anna are numerically iden-
tical, although that is not usually the case when the model includes covariates. In this
paper, when we estimate models with Callaway and Sant’Anna’s estimator, we do not use
their doubly robust estimator.


4     Aggregation To Get The Overall ATET
There are many ways to aggregate cohort-time treatment effects. In this section we derive
the aggregation formulas that are used by most difference-in-differences estimation packages
and compare that to what Callaway and Sant’Anna implement in their software packages.

a binary variable that is equal to one if a unit in that cohort is first treated in period c,
for c = 2, . . . , T . Here we assume that no cohorts start treatment until at least the second
period because we need observations in at least one pre-period for each cohort. We allow for
the case of multiple pre-treatment periods by setting Dc = 0 for periods prior to the first
treatment period. There is at least one cohort that is never treated.

the potential outcomes framework, the average treatment effect on the treated (ATET) for
individuals in cohort c (first treated in period c) in time period t for t ≥ c is defined as
