                               AT ET (c, t) = E [Yt (1) − Yt (0) |Dc = 1]                   (4.1)

where Yt (1) and Yt (0) are the values of potential outcome Y in period t when treated and not
treated, respectively. The AT ET (c, t) are referred to as the cohort-time treatment effects.

number of units that are first treated in period c that are sampled in period t. In the panel
data case Nct is the same in all periods t for cohort c. In the repeated cross section case, Nct
will differ in each period.

across all cohorts and time periods is the weighted average of the AT ET (c, t)’s, where the
weights are the number of observations for cohort c in treated time periods (time t ≥ c), and
C is the set of treated cohorts.

                     AT ET =        P       P                         Nct AT ET (c, t)     (4.2)
                                      c∈C     t≥c Nct       c∈C t≥c

time treatment effects using different weights. In section 3.2 of their paper, they present
several formulas “for aggregating group time average treatment effects into an overall effect of
participating in the treatment.” Their first aggregation formula (3.10 in their paper, slightly
modified here by changing g to c, G to C, and AT T to AT ET ) uses weights proportional
to the number of treated observations for a treated group (or cohort) during a treated time
period.

                                 T
                      O   1     XX
                     θW =                 1{t ≥ c}AT ET (c, t)P (C = c|C ≤ T )
                              κ c∈C t=2

where κ is the sum of the weights, 1{t ≥ c} is an indicator for post periods, AT ET (c, t) are
the treatment effects for cohort c at time t, and P (C = c|C ≤ T ) are the weights for each
                                                                        O
treated cohort. Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) explain on page 211 that θW is a weighted
average of each ATET that puts more weight on ATETs’s with larger group sizes. This
is also the formula for the weighted average ATET shown in the Stata documentation of
hdidregress postestimation.

                                                   6
    Callaway and Sant’Anna’s weights P (C = c|C ≤ T ) are not a function of time even
though the treatment effects AT ET (c, t) are a function of both cohort and time. The
condition that C ≤ T simply restricts weights to cohorts that are treated (never treated
cohorts have C = ∞). So in their formula, Callaway and Sant’Anna have a single weight for
each treated cohort in all treated periods.
   But what is calculated in Stata’s command hdidregress postestimation and in the
user-written package csdid is instead the following, with an additional term Nc,c−1 in both
the numerator and the denominator, representing the number of observations for cohort c in
the pre-treated period (t = −1):

                                 1                    XX
         AT ET =      P    P                                    (Nct + Nc,c−1 )AT ET (c, t)   (4.3)
                       c∈C  t≥c (Nct + Nc,c−1 )       c∈C t≥c

   In general, equation 4.3 does not equal equation 4.2. Only in the pure balanced panel
data case will equation 4.3 simplify to equation 4.2, because Nct = Nc,c−1 across all time
periods for cohort c. Furthermore, these weights differ by both cohort and by time, unlike
their formula.

all averages, except in the unusual case that all ATETs are identical. They specifically
mention ATETs, weighted by the number of treated observations in treated periods, and
equal-weighted ATETs as having a meaningful interpretation. At no time do they mention
including the number of observations in any pre-treatment periods as part of the weights. Nor
is that mentioned in the Stata documentation of hdidregress postestimation or csdid.
   Callaway and Sant’Anna also say that one might consider alternative weights, for ex-
ample, putting equal weight on each cohort so as not to put more weight on cohorts that
participate longer.

different weights, and that those different aggregated ATETs will have different interpreta-
tions and different numerical values (except in the extreme case of homogeneous treatment
effects across all cohorts and periods). Therefore, we agree with the theoretical part of the
Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) paper. Our concern is that the implementation of their code
yields a weighted average that is hard to interpret and is not what researchers expect.

effects, for example by cohort, by event time, or by calendar time (also discussed by Callaway

years four, six, and eight, respectively. There are 10 groups in each of the three treatment

time in the control cohorts, with some annual fluctuation. There is an additive error with
a normal distribution. The parallel trends assumption and the no-anticipation assumptions

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"example in two ways. First, we did 20 simulations which varied in the magnitude of the
true treatment effects, the number of observations per cohort and time, and the error terms.
The overall study design (9 periods, three treated cohorts, heterogeneous treatment effects
by cohort and time) remained the same as the earlier example.
   Second, we compared four different estimation methods using publicly available Stata
software. These estimation methods include 1) basic homogeneous treatment effects, often
called two-way fixed effects (TWFE), estimated by regress or didregress; 2) Deb et al.
(2025) FLEX with lags and leads, estimated by flexdid; 3) Borusyak et al. (2024) impu-
tation method with lags and leads, estimated by did imputation with additional dummy
variables spanning all treated cohort periods; and 4) Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), esti-
mated by hdidregress. As is well known, the homogeneous TWFE only estimates a single
overall treatment effect, essentially combining estimation and aggregation in the process of
estimating a single parameter. The other three estimators all estimate identical cohort-time
treatment effects in these simulations with no covariates. Therefore, any differences in an
estimated overall ATET is due to aggregation.
   We found surprising results, as shown visually in Figure 2. Each column refers to results


                                             13
 from one of twenty simulated data sets. The vertical axis is the magnitude of the overall
ATET, roughly 5.0. The black dots (connected by a line) are the expected ATETs, weighted
by the number of treated observations in treated periods; these vary across simulations
because of differences in the expected cohort-time treatment effects and variation in the
number of observations per cohort and period, creating different weights for each simulation.
The two concentric red circles show that FLEX and BJS imputation aggregate the same
cohort-time treatment effects to the same weighted ATET, and those are quite close to the
expected values, differing because of the random error term. In other words, these two
estimators use the same weights to estimate an overall ATET. As expected, the TWFE
ATET is quite different.
   Surprisingly, the Callaway and Sant’Anna ATETs are also typically quite far from the
expected ATETs. Again, any differences in the aggregated ATET is solely due to aggregation
weights, not to the estimated cohort-time treatment effects, which are the same as the other
three non-TWFE methods. In fact, in four of the simulations (2, 6, 7, and 19), the CS ATET
was further from the expected ATET, weighted by the number of treated observations in
treated periods, than the TWFE ATET. We have done numerous other simulations and
found that pattern persists. If researchers avoid TWFE because it biased and often far
from the expected value, then they should also be cautious about Callaway and Sant’Anna’s
weighted ATET.
   In addition, we explored using the method of de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020),
estimated by did multiplegt. Their method estimates two-by-two comparisons but they
include any not-yet-treated observations as part of the controls. Therefore, de Chaisemartin
and D’Haultfœuille and Callaway and Sant’Anna with the notyet option yield identical
estimated cohort-time treatment effects. However, they do not return identical overall ATET.
de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020) use weights based only on the number of treated
observations in treated periods, just like Borusyak et al. (2024) and Deb et al. (2025).
In summary, for balanced panel data, de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille is identical to
Callaway and Sant’Anna with the notyet option. But for repeated cross sectional data, de
Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille is different than the other methods because of the difference
in control observations, which affects the estimated cohort-time treatment effects.


                                             14
 6     When Weighting Matters Most
The aggregation weights matter. If the data set was a balanced panel, then the difference in
the weighting formulas would balance out, because Callaway and Sant’Anna’s weights would
exactly double the weights of the ATET, weighted by the number of treated observations
in treated periods,. However, in repeated cross-sectional data, the number of observations
typically differs from year to year in a cohort, so it matters whether part of the weights
include the number of observations from the pre-treated year.
    When will the weighting matter more? In brief, the weighting matters more when there is
more heterogeneity in the treatment effects, when there is more heterogeneity in the number
of observations, and when those heterogeneities are correlated. The weights produce bigger
differences between methods when the number of observations in the pre-period is relatively
large compared to the number of observations in the treated periods.
    In our empirical example the number of observations in the pre-period is larger than
in any of the later treated periods. When those pre-period weights are included, they give
more relative weight to the later periods. Because the treatment effects increase over time,
the Callaway and Sant’Anna weights put more emphasis on the later periods, which in
this example means a higher overall ATET. The heterogeneity in the treatment effects by
cohort and time is modest. We could have constructed an example in which the difference
in estimated ATETs was either much larger or much smaller.


7     Conclusions
We show that the weights used to aggregate estimated treatment effects at the cohort-
time level into an overall ATET matter. The weights are different in the Stata commands
hdidregress and csdid than what Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) discuss in their theo-
retical paper. For many simple difference-in-differences model specifications, the choice of
estimator yields identical point estimates of the group-time treatment effects. This should
result in identical estimates of the average treatment effect on the treated and other aggre-
gated treatment effects (such as overall, by calendar time, by cohort, or by time since start of
treatment). However, for the Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) method, the Stata commands


                                              15
 use weights based in part on the number of observations in the period just prior to the start
of treatment. This will yield different estimates of the ATET compared to other difference-
in-differences estimators whenever the data set has an unbalanced number of observations.
The difference will be greater when the number of observations in the period immediately
prior to start of treatment is relatively large and there is heterogeneity across cohorts and
over time; the difference will be zero with a balanced panel.
   Given the enormous influence and popularity of the Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021)
method for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects in difference-in-differences models
with staggered start time, and the common use of Stata software, we are concerned that
many published results have been calculated with a formula that is not what the researchers
intended.

  Heterogeneous Treatment Effects. American Economic Review, 110(9):2964–2996.

  indifferences with heterogeneous treatment effects: a survey. Econometrics Journal, 26:C1–

  regression with staggered implementation.

  treatment effects difference-in-differences estimator for repeated cross-sections.

Freedman, S. M., Hollingsworth, A., Simon, K. I., Wing, C., and Yozwiak, M. (2023). Design-
  ing Difference in Difference Studies With Staggered Treatment Adoption: Key Concepts
  and Practical Guidelines. NBER Working Paper 31842. https://www.nber.org/papers/
  w31842.

       Nonlinear Difference-in-Differences with Repeated Cross Sections

                                    By Jeffrey M. Wooldridge*

     I extend to repeated cross sections the nonlinear difference-in-differences (DiD) methods in

Wooldridge (2023) for staggered interventions with panel data. The key is a conditional parallel

trends (CPT) assumption imposed on a strictly increasing function of the conditional mean. As

with panel data, one can apply pooled quasi-maximum likelihood estimation (QMLE) to log

likelihoods in the linear exponential family (LEF) with cohort and time dummies included

flexibly. The resulting estimators are fully robust to distributional misspecification, only

requiring correct specification of the conditional mean.

     I show how to obtain both lags only (LO) estimators, where only current and lagged

treatment indicators are included, and leads and lags (L&L) estimators within one framework.

     The setting here extends the linear analysis in Deb, Norton, Wooldridge, and Zabel (2025)

[DNWZ (2025)]. Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) [CS (2021)] propose doubly robust estimators

that combine regression and propensity score weighting, but the conditional parallel trends

assumption is stated in levels. The same is true in Borusyak, Jaravel, and Spiess (2024) (who

propose a two-step imputation estimator) and DNWZ (2025) (who show imputation and pooled

ordinary least squares are identical under certain conditions).

                          IV. Practical Considerations and Extensions

                           A. Clustering Standard Errors and Inference

     Above, we assumed the observations are independent across i. In this scenario, one only

needs to make inference robust to misspecification of the assumed LEF density. In the linear

case, this leads to the usual heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.

      Often a case can be made to cluster standard errors with repeated cross-sectional data. For

one, the data may be obtained from a cluster sampling scheme. For example, if census tracts are

sampled and then people are sampled from the tracts, one should cluster at the census tract level.

If stratified sampling is used, it is often straightforward to apply the pooled estimation method in

Procedure 1 with sampling weights and clustering.

     Even without a cluster sampling scheme, one may need to cluster standard errors to account

for the treatment assignment – a case studied in Abadie, Athey, Imbens, and Wooldridge (2023).

For example, a treatment might be assigned at the census tract level, where all units are assigned

the same cohort Dg . In order to reflect the uncertainty due to clustered assignment, the standard

errors should be clustered at the census tract level.

                               B. Aggregating the Treatment Effects

     Rather than report a full set of ATT estimates for each treatment cohort, it is common to

aggregate the effects by exposure time and, in the case of leads and lags, time until exposure. In

the balanced panel data case, one typically weights the estimates τˆgt by the relative cohort

shares, which vary by exposure time in the staggered case. One can also obtain a single weighted

                                                   7
 average of all of the τˆgt across treated periods; see Wooldridge (2025). In the leads and lags

cases, we can also weight the leads by cohort shares to produce a single event study plot, where

τˆg , g −1 = 0 as the normalization.

      With repeated cross sections the weighting issue is more subtle, as discussed in CS (2021).

One simple strategy is to compute weights that vary by t as well as by g, based on sample sizes

N gt , the number of units in cohort g in period t. Choosing weights in this way is equivalent to

computing the average partial effect (APE) with respect to Wi , t (i ) and then aggregating buy the

appropriate subsample. For example, to obtain the estimates by exposure time in the lags only

case, one computes the APE with respect to Wi , t (i ) in the pooled estimation and then averages

over all observations corresponding to exposure times of zero, one, two, and so on. In the leads

and lags case, one can get the aggregated pre-trend effects by introducing a new binary indicator,

NWi , t (i ) = 1 − Wi , t (i ) , and multiplying it by the pre-treatment terms in (7). Then, compute the APE

with respect to NWi , t (i ) and average over all observations corresponding to times until treatment.

      In the nonlinear case, there is a subtle point about obtaining an aggregate version of the

event study graph. Namely, the CPT assumption holds on the linear index, not necessarily the

conditional mean. To detect violations of PT it makes sense to aggregate the δˆgs in an event study

plot. In leading cases, this will produce aggregated effects on the log odds (logit) or on the log of

the mean (exponential).

      Statistical packages, such as Stata, that have features for computing APEs also will report

standard errors of the weighted effects. Even if the standard errors are not clustered, we still need

to know that there are sufficient observations within each cohort/time-period cell in order for the

standard errors to be reliable. In some cases, we may need to impose restrictions directly on the

                                                       8
 model, rather than estimating the most flexible LO or L&L model. For example, if some treated

cohorts have only a small number of units, we might impose constant effects by exposure time,

which means collapsing the dummies Dg ⋅ fst into dummies that vary only by s − g , s = g , ... , T

(LO) and then adding s = 1 , ..., g − 2 for L&L. In extreme cases, we might need to impose a

constant effect, which means replacing all treatment dummies with the single indicator Wi , t (i ) .

We can always compare this coefficient with the weighted average from the fully flexible

estimation to see if imposing a constant effect changes the results. The reason for imposing a

constant effect is so that we can better trust the inference.

                                            C. Heterogeneous Time Trends

       One approach to accounting for violations of PT that occur even after including covariates

is to assume relative simple heterogeneous trends in the absence of the intervention. In particular,

with at least two pre-intervention periods per treated cohort, one can include in (6) Di , t (i ), g ⋅ t , and

                          
even Di , t (i ), g ⋅ t ⋅ X                . The coefficients on the Di , t (i ), g ⋅ t can be used to test for pre-trends. Like in
                            i , t ( i ), g



the panel data case in Wooldridge (2023), such tests do not suffer from contamination bias

provided the covariates are included flexibly, as in (6).

       Including cohort-specific trends can be costly in terms of precision because their inclusion

creates collinearity with the treatment indicators. Of course, using a pre-test to decide whether to

drop these terms can be problematical -- just as when using the leads and lags approach.

                                                D. Empirical Application

data in DNWZ (2025), which includes more than 500,000 individual observations with

assignment at the PUMA level (of which there are 682), is available on request from the author –



                                                                  9
 including Stata code. The intervention is adoption of the Secure Communities immigration

enforcement program in the United States, and the outcome variable is participation in SNAP, a

government nutritional program. The logit model proposed here is compared with a linear

probability model similar to that used in DNWZ (2025).

content.text:
Read the aggregation paper and the 2026 AEA preview end to end. Several things land, and one of them is a specific instruction for the position this design is actually in.

The aggregation finding is sharper than the grep suggested. `hdidregress` and `csdid` weight by `N_ct + N_{c,c−1}` — treated observations *plus* the pre-treatment period count — where Callaway and Sant'Anna's own paper specifies weights proportional to treated observations only. In their simulation the true ATET is 2.804 and the Stata implementation returns 3.255, a 16.2 percent gap, and in four of twenty runs the CS aggregate was further from truth than plain TWFE. Their conclusion is blunt: if researchers avoid TWFE because it lands far from the expected value, they should be equally cautious here. It vanishes on a balanced panel — ours is — but the discipline transfers: the weights must count only the observations contributing to the numerator, and I should state mine explicitly rather than inheriting them.

The 2026 preview gives the cleanest statement yet of the centering rule and, crucially, of what `β_g` means. Covariates are centered as `X̃_tg = X_t − E(X_t | D_g = 1)`, and the reason is that this makes `β_g` "interpretable as average selection effects" — the average difference in `Y_t(∞)` between cohort `g` and the never-treated group. So the selection block isn't nuisance at all; centering is what converts it into a reportable quantity. He also notes CPT generally does *not* hold for `E[Y_t(∞)|D,X]` itself, with exactly two exceptions: no selection into treatment, or time-constant covariates with time-constant `γ_t` and `π_t`.

The instruction that matters most for seventeen policy paths is in Section IV.B. When cells are thin, "we may need to impose restrictions directly on the model, rather than estimating the most flexible LO or L&L model" — collapse `D_g · f_st` into dummies varying only by `s − g`, and in extreme cases replace all treatment dummies with the single indicator `W_it`. Then "compare this coefficient with the weighted average from the fully flexible estimation to see if imposing a constant effect changes the results. The reason for imposing a constant effect is so that we can better trust the inference." That is the opposite of the direction I've been pushed all session, and it comes from Wooldridge directly: with sixteen design degrees of freedom, restriction buys trustworthy inference, and the check is whether the restricted coefficient matches the flexible weighted average.

He also confirms the clustering rule for this exact structure — assignment at a higher level than the unit, cluster there, citing AAIW — and repeats the cohort-trend caution: `D_g · t` terms create collinearity with the treatment indicators, precision suffers, and pre-testing whether to drop them is "problematical," the same objection as pre-testing on leads.
Keep reading Wooldridge

Anticipating the general recommendations below, in applying DiD to limited dependent

variables it will make sense to compare DiD estimates from linear regression to a nonlinear

method that exploits the special nature of Y it – provided, of course, that the ATTs are properly

computed for the nonlinear model.

3.2. Adding Covariates
   It is straightforward to modify the index PT assumption to allow for covariates. First, we

specify the no anticipation assumption conditional on the covariates.

   Assumption CNAC (Conditional NA, Common): For a 1  K vector of time-constant

covariates X,

                     EY t 1|D  1, X  EY t 0|D  0, X, t ∈ 1, . . . , q − 1.            (3.19)

With the addition of covariates, we assume that the pre-intervention ATTs are zero for each

subpopulation indexed by X.

   Assumption CIPTC (Conditional IPT, Common): For a 1  K vector of time-constant

covariates X and a function G satisfying the requirements in Assumption IPTC,

                EY t 0|D, X  G  D  X  D  X   t  X t , t  1, 2, . . . , T,     (3.20)

where D is the binary treatment indicator and where we take  1 ≡ 0,  1 ≡ 0 as normalizations

to define  and . 

imposes functional form restrictions (unless X includes mutually exlusive and exhaustive

binary indicators that partition the population). For flexibility, we can choose X to be functions

of underlying control variables, such as in the common practice of including squares and

interactions of underlying variables. Once we settle on the functional form

the substantive restriction imposed on the linear index in (3.20) is that the coefficients on terms

involving D are time invariant. In the linear case the restriction becomes

which does not depend on D. Wooldridge (2021) used this assumption to derive POLS

estimators of the  r .

but not on D.

content.text:
Read the rest of the 2023 paper, the aggregation paper end to end, and the 2026 preview. Several things consolidate, and one changes what I'd recommend for this design.

Proposition 4.1 is the payoff of the canonical-link restriction: with `G⁻¹` the canonical link for the chosen LEF density, the pooled QMLE estimates and the imputation estimates are numerically identical, so "we can use a pooled QMLE in the LEF without adding additional assumptions and consistently estimate the ATTs." He defends the restriction on practical grounds — it limits the researcher's choices to logistic or exponential, with the estimator pinned by Table 3.1: linear/normal giving pooled OLS, logistic/Bernoulli for binary or fractional, logistic/binomial when there's a known upper bound `B_it`, exponential/Poisson for nonnegative outcomes with no natural bound. There is a subtle consequence I hadn't appreciated: under the canonical link the mean function "is only assumed correct when `W_it = 0`," which is far weaker than it looks from the pooled specification.

Two recommendations now appear three times each across these papers, which makes them worth acting on rather than noting. First, `X` built from exhaustive and mutually exclusive indicators makes the linearity restriction vacuous rather than maintained — my covariate block is entirely continuous, and swapping part of it for bin indicators is free in the region ledger. Second, when cells are thin, impose restrictions: collapse `D_g · f_st` into exposure-length indicators `Z_ith`, or in the extreme case use `W_it` alone, then check the restricted coefficient against the flexible weighted average. His reason is explicit — "so that we can better trust the inference." With sixteen design degrees of freedom that argument applies here with more force than in his `N → ∞` setting, and it cuts against the direction I've been pushed all session.

He also notes covariates help precision even when parallel trends holds unconditionally, purely by reducing noise, and that the support condition `Supp(X|D=1) ⊂ Supp(X|D=0)` should be checked even though a parametric `G` technically removes the need for overlap.

On the aggregation paper: the Stata implementations weight by `N_ct + N_{c,c−1}`, adding pre-period counts that Callaway and Sant'Anna's own text never mentions, producing a 16.2 percent gap from truth in their simulation and, in four of twenty runs, landing further from the target than plain TWFE. It vanishes on a balanced panel like ours, but the discipline stands: weights must count only the observations entering the numerator, and mine should be stated rather than inherited.
Even more Wooldridge

   I now report on Monte Carlo simulations when Y it is binary or nonnegative with mass at

6.1. Binary Response with Common Timing
    In this case the potential outcomes, Y t 0 and Y t 1, are binary. There are T  6 time

periods with a common intervention time at q  4. In generating the data, the difference in the

means of the underlying latent variables, EY ∗t 1 − EY ∗t 0, changes across t  4, 5, and 6.

[Because of the nonlinearity of the model, the ATTs defined in terms of Y t 0 and Y t 1 would

change over time even if EY ∗t 1 − EY ∗t 0 were constant across t.] The single

(time-constant) covariate, X, is generated as the average, over the six time periods, of

independent exponential random variables with unit means. Treatment status, D, follows a

logit:

                                      D  1−0. 5  X − 1  V  0,                                      (6.1)

where V is independent of X with a logistic distribution. This mechanism is used for all

where the U t 0 follow logistic distributions with a common effect C and independent

idiosyncratic shocks. This mechanism ensures the potential outcome Y t 0 is correlated with X

as well as with treatment status, D, and that U t 0 has substantial serial correlation. In the

treated state, Y t 1  Y t 0 for t ≤ 3 to ensure no anticipation. Then

           Y t 1  10. 5  X − 1 − 2D  0. 2  f5 t  0. 3  f6 t  U t 1  0, t  4, . . . , T,   (6.3)

where U t 1 depends on the same heterogeneity as U t 0 with separate independent shocks

and also has a logistic distribution. This formulation implies that the index inside the logit

treatment effects on the binary outcomes do vary with X because of the nonlinearity. The

parallel trends assumption, conditional on X, is in force for the linear index.

T −1 ∑ t1 PY t 1  1 ≈ 0. 405, and so there is reasonable balance in both potential outcomes

between zero and one. The ATTs – the target parameters – are obtained by averaging across

the 1,000 Monte Carlo replications. The logit conditional mean is estimated using pooled logit

and the linear mean is estimated using pooled OLS. The R-squared from the linear POLS

estimation is about 0. 205, which seems realistic given that D, year dummies, and the covariate

are controlled for flexibly.

      The method proposed by Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), where the comparison group is

the never treated group (the default in Stata), is also included in the simulation . The two tests

for pre-trends are computed for the pooled logit and pooled OLS estimation. The findings are

reported in Table 6.1.

cross-sectional units, all three approaches show little bias when compared with the sample

ATTs (which are averaged across the 1,000 simulations and should be close to the population

Carlo standard deviations no more than 69% of the linear model SDs. Not surprisingly, the CS

(2021) estimators, which use only the single period prior to the intervention as the control

period, are the least precise. Given that the logit model is correctly specified we hope that the

parallel trends tests in the logit estimation have rejection frequencies close to the nominal size,

The parallel trends tests don't have the power to catch this kind of misspecification, which is exactly what I'm seeing in my binary outcome analysis where I got sign reversals across different specifications and the PT tests weren't flagging problems.…

nonlinear model, such as logit, and hopefully draw robust conclusions.

promising. The event-study-type test rejects in the linear case 99.5% of the time, and the

heterogeneous trends test rejects in 999 out of 1,000 replications. Therefore, one would

conclude that the PT assumption is violated in the linear model. Because the observed Y it is a

simulation for count data in Table 6.5, the POLS estimation of the linear model [and CS

smaller in magnitude.) The exponential mean is correctly specified so the absence of bias for

the Poisson QMLE is not surprising. Because the outcome variable is not close to having a

Poisson distribution, and fairly strong serial correlation is present, there is no guarantee that the

Poisson QMLE using the exponential mean is efficient. Nevertheless, in this scenario the

Poisson QMLE is the most precise of the three estimators. For example, for  46 , the POLS and

CS (2021) SDs relative to the pooled QMLE are about 1.33 and 1.60, respectively. As before,

CS (2021) is the least precise by some margin because it uses only the never treated group as

the control group for each cohort and time period.

    The linear model is not systematically rejected using the PT tests – a sensible outcome

because the POLS estimators show essentially no bias. The event-study-type test for pooled

Poisson appears to reject somewhat too often: 15.9% for a nominal 5% test and the

heterogeneous trend test rejects slightly too often. The findings suggest that, with this kind of


                                                     55

similar estimates, with the precision of the pooled Poisson estimator probably being better.

Because the observed outcome is nonnegative with a corner at zero, the exponential mean

model estimated by Poisson QMLE suggest itself a priori as an attractive alternative or

supplement to the linear model.

solutions to follow, say, Tobit models, or two-part models. Then, the exponential mean would

also be misspecified. Preliminary simulations show that both linear and exponential model can

well approximate the ATTs even with more than 50% of the outcomes at the corner.

content.text:
The simulations are where this stops being abstract, and Table 6.5 is the one that should worry me most about what I've been reporting.

Count outcome, staggered intervention, exponential mean correctly specified: pooled Poisson QMLE is essentially unbiased across all six cohort-time ATTs, while pooled OLS carries severe downward bias — `τ₆₆` has a true value of 6.34 against a POLS estimate of 1.59, a quarter of the truth — and Callaway–Sant'Anna sits in between at 4.62. Poisson is also the most precise. Crucially the diagnostics *work* here: the event-study test rejects the linear model 99.5 percent of the time and the heterogeneous-trend test 999 times in 1,000, while both tests behave correctly under the exponential model at 8.9 and 6.4 percent.

Table 6.2 is the darker one. Binary outcome, index parallel trends satisfied, and pooled OLS and CS both return estimates that are *negative* when the true ATTs are positive and large — and "the tests of parallel trends have no power for detecting the misspecification." A linear model can be badly wrong on a binary outcome with no diagnostic warning at all. That bears directly on `any_application`, where I saw sign flips across specifications and had no way to adjudicate them.

He is not one-sided about it. Table 6.4 flips the result — with uniform errors the logit carries a *severe upward bias* while linear and CS are nearly unbiased, and Table 6.6 shows a corner-solution outcome with 36.8 percent zeros where POLS shows no bias at all and only loses precision, with relative standard deviations of 1.33 for POLS and 1.60 for CS against pooled Poisson. His conclusion is comparative rather than prescriptive: "one can try a linear analysis along with a sensible nonlinear model, such as logit, and hopefully draw robust conclusions," and he flags obtaining diagnostics that reject a misspecified linear model as an open research problem.

For this design that maps cleanly. Certified positions, certified hours, applications and employer counts are nonnegative with mass at zero and no natural upper bound — Table 3.1 says exponential mean with Poisson QMLE, and Table 6.5 says the linear model can be badly biased there with the PT tests loudly telling you so. `any_application` is binary, where Table 6.2 says the linear model can be badly biased with the tests telling you nothing. The one piece of good news is that the PT diagnostics I can run cheaply — the heterogeneous-trend test in particular, with the best size properties in his tables — would give real evidence on whether the linear specification is adequate for the count outcomes, without committing to estimate anything nonlinear.
Vastly more Wooldridge

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"7. Empirical Application
   I apply nonlinear DiD to the data in Di Tella and Schargrodsky (2004), who study an

intervention in July 1994 where more police were assigned to certain blocks in Buenos Aires,

Argentina after a terrorist attack on the main Jewish Center in Buenos Aires. Of 876 blocks, 37

were provided with extra police to protect Jewish centers. While the number of treated units is

relatively small, it is still more than in policy interventions using, say, the 50 states in the

United States.

   The data are reported monthly, running from April through December of 1994. Because the

terrorist attack occurred midway through July, a case can be made for dropping July and using

April, May, and June as the pre-intervention months and August through December as the

post-intervention months. I take that approach here.

   The outcome variable, thefts, is reported monthly, measured as the weekly average number

of automobile thefts. More than 78% of the outcomes are zero, with increments of 0.25 up

through the maximum of 2.5. Di Tella and Schargrodsky (2004) used a standard linear DiD


                                                   56
 analysis with several robustness checks, such as including covariates and looking at spillover

effects (for which they find no evidence). Here I estimate a linear model and an exponential

model allowing for five different treatment effects by month.

      Without covariates, the linear estimation is a standard DiD where thefts is averaged over

the three pre-intervention months, and this is subtracted from the outcome in a particular

treated month. This adjusted outcome is averaged across the treated and control blocks. As a

comparison, I use an exponential model – which has a different underlying PT assumption –

estimated by pooled Poisson regression. Also, the Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) estimates

are reported in the case of estimating separate effects. Without covariates and with common

timing, the CS (2021) estimates are 2  2 DiDs using June as the only control period and using

each of August through December as treated periods. In other words, the data on April and

May are ignored. The estimates without covariates are given in Table 7.1.

    Column (1) effectively reproduces the constant effect specification of Di Tella and

Schargrodsky (2004) when July is not included. It implies that the presence of more police

reduced car thefts by about 0. 087 per month, on average. The estimate in column (2) is

obtained by mimicking the linear analysis, where the time-varying treatment indicator is

included along with the indicator of being a treated unit and a single post-intervention period.

The estimate from the exponential model is practically the same, and even slightly less precise.

   Columns (3), (4), and (5) show estimates allowing for a different TE in each month. Again,

there are no practical differences between the linear and exponential estimates, with the latter

having slightly larger standard errors. The parallel trends test have large p-values, providing no

estimation of the linear and exponential models. Thes estimators are more precise than the CS

estimators, which show a similar pattern but are somewhat larger in magnitude. One advantage

presence of a bank on a block drives the effects to essentially zero, a finding that may be

obtain very different estimates.

    I now discuss some extensions that are straightforward to implement in the current

framework.

explainable by the idea that car thieves may already think the police presence and other

security is high near blocks that house a bank. One caution is that the estimated effects are

 forms leads to very similar estimates. The simulations in Section 6 demonstrate that in some

cases one will get very similar estimates (on average) and, at least in principle, it is possible to

obtain very different estimates.

8. Extensions
    I now discuss some extensions that are straightforward to implement in the current

framework.

An approach that has a similar flavor to Procedure 4.1 is the “build-the-trend” (BTT)

estimator in Callaway (2023), which uses all pre-treatment periods to weight pairwise

differences and uses all not-yet-treated units as controls. However, the BTT estimator is

a formula based on inverse probability weighting; it is not motivated as just one of many

special cases that is justified by the conclusion of unconfounded treatment. The estimator

is different from that in Procedure 4.1 when we use IPW; moreover, BTT does not handle

heterogeneous trends, an extension of our approach that we consider in Section 5.

   Procedure 4.1 can be compared with the Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) approach with

staggered interventions. CS (2021) suggest using a long difference of the form


                                     Y̊irg ≡ Yir − Yi,g−1                             (4.12)


and then choosing control groups from cohorts {r + 1, . . . , T, ∞}. The transformation in
                                                                             1
(4.12) ignores control periods prior to g − 1, whereas (4.11) gives weight (g−1) to all pre-

treatment outcomes.

   A sketch of an identification argument that mimics that in Section 4.1 for the CS (2021)

approach is instructive. For g ≤ t ≤ T , write

                                                                              
      Yt (g) − Yt (∞) = Yt (g) − Yg−1 (g) − Yt (∞) − Yg−1 (∞) + Yg−1 (g) − Yg−1 (∞) .


Imposing a no anticipation assumption


                            E[Yg−1 (g) − Yg−1 (∞) | Dg = 1] = 0,




                                             20
 implies

                                          
          τgt = E Yt (g) − Yt (∞) | Dg = 1
                                                                       
             = E Yt (g) − Yg−1 (g) | Dg = 1 − E Yt (∞) − Yg−1 (∞) | Dg = 1 .             (4.13)


The first part is always identified because

                                                                    
                    E Yt (g) − Yg−1 (g) | Dg = 1 = E Yt − Yg−1 | Dg = 1 ,


and so we can average the “long” difference of the units in cohort g. For the second part

of (4.13), we can impose a conditional parallel trends assumption

                                                                          
          E Yt (∞) − Yg−1 (∞) | DS , . . . , DT , X = E Yt (∞) − Yg−1 (∞) | X ,          (4.14)


which is the same as saying that the vector of cohort assignments, (DS , . . . , DT ), is uncon-

founded with respect to Yt (∞) − Yg−1 (∞) conditional on X.

   Now the argument is the same as in Section 4.1: we can apply any treatment effect

estimator based on unconfoundedness, and we can use the not-yet-treated units at time

t—so cohorts h ∈ {t + 1, t + 2, . . . , T, ∞} as the control group.

   As discussed in Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), equation (4.14) only requires the CPT

assumption to hold starting from period g − 1 and allows violations before g − 1. While

Marcus and Sant’Anna (2021) describe a potential bias–variance trade-off from using more

pre-treatment periods, such a trade-off does not always exist. Wooldridge (2025b) notes

that if CPT fails into the treated periods, the CS (2021) estimator can have more bias than

the extended TWFE (ETWFE) estimator. Like the ETWFE estimator, our approach uses

all pre-treatment periods, and so it can have less bias than CS (2021) when CPT fails.

Unfortunately, we cannot know when that will happen.




                                               21
 Information Set Comparison. Assuming the parallel trends assumption holds, we

next compare the information sets used by the rolling, CS, and Wooldridge approaches.

Table 1 summarizes the pre-treatment information used by each estimator. To illustrate the

comparison, we consider treatment cohorts g ∈ {4, 5, 6} and focus on estimating AT T (4, 5),

denoted by ⋆. Shaded cells indicate the pre-treatment outcome observations used by each

estimator when estimating the target parameter.

           Table 1: Pre-Treatment Period Information Used by Each Method
                CS (2021)               Rolling Method              Wooldridge (2025b)
  time   g=4      g=5     g=6         g=4    g=5     g=6           g=4    g=5     g=6
    1
    2

    4
    5    ⋆                            ⋆                            ⋆
    6



   The regression-based approach in Wooldridge (2025b) uses all available pre-treatment

information and can be the most efficient among the three under a correctly specified linear

conditional mean and standard error-components assumptions. However, this efficiency

comes at the cost of potential bias if the conditional mean is misspecified.

   The rolling method uses less information than the Wooldridge approach because it rules

out bad comparisons; for example, when estimating AT T (4, 5), both the rolling and CS

approaches exclude group 5 at t = 5, since it is already treated. This may sacrifice some

precision relative to Wooldridge, but, like CS, it accommodates doubly robust estimation.

At the same time, compared with CS, the rolling method uses more pre-treatment infor-

mation through the demeaning transformation, which can improve efficiency.

   In this respect, our rolling estimator can be viewed as a middle ground between the CS

(2021) and Wooldridge (2025b) approaches: it preserves the clean-comparison logic of CS

while using more pre-treatment information, and it sacrifices some of the information used

by Wooldridge in exchange for greater robustness to model misspecification.

T by modifying the parallel trends assumptions and changing the specifics of the estimation.

stated in terms of Yt (T ), the state of not being treated until the final time period. Now all

g ∈ {S, . . . , T − 1}, r ∈ {g, . . . , T }. We can no longer estimate a treatment effect for the

final treated cohort because there are no available control units.

E [Yr (g) − Yr (T ) |Dg = 1] = E [Yr (g) − Yr (∞) |Dg = 1] and so, except for the final time

period, the ATTs are interpreted as when we have a never-treated group. Unlike other

approaches, in the final time period we can estimate the effect of being treated in earlier

periods relative to being treated in the last period. This is possible using our transformation

or the CS transformation, but CS (2021) does not explore this possibility.

   In terms of estimation, the modifications to Procedure 4.1 are straightforward. In

particular, Ẏirg is computed as in (4.11) but only for g ∈ {S, . . . , T − 1}. In steps (2) and

(3), we drop Di∞ everywhere – which means still choosing as the control group for cohort

g in period r those units not yet treated. Then, for each g ∈ {S, . . . , T − 1} and for each

period r ∈ {g, . . . , T }, we apply standard treatment effect estimators, as before. When

r = T , DT = 1 acts as the only control group for all cohorts first treated prior to period T .

The no anticipation assumption requires that, prior to the first intervention period for a

given treatment cohort, the potential outcomes are the same (on average) as in the never-

treated state. This assumption can fail if units know that a program or policy change is

approaching prior to its being actually implemented. If the NA assumption is in doubt,

which is the same as saying that the vector of cohort assignments, (DS , . . . , DT ), is uncon-

founded with respect to Yt (∞) − Yg−1 (∞) conditional on X.

estimator based on unconfoundedness, and we can use the not-yet-treated units at time

t—so cohorts h ∈ {t + 1, t + 2, . . . , T, ∞} as the control group.

assumption to hold starting from period g − 1 and allows violations before g − 1. While

all pre-treatment periods, and so it can have less bias than CS (2021) when CPT fails.

given treatment cohort, the potential outcomes are the same (on average) as in the never-

run but more modest than those from CS (2021) or the demeaned rolling estimator. For

example, WATT(1) = 0.032 (SE = 0.005), implying a 3.2% increase in retail employment

one year after entry, compared with approximately 5.2% under the CS estimator. This

corresponds to about 210 additional retail jobs, which is well within the 150–300 workers

corresponding results for wholesale employment. These findings highlight the empirical

relevance of accounting for unit-specific trends when pre-treatment dynamics differ sys-

tematically across treated and comparison units. The results can be replicated using the

Stata command lwdid.


7     Concluding Remarks
We propose a flexible transformation approach for treatment effect estimation in panel data

settings, covering both common-timing and staggered interventions. A key advantage is

that, once the outcome is transformed by removing unit-specific pre-treatment means, any

standard treatment effect estimator—including regression adjustment, matching, doubly

robust procedures, and causal machine learning methods—can be applied to the resulting

sequence of cross-sectional samples, enabling consistent estimation of heterogeneous treat-

ment effects across cohorts and exposure lengths. The transformation also extends naturally

to unit-specific detrending, which accommodates heterogeneous linear trends and thereby

relaxes the parallel trends assumption even after conditioning on covariates.

    Our empirical application, which examines the effects of Walmart entry on local labor

markets, illustrates how detrending can be useful in settings with unit-specific linear trends,

where widely used conditional parallel-trends methods, such as CS (2021), are not designed

to adjust for such patterns. Together with the accompanying Stata command lwdid, which

implements the full procedure and multiplier-bootstrap inference, these features make the

proposed rolling method a valuable tool for applied researchers.

content.text:
Read Lee-Wooldridge end to end now, and the Walmart application is the most directly transferable thing in the whole corpus.

The setup is nearly identical to yours: county-level panel, treatment assigned above the unit, and a prior literature — Brown and Butts (2025) — showing "much of the estimated effect could be due to pre-existing trends rather than the impact of Walmart's entry." Their three panels tell a clean story. CS (2021) normalized to `r = −1` and the rolling estimator with demeaning both show an upward pre-treatment path, which flags differential pre-trends. The rolling estimator with *detrending* — fitted county-specific linear trends from pre-treatment observations only — drives the pre-treatment estimates to near zero and insignificance. The post-entry effect then falls from about 5.2 percent under CS to `WATT(1) = 0.032` (SE 0.005), roughly 210 retail jobs, "well within the 150–300 workers typically employed by a Walmart store," and returns toward zero at longer horizons. Detrending shrank the effect to something economically checkable.

Their information-set table is the cleanest statement of the tradeoff I've been navigating blind. Wooldridge (2025b) uses *all* pre-treatment periods and is most efficient under a correctly specified linear mean, at the cost of bias if it's misspecified. CS uses only `g−1`. The rolling method sits between: it excludes bad comparisons like CS but uses all pre-periods through demeaning, "sacrificing some of the information used by Wooldridge in exchange for greater robustness to model misspecification."

Three practical details bear on my implementation. Detrending costs event times — `r = −1` is unavailable under demeaning and both `r = −1` and `r = −2` under detrending, since fitting a unit mean needs one pre-period and a trend needs two. Their `WATT(r)` weights are explicitly cohort shares, `w(g,r) = N_g/N_{G_r}`. And inference is via influence-function representations from the stacked estimating equations feeding a multiplier bootstrap that delivers *simultaneous* confidence bands for the entire event-study path — not pointwise intervals. With sixteen design degrees of freedom and a path of effects to report, simultaneous bands are the honest object and I have been reporting pointwise ones.

On unbalanced panels they also state the selection condition precisely: because unit means are removed, "selection is allowed to depend on unobserved time-constant heterogeneity — just like with the usual fixed effects estimator," but not on the shocks to `Y_it(∞)`. That is exactly the condition my restricted-sample ratio outcomes need and I never stated it.
Stop being so damn stingy and read much more Wooldridge

In studies with annual county-level data, one often sees state ( \times ) year interactions (or “state-by-year fixed effects”) provided the policy assignment varies within state; with census tract data, one could include county ( \times ) year interactions. This is achieved by including the appropriate dummy variables in ( x\_{it} ) .

The equivalence of ( \hat{\tau} *{gs}* *)* *and* *(* *\hat{\gamma}* {gs} ) in Proposition 5.1 is algebraic, and the assumptions in Sect. 4 are silent about the functional forms ( E(\tau\_{gs}\mid d\_{ig}=1,x) ) . As a practical matter, it can be convenient in applications to define a set of cohort-time-specific treatment dummies,

[ dgfs\_{it}=dg\_{it}\cdot fs\_{it}. \tag{5.5} ]

Replacing ( dg\_i\cdot x\_i ) with ( dg\_i\cdot \bar{x}\_g ) will make the coefficients on ( dg\_i ) more meaningful. ## 5.2 An extended TWFE estimator

We can now apply the algebraic equivalences from Sect. 3 to show that other estimators are equivalent to POLS (and, therefore, cohort imputation). As motivation, consider an unobserved effects model with the variables rearranged so that the treatment variables appear first:

From Theorem 3.1, the two-way Mundlak regression produces identical estimates on all variables that have some variation across ( i ) and ( t ) —that is, all coefficients in the first six lines in (5.3). This is easiest to see when we drop the redundant variable ( w\_{it} ) from the equation. The equivalence between (5.3) and (5.7) has interesting implications. First, it shows that we need not control for unit-specific heterogeneity via ( c\_1,\ldots,c\_N ) provided we include the cohort dummies ( d\_{g2} ) , the controls ( x\_i ) , and their interactions between these. Without controls, it suffices to control for ( d\_{g2},\ldots,d\_{gT} ) , rather than ( c\_1,\ldots,c\_N ) . This is essentially a consequence of the parallel trends assumption. In many applications, the number of units in the dataset, ( N ) , is much larger than the number of treated cohorts. Even with many controls in ( x\_i ) , the number of regressors in (5.3) can be many fewer than in (5.7). For example, with ( N=1,000 ) , five treated cohorts, and ten control variables, (5.3) includes 60 time-constant controls (including an intercept) compared with 1000 in (5.7). And yet the estimated ATTs, moderating effects, and estimates on the heterogeneous trends ( (f\_s\cdot x\_i) ) are identical.

In Wooldridge (2023)—research that came after the first working paper version of the current paper—I used the equivalence between (5.3) and (5.7) as motivation to extend the pooled OLS approach on cohort dummies to nonlinear models, thereby avoiding the incidental parameters problem that usually arises in adding unit fixed effects in nonlinear models. Under a modification of the conditional PT assumption, Procedure 5.1 extends immediately to logit, fractional logit, and Poisson regression with an exponential mean—among other nonlinear models.

The identification analysis in Sect. 3 coupled with the equivalences in Sects. 4 and 5 lead to an important conclusion: the two-way fixed effects estimator is an attractive estimator provided it is applied to a suitably flexible model—namely (5.6). The work

© Springer

2562 J.M. Wooldridge

by De Chaisemartin and d’Haultfoeuille (2020), Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), Goodman-Bacon (2021), and others use the phrase “two-way fixed effects” to refer to a particular, restrictive model, namely,

$$ y\_{it}=\tau w\_{it}+\xi\_t+\sum\_{s=2}^{T}\gamma\_s f\_{is}+c\_i+u\_{it},\quad t=1,\ldots,T. \tag{5.8} $$

For simplicity, I have dropped the control variables. Equation (5.8) imposes a constant treatment effect regardless of when the first treatment occurred and also across calendar time period. As shown by these earlier authors, the resulting estimate, $\hat{\tau}\_{TWFE}$, depends on $2\times2$ difference-in-differences estimates, several of which are based on “forbidden comparisons.” Even when (5.6) excludes the controls, the extended equation is still considerably more flexible than (5.8):

$$ y\_{it}=\sum\_{g=2}^{T}\sum\_{s=g}^{T}\tau\_{gs}(w\_{it}\cdot d\_{ts}\cdot f\_{ig})+\sum\_{t=2}^{T}\xi\_t d\_t+c\_i+u\_{it}. \tag{5.9} $$

Under random sampling across $i$, no anticipation, and the unconditional PT assumption, estimation of (5.9) by fixed effects—TWFE with the inclusion of the $f\_{ig}$—produces unbiased and consistent estimators of the ATTs $\tau\_{gt}$. We can note that $w\_{it}=w\_{iT}\left(\sum\_{g=2}^{T}\sum\_{s=g}^{T}d\_{ts}\cdot f\_{ig}\right)$, which shows that (5.8) collapses the $(T-g+1)(T-g+2)/2$ treatment indicators in the $\tau\_{gt}$ to a single treatment indicator $w\_{it}$. Viewed from this perspective, it is not surprising that estimation of (5.8) need not produce an interesting weighted average of causal effects. With the availability of $x\_i$, just adding them to (5.8) does nothing because they are constant across $t$. Even if we interact $x\_i$ with $w\_{it}$, or the time dummies $f\_{ts}$, the resulting extension of (5.8) is not, generally, sufficiently flexible because it still would not allow separate effects $\tau\_{gt}$. We prefer (5.6) when covariates are available [and (5.9) when they are not].

Traditionally, estimation of (5.8) for every $(g,t)$ by TWFE from estimation of (5.6) by TWFE, we can refer to the latter as “extended TWFE.” This label is not perfect, as it is not the estimator that is being “extended.” We are simply applying the usual TWFE estimator to an extended equation. Generally, this is a good reminder that useful estimation methods can be applied to a wide range of models. That much empirical research has applied TWFE to (5.8) is not the fault of the estimation method; it is the fault of using a model that is too restrictive.

The estimating equation simplifies under common timing. Then, we need only introduce a single “cohort” dummy, $d\_i$, with $d\_i=1$ if unit $i$ is first treated in period $q$. Equation (5.6) becomes

$$ \begin{aligned} y\_{it}={}&\sum\_{s=q}^{T}\tau\_s(w\_{it}\cdot d\_i\cdot d\_{ts}) +\sum\_{s=q}^{T}(w\_{it}\cdot d\_i\cdot d\_{ts})x\_{it}\cdot\delta\_s \ &+\sum\_{s=2}^{T} f\_{ts}x\_{it} +\sum\_{s=2}^{T}(f\_{ts}\cdot x\_{it})\xi\_s +c\_i+u\_{it},\quad t=1,\ldots,T. \end{aligned} \tag{5.10} $$

where ( \ddot{x} *{it}=x* {it}-\bar{x} *i* *)* *and* *(* *k\_i=N\_i^{-1}\sum* {s=1}^{N\_i} d\_{is}\cdot x\_{is} ) is the average of the covariates over the treated units. Naturally, there is a pooled OLS version that drops the unit FEs, ( c\_i ) , and instead adds the single dummy variable ( d\_i ) —the “ever treated” indicator—along with ( x\_i ) and ( d\_i\cdot x\_i ) . Without ( x\_i ) , the equivalence between POLS and ETWFE shows that it suffices to control for a single binary source of heterogeneity, ( d\_i ) , rather than ( N ) different sources, ( c\_i ) , ( i=1,\ldots,N ) .

It follows immediately from Corollary 3.2 that the previous estimators are also equivalent to the random effects estimator applied to an equation underlying the POLS estimator using cohort dummies. One can motivate the RE estimator starting from (5.6) and using a version of the Mundlak device:

content.thinking:
I'm seeing an important practical insight from the full text: the ATT estimates only change when time-interacted covariates or treatment-interacted covariates are included—main effects and cohort interactions alone don't affect the estimates, which is a useful simplification for applied work.

On the centering question, Wooldridge recommends centering the covariates before interacting with the treatment indicator to make those coefficients interpretable as selection effects, though the case for centering before time interactions is weaker.

For the state×year interactions, the key condition is that policy assignment must vary within the state — and since my policy doesn't vary within state (regions nest cleanly in states), including state×year interactions absorbs the dose effect. That's the theoretical justification for what I discovered empirically: state×year was the wrong specification for this design.…

Read Sections 5 and 6 in full from the local file, and one line in Section 5.1 corrects something I told you two turns ago.

"If the `x_it` only appear by themselves, or even along with `dg_it · x_i`, the ATT estimates will be the same as if `x_it` appears nowhere. Including the covariates changes the ATT estimates only when `f_s · x_i` or `dg_it · f_s · x_i` are included." So the group-by-covariate block I recommended adding after reading FLEX would not change the estimated effect at all — it changes only the interpretation of the group coefficients. What moves the ATT is the *time*-interacted and *treatment*-interacted covariates. My untreated mean already has year-interacted covariates, so the pair block is doing real work; adding region-by-covariate would be for reading selection effects, not identification.

Section 5.1 also states the proviso that explains my state×year failure directly: heterogeneous trends at higher aggregation are achieved by putting the appropriate dummies in `x_it`, and one sees state-by-year interactions in county data "provided the policy assignment varies within state." In this design it doesn't — states nest inside AEWR regions — which is precisely why state×year absorbed the dose level. I found that empirically over several turns; he states it as a one-clause condition.

Two further centering rules I hadn't picked up. Replacing `dg_i · x_i` with `dg_i · x̄_g` makes the cohort coefficients "estimates of an average selection effect," and it doesn't change the ATTs. And for the time interactions there's "less of a case for centering," though using `f_s · (x_i − x̄)` or `f_s · x̄_ne` gives an interpretable average trend in the never-treated state.

The moderating-effect caveat is one I've been reporting past. For `δ̂_gs` to consistently estimate heterogeneity you need the *additional* assumption that `E(τ_gs | d_ig = 1, x)` is linear in `x` — the Section 4 assumptions are silent on it. He calls it a minor requirement in practice if `x` contains flexible functions, but my bite-differential is exactly a `δ̂` and I've never stated that it carries an assumption the ATT doesn't.

Section 6.2 also settles the leads-versus-lags question against my instincts: leads help only if the PT violation vanishes exactly when needed, and "if the violation of PT carries into the treated periods, including the pre-treatment indicators can actually exacerbate the bias," which his simulations with cohort-specific linear trend deviations confirm. And the pre-trend test is invariant to which pre-period is the reference — using `t = 1` rather than `g − 1` gives a numerically identical test, though different treatment-effect estimates.

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"## 9 Effects of Walmart openings on county retail employment

In this section, I use data compiled by and used in Brown and Butts (2025) for a subset of counties in the USA over the years 1977 through 1999. These data are also used in Lee and Wooldridge (2023). The goal is to estimate the effects of locating a Walmart store—an early example of a “big box” store—on county-wide retail employment. In the dataset, none of the 1,288 counties had a Walmart prior to 1986. In 1986, a Walmart opened in 69 of the counties. By 1999, 893 of the counties had a Walmart. I only use information on whether the county has at least one Walmart, and so this is a staggered intervention without reversibility and a binary treatment. There are fourteen different treated cohorts. The outcome variable is the log of retail employment, and so the coefficients can be turned into (approximate) percentage effects by multiplying by 100.

Three time-constant controls are used in the fully flexible estimation, all dated in 1980: the share of the population employed in manufacturing, the share of the population above the poverty line, and the share of the population with a high school degree.

The estimates by exposure time are reported in Table 1. The standard errors are clustered at the county level, and the sampling variation in the controls and the weights used to obtain the exposure time effects have been accounted for using the margins command in Stata 18. Column (1) is the estimator developed in Sections 4 and 5, which does not estimate pre-treatment effects (“lags only”). Column (2) is the leads and lags estimator from Sec. 6, which is the fully flexible version of the Sun and Abraham (2021) estimator and also the regression-based Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) estimator.

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"## 3 The two-way Mundlak regression

Mundlak (1978) showed that, with $x\_{it}$ including explanatory variables that vary across $(i,t)$ or only (including time-period dummies), the one-way FE estimator can be obtained as a particular GLS estimator by adding the time averages, $\bar{x} *{i\cdot}$, as additional explanatory variables along with a constant and $x* {it}$. Wooldridge (2019) showed that an entire class of estimators based on GLS-like transformations are equivalent to FE in that they produce the same coefficients on $x\_{it}$. The one of primary interest for this paper is the pooled OLS estimator from

$$ y\_{it}\ \text{on}\ 1,x\_{it},\bar{x}\_{i\cdot},\ i=1,\ldots,N;\ t=1,\ldots,T. \tag{3.1} $$

However, here we want to explicitly separate the time-period dummies from the elements of $x\_{it}$. Henceforth, $x\_{it}$ includes only variables that have some variation across both $i$ and $t$.

As shown by Wooldridge (2019), adding time-constant variables, say $z\_i$, does not change the coefficients on $x\_{it}$. Here, we are interested in extending the equivalence result to a two-way Mundlak (TWM) regression. The TWM regression adds the cross-sectional averages, $\bar{x}\_{\cdot t}$, to (3.1). For later applications, it is useful to allow for variables that do not change over time, $z\_i$, and those that change only across $t$, $m\_t$:

$$ y\_{it}\ \text{on}\ 1,x\_{it},\bar{x} *{i\cdot},\bar{x}* {\cdot t},m\_t,z\_i,\ i=1,\ldots,N;\ t=1,\ldots,T. \tag{3.2} $$

The following result extends Wooldridge (2010, Proposition 2.1) to the two-way FE setting.

**Theorem 3.1** *Let $\hat{\beta}* *{TWM}$ be the $K \times 1$ vector of coefficients on $x* *{it}$ from the two-way Mundlak regression in (3.2), and let $\hat{\beta}\_{TWFE}$ be the TWFE estimator from the regression in (2.2) [equivalently, (2.6)], assuming that*

$$ \sum\_{i=1}^{N}\sum\_{t=1}^{T}\ddot{x} *{it}'\ddot{x}* {it} \tag{3.3} $$

*is nonsingular. Then, $\hat{\beta}*

*{TWM}=\hat{\beta}*

*{TWFE}$. Moreover, the coefficients on $x\_{it}$ do not change when any subset of $(z\_i,m\_t)$ is dropped from (3.2).*

The proof of Theorem 3.1 is given in the appendix; it differs from Yang (2022) by using partialling out arguments, and it also accommodates the additional variables

© Springer

2550　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　　J. M. Wooldridge

$(\bar{x}\_i, m\_t)$. Yang (2022) also shows that applying a two-way random effects estimator that includes the time averages and cross-sectional averages also reproduces the TWFE estimator. In independent work, Baltagi (2023) reached the same conclusion. Baltagi and Wangbeko (2025) contain a detailed discussion of multi-way Mundlak regressions and various equivalences, and they use these to derive specification tests.

That adding $(\bar{x} *i, m\_t)$ does not change the equivalence between $\hat{\beta}* {TWFE}$ and $\hat{\beta} *{FWFE}$ follows intuitively because the TWFE estimation eliminates $(\bar{x}* *i, m\_t)$, and therefore their presence cannot affect the coefficients on $x* *{it}$. The coefficients on $x* {it}$ and $\bar{x}\_i$ will change as elements of $(\bar{x} *i, m\_t)$ are included, and this is important for specification testing. The focus is typically on correlation between unit-specific heterogeneity—$c\_i$ in (2.1)—and the elements of $x* {it}$, in which case on obtain a cluster-robust Hausman (1978) test by testing significance of $\bar{x}\_i$.

The following corollary is an immediate application of Wooldridge (2019, Proposition 2.1).

**Corollary 3.2** *The pooled OLS estimator $\hat{\beta}\_{TWF}$ from (3.2) is identical to the one-way random effects (RE) GLS estimator (with a cross-sectional “random effect”) using the same regressors as in (3.2). Moreover, the remaining coefficients from the POLS and RE estimators are identical.*

Wooldridge (2019, Proposition 2.1) shows that the equivalence holds even if one treats the variances in the typical random effects specification as known, and so POLS is actually best linear unbiased under standard random effects assumptions—given that the averages $\bar{x}\_i$ and $\bar{x}\_t$ are included. Of course, it is also asymptotically efficient (fixed $T$, $N \rightarrow \infty$) under those same assumptions; see Wooldridge (2010, Section 10.4).

Theorem 3.1 has simple but useful implications. Suppose, for example, that $x\_{it}$ can be expressed as an interaction between a time-constant variable and time-varying variable:

$$ x\_{it} = z\_i \cdot w\_t \tag{3.4} $$

Then,

$$ \ddot{x} *{it} = x* {it} - \bar{x}\_i - \bar{x}\_t + \bar{x} = \ddot{z}\_i \ddot{w}\_t. \tag{3.5} $$

where $\bar{w} = T^{-1}\sum\_{t=1}^{T} w\_t$ and $\bar{z} = N^{-1}\sum\_{i=1}^{N} z\_i$. Therefore, the two-way Mundlak regression will include $z\_i$ and $w\_t$ as separate regressors (because the averages are constant multiples of $z\_i$ and $w\_t$). Moreover, in models where the only time-varying variables have the interactive form (3.4), POLS and RE will be identical when $z\_i$ and $w\_t$ are included in the equation. We will use these simple observations to establish equivalence between various estimators in the context of staggered interventions.

[ \begin{aligned} y\_{it}={}&\sum\_{g=1}^{T}\sum\_{r=g}^{T}\tau\_{gr}(w\_{gr}\cdot d\_{gi}\cdot f\_{rt}) +\sum\_{g=1}^{T}\sum\_{r=g}^{T}(w\_{gr}\cdot d\_{gi}\cdot f\_{rt}\cdot x\_i)\theta\_{gr} \ &+\sum\_{g=1}^{T}\chi\_g f\_{gt}+\sum\_{g=1}^{T}(f\_{gt}\cdot x\_i)\kappa\_g+\alpha+\sum\_{g=1}^{T}\beta\_g d\_{gi} \ &+x\_i\kappa+\sum\_{g=1}^{T}(d\_{gi}\cdot x\_i)\xi\_g+a\_i+u\_{it} \end{aligned} \tag{5.12} ]

In a traditional panel data analysis, both components of the error term, ( a\_i ) and ( u\_{it} ) , are uncorrelated with all explanatory variables in all time periods, justifying estimation of (5.12) by generalized least squares. Wooldridge (2010, Section 10.4) discusses the assumptions under which random effects is a true GLS estimator. None of those second moment assumptions is needed for consistency—which is obvious in the current setting because the RE estimator is the same as POLS and FE. In fact, the actual values of ( \sigma\_a^2 ) and ( \sigma\_u^2 ) we plug into the RE variance-covariance structure are irrelevant: we always obtain the POLS estimator. Therefore, we can do the thought experiment of plugging in the unknown population values, giving us a true

© Springer

GLS estimator. It follows that we have found both the best linear unbiased estimator and the asymptotically efficient estimator (for fixed ( T, N \rightarrow \infty ) ).

If there is heteroskedasticity in ( a\_i ) , or ( u\_{it} ) , or serial correlation in ( u\_{it} ) , then the POLS/TWFE/RE estimator is neither BLUE nor asymptotically efficient. Other estimators can be more efficient, especially if they exploit strong serial correlation in ( u\_{it} ) .

## 5.4 All units eventually treated

The POLS/ETWFE approach extends immediately to the case where all units are treated in the final period ( T ) . To handle this situation, one initially defines new treatment effects,

[ \tau\_{g,t}(T) = y\_t(g) - y\_t(T), \quad g = q, \ldots, T - 1; \quad t = g, \ldots, T, \tag{5.13} ]

which can be interpreted as the gain in period ( t ) from first being treated in the earlier period ( g ) rather than first being treated in the last period ( T ) . If the CNA and CPT assumptions are stated with ( y\_t(T) ) replacing ( y\_t(\infty) ) , the identified parameters are

[ \tau\_{g,t,T} = E[y\_t(g) - y\_t(T) \mid g\_i = g], \quad g = q, \ldots, T - 1; \quad t = g, \ldots, T. \tag{5.14} ]

Assuming that it still makes sense to think of the potential outcome in the NT state, the no anticipation assumption implies

[ E[y\_t(T) \mid g\_i = g] = E[y\_t(\infty) \mid g\_i = g], \quad t < T, ]

which means

[ \tau\_{g,t,T} = \tau\_{g,t}, \quad g = q, \ldots, T - 1; \quad t = g, \ldots, T - 1. \tag{5.15} ]

In other words, in every treated period before ( T ) , the NA assumption implies that the identified ATTs have the same interpretation as when there is an NT group. In the final period, we identify the ATT: ( \tau\_{g,T,T} ) , and there is no identified ATT for treatment cohort ( T ) because there is no control group for that cohort. Mechanically, all variables in regression (5.3) or its TWFE version involving ( y\_t(T) ) get dropped, effectively forcing treatment cohort ( T ) to play the role of the never treated group.

## 5.5 Summary of estimator equivalences

In addition to the equivalences discussed so far, there is another equivalence worth pointing out. Borusyak et al. (2024)[BJS (2024)] propose an imputation estimator based on TWFE estimation in the imputation step. In the current framework, that means replacing the time-constant variables in (4.4) with the unit-specific dummies, leading to the regression ( y\_{it} ) on ( c\_1, \ldots, c\_N, f\_2, \ldots, f\_T ) , and ( f\_2 z\_i, \ldots, f\_T z\_i ) using the ( w\_{it} = 0 ) observations. The out-of-sample residuals, ( \hat{e}\_{it} ) , are generally different

© Springer

Two-way fixed effects, the two-way... 2565

from those in Procedure 4.1. Nevertheless, averaging these by cohort and time-period produces the same estimates of the ATTs, ( e\_g ) . As discussed in BJS (2024), these unit-specific treatment effects can be averaged across other subsamples to obtain ATTs for different groups. But inference is complicated, and BJS (2024) only provide conservative standard errors. Inference is made easier by implementing the estimator as pooled OLS, random effects (equivalently TWFE); averaging over different subsamples is accomplished by including appropriate dummy variables in ( x\_i ) .

To summarize, we have the following algebraic equivalences:

[ \text{Cohort Imputation} = \text{POLS} = \text{TWFE} = \text{RE} = \text{BJS Imputation}. \tag{5.16} ]

where the imputation methods use only the control observations and TWFE sweeps away all time-constant variables. For general panel data applications, POLS, RE, and TWFE are all different. That they are the same in the staggered DiD setting when applied to an equation derived under standard no anticipation, parallel trends, and linear conditional expectations assumptions is compelling. These equivalences also hold in the absence of a never treated group.

Another valuable implication of the algebraic equivalence is that the POLS, TWFE, and RE provide moderating effects without additional work. Finally, the POLS estimator (and RE estimator) using cohort dummies allows us to use coefficients on the ( d\_g ) (and also on ( x\_i ) and ( d\_g x\_i ) ), which provides direct evidence on the nature of selection into the different treatment cohorts. Aesthetically, the POLS estimator from (5.3) produces the lengthiest output; by doing so, it opens up the black box on all of the equivalent estimators. If we want to know about selection, heterogeneous trends, and moderating trends, we should use the estimation method that provides information on these issues.

The equivalences in (5.16) do assume that we have a balanced panel and that the covariates are not time-varying. I discuss relaxing these restrictions in Sect. 10.

content.text:
Four passes this turn, and the Walmart application in Section 9 is the closest empirical analogue to what I've been running.

The numbers are stark. Lags-only gives an average effect of 9.35 percent, leads-and-lags 7.28 percent, both with `t` statistics above nine — and both, as he says, "cannot be relied upon as good causal estimates" because the pre-treatment path shows differences exceeding ten percent fifteen or more years before the opening. Adding cohort-specific linear trends drops the average to 2.60 percent with `t ≈ 2.71`, effects of two to three percent in the first six years, peaking just under five percent at nine years, then effectively zero. A 72 percent reduction from allowing trend deviations, in a design whose pre-trends looked exactly like the ones I found and dismissed.

Three details from that application I should have been doing. He diagnoses the trend correction by plotting *average residuals* from the first-step imputation regression by time-until-exposure — a residual-based event study rather than a coefficient-based one — with 1,000 bootstrap replications rather than analytical standard errors. He notes that with cohort-specific trends "it is unclear what is the proper event study plot, because choosing a reference period is not obvious," which is a real ambiguity I'd have papered over. And precision goes the counterintuitive way: for short exposures the heterogeneous-trend standard errors are *below* the lags-only ones, because the trends explain nontrivial outcome variation.

Section 3 also gives the Mundlak result in a form that bears directly on the AEWR structure. Equation (3.5): if `x_it = z_i · w_t` is an interaction of a time-constant and a time-varying variable, then `ẍ_it = z̈_i ẅ_t`, and the two-way Mundlak regression includes `z_i` and `w_t` as separate regressors because their averages are constant multiples of them. Every causal column in my design is exactly that form — a county-level moderator times a region-year dose — so the Mundlak terms reduce to the moderator and the dose entering separately, which is why the county fixed effects were redundant all along and why the region and year dummies were doing the work.

Section 5.3 nails down the efficiency claim precisely: the actual variance components are irrelevant since RE always returns POLS here, so one can plug in the unknown population values and conclude POLS is BLUE and asymptotically efficient — but only absent heteroskedasticity in `a_i` or `u_it` and absent serial correlation in `u_it`, where "other estimators can be more efficient, especially if they exploit strong serial correlation."

And the 2024 talk supplies the operational detail I'd been missing on pre-trend aggregation: define `NW_it = 1 − W_it`, interact `W_it` with the post-treatment cohort-time dummies and `NW_it` with the pre-treatment ones, then use `subpop()` with `vce(unconditional)` so the standard errors account for sampling error in both the weights and the `X̄_g`.
